'I've got a band now' - Club anthem star Shygirl on why she's switching up her sound

BBC News Mon, 09 Nov 2026 11:09:08 GMT

Hard-hitting beats, club anthems and unapologetically sexy lyrics are what Shygirl is known for.

But the singer and DJ - real name Blane Muise - has introduced a different sound for her second album, Swallow!, which dropped on Friday.

Shygirl hasn't totally left her electronic roots behind though.

You can still hear the sweat-soaked energy of Charli XCX's 365 remix and relentless pulse of 2024 hit mr useless on her latest record.

But there's also guitar strums, heartfelt songwriting and a dreamy haze, giving it an indie edge.

"I've learned over the 10 years I've been making music to have this confidence and to not be afraid of failure," she tells BBC Newsbeat.

"The big part of starting this record was wanting to have natural instrumentation and not feel like that was barred from me."

Shygirl puts the change down to a desire for a more "authentic" sound - a growing trend among British electronic artists who've been bringing a rockier influence to their music.

Asked why she took this musical direction, the 33-year-old says it was down to "the nostalgia of the indie sound".

"I felt the familiarity of that feeling, embracing the teenager within and the angst that I had and all the sounds that coloured that environment," she says.

Long-time producers Karma Kid and Casey MQ were "surprised" when Shygirl told them about her desire to work in more indie sounds, but she says the pair trusted her with the new direction.

Fans have been patiently waiting for something other than singles since her debut album Nymph was released in 2022.

The question now is whether they'll relate to this more rose-tinted version of Shygirl.

"It's not like I changed overnight," she insists. "In fact, it was because I was the girl I was in all the other songs that I became who I am now."

There are clear signs that Shygirl is entering a new chapter.

She cleared her Instagram feed before beginning the album rollout, and the artwork shows a bird hatching from an egg, symbolising rebirth.

But she points out the journey is an "evolution" rather than reinvention.

"I think it's less about moving away from me, but I would hate to repeat myself," she says.

"I would only wish to pick up the same tool if I felt like I had grown somewhat or had a renewed expertise for it."

That growth can be heard in tracks like Live the Life You Like - one of Shygirl's favourites on the album.

It features a gritty bassline and a manipulated riff that echoes a klaxon, which she describes as giving off "punk energy".

Leaning into that side of her sound has only made her more excited to take the record on a tour, starting with Europe in March.

"I've got a band now," she reveals with a grin. "I work with a drummer and a multi-instrumentalist and sometimes a bassist.

"It's just so fun to share the stage and be so inspired. We've rehearsed, but there's still so many moments for spontaneity and for us to look at each other and vibe."

Shygirl's the latest artist known for electronic music who's embraced a more organic sound.

Her close friend Charli XCX featured a rockier, guitar-driven style on her latest album Music, Fashion, Film.

One of the standout tracks on that album for Shygirl is SS26, because "her voice is so natural and exposed".

"You forget other people don't know that voice and they need to get to know that starting point to be able to appreciate everything else."

Shygirl believes that same stripped-back approach is shaping much of the current wave of British dance music, including her latest album.

"There's so many of us now, especially coming from the Brit pack, that are doing the same thing," she says.

Artists like PinkPantheress and Fred Again have also spoken about bringing indie influences into electronic music, something Shygirl says is "a reflection of what is going on in the world".

"I think there is a natural desire to have a sense of truth or something grounding," she says.

"And what is more grounding or more truthful than knowing exactly where a sound comes from."

So with artists borrowing more and more from across the musical spectrum, does genre still matter?

For Shygirl, it's less about what box listeners put her music in and more about whether it connects with them.

"Regardless if they like it or they hate it, I want someone to feel something. To be apathetic to my music would be the biggest insult to me."

Usman Khawaja is "100% accurate" in his recounting of the Australia ball-tampering scandal in 2018, says former team-mate David Warner.

Ex-opener Warner also said Cricket Australia's investigation process following the incident was "rushed and botched".

Australia were found to have used sandpaper to alter the condition of the ball during the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town.

Warner and captain Steve Smith were banned for a year and fellow batter Cameron Bancroft for nine months.

Khawaja last week said the entire Australia team knew about the use of sandpaper, despite consistent denials from the bowlers that they had knowledge of the plan.

Warner, who retired from international cricket in 2024, said in a video statement on Instagram:, external "It's been eight years since I spoke on this topic. And Ussie, I throw my full support behind you.

"I thank you for what you've done. It's 100% accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."

Former batter Khawaja has said he was shocked not to be asked to provide evidence during Cricket Australia's investigation.

"In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth," he wrote.

"The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now."

In response, Warner said: "This is Usman's story. This is what Usman believes. Ussie wrote down every single thing from that day on.

"This whole interview process was rushed and botched. Ussie was sitting next to Cameron Bancroft. Ussie was not interviewed.

"How is that a thorough investigation? It baffles me. We're not here to point fingers and we're not opening old wounds. It's about accountability, transparency, ensuring that the truth is properly examined.

"Perhaps it's time people stop scrutinising the person asking for accountability and start asking those responsible for the investigation to provide it."

While Smith, Warner and Bancroft - all batters - were punished, there was never an explanation of how bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon did not notice a change in the state of the ball.

Cummins has been Test captain since 2021 and all four players remain fixtures in the Australia red-ball side.

The quartet released a joint statement in 2021 which said they "did not know a foreign substance was taken on to the field".

Warner said in his video that there were "a lot of statements and inaccuracies over the last eight years that were out in the media by people. And there was a lot of people who stayed silent."

The 40-year-old, who scored 8,786 runs in 112 Tests, said he delayed his reponse to Khawaja's comments so he could explain the incident to his daughters.

"I had to tell them exactly what had happened," said Warner. "My 12-year-old, Ivy, wanted to know why we were holding her, why there were so many cameras, why we were all crying on TV. That was a hard thing to do.

"But one thing I did say is, 'Girls, tell the truth, because lies will eventually get out'.

"It's a very tough time. This is for everyone in Australia. It's been the question everyone's been asking.

"It's been a tough time for my family, Steven and Cameron, no doubt. But this is what needed to come out. I fully support that, Ussie."

Cricket Australia has not said it will re-open the investigation into the events at Newlands in 2018.

"During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case.

"All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process."

Experienced batter Marnus Labuschagne has been dropped for the Tests.

Chair of selectors George Bailey said: "At this stage we won't be considering Marnus for selection for certainly that first Test, but for the New Zealand series."

James Bond: What we know so far about the next 007 film

BBC News Mon, 09 Nov 2026 06:47:09 GMT

When a bartender asked James Bond in 2006's Casino Royale whether he'd like his vodka martini shaken or stirred, the irritated spy replied: "Do I look like I give a damn?"

Such throwaway lines were a clever way of signalling to the audience that this was a new era for 007 - and that the film series launched in 1962 was being overhauled with the arrival of Daniel Craig.

Over the next few films, producers struck a balance between nodding to the past while also moving away from some of the cheesier elements of the series, no longer sticking rigidly to all of the tradition and tropes of Bond.

"Were you expecting an exploding pen?" Ben Whishaw's Q later asked the secret service agent in Skyfall. "We don't really go in for that anymore."

Two decades on from Craig's debut, the series is about to be rebooted once again, with a new actor and new creative team. It's an exciting time for Bond fans as they wait to see what shape the next era will take. Here's what we know so far.

After years of speculation, the wheels are firmly in motion and we expect to hear who the new James Bond actor is in November or December.

Speaking in August, producer Amy Pascal told Deadline: "I would say the end of the year is a good bet. We are being really, really methodical."

The final screen tests reportedly took place in late October, so, unless something unexpected happens, it should not take much longer for producers to make their decision and the actor to sign the contract.

After that, it's just a matter of how the announcement will be made. In an earlier era, Bond actors were revealed with a traditional photo call or press conference.

But now that the franchise is owned by Amazon MGM, some expect the company to make the announcement via its own Prime Video streaming service.

A handful of actors are thought to have made it to the final screen tests to take on Britain's biggest film role. The three frontrunners are thought to be:

Other actors in the frame include:

But remember, Craig was a surprise choice in 2005, so don't bet against a wildcard candidate whose name has not yet been widely reported.

The film is expected to go into production in 2027, before its release in 2028. No exact dates have been announced.

Film schedules can be notoriously fluid, but it's clear that development is well under way, with the director and writer already in place.

It will be the 26th film in the official film series, but the title has not yet been confirmed.

The movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, known for Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival, Blade Runner 2049 and the recent Dune trilogy starring Timothée Chalamet.

"Some of my earliest movie-going memories are connected to 007," the French-Canadian director said last year. "I grew up watching James Bond films with my father, ever since Dr. No with Sean Connery. I'm a die-hard Bond fan. To me, he's sacred territory."

He added: "I intend to honour the tradition and open the path for many new missions to come. This is a massive responsibility, but also, incredibly exciting for me and a huge honour."

Bond 26 will be written by Steven Knight, known for TV series such as Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer, Locke and The Girl in the Spider's Web.

Knight has said it had always been on his "bucket list" to write a Bond film, adding that he felt he was "doing my duty for King and country" by joining the franchise.

He told the BBC he planned to "write the character, not the actor", adding: "The thing with Bond is it's its own universe and franchise. So there are certain rules.

"Obviously you have to move it along, but I love where it sits. I love that it's British. I love that it's not DC or Marvel... So I feel a responsibility to the text."

Only six actors have played James Bond.

You might have noticed some overlap in the above dates.

That's because Connery returned to the lead role for 1971's Diamonds Are Forever, after Lazenby took his place for 1969's On Her Majesty's Secret Service.

Connery also later appeared in 1983's Never Say Never Again, a Bond film produced by a different studio and not part of the official film series.

If you discount the films not in the official series, there have been 25 Bond films in total. In order, they are:

With the change in ownership and a new creative team now in place, the new Bond film is likely to make a fresh start.

It would be difficult to continue the story chronologically given the ending of 2021's No Time To Die, but that still leaves producers with plenty of options.

A different version of James Bond, who exists in a different universe, would be easily pulled off in an era where audiences are used to major film franchises restarting in a different world or timeline.

Bond 26 could even be set in a significantly earlier era - an idea that gained more popularity after Tony Gilroy revealed he and fellow director Steven Soderbergh previously pitched a 1960s version of Bond.

Separately, actor Ralph Fiennes recently said he had once been in talks to play Bond, and had suggested producers make a "black and white and very sort of film noir-y" version set in the 1950s.

Neither idea materialised, but the suggestion went down well with some Bond fans, who noted a period piece would help make the film truer to Ian Fleming's original character and books.

Exactly what shape the next film takes will become clear at a later stage. For now, fans are hoping that Christmas could be about to come early this year, as the world awaits the imminent announcement of the next actor to play 007.

Cruise ship pianist rescued from sea after nine hours in Pacific Ocean

BBC News Mon, 09 Nov 2026 02:50:13 GMT

A cruise ship pianist was found treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast after falling overboard, according to US media reports.

Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island on Friday and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.

"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in," Grant Garrett was quoted as saying, recalling the moment he and Sean Norton spotted him.

The man, who has not yet been identified, was taken to hospital in a stable condition, the US Coast Guard told the BBC, adding it was investigating the incident.

The fishermen say the man identified himself as a pianist on a 14-deck cruise ship called the Ovation of the Seas.

"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.

The Coast Guard said in a statement it had received a report from "a Good Samaritan who recovered a conscious individual from the water".

The person was handed over to Newport Beach Lifeguards, who confirmed he was an employee of the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship, it said.

Lifeguard officials believe he may have fallen overboard at around 02:30, about nine hours before he was discovered.

"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean," Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS.

Norton credited the man's survival to unusually warm ocean temperatures.

"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees," Norton said, which equates to about 24C.

"A different year, no way he makes it," Norton said.

The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring the Pacific, with ocean temperatures about 3.05C above average.

In a statement to the BBC, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson said: "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time.

"To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."

What's your love language - and does it actually mean anything?

BBC News Mon, 09 Nov 2026 00:55:35 GMT

I'm "words of affirmation", and so is my husband. This is supposedly our shared love language.

But, while we do like receiving compliments, they make us both feel a bit awkward.

Despite this, our result was confidently defined when we took the original Love Languages Quiz online, a personality test published by US pastor Gary Chapman who first came up with the five types of expressing and receiving love in 1992.

I'm sceptical. Does the theory really know more about us than our own lived experience of a 10-year marriage?

The five love languages are: Quality Time, Acts of Service, Words of Affirmation, Receiving Gifts, and Physical Touch - and they feel more ubiquitous than ever.

Contestants on dating shows ask each other their love languages; "My love language is…" is a common prompt on dating apps.

According to the Love Languages website, my husband and I are just two out of more than 150 million people to have taken this particular quiz.

Even though we scored much lower on some of the other languages, they speak more directly to us.

For example I love spending "quality time" with my husband, and feel much more loved by him making lists of films to watch with me than when he pays me a compliment.

But where did the idea of these five neat categories come from? And are they relevant for modern dating and relationships?

Unlike other relationship theories - such as attachment theory - the concept of love languages doesn't have scientific origins.

Chapman said the theory came to him after observing couples during counselling sessions he held in his parish.

Counselling psychologist Dr Sarah Emmerson told the BBC that love languages are still mentioned regularly in her sessions.

"There's almost no-one out there who hasn't taken that quiz," she said. "[Couples] quite frequently bring that in and say, 'So my partner is Physical Touch and I'm Acts of Service, so this doesn't work'.

"Research has proven that there isn't a lot of validity to the idea that there are only five ways in which people show love, and that everybody fits neatly into these categories. But people still gravitate towards it, and we have to wonder why that might be."

For some, talking about love languages can simply be a useful introduction to thinking about how they communicate their needs to their partner.

Psychotherapist Georgina Sturmer said that it helps people think about "what you really like in a relationship, and what do other people really like" but points out it's "hugely limited" and risks "oversimplifying everything".

In recent years, many therapists have also warned that Chapman's examples refer too readily to scripture and unequal relationship dynamics.

In the Love Languages book Chapman describes counselling a woman, Ann, whose husband of 10 years is hostile and verbally abusive towards her, including frequently telling her he hates her.

His love language, Ann tells Chapman, is specifically sexual physical touch.

When Ann says she finds it "hard to be sexually responsive" to him, Chapman advises her that she should "rely heavily upon [her] faith in God" to make herself have sex with her husband more often.

This example also exposes another problem - that love languages can be used to coerce partners into showing or receiving love in a way they're not comfortable with.

"There's a risk if someone says, 'well my love language is receiving gifts, so you must give me gifts all the time, or my love language is physical touch, so you must be physically intimate with me all the time," Sturmer said.

The BBC has contacted the Love Languages team for comment.

So what can couples do if they want to understand each other, and themselves, better?

Listen to your partner: "Don't just wait until you can speak, but try to hear what they are saying and acknowledge their feelings," Dr Emmerson said.

Share how you feel using "I" statements, so you avoid blame: "If you reframe your words to lead with your own feelings, it helps you to express what's going on without leaving the other person feeling criticised," Sturmer explained.

Remember that disagreements are normal: "Healthy relationships often feature debate and disagreement," Sturmer said. "The challenge is not about avoiding rupture, it's about finding ways to repair it that can leave the relationship feeling stronger."

But, Dr Emmerson added, you should "pick the right time to talk about things that are difficult - not late at night, not when they've just come through the door".

Respond to bids for connection: Dr Emmerson said you should "try to be emotionally responsive to your partner when they are seeking connection" - even if they're doing so in subtle ways.

"This could be asking for a hug, or just telling you about something they just saw on their phone."

Antipersonnel mines have returned in Ukraine and now threaten the world

New Scientist November 08, 2026

Antipersonnel (AP) mines seemed to be on the way out in 1997, when 122 countries signed the Ottawa Treaty to ban them. But in 2026, such mines are making a comeback.

“These things are both cheap to produce and offer a level of sophistication that actors couldn’t hope to reproduce for a hundred times the price only a few years ago,” says Seán Moorhouse, an explosive ordnance disposal consultant.

How Ukraine became a drone factory and invented the future of war

AP mines come in two forms. Blast mines, weighing 100 grams or less, are typically scattered by aircraft. Activated by pressure, blast mines are designed to maim. Larger fragmentation mines, laid by combat engineers, have tripwires and spray lethal fragments in all directions.

Advertisement

Moorhouse notes that three technologies have enabled the resurgence of AP mines in Ukraine: 3D printing, microcontrollers and drone delivery.

3D printing enables any frontline unit to produce its own mines. Different shapes, sizes and colours proliferate, making mines harder to spot. Some, like the curved, green Caterpillar, blend in with vegetation. Urban mines, meanwhile, may look like pieces of brick or concrete.

Free newsletter

Fragmentation mines can be triggered by microcontrollers connected to sensors rather than tripwires. In Ukraine, the most common type, nicknamed Jonik (“little soldier”), is magnetic and sensitive enough to be set off by a rifle carried nearby. Doppler microwave sensors detect movement; others sense body heat or vibration. A new variety is triggered by the approach of any Bluetooth device.

Drone delivery of both blast and fragmentation types has been transformational. Drones slip far behind the lines to place mines precisely on tracks and paths, or around trenches, giving a greater chance of finding a victim than random scattering. Human rights organisations and a UN commission have reported that Russian forces are using drones to drop AP mines to target civilians in the city of Kherson.

The combination of these technologies makes mines both deadlier and more accessible. “The triad of drone delivery, 3D printing and microcontrollers will proliferate worldwide,” predicts Moorhouse.

Fully autonomous drones have killed human soldiers for the first time

Networks of soldiers and volunteer groups produce mines in garage workshops in Ukraine and Russia. The technology is easy to replicate.

“These simple devices can be rapidly produced by any group with access to explosives, enabling a significant expansion of mine warfare,” says Roy Gardiner at the non-profit group Defense Tech for Ukraine.

AP mines present a threat to civilians for decades after a conflict. When the Ottawa Treaty was signed, this lasting danger outweighed any military value. The calculus seems to have changed. Ukraine suspended its implementation of the treaty, and others have also changed their minds.

“Now we see five countries pulling out of the Ottawa Treaty [Poland, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia], which suggests that mines have some utility,” says Moorhouse.

He says demining agencies need to act urgently to adapt to the challenges of new AP mines and update their training and awareness programmes. Technology may mitigate the problem, with AI-enabled drones beginning to play a role in mine detection and disposal. But Moorhouse warns the risk from AP mines is growing rather than shrinking, and many states and non-state actors are likely to adopt these cheap, accessible and effective weapons, despite the human cost.

COP climate summits might yet have a useful future – here’s how

New Scientist November 07, 2026

At a certain point, it becomes impossible to convey the urgency of the climate crisis in words. Calls to “intensify efforts” to cut emissions or countries “expressing alarm” at the pace of climate change start to ring hollow after years of rising emissions. At a certain point, you have to ask, what difference will another carefully worded declaration really make?

This is a live question: next week, countries will gather at the COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, to progress the global response to climate change. For the seasoned attendee, these gatherings follow a predictable rhythm: some pomp and ceremony at the start when the world leaders are in attendance, followed by a quiet first week of backroom talks, escalating tension and fights over finance in the second week, all rounded off with a late-night showdown as countries argue over the wording of a final agreement.

In the context of ever more dire warnings from scientists and increasingly severe real-world climate disasters, this is an event cycle that is wearing thin. To many of those in attendance – and millions more looking on from afar – it is becoming increasingly clear that COP summits are failing to deliver meaningful progress.

Advertisement

This is a relatively new problem. For decades, the job of a COP negotiator was to forge some kind of global agreement to address climate change. That was no mean feat, and it took years of hard work and dedication to deliver the Paris Agreement in 2015. After the treaty was struck, climate negotiators then spent a few years busily drawing up the rules that would govern how the agreement would work in practice. But with that work largely completed by 2021, since then, COP summits have been left to drift, plagued by arguments over finance and bewildering last-minute disputes over the wording of seemingly uncontentious statements. At last year’s summit, for example, countries couldn’t agree on even mentioning fossil fuels in the final agreement.

COP31 will largely follow the same format. Arguments are already brewing over funding, negotiators are flexing their pens to hammer out details of new bureaucratic mechanisms, and hosts Turkey and Australia are limbering up for fresh disputes over which adverbs to deploy in a final agreement. This is your official warning: COP31 will not be the meeting that saves the world from climate peril.

But there could be one bright spark at the summit. An electrification pledge being touted by the Turkish presidency would see countries promise to increase electricity’s share of their final energy consumption to 35 per cent to 2035.

Focusing the climate effort on electrification is a smart move. In the current landscape, with disinformation rife and a climate denier still in the White House, electrifying stuff is probably our strongest climate weapon. High oil and gas prices and geopolitical instability make the energy security benefits of electrification obvious, while cheap green power could ease cost of living pressures in high-income countries and unlock development in low-income nations.

Electric power is also just so much more efficient than burning fuel. Electricity currently provides about 23 per cent of the energy delivered to consumers, but it powers sectors that make up 46 per cent of the global economy, energy analyst Jan Rosenow pointed out recently. If the world’s economy transitioned to a highly electrified state, powered by renewables, total primary energy use – the raw inputs into the energy system – would fall by almost 50 per cent, Rosenow’s analysis shows. Electrifying stuff is a common-sense move, before you even get to the climate benefits.

Plenty of richer countries are not moving fast enough on this stuff. China and Indonesia are ahead of both the US and the UK on electrifying their economies, while India and Brazil are catching up fast. We could learn a lot by looking beyond our borders. Annual climate meetings should become an opportunity for countries to swap notes and share best practice on the energy transition, not fight over the wording of virtue-signalling statements.

For too long, COPs have been generating a lot of words and not much action. But efforts are under way behind the scenes to redesign these meetings as useful events for the clean energy transition. The push for electrification offers a hint of what this could look like. If it delivers, COP summits might yet have a useful future.

Cold therapy may be worse than doing nothing for post-exercise recovery

New Scientist November 09, 2026

Plunging into an ice bath after a workout may be worse for your muscle recovery than doing nothing. Cold therapy is a popular intervention after rigorous exercise, like marathons, to relieve soreness and dampen the inflammation that can impair muscle recovery. But in a new study, adults who had ice baths after intense leg exercise showed markers of muscle damage for longer than those who just rested.

“Ice baths have long been considered a go-to recovery strategy in sport, so many people might expect them to outperform doing nothing,” says Freya Bayne at the University of East London. But emerging studies suggest that cold therapies slow muscle-protein synthesis by restricting blood flow and reducing the supply of nutrients to the muscles. “The [latest] study contributes to a growing conversation that recovery strategies should be selected based on the desired outcome, rather than assuming one approach works for everything,” she says.

Cold-water swimming has benefits for the brain as well as the body

The use of cold therapy – from ice baths and cold showers to open-water swimming – dates back centuries. Some studies suggest that cold therapy, particularly if it involves open-water swimming, benefits our mental health. But other claims, such as those made by Wim Hof around ice baths improving athletic performance and immune health, lack good scientific evidence.

Advertisement

Focusing on muscle recovery and soreness, Bayne and her colleagues compared cold therapy with other post-exercise interventions.

Forty adults who regularly strength-train had the strength of their quadriceps measured via a machine that also controls movement. While seated, the participants pushed against the machine as hard as possible while it kept their knee in a fixed position. They then performed a high-intensity knee-extension exercise using the same leg. This involved them trying to straighten their knee as much as possible while the machine pushed it back towards a bent position, causing the quadriceps to lengthen.

Free newsletter

Similar movements occur when lowering into a squat or running downhill. These can cause small tears to muscle fibres, which trigger an inflammatory response and lead to muscle soreness. This discomfort usually kicks in within hours of doing a new or particularly intense workout, peaking between 24 and 72 hours, and fading after a week.

Straight after exercising, the participants’ muscle strength was measured again, revealing a loss of 36 per cent, on average. They were then randomly assigned to one of four recovery strategies: cold-water immersion at 9°C (48°F) for 15 minutes, hot-water immersion at 42°C (108°F) for 30 minutes, hot-air exposure at 30°C (86°F) for 30 minutes, or passive rest at room temperature for 30 minutes. Cold-water immersion is typically a short treatment to reduce the risk of hypothermia, which is why it was offered for just 15 minutes.

After 72 hours, those who simply rested had recovered strength to a similar extent as those in the hot-water and hot-air groups, with all three groups regaining around 89 per cent of their maximum muscle strength. The cold-water group recovered about 82 per cent of their maximum strength.

Less than 4 minutes of vigorous exercise a day could halve your dementia risk

Self-reported pain and muscle soreness significantly increased in all groups at 24 hours after exercise, with none of the groups reporting a significant reduction by 72 hours. The cold-water group did report less pain at 24 hours relative to the other groups, but this had increased by 48 hours, suggesting the cold-water therapy had only temporarily masked pain.

Blood samples showed that levels of creatine kinase-MM, an enzyme in skeletal muscle cells that enters the bloodstream when muscles are damaged, returned to normal levels faster in the hot-water group than in the control and hot-air groups. In the cold-water group, levels remained 25 per cent above normal, even after 72 hours.

It is possible that changes to the interventions, such as repeating them or applying heat or cold therapies more locally to the affected area, would also change the results, says Bayne.

There are huge benefits to ringing the changes when it comes to exercise, finds committed runner Grace Wade when she analyses the science

Ken Nosaka at Edith Cowan University in Western Australia says that much of the evidence supporting cold therapies is anecdotal. “It is interesting that the authors found that none of the thermal recovery strategies were effective in alleviating pain and muscle soreness, but importantly none of them had negative effects,” he adds.

But it remains to be seen whether each recovery strategy has longer-term benefits, or whether different types of exercise would have different outcomes. “Athletes and recreational exercisers experience muscle fatigue and recovery demands in many different contexts,” says Bayne.

Mike Tipton at the University of Portsmouth, UK, says the findings shouldn’t stop athletes using ice baths altogether. “[It] may assist with repeated bouts of continuous activity in the heat as well as blunt perceived muscle soreness and fatigue during multi-day events where rapid recovery is required,” he says.

A true paleo diet would include a lot more insects

New Scientist November 09, 2026

There is a cliché in journalism where you say that something or other “is having a moment”. In 2024, Sabrina Carpenter released Espresso and suddenly she was having a moment. Right now, the cast of Celebrity Traitors are all having a collective moment.

For much of the 21st century, entomophagy – the eating of insects – has been having a moment. The first edible insect farm opened in the US in 2014, and many have followed its example. Insects are high in protein and there is evidence that farming them produces fewer greenhouse gases than conventional meats (alongside other environmental benefits). Magazines like New Scientist have run countless stories about edible insects. Insect-based food companies have launched to enormous buzz (sorry, not sorry).

Yet entomophagy hasn’t really taken off (again, not sorry). While edible insects are commonplace in many cultures, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, nowadays they are falling out of favour. In Europe and the US, they have long been viewed with disgust.

Advertisement

The overlooked power of diet for improving your mental health

Western culture reflects this. Try to think of an example of a fictional character eating insects. Did your mind instantly go to the vampire’s familiar Renfield in Dracula, endlessly chowing down on creepy-crawlies while also serving his evil master? Or maybe the, er, let’s go with “problematic” dinner sequence in Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom?

The thing is, this cultural belief that insects are gross is just that: cultural. There are insects you absolutely shouldn’t eat because they carry diseases or are poisonous, but many others are safe and nutritious. As I said, plenty of societies use insects as food.

How far back does this practice extend? When we talk about prehistoric foods, we often focus on large mammals like deer or mammoths, or cereals like wheat and barley, or – if you go back a few million years – grasses and sedges. We don’t often talk about Neanderthals or Homo erectus munching on crickets. But maybe we should.

Our evidence about prehistoric entomophagy is partial and scattered. That is partly because archaeologists haven’t often actively searched for it, says Lisa-Marie Shillito, an archaeologist at Durham University in the UK. “We don’t always recognise things that we’re not looking for,” she says. Insect remains are often found on archaeological sites, but often “people just assume it’s contamination or pests”.

Some of the best evidence comes from fossilised human faeces, known as coprolites, which can contain bits of insect exoskeleton and other traces. Unfortunately, “they’re not routinely collected in the same way that other artefacts are”, says Shillito. “They can be surprisingly hard to recognise” and may be mistaken for lumps of clay. Only a handful of researchers specialise in coprolites, including Shillito. “I’m kind of known, I guess, as being the expert in ancient poo.”

Shillito has now brought together a lot of evidence about insect-eating in prehistory in a synthesis paper published in World Archaeology on 27 October.

The first thing to note, Shillito says, is the practice is “really geographically widespread”. Some of the best evidence comes from the Americas, where coprolites have been more routinely studied. Shillito highlights Paisley caves in Oregon, which has evidence of human presence from around 14,300 years ago: one of the oldest such sites in the Americas. In 2020, she and her colleagues studied coprolites from the caves and found evidence that people were eating, among other things, insects.

Specifically, “big juicy ones”, says Shillito. These included ten-lined June beetles (Polyphylla decemlineata), which grow to almost 3 centimetres in length. The team also found the remains of Jerusalem crickets, which is an inaptly named group since they aren’t crickets and don’t come from Jerusalem. They are related to the oversized wētā insects of New Zealand, albeit not quite as large. “If you’re hunting and gathering, they’re quite meaty-looking things that you might just pick up and eat,” says Shillito.

A more subtle piece of evidence comes from the Bonneville Estates Rockshelter in Nevada. A coprolite from this site contained the eggs of parasitic worms called acanthocephalans. These parasites use insects and other arthropods as intermediate hosts – so the person who was infected may well have eaten insects.

On the other side of the world, at Cloggs cave in Australia, researchers have found evidence of Aboriginal Australians eating bogong moths (Agrotis infusa). These moths migrate in huge numbers every year, and it seems the Indigenous peoples took advantage of this. A grindstone from the site had the remains of ground and cooked bogong moths from about 2000 years ago.

There is also evidence that people were using bees as a food source thousands of years ago. In Nigeria around 3500 years ago, farmers and foragers lived alongside each other. A 2021 study of pottery vessels from the Nok culture found that many of them had telltale lipids. This reveals the people were eating honey or other items from beehives, perhaps including bee larvae. Likewise, in Egypt there are pottery vessels with traces of beeswax from at least 8000 years ago.

So far, all these examples have been from the relatively recent past: the last 20,000 years. But our species has been around for 300,000 years, at least, and human evolution spans 7 million years or more. Were our more distant ancestors eating insects too?

The first thing to say is that non-human primates, which are our closest living relatives, absolutely eat insects. A 2012 review found it was a common behaviour and that non-human primates tended to go for insects with a high protein-to-fat ratio – suggesting that insects are a significant source of protein for them. This hints, though of course doesn’t prove, that the most recent ancestor we share with apes also ate insects.

There is some evidence that this behaviour was carried through. In studies published in 2001 and 2008, two researchers – Lucinda Backwell at the University of the Witwatersrand in South Africa and Francesco d’Errico at the University of Bordeaux in France – described bone tools found at sites in South Africa. They argued that the pattern of wear on the bones was consistent with digging into termite mounds. The tools are over 1 million years old and may have been used by Paranthropus, extinct hominins related to our genus, Homo.

Likewise, in a 2014 study in the Journal of Human Evolution, researchers compiled isotopic data from early Homo specimens, and from older Australopithecus. The mix of carbon isotopes found in the remains gives us a broad-strokes picture of what the hominins ate. It seems they were eating at least some animal material, and at least some of that may have been insects.

Some readers may also remember an intriguing study published in 2025. It re-examined isotopic data from the bones of Neanderthals. Because living organisms tend to accumulate the heavy isotope nitrogen-15, and lose the lighter one nitrogen-14, organisms higher up the food chain tend to have more nitrogen-15 than those at the bottom. Neanderthals have sky-high levels of nitrogen-15.

We have an unprecedented choice of food, yet our diets are worse than ever, says palaeoanthropologist Daniel Lieberman. So what can evolution tell us about how to eat better?

One interpretation is that Neanderthals ate meat and little else: you could conclude they were “hyper-carnivores”. However, this doesn’t make a lot of sense, partly because eating just meat is dangerously unhealthy, and partly because there is plenty of evidence from other sources that Neanderthals had varied diets. So instead, researchers have suggested that Neanderthals sometimes ate the maggots that were feasting on rotting meat.

One of the authors of that study is Julie Lesnik at Wayne State University in Detroit, Michigan. In her 2019 book Edible Insects and Human Evolution, Lesnik argues that insects are both abundant and relatively low risk, making them an ideal food source. She suggests that mothers could have safely gathered insects while also carrying their babies. Of course, that assumes women weren’t hunting large animals alongside the men, an assumption that looks decidedly shaky – but that aside, it seems a reasonable hypothesis.

Nevertheless, there is a huge amount we still don’t know about insects in prehistoric diets. “How important were they?” asks Shillito. “How did that change over time, and why, in different parts of the world?”

Insects were probably seasonal foods in many places, Shillito suggests. “They’re not around all the time.” This may help to explain why it is tricky to find hard evidence of entomophagy in the archaeological record. “We’ve got this tantalising evidence,” says Shillito. Now, she wants to look more systematically.

The obvious takeaway from all this is that everybody banging on about the so-called paleo diet needs to rethink. Less red meat, more grasshoppers and beetles. It’s (probably) what our ancestors did!

Your body changes as you age and so should your diet – here’s how

Finally, let’s go back to where we started. In the past 20 years there has been a lot of coverage of the environmental and food-security benefits of eating insects. Yet, insect products aren’t supermarket staples, at least not where I live. If the wheel is turning, it’s only turning slowly.

That leads me to a book chapter by the entomologist Friedrich Simon Bodenheimer. He begins: “It has been known for many centuries that insects are eaten as delicacies in many parts of the world. Reports have come down from antiquity of insects, especially locusts, being eaten by primitive peoples. Honey has been known as a prized food from time immemorial. Yet entomophagy, apart from honey consumption, has always been regarded as a curiosity or as barbarism.”

Bodenheimer goes on to say that he began examining the subject “largely out of curiosity”, only to be taken aback by the sheer scale of entomophagy. “It is actually astonishing that the real and basic importance of insects as food for early and primitive man has been so long ignored.”

Savvy readers may have twigged from archaic terms like “barbarism” and “primitive man” what the punchline is going to be. Yes, this chapter is old: Bodenheimer published it in 1951.

We keep rediscovering the fact that humans have routinely eaten insects, and we keep being surprised by it. At some point, we should stop being surprised.

X chromosome gene may reduce autism rates in women and girls

New Scientist November 09, 2026

A single gene on the X chromosome may help explain why autism is less common in women and girls. The gene, ZFX, has powerful effects on a set of genes that contribute to the risk of autism, and is expressed more in women than in men.

“It’s about the fact that ZFX has a relationship with these other autism-associated genes,” says Rebecca Andersen, a neurogeneticist at Boston Children’s Hospital in Massachusetts. This one gene can keep other genes turned on when they might otherwise be deactivated, she says, reducing the chances that girls will develop autism.

Autism is a developmental condition. Autistic people have a variety of traits that can include difficulties with socialising and communicating, unusually high sensory sensitivity that can cause them to become overwhelmed, and restricted behaviours and interests.

Advertisement

A revolutionary new understanding of autism in girls

Many studies have found that autism is more common in males than in females: up to four times as common. “That specific number is contested,” says Andersen, partly because we now know that autism presents differently in females, including subtler effects on socialising. Furthermore, women and girls with autism often “mask” or “camouflage” their autistic traits, enabling them to pass as neurotypical at the cost of their mental health. This means females often go undiagnosed, or are diagnosed later in life, skewing the figures.

Nevertheless, many autism researchers believe there is a “female protective effect”: something about being female makes people less likely to be autistic. Notably, women diagnosed with autism tend to have more autism-linked mutations than men diagnosed with autism. This suggests there is a requirement for a “greater genetic load in females in order to manifest with autism at all, or to manifest to a degree that would be diagnosed”, says Andersen.

Understanding this requires understanding the genetics of autism. “We’ve long known that there’s a very strong genetic component to autism,” says Andersen. “There have been a lot of large-scale sequencing studies that have identified hundreds of different genes that are implicated in autism,” she says. “It’s been really perplexing to understand how so many different genes could all be relevant for autism.”

Free newsletter

To figure out how these genes work together, Andersen and her colleagues grew neural progenitor cells – which develop into neurons – in culture. They then targeted each of 20 genes, all known to be associated with autism. Rather than deleting or mutating the genes, they used a version of the CRISPR gene-editing technology to break down the RNA produced when the genes were expressed. Reduced expression of these genes is thought to increase the chances of developing autism. “We could target the RNA for degradation and have very rapid changes in expression levels of those genes,” says Andersen.

To their surprise, the researchers found that reducing the expression of any one of these genes tended to also significantly reduce the expression of most of the others. “Across almost all of our perturbations, they just looked very similar to one another, and in particular, how much they affected the other autism-associated genes,” says Andersen. “It seemed to make sense that they would have to converge in some way, in order to be related to autism, but we didn’t necessarily expect to find such a strong degree of convergence.”

What if the idea of the autism spectrum is completely wrong?

The researchers then built a model of the interactions between the genes. This enabled them to identify a core of 70 genes, all of which strongly regulate the 20 autism-associated genes, and also regulate each other. Andersen calls these genes the “central hub”.

“This provides strong evidence that apparently distinct genetic causes of autism may converge on common pathways,” says Louise Gallagher at the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto, who wasn’t involved in the study.

Having identified these core genes, the team then identified a set of 82 genes that were expressed less when the autism-related genes were suppressed, and which are known to be more heavily expressed in female brains compared with male. This led the researchers to ZFX, which is found on the X chromosome. Females have two X chromosomes, but males have one X and a smaller Y chromosome. This means females have two copies of ZFX – and unusually for genes on the X chromosomes, both copies are expressed.

Simon Baron-Cohen’s influential research helped pin autism as a particularly male condition. As studies increasingly broaden our view of autism, has his perspective changed?

“We found that ZFX was very related to many of these different autism-associated genes,” says Andersen. This means ZFX could act as a buffer. A girl could have a lot of mutations that reduce the expression of autism-associated genes and thus increase her probability of autism – only for the ZFX to increase the expression of those genes and reduce her chances of autism.

“That’s very interesting and biologically plausible,” says Gallagher. However, the claim rests on the team’s model of the interactions between the genes. “The paper doesn’t show that increasing ZFX expression rescues the consequences of the variants.” That would require additional experiments.

“It’s also unlikely that something as complex as the female protective effect will be attributable to a single gene,” says Gallagher. “It could be related to other sex-linked genetic mechanisms, hormonal influences and broader differences in developmental biology.”

Is Schrödinger’s cat both dead and alive? No, it’s just haunted by its past

New Scientist November 09, 2026

Today, for breakfast, I had a smoothie. This isn’t unusual: I drink the same smoothie every weekday morning. At some point in the past, I discovered I particularly liked it and made it a habit. It is a simple example of something that makes intuitive sense – that our past experiences determine our present actions, and they, in turn, determine our future trajectories.

But what if I told you that the past never actually existed? Or, at least, that it doesn’t matter? It sounds left field, but I would only be channelling an assumption that lurks within many laws of physics largely unchallenged: that the present moment is all we need to know about to predict the future. Without making this assumption, the amount of information you need to predict the future is at risk of dramatically blowing up, rapidly making it impractical to say anything at all.

Or so we thought. Now, there’s a move afoot to reclaim the past for physics. Its proponents think that could resolve long-standing questions at the core of quantum theory, such as why it is so weird as it is, but equally not as weird as it could be – and, along the way, clarify the true nature of time itself. “I think it’s a big deal. I think it will be a big thing for the foundations of physics,” says quantum information researcher Jacob Biamonte at École de Technologie Supérieure in Montreal.

Advertisement

To begin to understand how physics cancelled the past, imagine a game of marbles. To predict where any marble will be in a second’s time, all we need to know is its current position, speed and direction of travel, all effectively ignorant of the marble’s deep past. We then roll the relevant physical laws – in this case, Isaac Newton’s laws of motion – forward into the future. We don’t need to know anything about the collisions that brought the marble to its present position – luckily, as calculating the myriad past possibilities might rapidly overwhelm our computational ability.

The daring idea that time is an illusion and how we could prove it

The marble’s present is agnostic about its past, and its past is largely immaterial in determining its future, so long as we know about the present. It is like saying that all that matters with my smoothie choice is that memories of past mornings are stored in my present mind. Even if the past vanished entirely, I can continue my breakfast routine. In this way of thinking, there’s no way of telling if the universe began just 5 minutes ago.

This principle of neglecting the past is called Markovianity, after Andrey Markov, the Russian mathematician who laid the groundwork for the idea. And it is everywhere in physics – even in quantum theory, our best stab at characterising how the weird realm of particles behaves.

Unlike objects in the classical world, quantum particles can appear to be in a mix of different states at once – in multiple positions, for example. This leads to dramas such as the infamous Schrödinger’s cat thought experiment, in which a cat is kept in a box in a quantum “superposition” of being alive and dead. Each of the two states can be assigned its own probability, encoded in a mathematical object called the quantum wave function.

Just as with classical mechanics, standard quantum mechanics doesn’t much care about the cat’s past. As far as its future goes, there are two possibilities. You can keep the box closed, in which case, all you can say is a matter of percentages – the cat could be alive or dead and currently seems to be existentially fuzzy. Or you open the box, in which case, the cat’s wave function “collapses” into a single, definitive state and the animal is definitively dead or alive, too.

Key oddity of quantum physics may run even deeper than anticipated

Schrödinger’s cat lifted the lid on a load of problems that physicists and philosophers have anguished over in the century since the inception of quantum mechanics. What physically happens when you open the box – is it you who somehow potentially kills the cat? What about the nanosecond when you have just barely moved the lid – is the cat somehow slightly less mixed at this time? What, indeed, does anything about the wave function say about the cat in the real, physical world? Is the wave function itself “real”? “It’s been 100 years, and we still don’t have a consensus on the right way to think about quantum theory,” says philosopher David Glick at the University of California, Davis.

Jacob Barandes, a philosopher of physics at Harvard University, thinks he has identified the problem. He says that the shenanigans surrounding the wave function are merely a smokescreen, behind which the true culprit for the cat’s bizarre situation is hiding: the influence of the past.

In a paper published last year, he showed that something like quantum theory can be built on equations for inherently probabilistic, non-Markovian processes that are always influenced by their past. In this world, cats are never simultaneously dead and alive; rather, everything is inherently chancy, and the past indispensable.

Here, the wave function doesn’t represent any physical reality, but is just a form of mathematical bookkeeping for all the ways in which the past touches the cat from across time. Let’s go back to our marble and make it quantum. Barandes likens this marble’s wave function to a collection of “ghost marbles”. Each of these ghost marbles embodies the real quantum marble’s state but, say, 1 second ago – or 2, or 3, or as far back as you like. “Each ghost marble is a little weird. It’s invisible. It’s unobservable,” says Barandes. But if you have information about the ghost marbles, you can predict what the real marble can do next. Consequently, the world that contains real and ghost marbles seems to follow tractable, Markovian laws, because everything about the real marble’s past is encoded in the ghost marbles’ present. The price of pretending that the past doesn’t matter is filling the universe with ghosts. The quantum wave function is just an elegant arrangement of such spectres.

Barandes thinks our mistake is to read physical reality into this spooky parlour trick. In his alternative framework, quantum peculiarities such as superposition states and wave function collapse are consequences of treating the wave function as something overly real. We can’t know what state Schrödinger’s cat is in, not because its state is somehow existentially fuzzy, but because quantum objects are inherently a little random. “They’re always behaving probabilistically, in a chancy way that depends on the past,” says Barandes. Acts of measurement, such as opening the cat’s box, aren’t special, but merely physical interactions that make the object “forget” some of this past, suppressing some of its chanciness and history-ladenness.

Subscriber-only newsletter

This picture provides a way to counter the objection that calculations become intractable if you must account for the whole prior history of the universe. In standard quantum theory, it is well accepted that as objects get larger and interact with more of their environment, they lose their quantumness. In Barandes’s picture, that maps onto objects relinquishing some of their past and becoming more Markovian as the past recedes into the distance.

His framework hasn’t yet produced a distinct, experimentally testable prediction, but it has already had one notable win: explaining the degree to which quantum objects can be correlated, thanks to the phenomenon of quantum entanglement.

When two quantum objects are entangled, the results of measurements of their properties maintain a correlation, even if they are first pulled very far apart. These correlations are stronger than would be possible with any non-quantum connection – by a maximum of about 41 per cent, a number known as the Tsirelson bound. Mathematician Boris Tsirelson derived this number in 1980 from standard quantum theory, but Barandes says it had never been explained beyond being a quirk of complicated mathematics. Later, in 1994, physicists Sandu Popescu and Daniel Rohrlich showed that some hypothetical theories could, in principle, achieve correlations 100 per cent greater than non-quantum theories without information being exchanged faster than light speed, which would contradict Albert Einstein’s special theory of relativity. “Forty-one per cent is not even half of 100 per cent, so why so little?” asks Barandes.

His framework elegantly brings this back to the speed of light. In a universe of quantum marbles, each marble moves in its slightly random and history-laden way, but because it can’t move or communicate with other marbles faster than light, those parts of its past that lie beyond a horizon of influence set by the speed of light can be neglected. Working with David Kagan and Mahmudul Hasan at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, Barandes has calculated that this constraint is exactly what keeps the strength of quantum correlations from exceeding the Tsirelson bound.

For 100 years, quantum theory has painted the subatomic world as strange beyond words. But bold new interpretations and experiments may help us to finally grasp its true meaning

Simon Milz, a physicist at Heriot-Watt University in the UK, is intrigued. Standard quantum theory is very abstract and mysterious, so there is value in uncovering processes that offer some underlying picture, he says – and the Tsirelson bound is one of the most talked-about things in quantum information theory. “It’s quite an interesting thing to find a new principle that leads to it,” says Milz.

David Wallace, a philosopher of physics at the University of Pittsburgh in Pennsylvania, echoes that. But he is uncertain how far Barandes’s approach can go, in particular because of the way it denies the wave function any physical reality. Standard quantum theory works incredibly well as a description of our world, he says. “If you just take quantum mechanics as we find it, there doesn’t seem to be any way to read it that doesn’t basically commit you to the wave function representing physical goings-on,” he says.

He would like to see the framework reproduce more complex calculations, such as from quantum field theories that underpin the standard model of particle physics. Historically, this is where non-standard interpretations or reformulations of quantum physics have tended to fail. Barandes says that his framework ought to work for quantum fields, and he plans to extend his work in this direction.

His isn’t a lone, quixotic quest to bring the past back into physics. Cristian Mariani at the University of Italian Switzerland in Lugano works on an unorthodox approach to quantum theory known as spontaneous collapse. It depicts wave function collapse as something that doesn’t happen only when you try to measure things, but can spontaneously occur at any time. Spontaneous collapse models produce predictions that are distinct from those of standard quantum theory, but no experiment has yet provided enough reason to reject standard quantum mechanics in favour of spontaneous collapse. But if quantum laws are amended in a non-Markovian way, allowing spontaneous collapse models to become history-laden, then new experimental tests open up, says Mariani.

Where exactly does the quantum world end and concrete reality begin?

Questioning the role of Markovianity in quantum physics is important in itself, he says. “In physics, and in philosophy of physics, this was the kind of assumption that we made without explicitly defending it.” In part, that’s because of the mathematical complexities of non-Markovian theories, and the enduring appeal to philosophers of Occam’s razor, the idea that the simplest solutions are the best. Grappling with the assumption might lead researchers to rethink the nature of physical laws themselves, says Mariani.

It isn’t just our understanding of quantum theory that could be sharpened up, either; so could our conceptions of time and the significance of the present moment. Until the 20th century, philosophers had long argued that the present moment is privileged. In the sense that the past has ceased to be and the future is yet to exist, you might indeed argue that only the present can claim to be truly real. This point of view is known as presentism, and it depicts us as observers living on a wavefront of “now”, ploughing from the past into the future.

Einstein’s space- and time-warping theories of relativity seemed to put paid to that privileging of the present. Within relativity, it is impossible to get all observers to even agree on a single, simultaneous “now”. The alternative view, which Einstein’s relativity is more friendly towards, is called eternalism. It states that all of the past, present and future exist simultaneously. We exist at a fixed point in this block of space and time, and the flow of time past us is essentially an illusion.

Since the advent of Einstein’s relativity, “most people think that presentism is always on the defensive”, says philosopher David Builes at Princeton University. In 2025, he and his Princeton colleague Michele Odisseas Impagnatiello went on the offensive, arguing that presentism is backed by centuries of experiments whose outcomes haven’t deviated from predictions of Markovian laws of physics that only really require that the present be real. “This isn’t an argument from the armchair; it’s an empirical argument,” says Impagnatiello. Conversely, the pair argue, if a non-Markovian, history-laden interpretation of quantum physics prevails, it will force them to abandon presentism.

We’re a long way off any such proof as yet. “Ideally, we would have a case in which a non-Markovian interpretation is superior in the sense that it makes novel predictions that orthodox quantum mechanics doesn’t make,” says Impagnatiello – a view echoed by Wallace.

Barandes says that one place where his framework may touch the world of experiments is in quantum computing. Quantum computers derive enhanced capabilities through superposition and entanglement effects that, in Barandes’s view, are all really fronts for influences of the past. “A quantum computer is secretly a non-Markovian computer,” he says. “It’s not just the present arrangement of the bits that matters, but also the past arrangements.” There are currently only a few cases where researchers have unambiguously proved that using quantum computers is the only way to solve a particular problem. Thinking about them in a non-Markovian way might lead to the identification of new situations in which they are clear game changers, says Barandes.

What exactly would a full-scale quantum computer be useful for?

Glick agrees there is general value in seeing how far weakening or dropping the Markovian assumption can get us, even if other descriptions of nature never get fully ruled out. “At a certain point, we might find that, well, it’s better to drop that assumption, that then we get a more fruitful result,” he says. “That’s not a direct, empirical kind of confirmation or disconfirmation, but this is how science often works.”

Taking the past seriously touches the foundations of physics in a sweeping and profound way, and that makes it worth pursuing, says Barandes. “I think that this framework may have something to tell us about the way the world really is,” he says. “As a philosopher, I care about that.” It’s certainly food for thought as I prepare my morning smoothie.

Prehistoric Britons may have made giant stone axes to show off

New Scientist November 09, 2026

More than 300,000 years ago, hominins in Britain were crafting huge, skilfully shaped handaxes whose primary purpose may have been for showing off.

Giant ficrons, weighing up to 3 kilograms and measuring up to 30 centimetres long, were fragile and impractical to wield – but tricky and time-consuming to knap. Accomplished stone tool-makers thus probably fashioned these rare knives not for cutting but as a sort of prehistoric status symbol, says Malaika Standley Barrow at University College London.

A cave in France is revealing how the Neanderthals died out

“These giant ficrons really are lovely, and it seems they’re meant to visually stand out and be appreciable to other group members as something unusual and interesting to look at,” she says. “So there’s definitely some prowess or something – or maybe a creation of social bonds through the act of doing this together.”

Advertisement

Ficrons are Stone Age handaxes carved from flint with curved sides, rounded bases and remarkably pointed tips. Named for the sharp iron tips of poles once used to propel French boats through shallow water, these tools have appeared in archaeological records in Britain since the late 19th century, particularly along the Thames and its tributaries.

Most ficrons are similar in size to other handaxes from this period, measuring about 8 to 15 centimetres long, and probably worked as cutting or butchering knives. But a few stand-out ficrons exceed two or even three times the usual length and 10 times the weight – and scientists don’t know what purpose they might have served.

Subscriber-only newsletter

To address that question, Standley Barrow and her colleagues examined 817 ficrons and other handaxes from seven archaeological sites across southern Britain, stretching across the Thames valley, Kent, Hampshire and Devon. Among those tools were seven giant ficrons measuring at least 22 centimetres long.

3D scans and measurements revealed that six of the seven giant ficrons had extremely exaggerated proportions compared with smaller handaxes from the same sites. The giant handaxes also tended to be more symmetrical and have straighter edges than smaller versions, suggesting they were crafted with more skill and precision. This means these larger axes weren’t simply scaled-up versions of standard ficrons, but probably deliberately crafted to be visually distinct, says Standley Barrow.

The researchers then commissioned experienced flintknappers to make 10 giant and 10 normal-sized replica ficrons from British flint. Next, they had 20 students use the replicas to cut through 10 pieces of rope attached to metal frames. Each student completed the task first with an ordinary-sized ficron, followed by a giant one.

Knappers like James Dilley at Ancient Craft in Norfolk, UK, found the giant ficrons particularly challenging to make, especially the fine tip. “You have to think of the flint as being very much like a piece of glass,” he says. “One misplaced strike and it will snap in half, and all that work has gone to waste. You need a lot more skill and experience to make one of these.” On average, knapping a giant ficron took about 45 minutes, compared with about 20 to 30 for smaller ficrons, he says.

Our ancestors probably used a wide range of plant-based tools that have since been lost to history. Now we’re finally getting a glimpse of this Botanic Age

Yet there seemed to be no practical benefits for this extra work: on average, the students took 22 per cent more time cutting the rope with giant ficrons, often resorting to using two hands to manoeuvre a heavy knife they found difficult to control. For butchering or digging, pressure on the blade would probably break the tip quite easily, Standley Barrow adds.

Even so, it’s possible the blade could have been used both ceremoniously and practically for delivering a killing blow to a wounded prey, known as the coup de grâce, she and her colleagues argue.

Luke Dale at Durham University, UK, finds that concept particularly compelling. The giant ficrons could have had limited practical use in a culturally important role and hold a prominent social function, he says.

The age of the tools suggests they were probably made by early Neanderthals. The exquisite craftsmanship of these objects points to an interest in aesthetics and cultural tradition, adding to the evidence that our ancient ancestors were more sophisticated than people often consider them to be.

“These were clearly intelligent archaic humans who could use technology to survive, and presumably had very recognisable social interactions with each other,” says Dale.

Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports DOI: 10.1016/j. jasrep.2026.106120

Weird ‘ultraquantum’ turbulence seen for the first time

New Scientist November 09, 2026

A type of turbulence that only exists in the quantum realm has been directly observed for the first time. This “ultraquantum” turbulence may be representative of what happens in many exotic settings, from liquid helium to neutron stars.

Turbulence refers to chaotic and irregular currents in a liquid or gas that is perturbed, like unruly versions of whirlpools you create by stirring a cup of tea. Many fluids we encounter daily behave this way, but fluids and gases in the quantum realm follow completely different rules. When perturbed and made turbulent, they remain largely still, but become pocked with thin, tangled, string-like whirlpools before quieting down into equilibrium.

No space, no time, no particles: A radical vision of quantum reality

To get a look at this ultraquantum turbulence, Sebastian Morris at the University of Cambridge and his colleagues started with thousands of potassium atoms that they had cooled very close to absolute zero – the coldest temperature possible – with lasers and electromagnetic fields. This made the atoms behave like a very dilute quantum gas.

Advertisement

With the same tools, the researchers corralled the atoms into the shape of a cylinder a few dozen micrometres in size. By controlling the atoms’ interactions with each other and their energies, they could also create a disturbance that would engender turbulence and vortices.

Imaging the whole cylinder would have hidden the tangles, so Morris and his colleagues used a sheet of laser light to isolate and image just one slice of it.

“As soon as I got the first pictures, I felt like, this is the one,” he says. “You can see these holes, these imprints of the vortex lines as they wind in and out of this imaged cross-sectional slice.”

Subscriber-only newsletter

The researchers took many images and studied the distribution of vortices as they tangled, fell apart, connected into rings or moved to the cylinder’s edge, tracing how the quantum fluid became less and less turbulent and disordered. Intriguingly, they found this process to be very similar to what had previously been observed in liquid helium, which is also a quantum fluid, but one that is a lot denser and whose atoms interact more strongly.

The way order forms is similar for the two systems, but nothing else is, says team member Christoph Eigen at the University of Cambridge. This exemplifies a universal behaviour for a whole class of quantum systems, one that ought to show up in other, even more dissimilar settings, says Zoran Hadzibabic, who is also at the University of Cambridge and worked on the experiment.

Quantum experiment settles a century-old row between Einstein and Bohr

Mathematical models for ultraquantum turbulence have existed for decades, but it is usually very difficult to image vortices, especially in a three-dimensional collection of atoms, says Thomas Gasenzer at Heidelberg University in Germany. The new work supports the models with precise and sophisticated experimental evidence, he says.

Davide Proment at the University of East Anglia in the UK says the new measurement is phenomenal and surpasses past investigations of ultraquantum turbulence. Future experiments aiming to image several slices of atoms simultaneously could reveal even more details of vortices’ behaviour, he says – and Morris’s team is interested in this idea too.

Because of the universality of the process, future experiments could also shed light on ultraquantum turbulence far away from the lab, says Gasenzer. “The same kind of [turbulence] dynamics has been proposed to happen, for example, in the dark matter halo of a neutron star, so maybe one should think about observables that could be compared between the two.”

Physical Review Letters DOI: 10.1103/lywd-gjg9

An unexpected feedback loop may be driving mega heatwaves

New Scientist November 06, 2026

Mid-latitude regions such as Europe are set to suffer more intense heatwaves than previously thought, according to new research that has uncovered a three-way feedback loop that amplifies extreme heat conditions.

Heatwaves across the world have shocked scientists with their scale and severity in recent years, with heat extremes dramatically outstripping both historical records and the predictions of climate models.

Extreme heat is now making cities unlivable. How can we survive it?

In the UK in 2022, temperatures exceeded 40°C (104°F) for the first time in history, despite predictions that such a milestone was probably still years away. Likewise, the 2021 heatwave in the Pacific Northwest saw temperatures hit extremes that far outstripped climate model projections.

Advertisement

Researchers have been scrambling to understand why very extreme heat is occurring more frequently, and with greater intensity, than expected at this level of warming.

One team thinks the answer lies partly in the soil. Scientists already knew that high-pressure systems allow more solar radiation to reach Earth’s surface, heating up the land. They also knew that higher temperatures dry soils more quickly, removing the cooling effect provided by evaporation, thereby further amplifying heatwaves.

Free newsletter

Now it seems that when temperatures climb high enough, dry soil, high pressure and extreme heat can amplify each other further, with dry soil helping to sustain high-pressure systems in the atmosphere.

“Basically, the soils that are affected by circulation pattern also start to affect back on the circulation pattern itself,” says Kai Kornhuber at the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis in Austria.

This three-way feedback effect makes extreme heatwaves 10 per cent hotter than they would otherwise be, according to the research by Kornhuber and his colleagues – a factor not fully accounted for in climate model projections.

This will have serious consequences for our ability to cope with future extreme heat. “Ten per cent hotter or colder can really make a difference between a heatwave and a record-shattering heatwave,” says Kornhuber. “We’re facing so many critical thresholds in social and biophysical systems that an extra 10 per cent can really lead to temperatures that are then quite damaging.”

Is a broken jet stream causing extreme weather that lasts longer?

This may include serious public health consequences, a breakdown of vital infrastructure such as transport links and energy grids, crop failures and the collapse of ecosystems.

As the world warms due to climate change, regions including Europe, Russia, North America, parts of South America and Australia will hit thresholds where this feedback effect is triggered increasingly often. Kornhuber says work is now needed to ensure climate models are properly including this feedback effect when projecting future extremes.

Dim Coumou at the Free University of Amsterdam says the work helps to solve “part of the puzzle” of why heatwaves are outstripping model projections in their severity. “It shows that climate models are not doing a good job in reproducing this feedback mechanism, and that is a concern,” he says.

Governments should urgently start to prepare for more extreme heat events, he adds: “A region like Europe has to prepare for more intense heatwaves in the coming decades.”

Science Advances DOI: 10.1126/sciadv. aeh9111
