Record-breaking, fast-spinning magnet could help uncover new physics

New Scientist November 06, 2026

A tiny magnet that levitates within a superconductor trap may be the fastest spinning object visible to the naked eye, and one of the fastest spinning objects ever made. In the future, it could be used in experiments searching for mysterious dark matter particles and aid the development of quantum technologies.

Superconductors are materials that conduct electricity with perfect efficiency, and they also expel any magnetic field that tries to permeate them – a phenomenon known as the Meissner effect. Because of this, a magnet placed above a superconductor experiences repulsive magnetic forces and starts to levitate. Tao Wang at the Agency for Science Technology and Research in Singapore and his colleagues have now set one such levitating magnet spinning at an unprecedentedly fast rate.

A miniature magnet rivals behemoths in strength for the first time

The researchers used a spherical magnet made from neodymium, iron and boron that was about 30 micrometres wide, similar to the width of a fine human hair. They placed it in a cylindrical container made from lead, then enclosed that container in a chamber devoid of air, or a vacuum chamber.

Advertisement

Next, they used liquid helium to cool the whole set-up to approximately -269°C (-452°F), only a few degrees above the coldest possible temperature. Under these extreme circumstances, lead behaved as a superconductor and the lack of air meant that the magnet could levitate within it without bumping into any particles. The team set the magnet spinning with a magnetic coil, ultimately pushing this tiny rotor to 138 million revolutions per minute.

Wang says the magnet’s spinning was also very stable: it would take 17 days for its spinning speed to decrease by 50 per cent, something that would typically happen more quickly due to interactions between the magnet and its environment. “In terms of how many turns it makes before slowing down significantly, this is in the same league as the Earth’s spinning,” he says. “This, so far, is the fastest magnetically levitated rotor.” The record for the fastest rotating human-made object is also held by a levitated sphere, but that one was nano-sized, so invisible to the naked eye, and levitated by laser beams.

Physics of light and magnetism rewritten after almost two centuries

Because the rotor experiences essentially no friction, and it is magnetic and cold, its behaviour is very sensitive to its environment, which makes it a promising sensor. The team has already successfully tested it as a gauge of vacuum at very low temperatures. Wang says this could be useful for builders of quantum computers, which often must be kept extremely cold and isolated in order to work.

Benjamin Stickler at Ulm University in Germany says the levitated spinning magnet could also be used to precisely sense and measure magnetic fields.

It could also be a promising platform for tests of fundamental physics, such as looking for effects related to dark matter particles, or sensing gravitational waves at so far unexplored frequencies, says team member Andrea Vinante at the National Research Council in Italy. Additionally, at very low temperatures quantum effects become dominant, so it could even be used for explorations of quantum mechanics and its interplay with gravity at micrometre scales, he says.

Science Advances DOI: 10.1126/sciadv. aee6434

Thea Kilian appointed principal of St Cuthbert’s College in Auckland

New Zealand Herald November 09, 2026

Thea Kilian will formally take up her role as principal of St Cuthbert’s College from April 15, 2027. Photo / St Cuthbert’s College

One of Auckland’s most prestigious private girls’ schools has looked to Tauranga for its next principal after its former head resigned less than two years into the job.

ACG Tauranga executive principal Thea Kilian will take the helm at St Cuthbert’s College on April 15 next year, after Charlotte Avery decided to return to the UK for “family reasons”.

Kilian has worked in education for 28 years in New Zealand and South Africa, including more than 20 years in senior leadership at New Zealand schools. She also previously served as lead principal of the Oneroa Kāhui Ako.

Contact reporter Rachel Maher

The St Cuthbert’s College Trust Board said it was impressed by Kilian’s humility, commitment to teaching and learning, and belief in the potential of young women.

During the appointment process, Kilian told the board her first priority would be to listen and get to know the school’s students, staff and wider community.

“I believe young people thrive when high expectations are combined with genuine care, and I look forward to working alongside staff, students and families to ensure every girl feels known, supported and challenged to become the very best version of herself,” she said.

Kilian holds a Bachelor of Science, an honours degree in mathematics and a postgraduate diploma in higher education.

Both postgraduate qualifications were awarded with first-class honours.

Head of senior school Tom Curtis and head of junior school Fe Tomich will continue to lead the college alongside the wider management team until Kilian starts.

Kilian’s appointment follows the resignation of Charlotte Avery, who stepped down in June after less than two years as principal.

Trust board chairwoman Leigh Melville previously told the Herald Avery had decided to return to the United Kingdom for “family reasons”.

Avery joined St Cuthbert’s in August 2024 after 17 years as principal of St Mary’s School, an independent girls’ school in Cambridge, England.

St Cuthbert’s College is a private girls’ school in Epsom, with students from Year 0 to Year 13.

It opened in 1915 as the Auckland Presbyterian College for Ladies and moved to its current Market Rd site in 1925.

In 2026, annual tuition for New Zealand residents was $27,500 for Years 0 to 6 and $31,544 for Years 7 to 13, with boarding bringing the total for a senior student to $53,152 before levies and other charges.

Rachel Maher is the education correspondent for the New Zealand Herald. She also covers other topics such as Auckland issues, crime and local government. She started at the Herald as a breaking news journalist in 2022, before joining the Auckland team this year.

Carterton forestry owners are facing an average rates hike of 1260% under a council proposal out for consultation. Photo / Ivan Turdeich

Carterton council staff have advised against adopting a controversial rating review in its current form, following a public backlash and flawed economic modelling.

The advice, outlined in a report by Carterton District Council chief executive Geoff Hamilton, comes before a two-day hearing starting on Wednesday, with more than 50 of the nearly 500 submitters scheduled to speak.

Under the council’s proposal, forestry owners faced average rate rises of 1260% to help fund roading, and dairy farmers faced increases of 92% on average.

About 4700 residential and lifestyle properties would have had falls in rates of 14%.

“Given the feedback, submissions and updated modelling impacts, officers do not support proceeding with the changes as consulted on,” Hamilton said.

“Officers suggest the proposal may be more publicly acceptable where the scale, scope and/or speed of changes are reviewed following consideration of submitters’ feedback.”

If the council decided to continue with the rating review, Hamilton suggested staggering changes over a few years and limiting the proportion of council-funded non-weather-related roading costs that were recovered through variable targeted roading rates.

Hamilton said the primary reason the council decided to initiate the rating review was to consider options to adjust its rates distribution across different property types.

“Carterton has long been known for having the highest residential rates in New Zealand, according to the New Zealand Taxpayer Union (NZTU) tables,” he said in his report.

Of the 20 rural councils in New Zealand that responded to the 2024/25 NZTU survey, Carterton had the highest average residential rates, and the fourth highest among all territorial authorities.

Carterton was the only rural council with residential rates greater than rural rates on average.

The council’s rates review proposal included introducing a targeted roading rate and increasing the rural differential from 0.8 to 1.0 (the amount rural ratepayers pay compared to household and commercial rates).

The proposed targeted roading rate sought to collect roading revenue from ratepayers in a more proportionate way, following an assessment by Morrison Low which was commissioned by the three Wairarapa councils.

The assessment found dairy, forestry and pastoral farming collectively made up more than 68% of Carterton’s council-funded, non-weather-related, roading costs in the Wairarapa town.

The assessment was later found to have errors and consultation was extended when the modelling was corrected.

Hamilton said if the proposal was adopted, it would “benefit almost 4700 residential and lifestyle properties while negatively affecting around 500 productive rural rating units”.

Of almost 500 submitters, about 80% did not support council’s proposal, and only about 150 were from Carterton addresses.

The biggest themes that came across in feedback were concerns around economic impact, mismatch with the forestry harvesting cycle, and concerns with the modelling and council’s process.

- LDR is local body journalism funded by RNZ and NZ on Air

The young Kiwis heading to the world’s biggest climate change gathering

New Zealand Herald November 09, 2026

Caretaker Climate Minister Simon Watts will also go to the Cop31 conference. Photo / Mark Mitchell

By Kate Newton of RNZ

Pacific communities must be at the forefront of global climate change action, three young Kiwi activists heading to the world’s annual climate summit say.

Ataria MacDonald, Aigagalefili Fepulea’i-Tapua’i and Aditi Tiwari – all in their 20s – are among an estimated 80,000 people heading to Cop31, which kicked off in Antalya, Turkey overnight.

This year’s conference is taking place against a backdrop of global political upheaval, including ongoing disruption to fossil fuel supply chains.

That has sharpened many countries’ focus on electrifying their economies, and the transition to clean energy is a priority on this year’s “action agenda” – the practical discussions that sit alongside the formal negotiations.

New Zealand’s delegation is heading over at an unusual moment, with a caretaker Government in place after Saturday’s inconclusive election.

Caretaker Climate Minister Simon Watts will attend from November 15 to 18, and RNZ understands that Labour’s Deborah Russell and the Greens’ Francisco Hernandez will also go.

MacDonald, Fepulea’i-Tapua’i and Tiwari are not part of New Zealand’s official delegation, but will attend as “civil society” delegates, who represent communities, NGOs and other organisations all pushing for climate action.

MacDonald (Ngāti Manuhiri), 26, the aquaculture project manager for her iwi, is one of three iwi rangatahi attending the conference alongside chief executive Nicola Rata-MacDonald.

Ngāti Manuhiri’s rohe reaches from Takapuna to Mangawhai, and includes the islands of the Hauraki Gulf (Tīkapa Moana).

“One of the biggest issues I think we’re facing across Tāmaki and Hauraki Gulf is the sedimentation that’s happening,” she said.

While sedimentation itself is not directly caused by climate change, it is made worse by increasing storms and extreme rainfall, which increase bank and coastal erosion.

Mahurangi Harbour, in particular, has been badly affected by sediment run-off.

That had not only affected the iwi’s cultural practices, but hurt the wider community, MacDonald said.

“We have oyster farmers in that area that are no longer able to rely on that as their livelihoods and create a living from there.”

The invasive Caulerpa seaweed posed another existential threat to the health of the Gulf, and the risk of further pest species arriving was rising as New Zealand’s ocean waters warm.

“There are a lot of issues that are happening in our climate that aren’t actually caused by ourselves as a [Pacific] region, but we’re left dealing with the consequences.”

With tens of thousands of people going to COP, and hundreds of events, MacDonald said she would be “trying to find something micro in such a macro conference”.

“What we have established is an indigenous network online with groups, mobs from Australia, the Pacific region, and we are all collectively attending Cop31 to connect as indigenous people,” she said.

“It’s almost using a global context to actually connect at a regional level.”

The Pacific was originally set to play a significant role in this year’s Cop, with Australia bidding to host the conference in partnership with island states.

However, a late bid from Turkey resulted in this year’s unusual co-hosting arrangement and a shift from Adelaide to Antalya.

Australia has still pledged to represent the interests of the Pacific, but MacDonald said there would have been a much stronger attendance from Pacific island states if the conference was in Adelaide.

“We all were really banking on the idea that it would be closer to home.”

A pre-conference event was held in Fiji and Tuvalu in October, but many countries skipped it.

New Zealand was among the 50-odd nations that did attend, and Simon Watts signed the country up to the event’s concluding Taku Palasoa declaration.

Aigagalefili Fepulea’i-Tapua’i, 23, will head to Turkey firmly grounded in the Pacific.

She set up youth climate group 4 Tha Kulture while she was at Aorere College in Māngere, and is executive director of the Aotearoa Climate Action Network.

“The Pacific is not just a nice to have,” she said.

“We are there to represent people who are living through the everyday impacts [of climate change]. And it’s very easy for that to get lost when people are going through the motions of Cop.”

It was also easy for New Zealand to forget its place in the Pacific.

“We have this idea that we are part of the Anglosphere, where actually, when it comes to the climate context … what happens in the Pacific happens to us too, eventually,” Fepulea’i-Tapua’i said.

“So it’s really important that we support and stand in solidarity with the Pacific.”

Fepulea’i-Tapua’i said Watts “spoke very ambitiously” while he was in the islands about keeping the 1.5C Paris Agreement target within sight.

“I would love to see the New Zealand Government carry that through to Cop31. It needs to be more than words.”

She and other advocates from the Pacific would push hard for stable, meaningful climate finance, she said.

“We are there to represent those who are unjustly living through the worst impacts of climate change.”

Currently, climate financing was typically treated as a form of charity or aid – which did not recognise either the dignity of Pacific peoples or match the scale of the challenge they faced.

“We’re not victims - we are resilient people.”

The challenge was to support that “without it becoming an expectation that resilience is an endless resource”, Fepulea’i-Tapua’i said.

“Families can’t afford to constantly have to recover - whether that’s flooding or other natural disasters that come in future.”

Like Ataria MacDonald, she was expecting the conference to be “quite chaotic”.

“Things develop so fast that you have to be really, really responsive. But I think that it’s exciting. I think that any opportunity we have to speak truth to the experiences of the people that we represent is exciting.”

For Porirua climate advocate Aditi Tiwari, 26, that experience is so close to home it’s almost lapping at the door.

“Just a kilometre away from my house is the Pāuatahanui Inlet.

“We see how the community suffers from every single flood or every single season of rising sea levels,” she said.

“How are we going to combat that?”

Already this year, she has been part of a community effort to plant 10,000 natives along the inlet to help reduce shoreline erosion.

It’s that grassroots voice that Tiwari hopes to take to Cop31 as a delegate for the Global Shapers Community, a network set up by the World Economic Forum.

However, she’s travelling solo, paying her way to Turkey through crowdfunding, community raffles and support from friends and whānau in Porirua.

One of her grounding experiences as a teenager arriving in New Zealand in 2014 was learning about the concept of mana whenua and connecting that back to similar ideas in India, where she was born.

“It goes beyond beach cleanups or tree planting - it’s the feeling and the sense of belonging that you belong to the land,” she said.

“And what does that mean? What is your shared responsibility as someone who lives and breathes here? So I think that was my first connection to climate.”

One of her jobs while she is in Antalya is to deliver the joint statement from rangatahi who went to Aotearoa’s Youth Cop, held in Auckland in September.

“I consider myself very privileged to be able to go,” she said.

Young people had “incredible ideas” to contribute but often did not get a seat at the table.

“I’ve been told time and time again in the last two months that, at least we have you, who is going to represent us and take all our cool whakaro and all our knowledge, not just to the international stage, but also bring that back home and be able to share that.”

Cop31 will run until November 20, with a “cover decision” – a high-level political statement agreed on by all members – expected in the final days.

This year’s cover decision could include official acknowledgement that the world will exceed the 1.5C target and will need to pursue an “overshoot” scenario, where the temperature peak and the length of time the world spends above 1.5C are limited as much as possible.

A UN report published in September said that would require deep cuts to emissions, as well as removing carbon already in the atmosphere.

A path away from fossil fuels will also form part of this year’s discussions, after last year’s host, Brazil, put together a draft voluntary “road map”.

Last year, New Zealand opted not to join a push from about 80 countries to include developing such a road map on the formal agenda.

The New Zealand delegation did consider signing a separate Belém Declaration on the Transition away from Fossil Fuels but ultimately did not, after officials in New Zealand advised that Resources Minister Shane Jones did not want them to.

Explainer: What are physician associates, and how might they change health care?

New Zealand Herald November 09, 2026

About 50 physician associates were already working in New Zealand. Photo / 123rf

By Kate Green of RNZ

“Physician associate” is now a registered profession in New Zealand, after gaining popularity as a career in the US and UK. Groups such as the Resident Doctors’ Association have voiced concern about its introduction, saying money would be better spent on doctors and nurses.

But what does a physician associate actually do? And how can they help a health system in crisis? Health correspondent Kate Green reports.

Working in urgent care, you never know what’s going to walk through the door.

Andie Cook has been working as a physician associate in New Zealand for the past decade, and is currently based at an urgent care centre in Hawke’s Bay.

Coughs, colds, chest pains and respiratory illnesses are common, she says, as are injuries – especially fractures – and abdominal pain.

But it is not just urgent care where you can find a physician associate. They work in all areas of health, from general practice to hospitals.

As of October 1, the role is now officially recognised and regulated as a profession in New Zealand.

Formerly known as physician assistants, and more colloquially as PAs, these healthcare workers are more common overseas, particularly in places like the US, UK and Canada.

Despite currently lacking the ability to legally prescribe medication in New Zealand, they see patients, form diagnoses and treatment plans, and then, if medication is needed, they review the case with a supervising doctor, who can prescribe.

Overseas, PAs do have the ability to prescribe, and Cook hopes that will be the next step for the profession in New Zealand.

When the news of the role’s regulation was announced, Health Minister Simeon Brown said it demonstrated the Government’s commitment to patient safety and providing high-quality care. Many hope creating more pathways for people to work in healthcare will increase the number of appointments available for patients.

It also provides the about 50 PAs already working in New Zealand some comfort. Until that point, Cook explains, there had been no authority in place to back PAs in complaints or wrongful dismissals, and nothing to stop people claiming to be PAs without adequate training or qualifications.

“It means safety, not just for the patient, but for us as a profession.”

Cook has a bachelor’s degree and spent eight years in the US military as a medic before going on to train as a physician associate at the University of Utah.

“My master’s degree took 27 months of training of fulltime study - book work [and] didactic [work] for half, and medical rotations the other half.”

Next came the national board certifying examination, a five-hour test students must pass to be able to practise, followed by a six-year stint as a PA in the Air National Guard as an officer before moving to New Zealand.

The job is aligned with the medical model followed by doctors, Cook says – diagnosticians, rather than nurses – and the training is “very nitty-gritty, condensed, know what you need to know to get the job done, but not knowing it at that higher level that doctors know”.

“Even though we are not a doctor, we can still see a wide breadth and depth of patients to help open and ease the pressures on the doctor.”

Physician assistants are generally paid less than doctors. Cook says one advantage for clinics is being able to add another clinician to the team at a lower cost than employing another doctor.

The Medical Council offers four pathways to registration – the first three, by holding an accredited PA qualification already in Canada, the United States or the United Kingdom.

The fourth is for PAs already practising in NZ.

Medical Council chairman Dr Kenneth Clark says to register, someone must have three years of clinical practice experience within the past five years, working at least half-time, “in the same or a similar area of clinical practice to their proposed New Zealand position”.

“The New Zealand experiential pathway also requires at least 24 months of practice in New Zealand immediately before applying.”

The council assesses each application, including the applicant’s qualifications, work history, references and fitness to practise. Physician associates initially enter a provisional scope of practice, with council approval required for their position, primary supervisor and supervision plan.

“Physician associates must continue to work under a doctor’s supervision throughout their practice. Their primary supervisor must be a vocationally registered doctor. They may only work in settings where onsite supervision is available and must not be rostered to practise solo.”

Whether a GP practice chooses to employ a physician associate is at its own discretion.

Cook says she wanted to move to New Zealand, but knew it might be harder to find a job here – until one day she spotted a post on social media about an NZ-based clinic which employed a PA off the back of a trial, some years before.

“And they had such good success with her that they were reaching out to find another PA.”

Some groups are worried about the potential for confusion among patients about whether they are seeing a doctor or someone with a different qualification.

Clark says clear identification is an essential part of patient safety and informed consent.

“[The Medical Council’s] standards require physician associates to identify their profession clearly and tell patients they are not medical doctors. They must explain their role in a way patients can understand, including how it differs from other health practitioners’ roles.”

Cook says as a PA, she is used to explaining her role and her scope of practice. Role confusion is nothing new, and it isn’t limited to PAs.

“Public education is key to fix this.”

The Royal Australasian College of Physicians (RACP) is one group concerned about PAs becoming more common.

“We have concerns about safety, cultural competency when working with Māori patients, and precious resources being diverted away from existing training programs and the supervision of the next generation of doctors,” wrote its president, Dr Hamish McCay, in April last year when the prospect of regulating the profession was first raised.

Proponents of the role say regulation will hopefully lead to the creation of local training courses – but for now, the only physician associates working here have been trained overseas.

RACP Māori health committee chair Dr Matt Wheeler says health workers without local qualifications will lack cultural awareness, particularly when it comes to Māori health, and he is concerned this will increase health inequity between Māori and non-Māori.

Other groups, such as the Resident Doctors Association, have called it a cost-cutting exercise, and many have questioned whether doctors have time to supervise other staff on top of their own workloads.

But Cook says: “Once you make that relationship with your supervising doctors, you’ll find that most every doctor that you interview who has worked with a PA says it is not a burden whatsoever.”

For patients, she says the important thing is freeing up appointments.

“Patients want to get seen and treated in timely fashion.”

The New Zealand Trotting Cup is a highlight on the calendar for many Cantabrians, bringing together racing, fashion and plenty of festivities.

Thundering hooves and high-stakes racing are drawing thousands to the track today.

So the Herald is taking a trip down memory lane to revisit some of the standout looks and moments from Cup Days gone by.

Starting more than 120 years ago, Monte Carlo is pictured at New Zealand Trotting Cup Day at Addington Raceway in 1904.

A photo captured 16 years later, in 1920, shows race horse Reta Peta winning that year’s edition of the New Zealand Trotting Cup.

On Show Day in 1961, there was a major fire at Addington Raceway.

At 5pm, 20 minutes before the final race of the day, fire took hold in the southwest corner of the main Public Grandstand.

Cardigan Bay is pictured at the New Zealand Trotting Cup Day at Addington in 1963.

Cardigan Bay was called New Zealand’s greatest harness horse by many, winning 80 races in his career.

Neroship the horse is pictured winning a race at New Zealand Trotting Cup Day at Addington Raceway, New Zealand, in 1990.

Neroship’s trainer-driver, John Langdon, was born and raised in Christchurch and had wanted to win the New Zealand Cup since 1962, when then 15 he skipped school to watch the race.

Langdon died in Australia earlier this year, aged 78.

New Zealand’s 36th and first female Prime Minister, Dame Jenny Shipley, was pictured at the New Zealand Trotting Cup Day in 1999.

Shipley posed with the winning horse Homin Hosed and his trainer Bryan Macey, while donning a matching blue wide-brimmed hat and blazer, the same colour associated with the National Party she led at the time.

The picture was taken on November 9. Almost three weeks later, Shipley lost the election to Labour’s Helen Clark.

Eight years later, in 2007, former All Black Richie McCaw was another familiar face pictured at New Zealand Trotting Cup Day.

McCaw, sporting a handlebar moustache, had been named captain of the national team a year earlier.

High-stakes racing may draw thousands to the track, but the glamour of Cup Week is just as much a part of the occasion.

Pictured in 2007 are three women watching the judging of the Best Dressed Man competition.

Notable looks and competitions are also a staple of New Zealand Trotting Cup Day.

Pictured are contestants entering the Body Art competition in 2007.

With fashion a much-loved fixture of the day, many bring the glitz and glamour to the track.

Pictured is the winner of the Best Dressed competition, Cindy Randall, with Sam Britten at the New Zealand Trotting Cup in 2009.

From bold fashion statements to timeless race-day elegance, style has continued to evolve over the years.

In 2011, Wearable Arts contestant Bonita Muntz and designer Melodie McColl were pictured putting on the style at the Cup Day.

The photo was taken the same year a deadly earthquake struck the city.

The pair were among 22,000 people in attendance that year.

A sea of punters, in classic hats, fascinators and sunglasses, are pictured looking on to the track in 2012.

Each face shows a different reaction to what is happening on the track they are intently focused on.

Even 10 years on, in 2023, Cup Day fashion was still a key tradition of the day.

A photo shows a sea of fascinators and colour popping as attendees enjoy a day at New Zealand Trotting Cup Day that year.

‘Nail in the coffin’: Businesses say they could face closure if council rates change

New Zealand Herald November 09, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

By Ellen O’Dwyer of RNZ

A family-run cinema in Wellington says potential council rating changes could be the “nail in the coffin” for the movie theatre if it were forced to pay an extra $77,000 per year in rates.

A hospitality business owner is also alarmed that paying an extra $100,000 in rates could also force him to shut the doors in a struggling inner-city.

Wellington City Council is consulting on a possible shift to the way it calculates rates – from a capital value to land value-based rating system with feedback sought by November 15.

The council had put out a calculator tool for people to figure out their rates under the potential new system, but hadn’t included the impact of a separate proposal to reduce commercial rates – a business owner says that had shocked the community due to the apparent size of the increases.

Capital value rating calculates the bill based on the value of someone’s land and buildings, whereas land-based value assesses just the value of the land. The move was underpinned by a drive among some councillors to incentivise growth, and target land-banking in the city.

Penthouse Brooklyn Cinema general manager Fergus Kisby-Macleod said rates for the cinema and adjoining carpark could increase by over $77,000 under a land value system – according to the council’s calculator.

“I couldn’t believe it, I thought it was fake.”

The cinema and cafe were 1729sq m, and the carpark was 435sq m, Kisby-Macleod said. He said the cinema and carpark were both on a relatively big piece of land, not far from the centre city.

He said the possible increase could be the “final nail in the coffin” for the business, forcing it to close – or lead to an increase in ticket prices or shortening of opening hours.

“We’ve never really wanted to change operating hours because we’re trying to be a community venue and stay open seven days a week, but with these bottom line costs going up – just to open the doors in the morning before you’ve even started - to get another setback it makes it very hard to justify certain costs of opening for the day.”

Kisby-Macleod said the movie theatre had been family-run for 51 years, with his grandfather opening it in 1975. He said the business tried to keep ticket prices lower than other cinemas for the community, but this would have to change if the rating estimates eventuated.

Jeremy Smith, director of Trinity Group hospitality company, said his bar Lulu on Courtenay Place, which was 1080sq m, could face an increase of $102,000 in rates under a shift to a land-value system according to the calculator, from $68,000 to $170,000 per year.

“We definitely are not going to revitalise [Courtenay Place] ... if people can’t pay their bills they’re going to shut the doors ... we just recently had Dakota’s shut their doors, I know there’s quite a few others hanging on by their fingernails.”

The council was considering reducing commercial rates from 3.7 times residential rates to three times residential rates over several years. This hadn’t been included in the council’s calculator tool.

Smith, who was also on the board of Hospitality NZ, said if the council was considering lowering commercial rates, it should have “absolutely” factored that into the calculator for the change – but he expected many residents wouldn’t want an increase to their rates so businesses could lower theirs.

He said the calculator showed high-rise office buildings, like the Majestic Centre – which could have over $700,000 in savings, and the Deloitte high-rise, which could have over $1 million in savings – had large decreases in rates under the system, compared to smaller businesses.

“Whereas the smaller property owners, and the tenants in the buildings are going to be heavily penalised.”

Greens councillor for Wharangi/Onslow-Western ward, Rebecca Matthews, who’d been pushing for the change for six years, said the council wanted to hear from people about their concerns.

“Productive businesses don’t have nearly as much to be concerned about as unproductive major commercial land-holdings where nothing has happened.”

Matthews said land-value based rates was about driving affordable housing development in the inner city.

“Other cities, for example throughout Australia, have land value rates and have more thriving hospitality sectors than we currently have in Wellington. It’s not like in Wellington we don’t have an issue now with empty shops and businesses that are not active, so this is an attempt to revitalise the city.”

Mayor Andrew Little said the council was consulting because it wanted to hear people’s views on an issue that’d been hanging around the city for some years.

Work Auckland Council did some years ago showed roughly 60% of property owners would have a reduction, 40% would have an increase, Little said, but the extent of increases and decreases wasn’t clear.

“It would be good to hear from anybody affected by it, good or bad, so that we get a picture of what the impact could be, so that we then know what to do next.”

Little did not state his preference on either system. He said he wanted a rating system that was “fair”, and did not create disincentives for the development the city needed.

He said the proposal to decrease the commercial differential for businesses was quite a separate proposal the council was looking at, with different views around the council table.

Consultation closes on November 15.

Cop31 must deliver climate progress that people can see is real, host says

The Guardian Sun, 08 Nov 2026 13:24:00 GMT

High-stakes talks involving 190 countries begin on Monday as world grapples with El Niño supercharged by fossil fuels

The Cop31 summit must produce progress, “a tangible outcome ... that people can see is real”, its host has said as scores of world leaders and representatives of close to 190 countries gather in Turkey for the UN climate talks.

The high-stakes meeting begins on Monday, as countries around the world grapple with the strongest El Niño weather system on record, supercharged by fossil fuels, which is set to take hundreds of thousands of lives and cause damage costing trillions of dollars.

Friction is expected between the rich and poor worlds over who pays for the impacts of the climate crisis, and the slow pace of cutting greenhouse gas emissions. Temperatures have broken records this year, surpassing the limit of 1.5C above preindustrial levels aimed for in the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

Adão Soares Barbosa, the chair of the Least Developed Countries, a negotiating group of 44 nations, said: “Keeping 1.5C within reach by minimising the duration and magnitude of the overshoot, delivering accessible and predictable climate finance, strengthening adaptation, and addressing loss and damage [caused to poor countries by extreme weather] are not political choices but matters of survival. The credibility of the Paris agreement will be measured not by promises made, but by commitments fulfilled, and lives protected in vulnerable countries.”

Unusually, the talks will have dual hosts: they will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya but the formal negotiations will be presided over by Australia, following a compromise reached last year over their competing bids.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and president of negotiations for Cop31, told the Guardian in an interview: “We need a tangible outcome focused on implementation [of emissions cuts and finance] that people can see is real. We need progress, it needs to be a step forward on previous Cops.”

Australia also wants a “strong, ambitious outcome” to raise the plight of low-lying countries in the Pacific region for whom the climate crisis poses an existential threat. “We need to finally elevate some of the issues so important to our Pacific family,” Bowen said. “[Only] 0.2% of the world’s available climate finance goes to small island developing states for adaptation, for countries whose very existence is at stake.”

But climate advocates and more than 500 scientists in Australia said Australia must stop approving coalmines and gas projects if it wanted to escape the charge of hypocrisy.

The summit will have a notable absentee, with the US refusing to send a delegation for the second year in a row. The Trump administration wants no part of “extremist climate policies” embraced by other countries, according to a White House spokesperson.

Donald Trump expressed glee shortly before the US midterm elections about the huge profits made by oil and gas companies due to the Iran war, which he started and has caused an increase in living costs around the world. “I don’t give a damn,” the president said at a recent rally in Georgia. “I’m going to say it: we’re making a frickin’ fortune.”

However, a group of 20 Democratic members of Congress have made the trip to Antalya, buoyed by their party’s stunning success in the US midterms last week that will enable them to stymie Trump’s attempts to dismantle pollution rules and withhold financial support for clean energy.

Developing countries and civil society will seek to put climate finance and justice at the heart of the Cop31 talks. Rukiya Khamis, the east Africa programme manager at the 350. org campaigning group, said: “Across east Africa, people are facing the devastating impacts of a climate crisis they did not cause. From prolonged droughts to destructive floods, we are losing homes, livelihoods and access to food and water. Yet the money needed to respond to these impacts remains out of reach for many of the countries and communities most affected. It is fundamentally unjust that those least responsible are being left to carry the greatest costs.”

This summer more than 50,000 people died in Europe due to heatwaves, severe wildfire smoke shrouded swathes of North America and a glacier collapse in Nepal triggered a landslide that caused more than 1,500 deaths, while the El Niño weather event, described as “staggering” by scientists and still to reach its peak, is gathering strength.

However, while the pace of progress on cutting global emissions has been slow, the Iran war has spurred many countries to see fossil fuels as expensive and vulnerable to shocks, while renewables continue to plummet in price.

Simon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, said before the talks: “Climate impacts hit every population and every economy harder each year. [But] almost every major economy, and many medium-sized and smaller economies, now see climate action as a central driver of economic growth, jobs, and affordable and secure energy.”

Cop host Turkey also wants more countries to switch to electric technologies, such as electric vehicles and heat pumps, as these are many times more efficient than their fossil fuel counterparts. A target for 35% of global final energy to come from electricity by 2035 will be on the table, but faces opposition from some.

Both presidency countries rely heavily on fossil fuels. Australia is one of the world’s leading exporters of coal and liquefied natural gas. The centre-left Labor government has targets to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, and have more than 80% of its electricity generated by solar and wind by 2030, but is off track to meet them.

Labor also faces a political threat from the resurgent rightwing One Nation party, which dismisses climate science. One Nation and the Liberal and National party coalition want to scrap the net zero goal.

The UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: “This summer, we all felt it: climate change is here, in Britain, now. No country can tackle it alone, which is why Cop31 matters. The answer to high bills and climate change is the same – more clean, homegrown power, creating good jobs and warmer homes. Cop31 is about Britain’s national interest.”

The AI poster boy, the ‘Chinese spy’ and Trump: how an affair may have harmed US security

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 20:01:05 GMT

Jensen Huang’s close relationship with president means Nvidia CEO’s affair with woman alleged to be working for Beijing is a big deal

A hand on the back, a kiss on the cheek; the footage of Alice Huang’s interaction with Jensen Huang in a Taipei venue last year does not seem particularly remarkable at first glance.

But the Nvidia chief executive’s revelation on Sunday that he had an affair with Ms Huang has given it new significance.

According to reports, his lover, who is not a relation, was not just an executive at an Nvidia customer. She was also an alleged Chinese spy.

Nvidia has now launched an independent investigation into reports that the boss of a cornerstone company in the global AI boom has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

“While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” said the board.

Huang, 63, a poster boy of the AI boom in his trademark leather jacket, admitted there was “no excuse” for what he had done.

Aside from Huang’s dented personal reputation, what is the scale of the damage done to Nvidia and US national security?

The story started to emerge last year when the New York Times and Bloomberg raised questions about a Singapore-based buyer of Nvidia’s powerful chips, which have become the proverbial shovels in the AI gold rush. There were concerns that Megaspeed was flouting US restrictions on AI chip exports to China by diverting some Nvidia inventory to America’s arch AI rival. Nvidia and Megaspeed denied this.

Then last month came a further startling NYT report that Jensen Huang had formed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive, and that American officials believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Donald Trump had been told, but decided not to act on the information. It is now evident that the relationship was more than just close.

At the heart of the question of what China might have achieved through Alice Huang is the extremely close relationship between the CEO of the world’s second-most-valuable company and the president of the United States.

The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia appeared to have successfully leaned on the US commerce department to halt an investigation into potential chip smuggling on the part of Megaspeed. That pressure came through a Trump appointee, who allowed Nvidia to reach out about the case.

Responding to reports last year that it might have diverted Nvidia deliveries, Megaspeed said: “Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company, operating fully in compliance with all applicable laws, including US export control regulations.”

Trump has met frequently – at least seven times – with the head of Nvidia since the start of his second term. Huang has flown on Air Force One and taken calls from the president during public events.

Four of their meetings have touched on one of the most sensitive issues in US-China relationships: the controls that the US has put up around the export of the world’s most advanced AI chips, which are almost entirely sold by Nvidia.

Under the former president Joe Biden, the US put in place the Chips Act, a package of rules that introduced sweeping limitations on US tech companies and their overseas trading partners. These rules sought to control what semiconductor technologies US companies could sell to businesses based overseas – particularly those that might be put under pressure to transfer those technologies to China.

It also introduced strict licensing requirements that in turn limited what those partners could do with technology that they bought.

For Nvidia, this was bad for business. China was one of the largest markets for its GPU chips – accounting for roughly a quarter of its revenue in the years between 2020 and 2022. When the Chips Act passed, the company started to sell downgraded versions of its premier chips to China – for example, the A800 and H800. Some of these were then banned, forcing Nvidia to scramble even more.

Under Trump, things changed. The president first invited Huang to the White House just six days after he was inaugurated, to discuss AI policy and chip exports. The two then met again in July and August of 2025. This was followed by victories for Huang – Trump allowed Nvidia to export previously banned chips to China. Nvidia agreed, in turn, to give the US government 15% of the sales revenue.

Experts said the deal would help Beijing compete “on the AI frontier”, in other words develop AI systems to rival those being produced by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI.

Five months later, the tech boss appeared to win another startling concession, days after another meeting with Trump. The president agreed to allow the tech boss to export H200s – a far more powerful chip – to China, in exchange for 25% of the revenue.

“President Xi responded positively!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

It is not unusual for large technology companies to lobby for their preferred policies in Washington; nor is it unusual for Trump to give access – and favourable deals – to men he likes.

But one more thing is now apparent – during this crucial year for his company, Huang was also intimately involved with a reported Chinese spy. The two were first photographed together in mid-2024. Five months after Trump took office is when the two were filmed at the Taipei restaurant. This would have been at the height of Huang’s lobbying push, shortly before Trump agreed to let Nvidia sell the H200s.

What could Alice Huang have gleaned – and passed on – during this affair? Plenty. Glimpses into US policy as it was being made, and to Trump’s own chaotic thinking on AI. And perhaps a world of tips beyond the confines of the White House.

Huang was a key figure for government after government as they formulated their AI policy. He met world leaders from South Korea to Saudi Arabia that year; he joined the then UK prime minister, Keir Starmer, on stage in London.

He would have known the details of the most important tech policy for many governments on Earth – their AI ambitions – because his company was often the only one that could make these ambitions happen. That is certainly true for Britain.

For all the intellectual feats of the systems powered by Nvidia technology, it is Huang’s human intelligence that is most valuable to America’s competitors.

Tommy Walsh, co-presenter of BBC’s Ground Force, dies aged 69

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 19:59:36 GMT

Former builder got his big break after restoring the home of a producer who was working on a precursor to the show

Tommy Walsh, the building and DIY expert who appeared on television shows including Ground Force, has died aged 69 after a long illness.

Walsh started his career as a professional builder before rising to fame alongside Alan Titchmarsh and Charlie Dimmock on the popular BBC garden makeover show from 1997 to 2005.

He went on to front programmes including Clean It, Fix It and Cowboys and Angels and joined the BBC show Homes Under the Hammer in 2021, following renovation projects and attending property auctions.

Walsh’s agent, Debbie Schiesser, told the Press Association: “Tommy died peacefully after a long illness surrounded by his family.

“As this has only just happened, we would ask everyone to please respect the family’s privacy.”

Walsh, from Hackney in east London, ran his own property business before his television career. He got his big break after restoring the house of a BBC producer who was working on ideas for a show that would become Ground Force.

He told the BBC in 2004: “She asked me to look at a couple of pilots. One of them was the precursor to Ground Force, called Over the Garden Wall.

“It was like watching paint dry. It was terrible.”

Walsh turned down the chance to star on the show three times, but agreed when his eight-year-old daughter told him she had made a £10 bet with a boy at school that her dad was going to be on TV.

At its peak, Ground Force attracted 12 million viewers. In one episode, the team was flown out to South Africa to work in secret on Nelson Mandela’s garden, building a pergola and water feature.

Walsh attended Parmiter’s grammar school in Bethnal Green, east London, and played football for the Old Parmiterians.

The club wrote on X: “It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of Tommy Walsh. A Parmiters boy he played for the club for many years in goal but made a great career as a TV personality in shows such as Ground Force. He will be sorely missed. RIP Tommy.”

He was married to Marie Walsh and was a father to three children: Charlotte, Natalie and Jonjo.

Huang’s defenders framed his affair as a personal lapse in judgment rather than evidence of treachery against the United States, which has imposed strict limits on what chips Nvidia can sell to China.

Huang, who has been married to his wife, Lori, since 1985, admitted in an email to employees on Sunday that he had an affair and that he would cooperate with an internal investigation. Nvidia’s board of directors put out a statement the same day that the company was launching a probe regarding reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

The chip mogul is alleged to have had a relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman that US intelligence services suspect of spying for the Chinese government, according to The New York Times. Trump was reportedly briefed on the relationship last year, the Times reported, but took no action. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are unrelated, with the latter being one of the world’s richest men and CEO of Nvidia, worth more than $4tn, for the past 33 years.

US intelligence agencies believe Alice Huang, acting on behalf of Beijing, pushed Jensen Huang to lobby Trump for relaxed export controls on Nvidia’s sales in China, which he has done multiple times publicly. Nvidia said in a statement that neither trade secrets nor US national security had been compromised.

The affair and alleged intelligence operation involving Huang could have far reaching implications for Nvidia and the tech industry, which are already enduring a period of high market volatility. Huang’s leadership of Nvidia, which is deeply financially intertwined with other leading tech companies like OpenAI, has long been viewed as crucial to the company’s success and stability.

Musk posted “I agree” in response to prominent venture capitalist Shaun Maguire’s defense of Huang. “Two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” Maguire posted. He stated the Nvidia CEO “did something incredibly dumb” but that he is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation”.

“Let’s also not nuke our AI industry because China ran a successful intel op,” Maguire added in a separate post.

Bill Ackman, the US hedge fund manager and pro-Trump billionaire, meanwhile, suggested that Huang is “human” and deserves public support over the affair.

“He is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes,” Ackman posted. “He takes full responsibility as he should. We should all support him and his family. Onward.”

Ackman followed up with another post later clarifying that he wasn’t suggesting Huang “gets a free pass” but that he was “hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security”.

China has meanwhile denied allegations of an intelligence operation targeting Huang, with the Associated Press reporting that foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun rejected the allegations as “entirely baseless vilification and smearing”.

Nvidia and its chips have been an integral part of the AI boom in recent years, with hundreds of billions of dollars committed to building out projects such as datacenters and chip factories. In August, Nvidia agreed to provide a $105bn guarantee to help OpenAI lease an Ohio datacenter.

As Nvidia has grown in prominence, Huang has also become one of the world’s richest people and most influential figures in tech. He has taken calls from Trump in the middle of an all-hands company meeting and on stage at a conference, and attended state dinners with the president and accompanied him on a trip to China. Huang has also been a powerful voice on tech policy, weighing in on issues such as export controls of chips to China and regulation of open-source AI models.

Shares were down around 5% as of midday and were on track to wipe out around $200bn in market value. The losses extend a six-month slide for what was once the world’s most valuable company, with Nvidia shares down over 20% since May.

The Guardian view on Jensen Huang’s affair: why did Trump ignore the warnings?

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 18:51:10 GMT

The AI chip boss’s actions raise urgent questions about corporate influence, national security and the US president’s willingness to listen to intelligence warnings

It could be the plot of a spy thriller. One of the most powerful figures in the AI revolution admitted to having an affair with a Chinese businesswomen said to have passed intelligence to Beijing. When Donald Trump was briefed about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s liaisons with Alice Huang, he took no action. Perhaps he thought only marriage vows had been broken. Or perhaps Mr Trump was willing to overlook the conduct of a friend who championed his unpopular datacentre expansion, whose company donated to his White House ballroom and who echoed his opposition to AI safeguards against expert advice.

Nvidia became the cornerstone of AI by supplying brute computing power. As tech giants scrambled for the firm’s graphics processing units (GPUs), Mr Huang sold the picks and shovels for the AI gold rush – and amassed a $160bn fortune. When China joined the race for tech supremacy, Nvidia’s microchips became a national security issue. In October 2022, the US slapped export controls on GPU sales to China. Thirty months later, Nvidia was effectively banned from selling to Beijing. Mr Huang lobbied for looser controls. Such was his sway with Mr Trump that the White House scrapped Biden-era global AI chip restrictions and then permitted sales of Nvidia’s prized H200 processors to Chinese customers.

Democrats, buoyed by their midterms’ success, will be looking for answers. Asked whether he should have acted on the intelligence, the president replied: “No, I don’t think so.” That makes the question of his reasons unavoidable. There could be trouble at Mr Trump’s commerce department if it backed Mr Huang’s policy agenda and loosened export controls despite knowing of his affair with a Chinese spy. Reports suggest that the commerce department’s probe was halted after Nvidia called investigators. Congress clearly has grounds to investigate whether the Trump administration knowingly disregarded a foreign intelligence threat. Whatever happens next, Mr Huang’s admission is likely to be the beginning, not the end, of the saga.

Rumours had swirled for months that Nvidia’s boss had been in a “special relationship” with Ms Huang – an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that in 2025 was revealed to be under investigation for suspected diversion of restricted Nvidia chips to China. What makes this extraordinary is the possibility that Mr Huang’s romantic and commercial relationship exposed him to a Chinese intelligence operation. In May, analysts at Culper Research argued that Megaspeed brought Nvidia substantial revenues, allegedly backed by Chinese financing. Then Nividia’s boss publicly defended Megaspeed while secretly conducting an affair with its top executive. More than $300bn was wiped off Nvidia’s valuation as soon as Wall Street opened.

Industrial espionage is nothing new. Richer nations often block the export of their commercial secrets to prevent others from catching up. These challengers often go to extraordinary lengths to obtain new technology. Historically, diplomatic or military so-called honeytraps – spies sent to seduce victims to gain confidential information – have been more common than commercial ones. But in 2008, British spy agencies accused Beijing of a campaign to target businesses, using sex to pressure targets into cooperating. Whether that has happened here is unknown. But a president who promised to get tough on China needs to explain why his administration eased chip export controls despite warnings that the businessman lobbying for it might be compromised.

The Guardian view on the British Library: don’t privatise the reading rooms

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 18:50:54 GMT

Cybercriminals are to blame for the current crisis. But renting out study space will not lead to recovery

It holds two copies of Magna Carta, the charter that set limits on royal power in 1215. It has the sole surviving manuscript of the Anglo-Saxon epic Beowulf and notebooks by some of the most beloved authors in the English language: Jane Austen, William Blake, Virginia Woolf. Also in the British Library’s red-brick London building is the original, illustrated version of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland – given as an early Christmas gift to Alice Liddell in 1864. On handwritten drafts of Wilfred Owen’s tragic poem Dulce et Decorum est, visitors can see suggestions made by his friend Siegfried Sassoon.

But neither display cases filled with treasures such as these nor vast digital archives, basement storage rooms, six cafes and a shop have been sufficient to arm the library against a sea of troubles that first threatened it three years ago, when hackers raided its computers for personal data and demanded a £600,000 ransom. Its long-serving chief executive, Roly Keating, took the decision to step down once the worst of the cyber-attack – one of the most serious in the UK’s history – had been dealt with. His replacement, Rebecca Lawrence, lasted less than a year before resigning in the middle of a strike over pay. Now, a new row has broken out over plans to rent out three of the library’s reading rooms and outsource security.

The British Library is, of course, not alone in seeking novel ways to generate revenue from its open-access public building. Private and corporate private views are routine at blockbuster exhibitions; the early weeks of the British Museum’s Bayeux tapestry show were marred by a row about an ill-judged invitation to Peter Thiel, the tech billionaire. But reading rooms are unlike temporary exhibitions in that they are permanent. These are spaces designed for people to read and study in. Handing three of them over to a private contractor to operate commercially, as the British Library proposes, would change the character of a cherished institution.

Its new boss, Dr Paul Bate, has been in post for less than a week. He urgently needs to grip the situation and give a fuller account to staff, users and the public of what is going on. As an arm’s-length body, the library is overseen by a board. But since 84% of its £170m annual budget comes from the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, ministers too should be constructively engaged.

It is widely accepted that the damage to finances and morale caused by the hackers, following the Covid pandemic, lies behind the current woes. A report this summer from the public accounts committee of MPs blamed the government for the lack of a strategic approach to cybersecurity. Politicians must take responsibility for past mistakes and help England’s national library to avoid a protracted crisis.

As trade unions have pointed out, outsourcing the library’s security staff would be contrary to the government’s commitment to insourcing. Privatising sections would undermine a valued public space that is both open to all, and an essential component of a neglected higher‑education ecosystem. The British Library – formerly part of the British Museum – was established more than 50 years ago; the St Pancras building is approaching its 30th anniversary. As a national institution, it is a place in which everyone has a stake. The government must get behind it, and look for an alternative solution.

Brand’s sentencing, the culmination of a four-week trial at Southwark crown court, came after the four women described the impact of his crimes on their lives in victim impact statements. A woman who was raped by Brand said the attack had had lasting consequences.

“Even now, I feel that I am living with the trauma of what happened,” she said. “It is something I carry with me every day and it often feels never-ending.”

Brand, 51, appeared emotionless as he was jailed, but told his wife, Laura: “We’ll be OK,” as he was taken downstairs by the dock officers. His wife replied: “I love you,” before leaving the court in tears.

The disgraced comedian was convicted on Thursday of raping a 21-year-old fan and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.

After his convictions, the Metropolitan police revealed that Brand was under investigation over two further rape allegations.

On Monday, the judge praised the bravery of the women in the case. He also criticised Brand’s “staggering arrogance” before sentencing him to 10-and-a-half years in prison.

In his sentencing remarks, which were broadcast live, Bennathan told Brand: “I pause to pay tribute to the determination and bravery of all the women whose evidence I have been recounting. I do not increase your punishment because of it, but all those women had to face being confronted and being told they had lied, or twisted the truth and, or, they had agreed to your sexual demands: that was all done because of you, on your instructions.”

The judge said Brand had felt “entitled” to grab the breasts of his earliest victim, an MTV worker, at a birthday party in Soho, London, in 2004, because she had wanted to be introduced to him.

“In your trial you said you had never touched a woman sexually without her consent, and that included this woman. In the light of the jury’s verdicts, that was one of a series of lies you told,” the judge said.

The woman told the court that she was “extremely upset and traumatised” and felt “vulnerable” after the assault.

“There were many times I felt visibly sick at the sight of him parading around thinking he can get away with anything,” she said in her statement.

Brand’s second victim told the court that he had laughed after “mauling” her by squeezing her breasts and kissing her sloppily while she was working at the radio station Choice FM in 2005. She said he overpowered her during the “violent” and “frenzied” attack, which took place in front of his entourage.

The judge said: “No doubt your companions thought it was outrageous laddish behaviour that only you could get away with. It was outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal sexual offence, and as it turns out you haven’t got away with it.”

The judge said Brand was happy to exploit the fact that his youngest victim was a fan and showed his contempt for her by storing her number alongside the letter T for “tart”.

The woman told the court she had felt “anxious, humiliated and overwhelmed” after Brand anally raped her without a condom at his London townhouse. She was 21 when Brand picked her from a crowd after one of his performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009.

“I struggled to eat and sleep, and I found it difficult to cope with my emotions. The impact was so significant that I had to take time away from work, and for a period I returned to live with my parents because I did not feel safe,” she said in a victim impact statement.

The judge’s said Brand’s final offence showed his “staggering arrogance” and how his entourage indulged his “dreadful behaviour”.

Brand sexually assaulted the woman in front of his entourage during a recording project at Channel 4 in 2009 when he placed his head in her lap after she was forced to give him a massage.

The judge said: “The whole episode reeks of casual disrespect and your belief that fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live.”

Earlier Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, said the former TV personality was a “fundamentally different person today” and was not “in general terms, a rapist”.

In his submissions, he claimed: “This should be regarded as a man who went too far and overrode consent that had been given.”

There was also a submission in support of Brand from Andrew Sachs’s granddaughter, Georgina Baillie. She was at the centre of a 2008 scandal when Brand and Jonathan Ross put out a Radio 2 segment in which they left Sachs a voicemail claiming that she had been sleeping with Brand.

Winter said Baillie was among six people submitting character references, and said she had been sober for the last six years, and Brand supported her and paid for her to go into rehab for alcohol addiction.

Winter also told the court that Brand’s wife was standing by him before adding: “I’m afraid words are completely inadequate to truly try to convey to your lordship the total devastation she’s experiencing.

“Currently [they] are wrestling with how to exactly explain to a child who’s just turned 10 what has happened here.”

But in his remarks, the judge told Brand: “I am also very conscious that your imprisonment will deprive your children of the presence of their father: that sad loss to them, however, is caused by your serious offending.”

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio. org/rcip/internl. html

Revealed: Palantir lobbied minister to stretch AI tools’ reach to NHS GP records

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:58:05 GMT

Exclusive: WhatsApp messages show firm pressuring Zubir Ahmed MP to help bring sensitive data into its platform

UK politics live – latest updates

Palantir lobbied a health minister to consider extending its AI technology into GP records, stretching its reach into the NHS in a way doctors fear could undermine trust with patients.

The US company, co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel, used a direct WhatsApp channel to argue that “the logic of joining up primary and secondary [care] data is unarguable” and said its software was “ideal” for the job. The push came in February this year despite GP data being expressly ruled out of the scope of Palantir’s existing £330m contract with NHS England to run its federated data platform (FDP), which it says has helped cut surgery waiting times and discharge delays.

The messages – which were obtained under the Freedom of Information Act by Foxglove, a tech equity campaign group, and shared with the Guardian – appear to be between Palantir’s UK boss, Louis Mosley, and the former health minister Zubir Ahmed. They span several months from July 2025 to March 2026.

In the messages and a briefing document, Palantir urged Ahmed to “get out ahead of” likely “political” opposition from doctors and vocal critics of Palantir, such as the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, and Your Party, led by Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana. The firm also told Ahmed: “The FDP is already delivering very strong results – but will deliver even more benefits faster with the right ministerial sponsorship.”

Groups representing doctors and patients, including the British Medical Association (BMA), have opposed the integration of GP data into Palantir’s FDP, arguing there is a lack of trust in the company, which also works for the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). When Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government announced the deal with Palantir three years ago, it said: “GP data will not be part of the national platform.”

The lobbying emerges after it was reported last week that ministers were unlikely to end Palantir’s NHS data management contract imminently, defying campaigners and two House of Commons committees that wanted the company to be forced out as soon as spring. The Financial Times reporting, which suggested the Palantir contract would be extended, came amid concerns that removing the firm’s AI technology would be disruptive without an alternative lined up.

The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, last week told parliament the review was ongoing, but said there was “a huge long-term benefit to using the NHS to develop UK sovereign AI” – a sign that the government may seek a UK replacement for Palantir when the contract reaches its next end point in 2029. Bloomberg also reported that Tom Watson, a Labour peer hired as a full-time lobbyist by Palantir in September, recently wrote to Cooper urging her to keep the contract going, saying: “I want to ensure that Palantir UK rises to meet the government’s new social-value tests and helps build Britain’s sovereign technological capability.”

The WhatsApp logs released under the FoI Act show Palantir telling Ahmed that the benefits to the health system of applying its software – known as Foundry – to GP data could include “faster access to GPs … more effective and targeted management of frail patients, and more effective preventative care”. It also said Palantir’s software platform would “maintain local control of data”.

The Palantir executive’s name is redacted in the documents released by the Department of Health and Social Care, but Palantir did not deny it was Mosley. In one message, the minister praises a performance on a BBC One Sunday politics programme, just after Mosley had appeared.

“Great work [on] Kuenssberg btw,” Ahmed said.

The Palantir executive advised the minister that “the politics [of using GP data] is not straightforward – the previous government ruled GP data out of scope when announcing the FDP. So, as this moves forward, it will be one to get ahead of and explain, otherwise the opponents described above will make hay with it.”

Donald Campbell, the director of advocacy at Foxglove, said the WhatsApps showed Palantir “lobbying to hoover up yet more of the British public’s sensitive personal data”.

“It is appalling to see Palantir pressuring the minister to bring GP records into its platform, despite pledges from the government in 2023 that this would not happen,” Campbell said.

The correspondence “shows they knew just how sensitive this was” and it was “telling [that] they made this argument privately, via privileged access to the government”, he added.

Dr Tom Dolphin, the chair of the BMA council, raised concerns about “scope creep” with Palantir potentially accessing identifiable personal data in the GP record that could “undermine patient trust and threaten the doctor-patient relationship”.

“Patients must be able to seek care without worrying which operators might have access to duplicates of their personal information,” he said.

Marc Farr, the chair of the NHS Chief Data and Analytical Officer Network, said: “Palantir appears to be bidding to stretch the scope of its work for NHS England in a way that goes beyond statements from ministers and NHS leaders that GP data was not in the scope of the FDP contract and would require legislative change … As two separate select committees have noted, public trust and transparency is essential to us being able to realise the fantastic opportunities that technology and data offer.”

Palantir said: “We’ve long argued that data sharing can improve the NHS, for patients and taxpayers, and that our software helps different NHS organisations to do that, while ensuring they maintain full local control over their data. We’ve also always been clear that it is for the government to decide how they roll the software out. These exchanges reflect both of those points.”

The Department of Health and Social Care declined to comment.

Reform UK councillor in Sunderland handed community order after racist ‘joke’ about Nigerians

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:57:50 GMT

Glenn Gibbins sentenced to 150 hours of unpaid work by South Tyneside magistrates over 2024 Facebook post

A Reform party councillor who claimed racist comments about Nigerians were no more than a “bit of fun” has been handed a community order for posting grossly offensive material.

Glenn Gibbins, who was voted on to Sunderland council in May, wrote on Facebook in March 2024: “Carnt believe the amount of nigerians in town … should melt them all down and fill in the pot holes!!”

At a trial before a district judge on Monday, Gibbins, 66, said it was meant to be no more than “cheeky”, “naughty” and “tongue in cheek”. He said the post was not meant to be taken literally. “It was just a bit of fun.”

It was agreed at South Tyneside magistrates court in South Shields that the social media post was offensive – the question was whether it was grossly offensive.

District judge Zoe Passfield ruled that the post breached the Malicious Communications Act and was grossly offensive.

She said Gibbins “intention was to be grossly offensive to Nigerians as a result of his displeasure at the number of them in the city.”

Gibbins has been sentenced to a 12-month community order with 150 hours of unpaid work. Adam King defending, said they would be appealing against the decision to the crown court.

Prosecutor Emma Dowling said Gibbins’ post was talking about “exterminating” a group of people. “To say that it’s not to be taken seriously is to disregard history,” she said.

“The comment about melting them down conjures up despicable images.”

Godwin Ejeh, the leader of the Nigerian community in Sunderland, was called as a witness and recalled how he called an emergency meeting of Nigerians after the post came to light.

The mood of the meeting was “chaotic”, he said because of the “level of distress”. People were concerned for their safety and the safety of their children. People wanted an apology so decided a protest should take place outside city hall.

Ejeh, a Lib Dem council candidate in May, said the comments should never have been made. “We are talking about humans. It’s not something people should play with.”

Gibbins, who ran a mobile personalised gifts and T-shirt kiosk in a Sunderland shopping centre, said he would not have described himself as a political person before this year.

He said he thought he was approached by Reform in March to run as a councillor because of a T-shirt with Nigel Farage on it on a mannequin on his stall.

He had been asked to print the T-shirt by someone drinking all day in a nearby pub. That person was “clearly intoxicated”, Gibbins said, and forgot to pick up the T-shirt, so he put it on the mannequin.

When he got a call from Reform asking if he would run as a councillor he saw it as a way of getting some income during the normal summer lull for his business. “They explained they were looking for a candidate. I didn’t even know councillors got paid. I thought it would tide me over.”

King said his client’s social media post was not politically motivated. “Reform would do well to pay more attention to the people they put forward for election,” he said.

Gibbins made the post after a couple of beers and said they were not his words. He said he had been trying to repost something he read but failed so typed in the words himself. About six friends responded with laughter, thumbs up and heart emojis.

King said it was a “stupid, unfunny joke. We come across stupid, unfunny jokes all the time.”

He pointed to jokes by professional comedians that had not resulted in criminal proceedings, namely Jo Brand in 2019 on the BBC, making a joke about throwing battery acid on Nigel Farage; and Jimmy Carr when he made a joke about the Holocaust and Gypsies on his Netflix special.

King said courts in the UK had also asserted the importance of free speech in “full-throttled, uncompromising terms”.

Gibbins said he had been suspended by Reform, then reinstated, but was now suspended again.
