Iran was behind cyber-attack on French supermarket freezers, Paris says

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:54:40 GMT

French foreign minister vows European sanctions against Tehran over ‘unprecedented’ hacks last month

France has said Iran was responsible for a massive cyber-attack on supermarket freezers and chiller cabinets that was described by its foreign minister as being an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression”.

Jean-Noël Barrot said “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible, adding that the attacks – which took control of digital thermostats to push temperatures up to above 50C – constituted “a major violation of the nation’s interests”.

At a press briefing during the G7 summit in Paris, he said: “Thanks to the remarkable efforts of government agencies, I am able to confirm that the Islamic Republic of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards are responsible for this attack.”

He said the Iranian ambassador had been summoned “to protest in the strongest possible terms against this extremely serious act.”

Swathes of French supermarkets were hit in the cyber-attacks on 11 and 12 October. Some were forced to throw away entire inventories of perishable food.

Similar incidents have been reported since, including on supermarket fridges in other European countries last week and on a French blood bank.

The Paris public prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, said on Monday that specialist investigators and government agencies had identified “a modus operandi” characteristic of the Iranian group Shahid Kaveh, a cyber warfare unit linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC).

This included “the use of Farsi and IP addresses traced back to devices located in Iran”, she said.

Beccuau said her office had opened a investigation against the head of Shahid Kaveh, his deputies and “others who will be identified” on charges of “fraudulent attacks on an automated data processing system committed as part of an organised crime ring and of causing damage dangerous to persons”.

She said the offences were “aggravated by the fact they were committed to serve a foreign power – in this case Iran”.

Gérôme Billois, a partner at the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said Shahid Kaveh had been active since 2020 and was known to have carried out cyber-attacks mostly on water distribution systems in the US.

“Two countries are known for this kind of attack: Iran and Russia. Given that recent cyber-attacks on supermarkets and the blood bank in France concerned freezers it is reasonable to think Iran is directly linked to both,” he said,

“For the moment they are attacking easy equipment but as a state group that has the means, the determination and the time, we should be prepared to see attacks on other systems like water or electricity.”

During the attack last month, hackers remotely overrode the temperature setting on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets in as many as 700 supermarkets and shops across France, pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F) in some cases.

Thousands of tons of food had to be dumped and in some stores the extreme temperature rise sparked fires, triggering sprinklers and water damage.

Hackers last week accessed control systems at cold stores stocking blood products. The French blood service (EFS) said temperature and defrosting thresholds and been raised to “very high level” but that technicians had been alerted by alarm systems allowing them to disconnect the cold stores before the products were destroyed. It is not clear whether the two attacks are linked.

The following day retailers in 11 European countries including the UK, Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with refrigeration systems.

A regional branch of France’s Crédit Mutuel bank also reported losing more than €100m in a cyber-attack on Friday. The bank said it had recuperated some of the money.

The European Commission did not immediately comment on the French foreign minister’s statement. Kaja Kallas, the head of foreign affairs for the EU said: “We have the foreign affairs council next Monday, so we will have the opportunity to discuss this. These cyber incidents occurring in Europe, if attributed [to Iran], also call for a strong response on our part.”

In a significant decision this year, the EU designated the IRGC a terrorist organisation, ending years of division over the issue. The designation became possible after France dropped its long-held opposition, having previously feared it would damage diplomatic channels and the interests of French nationals in Iran.

High fossil fuel prices spread inflation ‘like a cancer’, UN climate chief tells Cop31

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:47:04 GMT

Simon Stiell makes opening address at summit in Turkey, where talks are under way about speeding up shift to electrification

A global fossil fuel price crisis is “spreading inflation like a cancer” around the planet, the UN’s climate chief, Simon Stiell, told the opening plenary of critical UN climate talks in Turkey.

Stiell joined Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia, which is leading the negotiations, in promoting renewable energy and a new electrification goal as an optimistic alternative to a planet still tied to oil, coal and gas.

Inside the tight security of the opening plenary on Monday, delegates from almost 200 countries watched a stirring short film with scenes of fire, flood and storms that proclaimed: “It’s time to reconnect with the planet we have grown apart from.”

Turkey said it expected 100,000 visitors, including national delegations, to attend the two-week talks, including at least 95 heads of state. A global leaders summit is scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday. But the talks are under increased pressure to deliver, after growing dissatisfaction with the snail’s pace of results.

The talks are opening as a historic El Niño builds in the tropical Pacific and months after a glacier collapse set off catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet, wiping away villages and killing at least 1,459 people, with thousands more still missing. Climate scientists confirmed this year that global heating would reach at least 1.8C – beyond the 1.5C temperature goal that countries promised to aim for at talks in Paris in 2015.

Last week Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, told the Guardian that although he still had faith in the negotiating process, “the fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast … and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.”

And in a statement the UN secretary general, António Guterres, urged leaders to “get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need”.

Stiell also said: “The urgency of this moment must drive us forward. Global heating is already costing the Earth,” adding that it was vulnerable communities paying the price and frustration at a lack of fairness was palpable.

US president Donald Trump’s war with Iran and the disruption of the key strait of Hormuz supply route for oil pushed up petrol prices around the world by 50%, raising inflation and slowing economic growth.

Stiell told delegates this “fossil fuel cost chaos” had “delivered a global shock wave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer”.

Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, the president of the negotiations, said in a speech that will set the tone for the talks that although the 1.5C Paris target will be overshot “we can return … if we work together and act with urgency, solidarity and resolve”.

With fists clenched in the final moments of a speech, Bowen urged delegates to show future generations that this generation was “equal to the challenge” and to “rise to this moment together”.

The countries pushing for the greatest action at Cop31 have stressed the 1.5C temperature rise limit can’t be abandoned and called for accelerated steps to provide finance to the places most vulnerable to climate impacts. The so-called high-ambition coalition said it has 20 country members pushing for major progress in Antalya. “That limit is in serious danger but overshoot should never become an excuse for inaction, every fraction of a degree matters,” said Jess Gasper, an environmental official for the Marshall Islands.

“We must limit overshoot and return to a safe temperature as quickly as possible.” Gasper said it took eight years to get international finance to build a single sea wall to help protect the Marshall Islands, a Pacific island nation acutely threatened by sea level rise.

“That example shows we need that money to adapt,” he said. “I refuse to accept that we experience displacement because the world fails to act.”

The talks began without a fight over the agenda, which was considered by many to be a good sign. There was confidence among delegates that a final decision from Cop31 would include reference to a new voluntary electrification goal being championed by the host, Turkey, and the president of the negotiations, Australia.

Bowen said he had spoken to countries around the globe that were represented at the talks and there was “enormous momentum” among them for electrification.

The goal, he said, was to raise the percentage of final energy consumption coming from electricity from the current one-fifth to one-third in the next ten years.

Dr Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency, said: “I have talked with many governments and I see there is a great appetite for many countries to be part of this historic decision [in Antalya].”

He told the Guardian: “The important thing is that we are entering the age of electricity and this [electrification goal] would give an extra boost to that movement.”

Countries agreed at the 2023 climate summit to triple renewable energy capacity by 2030. Birol said if countries endorsed the 2035 electrification target it would give an “unmistakable signal to markets” and a chance to increase both renewable and nuclear electricity.

How to get the buzz back on Britain’s high streets

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:25:00 GMT

Readers respond to an article about the decline of town centres

Sammy Gecsoyler’s report from Rotherham (‘It’s just vape shops, nail shops, charity shops’: can anything save the British high street?, 4 November) tells the story in its dates. One out-of-town retail park in Britain in 1981; 385 by 1996. Parkgate opened in 1987 and MPs warned that it would disembowel towns and villages. It did. Rotherham town centre is now 24% vacant, while retail park vacancy nationally sits at 4.8%. That is not a mystery. It is 40 years of planning policy.

We have since gone one step further by making home delivery cheaper than retail parks. Up to 3bn parcels a year now land on British doorsteps and not one of them passes through a town centre.

Andy Burnham’s £210m for high streets is welcome, but is a one-off against a structural problem. What a town centre needs is a reason for people to walk into it again, every week, without being told to.

So here is a proposal, given in written evidence to an inquiry by the Commons housing, communities and local government committee into revitalising high streets. Put £1 on every parcel delivered to a residential address. Charge nothing if it is collected from a shop, locker or pickup point in town. Ringfence the money by law and return it to the council area that the parcel landed in – 60% to transport and 40% to markets and high streets.

The pound is not the point; the exemption is. The cheapest way to receive a parcel would involve walking into a town centre. That would do more for Rotherham than any grant. Dan Johnson Co-founder, Crafty Vintage, Whalley, Lancashire

I run the Grumpy Cook, a community-focused cafe in Hastings. I’ve seen first-hand how difficult it is for independent businesses to survive, particularly in communities where disposable income is already stretched. That’s why I recently launched My Local First, a loyalty and rewards platform to bring independent businesses together. Customers earn rewards for spending locally, discover other independent businesses and have a reason to return. Businesses can participate for just £10 a month, without paying commission on their sales to the platform.

But high streets cannot thrive if the people living around them cannot afford to participate in their local economy. That’s why we’re also developing ways to connect affordable food and discreet community support.

We cannot expect councils or government grants alone to regenerate town centres. Nor can we expect individual businesses to compete with multinational corporations on their own. We need to start working collectively. My Local First won’t solve every problem facing Britain’s high streets. But it represents something I believe we’ve lost sight of: communities taking responsibility for their own local economies. Perhaps the answer isn’t simply saving our high streets. Perhaps it’s giving people a reason to believe in them again. Barry Ashley Hastings, East Sussex

As someone who grew up locally, I recognise the challenges in Rotherham. The new government strategy, Hope on the High Street, has some ideas – including a number of community-led schemes that we helped support at the Architectural Heritage Fund. Projects like High Street West in Sunderland – a mixed-use approach to derelict shops that delivered a cafe, music venue and workspaces. Or Valley Heritage’s development in Bacup, Lancashire, where a Grade II former bank has been split into co-working space and affordable housing.

Equally importantly, it’s about empowering these communities as they are passionate about their environment. Although there are many challenging town centres, a growing number offer a more positive future and could be replicated elsewhere. Matthew Mckeague CEO, Architectural Heritage Fund

Saving the British high street means accepting that retail can no longer be its primary purpose. Councils should acquire vacant or persistently underused sites and, where appropriate, replace poor-quality empty buildings with well-insulated, low-rise homes for renters and young professionals. New developments could be designed from the outset so that extra floors or modular homes can be added later as demand grows. That would cost more initially, but could reduce the disruption and expense of future expansion.

Housing alone, however, will not make a thriving neighbourhood. It should be interspersed with services and spaces that people genuinely need: walk-in health and mental health support, childcare, community and arts spaces, and other local amenities. There is a strong case for locating services closer to the communities they serve, rather than expecting people to travel elsewhere to find support. High streets should also include more and better green spaces, with trees, planting and small parks that give people somewhere pleasant to spend time, while at the same time responding to the challenge of climate change and air pollution.

Bring people back to the high street and businesses will have a reason to return too: cafes, hairdressers, independent shops and other everyday services. Councils should use planning and licensing powers carefully to encourage a balanced mix of businesses and avoid excessive concentrations of premises that can undermine the health and character of an area. The high street will not be saved by restoring the past. Its future could lie in becoming a place to live, meet, access services and build community, with retail as one part of a much broader purpose. Helen Roberts Sheffield

Is the party ending in Birmingham’s nightlife district?

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:24:39 GMT

Guardian readers reflect on rail development plans for Digbeth, and on 200 years of musical history – from Duran Duran to the club scene

Regarding your article on the threat to nightlife in Digbeth from proposals by the Midlands Rail Hub Alliance (‘It brings soul into this sterile world’: the Birmingham clubbers fighting to save their patch – and Britain’s nightlife, 3 November), as someone who spends a lot of time in this district of Birmingham, I think it’s also worth recognising that it is getting major investment, turning it into an area you want to visit and even live in.

There are new TV and film studios, street refurbishments, residential flats, a new tram route and better bus services. Access to the area is increasing. The new tram route – wholesale street redesigns, but mothballed until connecting tracks can be laid across HS2’s Curzon Street site – has been particularly painful during construction and has spurred mistrust from businesses.

The Midlands Rail Hub Alliance recently came forward with early and heavy-handed designs for a project half a century in the making. The proposals demolished too many buildings, many of which are currently leased from Network Rail. Naturally, business owners want certainty about their premises’ future, which is hard to guarantee early on, and we would complain if proposals were too advanced to change.

The project is transformational for rail travel within Birmingham and beyond. It means no longer being constrained by capacity at New Street station. One standout benefit is returning the cross‑city line, one of the busiest rail commuter lines outside London, to 10-minute frequency.

Network Rail mismanaged its stakeholder engagement approach, with some businesses finding out via X. However, my observation is that they are being listened to. Birmingham city council set out conditions for the scheme that formalised the concerns expressed by businesses and the mayor recently took political oversight of one the main organisations promoting the rail hub. We now need to take a breath and wait for fresh designs at the next consultation. Martin Price-Phillips Birmingham

Digbeth has always been home to fascinating units and great nights out but, unless on National Express coaches, it has never been easy to get to. During Covid we were told that access would be simplified with the new Digbeth tramline. After six years of construction and temporary traffic lights, the tram has still not made it to Digbeth. By the time it opens, it seems the tram will only take you to see the remaining interesting sites being demolished to accelerate train line updates. What Digbeth really needs is a joined-up approach to urban planning to ensure any future decisions do not undo the progress of past successes. Harry Shaw Cradley Heath, West Midlands

Of course Digbeth cannot be demolished! For about 200 years this area has been Birmingham’s mecca for many styles of music and its genres have moved with the times.

The London museum music hall, created in Victorian times, and the Digbeth civic hall, where the 1960s folk scene flourished and popular bands from the Cure to the B-52s performed, are just two examples. The Irish centre celebrated 50 years of traditional tunes, and a terrace house in a street called Cheapside gave birth to classics like Girls on Film and Rio. These are a few of the venues where music has been enjoyed and created in this historical industrial hub, situated next to the city centre. All have all contributed to international successes and have put Birmingham on the musical map.

At the moment Digbeth is celebrating a fabulous party scene and in time it will evolve again and produce another kind of venue that will be culturally driven and call people to celebrate en masse in an area where music is truly rooted. A transport hub does not fit the remit. Janette Brown Castet-Arrouy, France

Like fridges, heat pumps don’t need an annual service

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:24:07 GMT

Ground-source and air-source heat pumps are extremely efficient machines, writes, David Reynolds

I read Mary Massey’s letter (2 November) with some surprise. She said that her heat pump needs an annual service and that this year it cost about £350. My ground-source heat pump has been heating my house for 18 years and it does not need or get an annual service.

A heat pump is essentially a big refrigerator working in reverse, and how often do you have your fridge serviced? That is another benefit of heat pumps. It has no burner and so it is not continually deteriorating; nor is there a fire-safety issue.

The company that installed it told me that a service every few years to check the ground loop fluid density and an overall lookover is sufficient, providing it is working normally. It is an electrical device. My service costs about £170.

Ground-source and air-source heat pumps are extremely efficient machines and can provide up to about four or five times the efficiency rates of boilers that use burners. David Reynolds Diss, Norfolk

Obama granted me clemency after 23 years in prison. What will it take for Trump to do similar?

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:23:35 GMT

Danielle Metz wonders whether the president will extend the forgiveness he has shown the 6 January insurrectionists to other prisoners, in response to an article by James Rosen

I was granted clemency by President Barack Obama after serving 23 years behind bars (The US founders made a grave error in granting presidents pardon power, 1 November). When I think of clemency, I think about what it was designed to do. How it’s a way to show mercy when those who issued the verdict showed none. Incarcerated people sit in prison for years waiting for someone to show up and correct an obvious wrong. The president and the governor have the power to right that wrong. I can’t imagine it being taken away.

I think back to 6 January 2021, when the Capitol was stormed, and I witnessed the violence and chaos that erupted that day. I remember how frightening it was to watch. This was not scripted. This was horror in real time.

But I wonder, will our Donald Trump extend that same forgiveness to those who have been in federal prison for as long as four decades in some cases? Will he consider pardoning those who are not as financially equipped? Maybe not. But removing the hope for clemency only hurts those who are already suffering.

Women and men have sat in prison for what some would call a lifetime, and they are deserving of freedom. Yet no one has come to save them. We talk about abolishing or limiting clemency, but the ones who need it most are left out of the conversation. In the rush to correct one injustice, we risk ignoring another.

What will it take for the president to extend mercy to approximately 152,500 men and women in the federal prison system across the US? They are waiting for someone to show up as well. Danielle Metz Washington DC, US

Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:06:23 GMT

The chipmaker faces business risks and political scrutiny due to its over-reliance on founder and CEO Jensen Huang

Why is Nvidia’s Jensen Huang at the centre of a US-China row?

Too big – and too well-connected – to sack? One doesn’t have to be overly cynical to think Jensen Huang, the Nvidia boss, starts with one huge advantage as the chipmaker’s board starts its independent investigation into the alleged honeytrap spy scandal. The world of US big tech is not, to put it mildly, strong on checks and balances on a founder’s power.

Huang does not enjoy the supercharged voting rights that are par for the course elsewhere – his shareholding is a plain vanilla 3.6%. On the other hand, Nvidia’s board does not appear to have spent much time worrying about succession planning and “key person risk” or other standard concerns of corporate governance wonks outside the US.

There isn’t even a Nvidia board member with the title of chair. Instead, a “lead director” is “designated annually by a majority of the independent directors”, which sounds like a formula for ensuring the attention remains wholly focused on Huang, the sole executive member.

It’s the American way, of course: the cult of the superstar founder or chief executive runs deep and there is a fair argument that such set-ups encourage adventurous risk-taking in pursuit of grand corporate visions. But such governance arrangements look unsuited to situations where the behaviour of the boss is under scrutiny and the role of the board itself is being examined.

The investigation will examine whether Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort” but the independent directors stressed there is now “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

OK, but legitimate questions don’t end there. Did Huang break Nvidia’s internal code of conduct? Did he mislead the board about his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), the alleged Chinese spy? Was the board aware of US intelligence reports that Ms Huang had been hired by China’s ministry of state security to spy on the Nvidia boss, as reported by the New York Times? What security precautions were in place? Other boards in other countries might have insisted on suspending the boss until all the facts are in.

In the meantime, the defence of Huang from elsewhere has begun. “An honourable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it,” said Donald Trump. “Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” opined Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, the powerful Silicon Valley investor. Yes, there is little doubt the US tech and political establishment would like this saga to end up in a series of bland conclusions about an everyday infidelity.

Nvidia’s board, however, would be wise not to rely on the “irreplaceable” consensus holding, or the political heat going away. This affair will be trawled over by newly empowered Democrats in Congress because it touches on how forcefully – or not – the administration has been enforcing its own national security restrictions on chip sales to China. This process will go on for months. Huang’s personal relationship with Trump will come under the spotlight like never before.

Will the Nvidia boss, even if he is cleared by the board’s investigation, still look so all-conquering by the end? His lobbying clout in Washington will be diminished. And Nvidia’s shareholders, if they’re doing the job properly, will surely insist on far greater visibility on where the company’s chips end up.

There may come a point where it is in Nvidia’s own interests to move on from the Jensen Huang era. The 63-year-old deserves all his accolades for spotting the enormous AI opportunity for the GPU chips that originated in the world of video games. The rise of Nvidia has been extraordinary. But over-reliance on one individual is also a business risk. Time for some overdue succession planning – it may be needed.

I wrote Labour’s Brexit red lines. This is why it’s time to scrap them

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:00:14 GMT

The world has moved on since 2020 – in uncertain times, closer ties to Europe are the best way to peace and security

Chris Ward is Labour MP for Brighton Kemptown and Peacehaven

If offering the public some “breathing space” in the cost of living crisis was the mantra of last month’s budget, the political space it created to revisit our relationship with the European Union may prove more defining.

I’ve spent what feels like much of the past decade immersed in the Brexit debate – first as an adviser, then helping to craft the red lines that shaped Labour’s 2024 manifesto, and latterly as a Cabinet Office minister working on the EU-reset. In truth, the discussions we have had as a country and within my party on this issue have not really moved on since the moment we left on 31 January 2020.

There’s good reason for this. The red lines we drew up in the aftermath of the Labour leadership contest in 2020 – ruling out rejoining the EU, the single market, the customs union or restoring freedom of movement – were designed precisely to close down the debate and to narrow the target that Brexit had become for Labour. They enabled us to fight the 2024 election on a manifesto that was both pro-EU, by advocating a closer relationship, but also clearly stopping short of anything that looked like rejoining the bloc or relitigating the 2016 referendum. Schrödinger’s Brexit.

I still believe that strategically this was the right course for Labour, and the reset deal that – touch wood – will get over the line at this month’s UK-EU summit will demonstrate that real benefits can be delivered within those red lines, whether cheaper prices for businesses, a youth mobility scheme or the return of the Erasmus+ scheme.

By the next general election, however, those red lines will have served their purpose. They should be given a well-earned and dignified retirement. Frankly, they no longer speak to the world as it is in 2026, let alone as it may be over the years to come.

The major reason for this is not, in my view, an economic one. The economic case for rejoining either the EU or the single market (I personally have never understood the argument for the latter without the former) is basically the same as it was in 2016: that it will boost GDP, raise living standards, go some way to heal our public finances, and open access for British businesses to a market of 500 million people. All that comes, of course, with accepting freedom of movement and the other rules of the club. So far, so 2016. But pinning the case for a new relationship on old arguments risks both the same result and missing what has really changed.

Instead, it’s the huge geopolitical shifts and, above all, the new security and cyber threats the UK and Europe now face day in, day out, that demand we now reassess the depth and nature of that relationship. We should be in no doubt that – whether from Russia, China, Iran or elsewhere – these are of a different order and immediacy to in 2016. At the same time, the reliability of the US as our primary security partner can no longer be taken for granted. Donald Trump’s second term – which saw a British prime minister forced to twice scramble “coalitions of the willing” precisely because we could no longer rely on the Americans – should be seen as confirmation of this, not an aberration. It would now be brave in the extreme to continue to pin our future security – and that of Europe – on the outcome of US elections, or the false hope that, whoever is in the White House, we can still bank on the US as we did in 2016, let alone 1945.

after newsletter promotion

And so it is this question – how to ensure peace and prosperity in a time of growing global threats and US retrenchment – that should drive our foreign policy, our geostrategic choices and our domestic priorities for the years to come. That question was unthinkable in 2016, but it is unavoidable in 2026. It, of course, demands much greater urgency in increasing domestic defence spending, but it should also drive our future discussions with the EU.

The minimum we should now seek with the EU is a deep and enduring defence and trade partnership – pooling and rebuilding our defence and security might, and aligning our economic interests where possible.

Our primary goal should be to ensure that we are, together, better able to protect ourselves, and less dependent on a volatile US. Mark Carney’s push by Canada for “associate membership” and “the deepest possible partnership short of accession” with the EU stems from precisely this realisation. The very least Britain should now seek is a future relationship with the EU that is as ambitious.

Whether, ultimately, that deep security and economic partnership can only be achieved through formally rejoining the EU or through an associate deal should, of course, be part of the debate that has now been opened. But to fully capitalise on the political space we now have, we need to be clear as to why now is the right time to reopen the Brexit debate, what we are seeking, and why it is so important to our national interest. A re-run of the tired arguments of 2016 won’t do that. Defending red lines designed for 2020 won’t do that either. But appreciating the urgent strategic challenges of the decades to come just might.

Chris Ward is Labour MP for Brighton Kemptown and Peacehaven

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:00:14 GMT

Exclusive: MP Chris Ward believes ditching pledges and forming closer ties with EU would protect it from global threats

One of the architects of Keir Stamer’s Brexit red lines has called for Andy Burnham to abandon them at the next election, saying a new relationship with the EU would protect the UK from global threats.

The call is the latest voice from a prominent figure in Starmer’s administration for a faster transition to a far closer European relationship, after the former chancellor Rachel Reeves said it was right for Burnham to consider rejoining.

Chris Ward, one of Starmer’s closest confidants in politics and one of the ministers who worked on the EU reset, said that it was the security relationship that meant a change was now imperative.

The Labour MP for Brighton Kemptown and Peacehaven said it was now time to give a “a dignified retirement” to the red lines, which rule out rejoining the EU, the single market, the customs union and restoring freedom of movement.

Ward also suggested there was little compelling argument for rejoining the single market without full EU membership, saying he had “never understood the argument for the latter without the former”.

But he said the main reason for abandoning the red lines was that the UK “could no longer rely on the Americans” which was a major geopolitical shift that merited an entire reappraisal of Britain’s diplomatic relationships. “That question was unthinkable in 2016, but it is unavoidable in 2026,” he wrote in an article for the Guardian.

Ward, who was Starmer’s chief adviser as shadow Brexit secretary and who co-authored the red lines in Labour’s manifesto in 2024, said that they had now outlived their usefulness and should no longer be part of Labour’s future thinking.

He remains close to the former prime minister and said that the drive to renew the relationship with the EU may prove the defining political moment of this autumn.

He said the party had agreed upon the red lines in the manifesto because they were “designed precisely to close down the debate and to narrow the target that Brexit had become for Labour”.

“I still believe that strategically this was the right course for Labour, and the reset deal that – touch wood – will get over the line at next month’s UK-EU summit will demonstrate that real benefits can be delivered within those red lines, whether cheaper prices for businesses, a youth mobility scheme or the return of the Erasmus+ scheme.

“By the next general election, however, those red lines will have served their purpose. They should be given a well-earned and dignified retirement. Frankly, they no longer speak to the world as it is in 2026, let alone as it may be over the years to come.”

Ward said it was well known that rejoining the EU or single market would have economic benefits but said supporters of rejoining should make a different argument.

“Pinning the case for a new relationship on old arguments risks both the same result and missing what’s really changed,” he wrote.

“Instead, its the huge geopolitical shifts and, above all, the new security and cyber threats the UK and Europe now face day in, day out that demand we now reassess the depth and nature of relationship.”

Burnham will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin on Thursday, expected to be used to see Labour’s reset deal over the line and to meet many European leaders for the first time.

Burnham will also meet European leaders on the sidelines to set out his ambitions for further integration after he announced his intention to seek a closer and more permanent relationship – including potentially rejoining the bloc.

Elon Musk and the tech bros banked on Trump and lost. Humbled, humiliated: what will they do next?

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 16:48:18 GMT

Democrats won seats on anti-datacentre tickets and Musk wasted nearly half a billion dollars. Big tech may be losing its grip, but it won’t go quietly

Photos That Precede Unfortunate Events: a couple of months back, Donald Trump hosted some of the world’s most powerful tech executives at the White House for a “Super Intelligence luncheon”, which by coincidence is also how my mum described her tuna sandwiches in a forlorn attempt to get me to eat them. Sitting either side of the president were Elon Musk, making a rare offline appearance in daylight hours, and Jensen Huang, the Nvidia chief executive carving out a precious slot in what we now know was an extremely busy schedule.

Over a delicious meal of microchips and rare-earth metals, the billionaires sketched out a utopian future of an AI industry unencumbered by regulation or safeguards, powered by their heroic strongman leader, a political genius effortlessly able to impose his will upon an entire nation. And perhaps it should have been apparent even at the time that these (mostly) men were putting their faith in a guy who had recently been defeated by pond algae. But as the drinks and the good times flowed, it was still possible to believe that the sun would never set on the thousand-year American superintelligence empire.

And so, while we’re all learning lessons from the resounding defeat delivered to Trumpism last week, might we start with a modest and sober reassessment of the Silicon Valley oligarch class? For years, we have been told that these are some of humanity’s greatest seers and visionaries, the Leonardos and Einsteins of the 21st century, the people best placed to plot a course for our species, despite for the most part not being able to smile without looking as though they were undergoing a juice enema.

As it turned out, this small band of brilliant clairvoyants somehow failed to anticipate the possibility that the deeply unpopular man they were clasping in a tender embrace would be subjected to an absolute democracy-mogging in just a few weeks, throwing their altruistic wet dreams into chaos. After all, last week’s midterms were not simply a rebuke to one man or one party, but to an entire ideology. Across the US, voters took their revenge not just on big tech, but on the politicians who had enabled it.

In Texas, Gina Hinojosa beat the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott, by promising an immediate moratorium on datacentre development, and despite being outspent almost eight to one, in large part by big tech donors desperate to preserve their tax breaks. In Ohio, the Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown described his opponent, Jon Husted, as “the face of datacentres”, a visually horrifying concept. In total, 46 of the 47 ballot measures relating to datacentres were defeated. By Thursday morning, the markets had responded with a devastating sell-off of tech stocks, the repercussions of which are still shaking out as you read this.

Should we read anything into the fact that the biggest progressive landslide in 52 years, catalysed by a concerted mobilisation of Black, Latino and young voters, was sufficient to send the financial markets into existential panic? Anyone able to join the dots for us there? Is it relevant that the São Paulo stock exchange plunged about 14% after Lula da Silva’s shock election victory in Brazil last month? Just what is it about the popular repudiation of hard-right autocrats that appears to spook the pillars of capitalism so much?

For the time being, big tech does not appear to be as politically polarising in Britain as it is in the US. This is largely because much of the recent acceleration has occurred under a Labour administration, in particular under the late lamented Keir Starmer, a prime minister who in retrospect may actually have been a semi-sentient chatbot all along. “We will test and understand AI before we regulate it,” Starmer once said, which he appears to have done by plugging it directly into his own mouth for two years. But this is an issue that will continue to rise in democratic salience, in part because it relies on the undemocratic manufacture of consent, an inexorable march deliberately designed to circumvent scrutiny.

after newsletter promotion

Take the UK government’s AI growth zones, designed to supercharge datacentre development by taking decisions on nationally significant infrastructure projects (NSIP) away from local councils. A recent report by Spotlight on Corruption found that over two years, ministers met only two community groups and no environmental organisations while developing the policy, while at the same time ministers and senior civil servants were hired to 38 roles at AI companies. Naturally, you are likely to hear very little opposition to any of this, either from the billionaire-owned press or the official opposition; indeed, Kemi Badenoch is perhaps the only major party leader you can imagine typing “what do I think of AI” into an AI prompt.

You will occasionally hear the assumption, made on both sides of the Atlantic and often on the flimsiest of evidence, that voters are increasingly fed up with democracy. But what if we’re getting this the wrong way round? What if, in fact, it is those who are supposed to be upholding democracy – the politicians and media and captains of industry, all slowly stewing in X-brained algorithmic talking points – who are beginning to tire of it? While Musk spends enormous chunks of his fortune trying (and failing) to tip the electoral scales in favour of the hard right, Reform UK rakes in £72m in donations from two cryptocurrency billionaires. Bonus question: do we think the brave men and women out there on the tech frontier will respond to democratic setbacks by demanding more democratic accountability, or less?

And, of course, in these febrile and fragile times you have to take your wins wherever you get them. But as any ChatGPT user will tell you, making bold claims on the basis of a bare minimum of data is always an exercise fraught with risk. Saying no once will never be enough. In a note to investors last week, Goldman Sachs wrote: “We expect the datacentre issue to somewhat fade in importance and any moratoria on datacentre development to be short-lived.” You can decide for yourself what it means by that.

Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnist

The hottest product in Britain this year? A 2kg bag of ice

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 16:41:58 GMT

As the UK endured record-breaking temperatures this summer, nothing grew in popularity on Deliveroo like sacks of sweet relief from the supermarket Iceland

Name: Iceland’s 2kg bag of ice.

Age: The first patents for commercial mechanical production date to the 1850s.

Appearance: Clear, cold.

Just normal ice, then. Ice in its most desirable form.

Cubes, you mean. A bag containing 2kg of ice cubes, as sold by the British supermarket Iceland.

What’s so desirable about that? “These ice cubes are better than anyone else’s and are great value for money,” according to a five-star review on Iceland’s website from Trevor P.

So Trevor likes ice. Not just Trevor. According to Deliveroo, Iceland’s 2kg ice bag was the “top trending” UK delivery order – a metric that marries year-on-year growth in orders, relative order volume in the local area and customer ratings – of 2026 so far.

Really? What came second? The diavola pizza from Monte Forte Neapolitan Pizza in Horsham, West Sussex.

How specific. But ice bag deliveries from Iceland were so popular in London that they came second in Deliveroo’s global ranking.

I guess it was a pretty hot summer. The hottest since records began.

How much would a 2kg bag of ice set me back on a scorching July afternoon? You can get one for £1 in the store.

That’s not bad, actually. But when you add in the Deliveroo surcharge, its small-order fee, the delivery fee, the bag charge and the service charge, it could cost as much as £8.

That’s ridiculous! As I’ve pointed out, you could get the same bag from the shop for a quid.

Yeah, but the shops are, like, hundreds of metres away. You could even make your own ice, in your own freezer, for a fraction of the cost.

But then I’d have to realise I’ll want a margarita hours before I do. I prefer to be spontaneous. Do you not see the irony of paying over the odds to have someone bring you a single bag of ice amid a climate crisis?

The climate crisis is why I want the ice. A climate crisis brought about in no small part by the rapacious demands of western consumerism, all because you can’t be bothered to fill your own ice trays?

OK, I do see the irony, but my hands are tied. No they aren’t! You can make better choices!

Anyway, it’s November now. I’m cold and I want soup. Well, the good news is you can probably make a lovely soup from things you already have in your kitchen.

I don’t like that kind of soup. What kind of soup do you like?

Soup from a man in a motorbike helmet. I despair.

Do say: “When we’re having ice delivered while the world burns, something is seriously wrong with our priorities.”

Don’t say: “This pizza from Horsham – can I get it delivered to Peterborough?”

Manchester United are deciding whether Michael Carrick should be sacked, with Jason Wilcox, the director of football, leading the review after the head coach was given the Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa games to turn results around.

Wilcox is consulting with Omar Berrada, the chief executive, before a recommendation regarding ­Carrick is made to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who ­controls sporting policy. United are in the Premier League relegation zone and have three victories in 15 games in all competitions.

Carrick came close to being removed after the 3-0 defeat against Bournemouth on 25 October. But after Wilcox and Berrada met the following day at the training ground to discuss his position, Carrick was given the three games until the international break to prove he and the players could reverse a dismal start.

United then lost 2-0 at ­Chelsea, beat Roma 3-2 at Old ­Trafford and shared a 4-4 home draw with Villa on Sunday. In each of the matches United were uneven. At Chelsea, ­Carrick’s side impressed in the first half but failed to convert chances before conceding twice after the interval, the second from a penalty after Lisandro Martínez was sent off.

In the Roma victory they were 2-0 behind in a poor opening 45 minutes before three goals in a rousing second one. On Sunday United twice trailed by two goals and entered added time 4-2 down, strikes from Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu rescuing a point.

After the Roma game Carrick urged his team to build momentum but within four minutes against Villa they were 2-0 down, continuing a pattern of conceding very early. In the 4-1 defeat at Como last month, Nico Paz scored after two minutes. This followed Pablo Barrios’s opener one minute into the 2-0 defeat at Atlético Madrid the ­previous week.

There is no plan to bolster Carrick’s coaching staff to try to help him and the team, it is understood.

If ­Carrick is removed, Eddie Howe remains Wilcox’s favoured candidate. The former Newcastle manager is taking a break from the game but would be open to considering the job.

A one-part wonder! The West End’s streamlined Harry Potter and the Cursed Child works like magic

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 15:11:19 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Palace theatre, LondonFive hours have been trimmed to three for this new version but it is packed with magic moments and superb performances

Ten years on from its premiere, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child has been transformed from an epic two-part play into a richly absorbing one-part production. A similar version is already running to great acclaim on Broadway but it still feels risky to tinker with a show that has come to feel like a fixed jewel in the West End. Happily, that risk has paid off and Cursed Child hasn’t lost any of its sparkle.

Admittedly, there are some drawbacks to reducing Jack Thorne’s ambitious five-hour script into a very tightly packed three hours. The plot can, at times, overwhelm. The story, which picks up nearly 20 years on from JK Rowling’s final book, focuses on Harry’s youngest son, Albus – freshly arrived at Hogwarts and determined to make a name for himself distinct from his famous dad. When Albus and his best friend Scorpius Malfoy stumble across a time-turner, the two unleash some seriously dark forces. It will take an incredibly complicated plot-twist, which I suspect only Thorne himself understands, to save the day.

Even with a streamlined script – key characters are cut and dream sequences nixed – the story can get in the way of John Tiffany’s spellbinding production. But, oh, the places that story takes us! There are brave boys swimming through shimmering lakes and frightened adults sliding through flaming fireplaces. Transporting telephone boxes and dazzling transformation spells. Exploding sweets. Glowing wands. And terrifying dementors, looming over us like some awful nightmare and whooshing right through the stalls and skimming over our upturned faces.

Woven through it all is Steven Hoggett’s beautiful movement direction, which keeps the production moving forward and creates a sense of mystery and magic at every turn. The huge ensemble cast – which seem to move as one – work wonders with their cloaks, sweeping them with precision and flair. All of this plays out on Christine Jones’s simple but stunning set, with its huge arches and great open dark spaces, which seem to hint at bigger, darker powers at play, just out of sight and beyond our control.

The show’s visual majesty is complemented by some fine performances, the very best of them laced through with sparks of humour. At the show I watched, Albus Potter was played by understudy Ewan Rutherford, who had a lovely flinty sort of defiance to him. Bill Stanley, on his West End debut, was especially good as Albus’s friend (perhaps crush) Scorpius – voice always on the verge of breaking, frightened of everything but all the braver for it. David Ricardo-Pearce’s Harry Potter is a man weighed down with responsibility, Thomas Aldridge’s Ron funny but just a little bit sad too and Naana Agyei-Ampadu’s Hermione commanding but vulnerable.

It’s a great cast but, even better in a celebrity-packed West End, there’s not a superstar in sight. The real star of this show is – with huge credit to illusionist Jamie Harrison – the magic we all come to believe in together. The portrait that talks. The stairs that dance. The man who flies. And the boy who lives.

At Palace theatre, London, until 5 September

Fancy an at-home coffee maker that can grind beans and make tasty espresso? Our expert put 14 to the test, including fully automatic and assisted models

The best coffee machine for your home

Laziness is akin to godliness. I know this for a fact because, every morning, my kitchen hosts a dishevelled re-enactment of Michelangelo’s famed fresco, the Creazione di Adamo (Creation of Adam). An outstretched arm extends a single finger, and lo – a bean-to-cup machine stirs, a grinder whirs, the smell of freshly ground coffee wafts, coffee drips and milk froths. Hopefully, my cup does not runneth over, for all the big mugs are in the dishwasher.

At its simplest, this is the appeal of a fully automatic bean-to-cup coffee machine. Turn it on, place a cup on the drip tray and lazily prod a button. The machine then freshly grinds the beans, brews the coffee and – if it has an automatic milk frother – optionally adds a layer of hot frothy milk to your beverage. Your role in the process is simple: decide whether you want an espresso, lungo, americano, cappuccino, macchiato, latte or cortado. Decisions, decisions.

In this roundup, I’ve collected the best bean-to-cup coffee machines that have passed through my kitchen in recent months (or in some cases, years), and tested them alongside a handful of less familiar models that have also earned their automatic barista accreditations. Think of this as a work in progress: I’ll be adding new models as and when they arrive in my kitchen – and prove themselves capable of making delicious coffee.

Note, there are different kinds of bean-to-cup machines, which require different levels of input to achieve different results. If you need a refresher, I go into the details at the end of the article.

Best bean-to-cup coffee machine overall and best on a budgetDe’Longhi Magnifica Start

Best bean-to-cup coffee machine under £1,000De’Longhi Rivelia

Best slimline bean-to-cup machineKitchenAid KF4

Best bean-to-cup machine for simplicityJura C8

Best bean-to-cup machine for coffee connoisseursSage Oracle Jet

Best high-end fully automatic bean-to-cup machineJura J10

Best value assisted machineNinja Luxe Cafe ES601

I’ve been reviewing tech and gadgets of all shapes and sizes for more than two decades, and I branched out into testing coffee machines about eight years ago. Whether it’s cafetières or capsule machines, manual espresso or fully automatic bean-to-cups, I’ve put hundreds of hours and – most probably – hundreds of kilograms of coffee into the pursuit of a pleasing caffeine hit. And yes, I’ve drunk a lot of the stuff too. At the time of writing, far, far too much. I’ll be going for a very long walk after I’ve finished writing this.

There’s a lot to consider with an automatic bean-to-cup coffee machine, so everything goes under the microscope. Some aspects are subjective (the ease of use, coffee quality and the overall design), while others can be measured – coffee temperature, noise, and how long the machines take to heat up.

I tested 14 models, taste-testing side by side against their nearest competitors to see how they performed for espresso, black coffee and milk-based drinks. Noise levels for grinding, brewing and milk frothing were measured with the Decibel X app on my iPhone to test comparative noise levels in A-weighted decibels (dBA), and my trusty Thermapen handles the temperature testing side of things.

If the best things in life are free, then the second-best things are cheap. And if you’re really lucky, simple. That’s the Magnifica Start to a T. This fully automatic bean-to-cup machine serves up good espresso, black coffee and cappuccino at the touch of a button, and it’s easy to use. Keep an eye on the sales, and you can pick it up for £300 or so.

Why we love it The Start looks good, with a mixture of matt and gloss black plastics and a little chrome here and there. It feels solid where it needs to: the drip tray and grounds bin slot out together, and the 1.8-litre water tank feels nice and sturdy.

De’Longhi includes a water filter in the box, which lasts about three months, depending on your usage and water hardness. A tester in the box allows you to set your water hardness so that the machine will prompt you to descale at sensible intervals.

The quality of the coffee is good. Feed it with decent beans, and the Start will reward you with a tasty, balanced cup. I had to reduce the grind size by a couple of steps to get a more robust espresso out of it, but it’s easy to tweak. Tapping the coffee bean control gives you three strength levels, too.

Milk texture is good – better than the pricier Philips. The foam is tight and creamy and lasts long enough to make for a pleasant drink. The lack of a dedicated hot milk button is an annoyance – but there is a trick. Use the pre-ground coffee option, but don’t add any coffee. You’ll get hot milk without the coffee, and the machine will chunter quietly in remonstration.

It’s a shame that … the milk carafe is small, and you’ll be refilling it regularly.

Machine type: fully automatic bean to cup Dimensions: 24 x 44 x 35cm (WDH) Water tank: 1.8l Time to heat up: 40secs Makes milk-based drinks? Yes, automatic Peak noise level: 55dB (brew), 60dB (steam), 75dB (grind) Warranty: two years repair or replace at De’Longhi’s discretion

For more, read our full De’Longhi Magnifica Start coffee machine review

The Rivelia dares to be different. It takes the fully automatic template – making gorgeous black and white coffees at the touch of a button – and adds the ability to quickly swap between coffee beans with its two interchangeable 250g bean hoppers.

It is pricey, with an RRP of £749, but keep an eye out for the regular discounts. If your budget can stretch a little further than the Magnifica Start, this is a big upgrade for sensible cash.

Why we love it The hoppers can be swapped in seconds. Twist the hopper to release it, and the touchscreen asks if you want to make a final drink from the coffee left in the chute, or purge it into the internal bin. Extra hoppers are £17.99 each; you can easily add a third or fourth.

The Rivelia’s slender design is less imposing than its rivals, and the touchscreen is a delight. It guides users through every step of the process, and the four individual user accounts allow everyone in the household to customise drinks to their preferences.

Crucially, the coffee is great. There’s a vast choice of short, long, milk-based and over-ice coffees here. Espresso is impressive: unlike most bean-to-cup machines I’ve tested, the finest of the 14 grind settings is so fine that it will slow the pour to a drip. That means syrupy, intense espresso is on the menu. The milk frothing is good, and you can adjust it from a light froth to a thicker, creamier foam – it’s not quite as smooth and glossy as the pricier Jura C8 below, though.

Adjustability is excellent. De’Longhi’s Bean Adapt feature adjusts the brewing settings to suit the type of beans you’re using, and the double-shot espresso does what it says on the tin – two separate brews are done one after another for an extra-strong cup. You can adjust the amount of milk froth, which is a welcome upgrade over cheaper models.

It’s a shame that … placing the colour touchscreen and buttons on the top of the machine puts the controls out of reach of inquisitive kids – but shorter people and wheelchair users will find them awkward.

Machine type: fully automatic bean-to-cup machine Dimensions: 24.5 x 43 x 38.5cm (WDH) Water tank: 1.4l Time to heat up: 38secs Makes milk-based drinks? Yes, automatic Peak noise level: 51dB (brew), 51dB (steam), 68dB (grind) Warranty: two years repair or replace at De’Longhi’s discretion

KitchenAid’s first foray into the world of fully automatic bean-to-cup machines was in 2024 – and with prices starting at £1,299, they weren’t cheap. Now comes a trio of more affordable models, listed by KitchenAid at £699 for the KF2, £749 for the KF3 and £899 for the KF4.

The KF4 is the most fully featured of the three. It has a large front-facing 8.8cm touchscreen, 24 recipes for both hot and iced coffees (although not cold brew), and four user profiles for saving your preferred recipes.

Why we love it Coffee is superb from the off. Espresso is rich and complex, and the various settings make it easy to get it just so. The grinding, steaming and brewing are refreshingly quiet, too.

The milk-based drinks are topped with a tight, creamy froth – among the best here. The loose carafe lid is an annoyance, but you can jam the tube into a jug or milk bottle if you prefer. Unlike the De’Longhi Rivelia, though, you can’t adjust the level of milk froth. It’s a choice of frothed milk or plain steamed milk.

For many kitchens, though, it will be the KF4’s dainty footprint that’s of most appeal. At 19.5cm wide, it’s one of the narrower models I’ve tested and will easily slot into any small gaps on your kitchen worktop. The retractable mains cable is a nice touch, too.

The touchscreen interface works well. It’s easy to swipe through the various recipes, and all the options are clearly presented. Unusually, there are temperature, strength and body options for each recipe too. The latter two adjust the amount of coffee used and the brewing time, which helps to dial in the perfect shot. You can pour two drinks simultaneously, too.

The space-saving design is great, but the rear-mounted water tank may be a tad awkward for some kitchens. You need clearance behind the machine to remove it, or space above it to refill the tank without taking it out.

Also, the setup instructions feel like an afterthought. The owner’s manual and quick start guide fall short for complete beginners, and the touchscreen’s setup diagrams could be clearer. Thankfully, once the machine is up and running, the interface is intuitive.

It’s a shame that … while the coffee is superb, it’s not light years better than the far cheaper De’Longhi Rivelia. If space is at a premium, though, you may be willing to pay the price – and the KF4 justifies it.

Machine type: fully automatic bean to cup Dimensions: 19.5 x 47.5 x 36cm (WDH) Water tank: 1.8l Time to heat up: 1min Makes milk-based drinks? Yes, automatic Peak noise level: 50dB (brew), 55dB (steam), 63dB (grind) Warranty: two years (limited five-year parts guarantee for burr grinder; 10 years repairability commitment)

The Jura C8 offers a winning combination of simplicity, potential upgrades and good coffee. The brand’s reputation for reliability doesn’t hurt, either. Don’t pay the £899 RRP, though; shop around, and you’ll often find it below £700.

Why we love it The design looks sleek – albeit by bean-to-cup standards – and it works well. The lack of a milk carafe seems like an oversight, but it’s not (you can buy a Jura one) – just pop the milk tube directly into a jug or milk carton, and it’s far easier to keep clean than the nooks and crannies of a carafe. You can upgrade to a Jura milk cooler for £225 if you’re feeling flush.

Where Jura’s pricier J10 makes a huge array of drinks, the C8 settles for four: espresso, black coffee, cappuccino and frothy latte macchiato. This simplicity is matched by the controls. The C8 has a black-and-white LCD screen with buttons on either side. The screen is basic, but that works in its favour – especially if you don’t want to be bamboozled with myriad recipes or by a touchscreen.

Espresso and black coffees don’t have the depth of flavour of the De’Longhi Rivelia at its best – and bitterness overwhelms if you dial the grind size too fine – but they’re still very good. Milk texture is also excellent: it’s far smoother than the cheaper machines here.

One nice touch is that the 2x Espresso or 2x Coffee options can pour two drinks via the dual spouts – or just one larger, stronger drink if you need it.

One minor annoyance: it won’t dispense hot water. You can increase the black coffee volume to fill your preferred cup, but that simply pushes more water through the coffee and increases bitterness.

It’s a shame that … you can’t make an americano without assistance from a kettle.

Machine type: fully automatic bean to cup Dimensions: 26 x 44 x 33cm (WDH) Water tank: 1.6l Time to heat up: 30secs Makes milk-based drinks? Yes, automatic Noise level: 50dB (brew), 47dB (steam), 65dB (grind) Warranty: 25 months repair or replace at Jura’s discretion

At this price, you have a choice: the finest-tasting coffee or the least amount of effort. The Oracle Jet offers the former: this is an assisted espresso machine that will give your finest independent coffee shop a real run for its money.

Why we love it If you want the best espresso – or espresso-based drink, such as cappuccino, flat white or even americano – then the classic manual espresso machine reigns supreme. The problem is that you need to know what you’re doing: the Jet’s solution is to guide you every step of the way with a big, colourful touchscreen.

It’s more involved than a single button press, but it’s not hard – it’s actually rather exciting. Slot the portafilter into place, and the grinder thrums into action, dispensing the perfect amount of coffee while the internal fan tamps it down just so. Move the portafilter to the brew group with a thunk and a twist, tap the touchscreen, and the espresso pours forth. Congratulations, you’re a barista.

Once you have your perfect espresso, all that remains is to create some perfectly steamed milk. Fill the supplied stainless steel jug with milk – there are settings for dairy, oat, almond and soy – and the Jet whips the milk to a silky, creamy froth in just over a minute. Combine the coffee and milk, and magic awaits.

It’s a shame that … it’s expensive. For this kind of money, you’d rather hope that it’d walk up the stairs and bring you coffee in bed every morning for the foreseeable future.

Machine type: assisted espresso machine Dimensions: 38 x 37 x 43cm (WDH) Water tank: 2.3l Time to heat up: 6secs Makes milk-based drinks? Yes, auto and manual steam wand Peak noise level: 46dB (brew), 58dB (steam), 66dB (grind) Warranty: two-year repair, replace or refund at Sage’s discretion

For more, read our Sage Oracle Jet review

Where Jura’s C8 distils the bare essentials of the brand’s bean-to-cup coffee machines, the J10 gives a more fully featured glimpse of its high end.

Why we love it As you’d expect for an RRP of £1,795, you get a nice bright colour touchscreen. The interface isn’t as pretty as the premium Sage alternatives, nor as intuitive, but it’s smooth and responsive. Flicking between the pages of drinks is easy, and a long press on each drink lets you fettle the recipes – of which there are 42.

All the staples are present and correct, and there’s a large menu of long, short, cold, hot, sweet and non-coffee drinks. The overall quality is great. Drinks are hot, flavourful, well-brewed and, where required, topped with a pleasingly fine microfoam. Almost every possible variety of coffee drink is on the menu, which is refreshing.

The design is classic Jura. The tall 1.9l water tank slots in snugly, and you get a single water filter in the box, which is rated to last for 50 litres or two months of use. The bottom tray slides out easily and splits into sections to make it easier to clean and dispose of used coffee grounds.

It’s a bit tightfisted of Jura not to include a milk carafe, but it’s not needed: simply pop the tube in a milk carton or jug, and it frees you from the faff of carafe scrubbing. I didn’t find the cold-brew drinks hugely impressive either – if you like the idea of the touchscreen and increased range of recipes, but can live without cold brew, save your money and step down to the Jura J8 instead.

Be in no doubt, the appeal here is the breadth of drinks, ease of use and the build quality and reliability. If you have this much to spend, though, choose carefully: if you’re willing to put in more effort, the Sage Oracle Jet makes vastly superior coffee. Think long and hard before splashing out.

It’s a shame that … cheaper models such as the De’Longhi Rivelia match it for espresso quality and breadth of drink choice. While the J10’s milk foam is tighter and creamier, the coffee isn’t better.

Machine type: fully automatic bean to cup Dimensions: 32 x 45 x 35cm (WDH) Water tank: 1.9l Time to heat up: 30secs Makes milk-based drinks? Yes, automatic Noise level: 50dB (brew), 47dB (steam), 65dB (grind) Warranty: 25 months repair or replace at Jura’s discretion

This is a very affordable assisted espresso machine. For an RRP of £579.99, the ES601UK serves everything from espresso to flat white, and cold brew to filter coffee. You have to lend a helping hand, but the automatic grind adjustment and automatic milk frothing mean that you don’t need to know what you’re doing.

Why we love it The versatility is impressive. Ninja supplies three baskets for the portafilter – single, double and quad – allowing it to brew everything from a single espresso to a brain-tingling quad espresso to a filter-style coffee with a coarser grind.

Milky coffee drinkers aren’t left out in the cold, either – well, not unless they want to be. The ES601UK’s proprietary milk jug uses a little whisk to froth up cold milk as easily as it steams and froths hot milk.

The big selling point isn’t just the range of coffee drinks it produces. The clincher is that, at its best, it can produce a stronger, better espresso or milk-based coffee than the fully automatic models here. And, as long as you feed it good-quality coffee beans, it’s not that much effort to do so.

While it’s far easier to use than a manual espresso machine, it’s not zero effort. The built-in grinder advises on the grind size and grinds the right amount every time, but you need to adjust this manually as instructed, press down the coffee grounds with the supplied tamper and slot the portafilter into place.

Consider the step-up ES701UK model. This swaps the manual tamping for a big lever that makes the process feel more immediate. If you’re on the fence between a fully automatic and an assisted espresso machine, it may swing the deal.

It’s a shame that … consistency is iffy. Coffee and milk temperature can vary, and my review unit started to overheat the milk after a few months. The two-year warranty is welcome.

Machine type: assisted Dimensions: 34 x 35 x 38cm (WDH) Water tank: 2l Time to heat up: 35secs Makes milk-based drinks? Yes Noise: 48dB (brew), 58dB (steam), 63dB (grind) Warranty: two years

For more, read our full Ninja Luxe Cafe review

Best for: ease of use

The LatteGo 5500 is one of Philips’ more upmarket models. The design looks good – and it’s practical. The 25cm width is a tad narrower than many machines, and that means it will slot into gaps on the worktop easily.

The Quiet Mark certification is welcome. The rubber-sealed bean hopper lid doesn’t just keep the beans fresher; it also makes for one of the quietest grinders here. Brewing and steaming are similar to the other models, though.

The controls work well. Nice, clear touch-sensitive buttons are adorned with drinks icons, and the colour touchscreen makes it quick and easy to adjust the drinks settings, from strength to size. Four colour-coded user accounts allow different people to set their own drink preferences, too.

For the money, though, the De’Longhi Rivelia feels more solidly built and makes a far better coffee. The LatteGo’s light, plasticky build is one disappointment, but the drinks could be better, too. The espresso at default settings is watery; you can improve it by grinding finer and making a smaller shot, but it still doesn’t match the De’Longhi models here.

The milk carafe design is wonderfully simple, but it creates a coarse, bubbly froth that’s bettered by the more affordable Magnifica Start. That it doesn’t prompt you to attach the milk frother is silly, too – forget to do so, and it just spurts steam all over the drip tray and worktop.

It didn’t make the final cut because … you can get better-quality coffee for less.

Machine type: fully automatic bean to cup; dimensions: 25 x 44 x 37cm (WDH); water tank: 1.8 litres; time to heat up: 45secs; makes milk-based drinks? Yes, automatic; peak noise level: 58dB (brew), 64dB (steam), 63dB (grind); warranty: two years

Best for: dual hoppers and hot, strong coffees

The Melitta Latte Select’s fully automatic design is reminiscent of Jura’s models – I suspect it’s built by the same OEM manufacturer – and serves 12 coffee recipes. The party trick? You can switch between two types of beans with the flick of a lever.

The split hopper is a mediocre design. The lever tilts a plastic gate to open or close the left- and right-hand sides of the hopper, but beans tend to slip through the gaps when it’s full. It works – but 100% effective it is not.

Still, it makes a mean coffee. The Latte Select uses larger doses of coffee than some of the other machines here; coffee temperature is hotter than average, and brewing temperature is adjustable. The result is that espresso is downright potent at the maximum strength setting, and the milk-based coffees are tasty, with a good, creamy milk foam.

The plastic milk carafe connects via a little rubber tube, but just like the Jura machines, you don’t have to use it – you can plonk the tube directly into a milk bottle or jug.

The body and parts feel light and plasticky; the hollow-sounding clunks and whirrs are a touch louder than its rivals, and the controls are fiddly.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the drink buttons are sensitive and easily pressed by accident.

Machine type: fully automatic bean to cup; dimensions: 26 x 48 x 35cm (WDH); water tank: 1.8 litres; time to heat up: 52secs; makes milk-based drinks? Yes, automatic; peak noise level: 53dB (brew), 57dB (steam), 67dB (grind); warranty: two years

Best for: super-hot manual milk frothing

The Cadorna does lots of things well. The chunky-looking control panel is easy to navigate, and it’s refreshing to have big, solid buttons to press rather than a touchscreen. User profiles are another boon, as everyone can customise the drink recipes to their tastes.

Espresso is good and strong – that makes the base for a great coffee, black and white. The simple interface plays a crucial part here: you can adjust shot volume, temperature and strength quickly and easily without consulting the user manual, which makes it easy to get a perfect shot.

Milk frothing is a manual affair, but it’s not hard. Grab your nearest metal milk jug, half fill it with milk, and dip the steam wand just below the surface. If you prefer your milk hotter, you can just leave it in a little longer and keep steaming. You still don’t get silky, perfect microfoam, though – it’s thick and frothy, and too coarse and stiff to create any latte art. You’ll need a proper manual wand for that.

It’s not the most handsome-looking or solid-feeling machine, either. It’s chunky and plasticky, and the 1.5-litre water tank and grounds bin clunk in and out inelegantly. It’s noisy, too.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s just too pricey at full price, and the manual milk frothing will appeal only to those who demand lip-scorchingly hot milky coffees.

Machine type: semi-automatic bean to cup; dimensions: 26 x 44 x 38cm (WDH); water tank: 1.5l; time to heat up: 28secs; makes milk-based drinks? Yes, manual steam wand; peak noise level: 58dB (brew), 52dB (steam), 69dB (grind); warranty: five years on parts (including two years parts and labour)

Well, there are lots. The tricky bit for buyers is that, rather unhelpfully, manufacturers have a broad definition of bean-to-cup, and they apply the term to a range of machines with a varied array of abilities. One thing they do all have in common is a bean hopper up top, which can be filled with coffee beans. Yes, they all brew coffee, but while some serve a milk-based coffee with a single press of a button, others require more effort.

Below, I’ve summarised the pros and cons of the three main types of bean-to-cup machines on the market in 2026, and given insight as to what they do differently.

Pros: Easiest to use Cons: Can be expensive

If you can see a milk carafe – or a milk tube – poking out of the side of a machine, then it’s almost certainly a superautomatic. As long as you keep the water tank, milk carafe and bean hopper topped up, one prod of a finger will summon a milk-based coffee – such as a cappuccino or flat white. Pricier models may provide more preset drink recipes (including cold brew), adjustable milk froth levels or the ability to swap between two types of coffee beans.

Pros: Normally cheaper; milk foam can be better Cons: More hassle

Semi-automatic bean-to-cup machines (confusingly referred to as automatic sometimes) require you to steam your milk manually with a steam wand. They serve espresso – and often long blacks or americanos – at the press of a button, but you’ll need to hold a steel jug of milk under the steam wand to create hot milk. Up your budget, and models with “pro” wands will create cafe-quality microfoam – if, that is, you have good technique. Most, however, use auto-frothing wands, which create a looser, more bubbly foam with minimal effort.

Pros: Best coffee and superior milk texture Cons: Require more effort

You’ll see manufacturers call these bean-to-cup machines, but they’re more involved than their semi- and fully automatic cousins. The more you spend, the more assistance you’ll get. Top-flight models hold your hand tightly: put the portafilter under the grinder, and they’ll grind the coffee and press it down, leaving you to move the portafilter to the brew group and press a button. If the grind is too coarse or too fine, they’ll prompt you to adjust it. Similarly, they froth milk to perfection: just put a jug of cold milk under the steam wand. For coffee quality, they trounce their automatic rivals, but effortless they are not.

For more: The best coffee machines for your home – tested How to make your coffee machine last longer The best espresso machines

Sasha Muller is a tech and consumer journalist, avid coffee drinker and craft beer enthusiast with more than two decades of experience in testing products and avoiding deadlines. If he’s not exploring the local woods with his kids, boring people talking about mountain-bike tyres or spending ill-advised amounts on classic drum’n’bass vinyl, he’s probably to be found somewhere swearing at an inanimate object
