‘A three-minute history of England written in the tour bus toilet’: how Tenpole Tudor made Swords of a Thousand Men

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 14:13:04 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

‘Dressed as knights, we’d walk onstage to the sound of the William Tell overture. I’d quote Henry V and the crowd would shout, “You’re the rightful king of England!”’

I’d worked up the basic idea on Stiff Records’ three-month tour of the northern hemisphere. It’s near-impossible to write songs on the road because you lack the basic solitude, so I’d retire to the tour coach latrine. The melody was really a boogie-blues progression, part-inspired by Norman Greenbaum’s Spirit in the Sky and Canned Heat’s On the Road Again. But lyrics only flowed when we came off the tour. Rehearsing near our favourite drinking haunt, the Castle on Holloway Road, London, provided the opening line: “Deep in the castle and back from the war.”

Swords is like a three-minute history of England. I like to think it could have been written at any time and been a popular folk song. Knights were the first superheroes, and the people buying the record in 1981 were 11-year-old boys. It became a playground craze: I’ve always felt I had the mind of an 11-year-old. When I’d recorded Who Killed Bambi a couple of years earlier, for publicity I’d fed Malcom McLaren the line that I was a direct descendent of Henry VIII. He thought it was hilarious.

With the release of Swords, we played up to the whole knights in armour thing, with doublets, hoses and tabards. Our live performances were very theatrical. Sometimes we’d walk on stage to the William Tell Overture and I’d declaim the St Crispin’s Day speech from Shakespeare’s Henry V. People would shout: “You’re the rightful king of England!” I’d say: “No I’m not!” They’d say: “Yes, you are!” It was in the fun, rocking tradition of Sweet, Slade and Status Quo, with a touch of music hall. Swords was one of the first pop videos on MTV. We hired members of the Sealed Knot historical reenactment society for the shoot.

One day, I was walking down the street and a policeman beckoned me over and said: “Are you the person responsible for Swords of a Thousand Men?” Given my permanently guilty conscience, I was terrified. But he just said: “Well done, congratulations,” and shook my hand. That was lovely.

I’ve been touring recently to promote my autobiography. Its title is a play on Swords – The Pen Is Mightier – and when I perform the number the audience sing the chorus for me. Those 11-year-olds are in their late 50s now. You always love the first record you bought, don’t you?

We’d been rushed into the studio to record tracks for our first album Eddie, Old Bob, Dick and Gary. When the mixes came back, we couldn’t hear a potential single among them. So when Eddie got his skeleton of an idea for Swords, its rhythmic, faintly rockabilly feel caught our attention. We worked it up outside the studio. Eddie loved the idea of chants you could sing on football terraces, hence the “Hoo-rah, hoo-rah, hoo-rah, yeah!” We took pride in our harmonies, something you hear on other singles like Wünderbar and Throwing My Baby Out With the Bathwater.

We recorded Swords at Island Studios with Alan Winstanley, who was also producing Madness. He was a master engineer. But although we’d got all the parts down, we still didn’t have an intro. I was influenced by the Stranglers’ JJ Burnel and wanted to write a bass intro that was instantly recognisable, but using as few notes as possible. The “dinga-dinga” bass start to Swords was it – as soon as the song comes on in a club, everyone knows what it is. But, on its own, it was too sparse. So the galloping horses were sourced from a sound effects LP in the BBC library. That horn you hear is me. I’d played bugle in a Boy Scouts’ band, so I borrowed a mate’s trumpet and blew that. Again, very minimalist, just two notes. Our drummer Gary Long overdubbed timpani, sitting in the corridor to get that big, ringing sound.

To me, Swords is a punk-psychobilly crossover, and it gave us a rockabilly-cum-psychobilly following. Our guitarist Bob Kingston had always looked like a 1950s’ ted with his greasy quiff. We did a gig at the Crystal Palace Bowl and got bombarded with mud and weeds, a trait of psychobilly fans.

Tenpole Tudor broke up too soon. I set up my own Panther Studios in Surrey. As well punk bands, these days I make ambient music. But 10 years ago, I was in a band, the Weird Things, that backed Eddie doing Swords at a show in London. It was brilliant being on stage with him again, doing what we used to do.

Edward Tudor Pole plays New Cross Inn, London, on 19 November. The Pen Is Mightier: Autobiography of a Punk Rocker is out in paperback

Felix Nmecha’s faith is forcing Borussia Dortmund into an uncomfortable debate

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 14:10:43 GMT

Midfielder’s spectacular strikes rescued a frustrating day, only for celebrations to reignite dialogue that has followed him through his career

It was just what they needed at just the right time. For a tricky first half and beyond, Elversberg had been a stone in Borussia Dortmund’s shoe, the promoted side not just keeping the home team at bay but keeping them honest, nourishing ambitions of their own. “The fatigue was clearly visible,” said the sporting director, Ole Book, to Sky after a week which had contained Der Klassiker in Munich and a hard-fought Champions League victory over Betis. “We were a bit too focused on managing the game, which was understandable.”

Enter Felix Nmecha. BVB have enjoyed a largely excellent start to the season, are unbeaten and level on points with Bayern Munich at the top; Bayern lead, unsurprisingly, thanks to their superior goal difference. It is a gap which has been widened by Dortmund being far from prolific, a facet which looked as if it might undercut their efforts to roll over their visitors on Saturday, especially in the absence of the injured centre-forward Serhou Guirassy.

Somebody was needed to break it open, and it was Nmecha. With two majestic sweeps of his right foot, two rockets from outside the area, he won the game for his team. His decisive moments of elevated quality pulled BVB away from their opponents when the game threatened to drift. “In terms of talent, qualities, and technique, he’s one of the best midfielders in the world. Add to that his finishing ability, and there aren’t many who are better,” Book beamed. That they go into the international break neck-and-neck with Bayern is all down to their No 8.

After scoring, Nmecha pointed to the sky, then mimed lifting a crown from his head and placing it on the ground. It was nothing new. He did the same, also in front of the Südtribune, the yawning, world-famous 24,000-capacity terrace in which much of the club’s hardcore support stand, after scoring against Paderborn in September. It was the same celebration that Nmecha used when he struck Germany’s opening goal of the World Cup against Curaçao.

The celebration is a nod to Ballers in God (BIG), the Christian group founded “to use the global platform of football to make Jesus known”, and in particular to their campaign The King’s Return. Yet this latest display provoked a response from BVB’s fan and support department. “When it comes to the values of our club,” it said in a statement the day after the Elversberg game, “discrimination, and the question of what kind of societal image of humanity is given space within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent.”

The German public broadcaster ARD has linked BIG to ultra-conservative positions on issues including homosexuality and transgender identity. “Footballers are role models for millions of people, especially children and young people,” the fan and support department continued. “If this reach conveys content that excludes certain groups in society, we cannot dismiss this as merely private religious practice. Where religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, our tolerance for intolerance ends.”

Reports suggest the club has been in dialogue with Nmecha since the Paderborn game, and a statement issued in response to Kicker’s inquiries said those talks would continue – while defending Nmecha. “For Borussia Dortmund, it is essential to take the concerns and needs of the fanbase seriously and to address them,” said the club. “Naturally, we also take the current media coverage and the associated questions and discussions very seriously.” Dortmund appear to have been careful not to use any images of the celebration on the club’s official social channels.

These issues and this dialogue have been almost a constant since Nmecha arrived in June 2023, as a de facto Jude Bellingham replacement. His faith had already been a key part of his social media messaging and, as his transfer from Wolfsburg neared completion, some fan groups voiced their opposition, pointing to Nmecha’s sharing of anti-trans posts by the American rightwinger Matt Walsh, among others. A bright yellow banner was hung outside Signal Iduna Park sprayed with the message “@BVB Steh zu deinen worten”, a message to the club to “stick by your words”. In June 2023 Nmecha posted: “I genuinely love ALL people and don’t discriminate against anyone.”

Dortmund’s motto, or marketing strapline, of Echte Liebe (true love), has been used in the last decade-plus to quantify exactly what makes the club special to audiences all over the world. What BVB believe elevates them is a connection with the fans, a mutual respect and understanding that goes way beyond what has increasingly become a company-customer relationship in modern times. Engaging with supporter concerns is important everywhere in German football and, arguably at Dortmund, there is a commercial imperative to visibly do so.

It was widely reported at the time of his arrival that Nmecha had a clause written into his contract that gave Dortmund the power to fine him if he made social media posts which they felt contradicted the club’s values. The club again had words with the player in 2025 after he posted a message of condolence to the family of Charlie Kirk (Nmecha deleted another post which said Kirk had “peacefully stood up for his beliefs and values”).

Hamburg 3-1 Mönchengladbach, Mainz 1-2 Bayern, Paderborn 2-2 Eintracht Frankfurt, RB Leipzig 5-2 Augsburg, Dortmund 2-1 SV Elversberg, VfB Stuttgart 1-0 Werder, Köln 1-2 Leverkusen, Freiburg 2-0 Union Berlin, Hoffenheim 2-1 Schalke

The difference now is that Nmecha, after a difficult start in Westfalen, has become one of Niko Kovac’s key players, and one of the most recognised in his position in Europe. He scored the first goal of Jürgen Klopp’s Germany tenure, and was linked with big-money moves to the Premier League last summer. So BVB must protect their present, in the sporting sense, their future, in the financial sense, and their very fabric, in terms of their continued relationship with supporters, already strained in recent years by their deal with the arms manufacturer Rheinmetall. For his part Nmecha has responded enigmatically and characteristically, quoting a Bible verse on his socials as a caption to snaps of the game. The one thing the club cannot say is that they never saw this coming.

Bayern remain on top but nothing is easy at the moment, even after their brilliant victory at Atlético in midweek. They closed out a narrow in at Mainz but Manuel Neuer was injured again, suffering a partial ligament tear of his right foot on the day he became Bayern’s oldest Bundesliga player at 40 years and 225 days, his sixth substitution in 2026. Whether he will – or should – return is now a fair question, with Jonas Urbig a ready-made replacement. Harry Kane provided assists for both goals to reach double figures in the category, his best-ever assist return in a season already.

The mood was not helped, however, by Uli Hoeness’ latest comments on Jamal Musiala, throwing doubt on whether he can recover his best level on the programme Der Sonntags-Stammtisch. “He’s still getting paid,” the honorary president underlined. “But imagine if FC Bayern were to say what he’s capable of now isn’t what’s stipulated in the contract?”

Even if there was another combination of the El Mala brothers – Malek setting up a goal for Saïd this week – for Köln in the derby with Leverkusen, the game had already been decided then, by a typically classy intervention by Patrik Schick.

A job that changed me: As a bookseller I realised reading is more than an insular pleasure – it builds connection too

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 14:00:12 GMT

I learned how to recommend the perfect book for a child whose parents were divorcing and how to identify something based on vague descriptors such as ‘the cover is orange’

Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email

I was in my early 20s when I landed my dream job. It was early 2018 and I had just started a master’s degree at the University of Melbourne, mostly because I didn’t know what to do with a bachelor of arts.

I had majored in creative writing without really thinking about a future career, certain only that I had always loved writing and reading books. But it turned out debating the pros and cons of Ernest Hemingway and penning poems about teenage breakups didn’t exactly land you a job.

So I returned to university, attempting to channel my hero at the time, Helen Garner.

Life felt listless. My submissions to literary journals were getting rejected. I was jumping from hospitality job to hospitality job while remaining terrible at hospitality. And studying media and communications was surprisingly uninspiring.

Then, one night, I went to a book launch at the Trades Hall in Carlton, lured by free drinks and its proximity to my house. There I met Christine Gordon, the programming and community engagement manager at Readings, the independent bookstore chain that was running the event.

I had emailed my résumé to Readings at least once a year since I had turned 16, without ever really expecting to hear back.

Bookstores had always been my safe space, my haven, and Readings was a cultural institution. I professed all this to Gordon, and instead of politely telling me to leave her alone, she said they could always use help with events.

With that, I was in. The shifts weren’t regular, but I was on the roster. Once or twice a week, I would head into the Lygon Street store and pick up boxes of books, an old computer and an Eftpos machine. Then I’d wheel it all haphazardly on a trolley to the event and sell the author’s books.

One of my early gigs was for Jordan Peterson at the Melbourne Recital Centre. I had no idea who he was and couldn’t understand why people were willing to line up for hours to get their books signed. At other events, I was often fan-girling, including when Helen Garner herself was among a group of speakers to appear at the Church of All Nations. She didn’t talk to me.

I had more luck at writers’ festivals, where authors usually had to sit with you to sign. Jimmy Barnes laughed at one of my jokes, but Irvine Welsh gave me the cold shoulder.

Sign up for our rundown of must-reads, pop culture and tips for the weekend, every Sunday morning

The events job eventually secured me permanent shifts at Readings Hawthorn – the same store I had visited almost weekly as a child. It felt like coming home.

I had some stumbling blocks, such as when I was given the responsibility to maintain the graphic novels section and, instead of arranging them in alphabetical order, as is custom, I created my own unique system based upon categories such as “feminism” and “coming of age”. But I made up for it with my whimsical charm (I hoped) and love of customers.

As much as I adored books, it was the customers who made the job so rewarding. One day a grieving husband who used to always visited the store with his wife, came in seeking a book to help him mourn. I recommended The Year of Magical Thinking and CS Lewis’s A Grief Observed, and we spoke about memories and of loss.

Elderly readers would often call up on the landline just to have a chat. For several months, we helped a man collect 100 hardbacks of his favourite books for his granddaughter’s 21st birthday. I will never forget him.

Our policy was not to bother people with chit-chat but let them come to us. If they wanted to sit for hours and leave without buying anything, that was OK too.

Then Covid hit, and suddenly the bookstore was shut for months. When we were able to reopen in limited ways, it was as though people had their sanctuary again.

Reading had always been an insular pleasure of mine, but working in a bookshop taught me about people – about connection and community that can be so hard to foster in large cities.

I learned how to recommend the perfect book for a child whose parents were divorcing, how to gently veer male readers away from sports biographies, and how to identify something based on vague descriptors such as “the cover is orange” (it was nearly always The Subtle Art of Not Giving a Fuck).

And I was changed by my colleagues, too, eccentric and wildly intelligent people – often writers or other creatives – who read voraciously and taught me about classical music, history and queer science fiction.

After a few wonderful years, my first journalism gig brought my time with Readings to a close. Bookstores, though, remain that sanctuary to me, and since leaving, I have dreamed, somewhat starry-eyed, of opening my own one day.

I still visit them at least once a week, and take pleasure in plucking books from my home bookshelf to recommend to friends. Whenever that time in my life comes up, I say resolutely: “That was the best job I ever had.”

‘Senna was Senna’: Wolff says it is too soon to compare Kimi Antonelli to F1 great

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 13:47:26 GMT

World champion idolises Brazilian who won three titles

‘He’s a Senninha and not a Senna yet,’ says Toto Wolff

Toto Wolff says it is too soon to compare his world champion driver Kimi Antonelli to Ayrton Senna but that the Italian may yet develop into a driver comparable to the Brazilian great whom Antonelli grew up idolising.

Antonelli sealed his first Formula One world championship at the Mexican Grand Prix and with a fifth place at Sunday’s São Paulo Grand Prix helped Mercedes secure their ninth constructors’ championship and their first drivers’ and constructors’ double since 2020.

The 20-year-old grew up watching film of Senna’s races, and was inspired by the Brazilian who won three titles before he was killed in a crash at the San Marino GP at Imola in 1994. Antonelli has adopted the No 12 for his car, in honour of the number Senna used in the early part of his career. He will retain the number next season, rather than adopting No 1, which is the right of the reigning world champion.

Expectations are high that Antonelli will go on to become a multiple world champion but in Brazil the Mercedes team principal cautioned that it was too early to be putting pressure on his driver to emulate a legend of Formula One.

“Comparing Kimi to Senna? I was always not very keen in having this comparison because Senna is a giant of the sport,” Wolff said. “Who he was as a person, who he was as a racing driver and I feel that setting these standards for a 20-year-old driver is a lot of pressure.

“That’s why I want to, how can I say, not compare him at this stage. He’s Kimi; Senna was Senna.”

Before the meeting at Interlagos Antonelli was welcomed by the Senna family at their estate and visited the Brazilian’s grave. He posted a picture of himself on social media sitting in Senna’s Lotus 98T, which the Brazilian drove to victory in the Spanish and Detroit Grands Prix in 1986 and bears the No 12. “I will carry these memories with me forever,” he wrote.

Senna’s niece, Paula, presented Antonelli with a sculpture she had made of her uncle and described her pleasure at seeing what “a special character” Antonelli was. Wolff said he appreciated how they had taken to the Italian, whom they called Senninha – “little Senna” – which is also the title of a comic book inspired by the Brazilian driver.

“It’s sweet to see that, how the Senna family embraces him. They say that it’s the first time that it looks like there is a second Senna,” Wolff added. “And that is the first time that you can say, OK, he’s a little bit like him. But maybe at that stage he’s a Senninha and not a Senna yet. So let the Senninha develop, let him become a Senna.”

Despite Mercedes clinching both titles with three races still to go and enjoying the quickest car for the first half of the season, Wolff does not believe the team are set to enjoy a period of dominance in the sport similar to when they won eight constructors’ and seven drivers’ titles between 2014 and 2021. Lens were humiliated by Como. The pain continued against Marseille

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 13:37:45 GMT

Pierre Sage led Lens to second and glory in the Coupe de France last season. A lot has changed in the last six months

The Lens striker, Florian Sotoca, was completely motionless as he looked into the middle space from the bench. The game, finely poised at 2-1 with a few minutes remaining, was not beyond his side, but that is not the story his troubled face told.

Marseille had just restored their lead thanks to a goal from substitute Keyliane Abdallah. Bruno Génésio’s men would go on to take all three points and continue their unlikely charge up the table, but the atmosphere at the Stade Bollaert-Delelis was morose before Marseille had even stepped on the pitch. The match did little to lift the mood at the end of a week in which Lens made unwanted history.

A pre-match banner unfurled by Lens fans that called the players a “disgrace” had not even been put away when a miscommunication between Jonathan Gradit and Samson Baidoo gifted Marseille the lead after 82 seconds. The former’s pass dribbled towards the goalline and was tapped in by Amine Gouiri from just a yard out.

It was a disastrous start for Lens, who recorded the joint-heaviest defeat in Champions League history last week. The 9-1 thrashing by Como was also the heaviest home loss in the competition’s history. Yannick Cahuzac, the Lens manager, called it a “humiliation”. The club’s president, Joseph Oughourlian, scrawled the words: “never again” inside the dressing room. Losing to Marseille on Sunday was not as chastening but the defeat posed more questions about the club’s recent decisions.

When Cahuzac, a friend of sporting director Jean-Louis Leca, stepped up from his assistant role in September to replace Dino Toppmöller, who lasted just six games, there were accusations of cronyism. Cahuzac’s stint so far has been a poor advert for the practice.

After three defeats in the league, winless in the Champions League, a derby defeat to Lille, a record-breaking loss to Como, and the wheels have well and truly come off at Lens; the jury is out on whether Cahuzac can set them back in motion. It was one of his former teammates, Florian Thauvin, who equalised for Lens against Marseille – his former club – with a close-range header. The playmaker, a harsh omission from Zinedine Zidane’s latest France squad, has been a rare bright spot in an increasingly gloomy situation.

Génésio said earlier in the season that these were the kinds of games Marseille could compete in but not win. But, as the French maxim goes, “le foot va vite” (football moves quickly). The tide has turned in Marseille; five league wins in a row have taken Marseille from the relegation zone to the Champions League places.

Génésio says his team’s fragile revival exists on “a knife’s edge”, however recent results – including a win at Bayer Leverkusen in the Europa League last week – have fed into growing optimism that his limited squad (both in quality and quantity) might avoid the abject season that fans had assumed was inevitable. The achievement belongs to Génésio, as does this win, secured by substitute Abdallah.

The academy product was banished to the reserves after his performance against Le Havre last month. Génésio criticised “a kind of lobbying around the young players” (from whom he did not specify) and held firm on his stance. He got the desired response. Re-integrated, Abdallah popped up at the back post to give Marseille a win that has taken them up to fourth in the table. They were second from bottom before the last international break.

Lens have replaced Marseille as France’s crisis club. After the match the home players did a tour of the pitch, applauding the fans for their support. In response, the fans unfurled a banner that read: “Shame on you.” Le foot va vite. Just six months ago fans packed into the Bollaert in the wee hours of the morning to welcome home their heroes after they had won the Coupe de France final. That feels like a lifetime ago for the players, fans and Pierre Sage, the manager who delivered that trophy.

“We are sick,” admitted Cahuzac after the match. There has been soul-searching but also plenty of finger pointing. Cahuzac says he “isn’t worried” about his job. Despite the growing pressure, he certainly has reasons to feel reassured but his friend, Léca, is also under a bit of fire after a second summer transfer window considerably less successful than his first. Jean-Clair Todibo, Thorgan Hazard and Franjo Ivanovic all arrived with high expectations but have fallen way short of them.

The fans had a banner for Léca, too, calling out his “shit interview” after the defeat to Como. They wanted an “apology”. They did not get one but it is certainly a sorry state of affairs at Lens.

Angers 0-2 Nice

Brest 2-0 Lyon

Le Havre 0-2 Lorient

Le Mans 1-1 Monaco

Lens 1-2 Marseille

Auxerre 0-1 Paris FC

Toulouse 3-1 Strasbourg

Monaco won their third game in a row in the Conference League last week, but their 1-1 draw at Le Mans was their fifth straight game without a win in Ligue 1. Filipe Luís says they need to “cleanse the minds” over the international break. When Monaco last won in Ligue 1 – against Lens in September – they were top of the table. They now sit seventh. The goals have dried up for Paris Brunner, Folarin Balogun – returning from injury – has yet to replicate the form that attracted Premier League interest and Matthis Abline put in an anonymous display against Le Mans. Monaco were reliant on a defensive blunder to open the scoring through Mamadou Coulibaly, who could be in trouble for a throat-slit celebration. Brunner was punished for a similar celebration earlier this season, although on that occasion it was directed towards the opposition fans. Le Mans, who equalised in the 90th minute through Erwan Colas, are also without a league win since September, but there was a strong show of support for manager Patrick Videira from the home fans, who also took a dig at the club’s unpopular football adviser Bruno Cheyrou. He evidently would not have popular support if he were to instigate a managerial change.

From cleansing minds at Monaco to exorcising demons at Nice. The club endured a shocking 2025-26 campaign, during which the relationship between fans, the players, and the club reached breaking point. It ended with Nice narrowly avoiding relegation to Ligue 2, thanks to a playoff win over Saint-Étienne. A new manager, Olivier Pantaloni, and a new sporting director, Roger Ricort, came in over the summer, but the players and Pantaloni continued to speak of the scars of the previous campaign. They showed in the opening four games, none of which Le Gym managed to win. Since then, however, only PSG have taken more points. Nice’s 2-0 win at Angers means they have picked up 15 points from their last possible 18. The club are now in European contention. Pantaloni is once again working his magic, just as he did at Lorient last season.

Trump is humiliated and angry – and Europe is where he’s free to lash out

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 13:10:43 GMT

The US president sees Europeans as the mirror image of his ‘woke’ domestic foes. They should brace for further betrayal this winter

Europeans have greeted the blue wave that crashed down on Donald Trump and his Republican party with jubilation and relief. Jubilation, because Trump’s second presidential administration has been the most destructive in the history of the transatlantic relationship. His disdain for Europe and his evident delight in attacking its governments – in particular that of Ukraine – have been hard to swallow.

Relief, because the midterm election results confirm that Europeans are not unique in being appalled by Trump’s actions: a large majority of Americans are too. I was in Washington immediately after the vote, and the mood was one of excitement and a newfound confidence. And like many Americans, in these results Europeans see hope that US democracy can be saved, American foreign policy moderated and the transatlantic partnership revived.

They are both right and wrong. Despite recent backsliding, democracy is alive and kicking in the US. The Democratic party, which for a long time seemed stunned and paralysed by Trump’s return to the White House, is bubbling with fresh energy and ideas. Its claim to be a big tent is no longer an abstract ideal but a reality, with a remarkable array of diverse and charismatic figures shining through – from the Christian progressive James Talarico in Texas to the democratic socialist Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who will be the first Muslim in the US Senate, and Georgia’s moderate Jon Ossoff.

The political power of a big tent is a lesson European liberals and progressives should heed, as many European countries head into crucial elections in the coming months facing strong headwinds from the far right.

The resounding defeat of Trump’s agenda – and in particular Americans’ stark rejection of the war on Iran, acknowledged explicitly by JD Vance and implicitly by Trump himself – could also lead Washington to soften its stance in the Middle East. Before the US midterms (and elections in Israel), the region had seemed set on a ladder of escalation; the Republicans’ drubbing could now force Trump to climb down. That will be good news if it happens. And European leaders, though largely sidelined, should do their utmost to encourage de-escalation by backing the diplomatic outreach of Gulf states such as Qatar.

But Europeans would be badly mistaken to think this mellowing will extend to US policy towards Europe and the war in Ukraine. Regarding Europe, the lesson Trump is likely to draw from the midterms is that his mistake – if he can bring himself to conceive of making any – was not being Trumpy enough, not lashing out hard enough at the continent’s liberal democracies.

After all, while Trump’s Maga base is sceptical of the Iran war, it applauds the normalisation of ties with Moscow and the withdrawal of support for Kyiv, and would be happy to see a more decisive US military disengagement from Europe. Trump’s decision to promote Stephen Miller to chief of staff points in that direction. While Miller has not played a prominent role on Ukraine so far, he is among the foremost proponents of the Maga worldview that might makes right. In the European context, this predatory approach often translates in the belief that Russia will (and therefore should) prevail. Over the past two years, Trump has humiliated and insulted Europeans, imposed punitive tariffs on them and threatened Greenland. In fairness, though, the US military disengagement from Europe and Nato has so far been limited.

Hemmed in on his Middle East adventurism, and having achieved most of what was within reach in Latin America – from the toppling of Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro to a string of rightwing electoral victories across the region, blunted only by Lula’s unexpected comeback in Brazil – Trump is left with Europe to lash out at. It would be surprising if he didn’t. While little can be expected from the resumption of Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, Europeans should brace for dirty tricks from the Trump-Putin-Xi Jinping trio, which may meet at the Apec summit in Shenzhen later this month, and from a Trump-hosted G20 in Miami in December. And it would be surprising not to see a further, uncoordinated US military pullback from Europe.

Trump and Maga have always seen Europe as the mirror image of their domestic foes: a bunch of presumptuous, woke, emasculated liberals. Now that those foes have made a comeback at home, Trump’s rancour towards Europe is likely to grow.

To imagine that the worst is over and that the transatlantic partnership will settle back to the good old days would be more than wrong. It would be delusional. The midterms may mark the beginning of the end for Trump, putting the US on track for a Democratic victory in the 2028 presidential election. But that road is long and strewn with obstacles. And even if a Democrat victory is achieved and the two sides of the Atlantic seek to pick up the pieces of their broken relationship, what they rebuild will look quite different. For a start, the US’s betrayal of Europe over the past two years can’t be quickly forgotten, but also the new class of Democrats emerging from this election lacks the commitment to Europe held by older generations.

after newsletter promotion

The transatlantic relationship can and will be rebuilt. But it will be narrower, more interest-based and less sentimental. Europeans should not look to the US midterms for a past to be revived. The time for transatlantic nostalgia is over.

Nathalie Tocci is a professor of practice at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, Europe, and a senior fellow at Bocconi University’s Institute for European Policymaking

Why is Nvidia’s Jensen Huang at the centre of a US-China row?

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 13:09:23 GMT

Donald Trump praised the chipmaker’s CEO despite reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish

Nvidia has launched an investigation into allegations that its chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been the target of a Chinese espionage operation.

Huang has admitted to having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who was reportedly central to the “foreign intelligence effort”.

Here are some of the key questions around the story, and its implications for US-China relations.

Nvidia, the maker of the computer chips crucial to developing and operating AI systems such as ChatGPT, and its CEO are reportedly the target of a Chinese espionage sting.

Nvidia has been selling its much sought-after chips to a little-known Singapore-based datacentre company, Megaspeed. US officials had been concerned that Megaspeed might have been helping Chinese firms bypass restrictions on chip exports to China, by diverting semiconductors – the computer chips that underpin most modern technology - to the US’s chief AI rival.

Those concerns about Megaspeed were first reported last year but the story became explosive when the New York Times reported last month that a Megaspeed executive, Huang Le – a Chinese citizen also known as Alice Huang – had developed a “close relationship” with the Nvidia boss. There were worries in US intelligence that Ms Huang, no relation to the Nvidia boss, was in fact a Chinese intelligence asset funnelling information to Beijing.

At the time Nvidia said its CEO’s interactions with the Megaspeed executive were “not unusual or unexpected” and the Singapore company had received “zero information relevant to national security”.

Then Huang admitted on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife.

In a message to company employees released on Sunday, Nvidia’s co-founder said: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

It is unclear how long the pair have known each other, but they were photographed together drinking whisky in a bar in Taipei after a technology trade show in June 2024.

Nvidia said it was “initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.

The statement added: “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

Jensen Huang said he supported the “investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company”.

In a statement to the NYT last month, Megaspeed said its “current leadership” took the matter “extremely seriously and is committed to getting to the facts behind these allegations”. It added that “outside counsel has been retained to conduct a thorough internal investigation and has notified the US government that we are fully committed to cooperating”.

Responding to reports last year that it might have diverted Nvidia deliveries, Megaspeed told Bloomberg: “Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company, operating fully in compliance with all applicable laws, including US export control regulations.”

Alice Huang has not commented.

Nvidia is a pivotal company in the AI boom, its chips being analogous to the shovels used by prospectors in a gold rush. It is worth $4.5tn (£3.3tn) and any serious knock to its value could have ramifications for valuations of US tech stocks, not just Nvidia. US tech stocks have been enduring a shaky start to the month after the success of anti-datacentre candidates in last week’s midterm elections.

“Nvidia is huge and at the heart of the AI supply chain, so what happens to this stock matters to the rest of the market. There is the potential for this story to knock sentiment, which is already pretty fragile,” said Neil Wilson, an analyst at the investment platform Saxo UK.

Dan Ives, a US-based tech industry analyst, said the scandal would result in “multiple congressional inquiries” and weigh on Nvidia’s share price.

“There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally,” he added.

The US president was reportedly briefed on US intelligence concerns about Nvidia a year ago, according to the NYT, and did not act on the information. He has been wary of disrupting a leading US company and his country’s already difficult trade relationship with China.

Trump said on Sunday he did not regret not acting on this intelligence. “No, I don’t think so. I think – you know, he’s an honourable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.”

Asked whether Huang would remain as CEO, Trump said: “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.”

Some other prominent figures weighed in on Huang’s admission. The billionaire investor Bill Ackman, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, said on X that the Nvidia CEO was an “incredible human”, but if “indeed this is more than an affair, then it is obviously a real problem”.

“I am hoping for a ​simple affair, not a risk to our national security,” he added.

Elon Musk commented “I agree”, on a post by the Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire that said Huang “did something incredibly dumb” that was “bad for America” but that “Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership“.

Huang owns approximately 3.6% of Nvidia and is worth $155bn, according to the Bloomberg billionaire index, which puts him in the top 10 of the world’s richest people.

The history of US-China tech relations is complex. US companies have long complained of industrial espionage, usually on the part of Chinese workers or academics with family in China, that makes them vulnerable to recruitment. The Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US thinktank, has tracked hundreds of instances of reported espionage, and says there are more than 1,200 lawsuits brought by US companies on the grounds of intellectual property theft.

However, US tech companies have at times opened themselves to this. Apple, for example, heavily relies on partners in mainland China to manufacture its iPhones – often because they were willing to do so at far lower prices than overseas competitors. These partners have in turn made profits by also manufacturing phones for companies like Huawei.

The situation at Nvidia may be raised next week, when Trump is expected to meet the Chinese president, Xi Jinping.

Under former US president Joe Biden, the US passed the Chips Act in 2022, a set of sweeping export controls designed to choke off China’s ability to make advanced semiconductors. There were multiple motives behind this: a sense of growing discomfort about the US’s declining share of the global chip market, a mounting sense of geopolitical competition between the US and China, and rumblings that AI might become very important, meaning that control of computer chip supply chains would be of greater import.

The Chips Act meant that most Nvidia chips – especially advanced chips – were banned from sale in China. Under Trump, this policy became more focused on cutting deals than coherent export controls.

Controversially, the president first banned Nvidia from selling H20s, a less-advanced model of chip to China, then pivoted to allow Nvidia to sell both H20s and then, later, the far-more-advanced H200 to America’s rival – all while the US government took a cut of the sales revenue.

Nvidia’s most-advanced AI chips – Grace Blackwells – are still banned from export to China.

Diversity, decency and a new south: who were the real winners in the US midterms?

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 13:00:10 GMT

Tuesday was a victory for equity and inclusivity and a rejection of hate and fear. The biggest losers? Megadonors and Super Pacs

Rather than regurgitate the particular wins and losses that occurred on Tuesday, I thought it more useful, at this point, to look at the big picture and identify the largest overall winners and losers for the country as a whole.

Biggest winner: a diverse, equitable and inclusive America. It’s Donald Trump’s DEI nightmare. Georgia voters elected Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black female governor in the country. Texas chose Gina Hinojosa, the state’s first Latina governor and first Democratic governor in more than 30 years. California elected Xavier Becerra, the state’s first Latino governor. New Mexico chose Deb Haaland, the country’s first female Native American governor. Florida elected Byron Donalds, the first Black governor in Florida’s history (a Republican).

For the US Senate, New Hampshire chose Chris Pappas, that chamber’s first out gay member. Minnesotans picked Peggy Flanagan, the first Native American woman elected to the Senate. Michiganders chose Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the Senate.

These are remarkable wins. Some are attributable to a surge in voting by Black people, many of whom were understandably incensed at efforts to push Black representatives out of Congress through overt racial gerrymandering. And by Latinos, enraged at ICE’s wanton arrests and detentions. Women upset by Republican efforts to outlaw abortion in their states. And LGBTQ+ people, angry about the blatant bigotry of Trump and his Republican enablers.

But many straight white men and women also disagree with Trump’s narrow definition of America. It turns out that the nation is far more diverse, equitable and inclusive than Trump or his Republican enablers want (or believe) it to be. They tried to make us fear and hate one another over our many differences. They indubitably failed.

Another winner: the new south. For as long as anyone can remember, the states that comprised the Old Confederacy have been regressive, conservative, intolerant and, at least since the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Republican.

No longer. On Tuesday, three of the four most populous southern states (Texas, North Carolina and Georgia) voted for Democrats up and down their tickets. Texas Democrats carried every statewide office from governor through lieutenant governor, attorney general, and even railroad commissioner. North Carolina and Georgia Democrats also scored stunning victories.

The biggest surprise was Annie Andrews’ win over Darline Graham in South Carolina’s Senate contest. As I write this, another possible gobsmacker: the Democrat Scott Colom may actually win the Mississippi Senate seat held by the Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Even Democratic losers in the south came remarkably close to winning: the Democratic Senate candidate Jamie Davis was within a hair’s breadth of victory in Louisiana. Florida’s Angie Nixon almost won the Senate seat there.

What accounts for this new south? Partly a large and growing professional class (in metro Atlanta, North Carolina’s “research triangle”, and Houston, Dallas, Fort Worth and Austin) combined with an increasing flow of young workers and their families from other states, seeking more affordable housing. Add to this, an abundance of Latino and Asian immigrants. All told, the new south is more tolerant than the old. Much of it is also more more educated.

A third winner: decency. During the run-up to the 2026 midterms, American voters were inundated with Republican attack ads, inflamed rhetoric, and personal smears against Democratic rivals. Those efforts backfired. Americans soundly rejected the politics of hate and fear, and embraced common decency.

Trump, JD Vance and RFK Jr did their worst to fuel Islamophobia against Michigan’s Dr El-Sayed. Trump claimed if El-Sayed won, he’d “invite hordes of jihadis to our shores”. RFK Jr baselessly linked El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood. Their fear-mongering obviously didn’t work.

Vance suggested that the Texas Democratic senatorial candidate James Talarico is gay. Another backfire.

Ohioans were so turned off by the Trump-endorsed billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad against his Democratic opponent Dr Amy Acton – using Acton’s mother, whom Acton hadn’t seen since she was 12, when her stepfather was accused of raping her – that the ad may have helped fuel Acton’s win, making her the first Democrat to win Ohio’s governorship since 2006. (Trump thought the ad was just fine, and Vance even blasted fellow Republicans who spoke out against the ad, calling their criticism “disgusting” and telling them to “stop whining” because “politics is a tough business.”)

Since Trump came on the scene, many Republicans have eagerly imitated his scurrilous character assaults. Such smears have become so common that we tend to forget that most Americans don’t particularly like this form of politics. They prefer Barack Obama’s tempered rhetoric and the late John McCain’s dignified and respectful way of disagreeing. Now, after the 2026 midterms, perhaps decency is back.

So who were the biggest losers? Besides Trump and his Republican sycophants, the biggest losers are the mega donors and Super Pacs that poured record amounts of money into failed Republican candidacies.

Top awards for strategic stupidity go to the crypto industry (which tried unsuccessfully to derail Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio); Aipac (which did everything it could to block El-Sayed and prevent any mention of Israel’s genocide in Gaza); the AI industry, which spent loads of cash trying but failing to allay voter’s concerns about datacenters; and Elon Musk, who sought, singlehandedly, to save Ken Paxton’s doomed Senate campaign in Texas.

Musk deserves his own special place in the loser’s circle. The richest person in the world became the poster child in the 2026 midterms for billionaire greed, legalized bribery, and corporate welfare. He sunk almost a half billion dollars into failed Republican campaigns, the most that any single human being has ever spent on elections – and for naught. After Tuesday’s blowout, shares in Musk’s SpaceX and Tesla dropped off a cliff.

Once they’re in control of Congress, Democrats will want to know what personal data and information Musk might have obtained when he ran his ill-fated “department of government efficiency”; what, exactly, happened with Ukraine’s Starlink access; and why the US government should continue to grant him an effective monopoly on satellites anyway rather than nationalize Starlink. To say Musk will be on the hot seat understates the temperature where he’ll be sitting.

In sum, considering the overall winners and losers from the 2026 midterms, I’d say America came out way ahead.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich. substack. com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

‘I’m surrounded by millions of people but I could still die from the heat’

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 12:00:08 GMT

Location: Mecca, Saudi Arabia

Disaster: Heatwave, 2024

This is Zirrar Ali’s story

After a transformative trip to Iran and one of its mosques, Zirrar started believing in God and writing about the soul of travel. Six years later, Zirrar and his elderly father were participating in the sacred five-day Muslim pilgrimage, the Hajj, when temperatures soared over 51°C. Temperature increases from climate change have made Hajj pilgrimages that happen in the summer, and even during the previously safer spring months, more dangerous.

By the age of 40, I had travelled so much that I was exhausted. I needed to be done with this experimentation of places and see the ultimate place, Mecca. There was always a pull to go back to the east. In my tradition, the only travel you were ever supposed to do is the great pilgrimage to Mecca. Abraham built the very first house of God in Mecca. God said to him: “Proclaim to the people the hajj; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every distant pass.” All souls go to that location; it’s a homecoming. Once I said I was going, my dad said: “OK, I’m going as well.”

A week before the hajj started, I flew into Medina and met my father. Medina becomes a warm-up. You learn the rituals and why you’re doing it. It’s regulating your nervous system to a different routine. It’s very peaceful. To protect you from the sun, they made special umbrellas. It has this coating for the sun. When it gets hot around midday, they release cooling vapour. Now you have shade and there’s water hitting you. There’s a deceptive feeling that it’s not hot.

At the beginning of hajj you go to the Grand Mosque in Mecca and do seven rounds around the Kaaba. It’s hundreds of thousands of people dressed in white, walking like a river and humming supplications to God. I remember covering myself with sunscreen thinking: “I’m going to be hot.” You’re in the open space, no roof, no air conditioning. But the weather was surprisingly cool. Maybe this is one of the blessings of God? I remember thinking: “How am I going to carry an umbrella and push my dad on a wheelchair at the same time?” I threw my umbrella away.

The second day everything shifted. The Day of Arafat. The most sacred day. You start from the outskirts of Mecca. Within two hours of the sun coming up, you start feeling the heat. As it got hotter, almost everybody within my group decided to stay indoors for some of the rituals. There’s a huge canopy set up, and they have air conditioning inside. They were sensible. I was stubborn. I didn’t want to spend this blessed day indoors because of the heat.

If your group hasn’t organised transportation, you have to walk between three places, wearing sandals. They’re quite close to each other, but because of traffic and lack of transportation, half an hour away becomes four hours. People don’t turn off the cars and buses because the air conditioning is keeping them cool. If you walk between buses, you get hit with the heat of diesel. Fumes permeate your nostrils, your skin.

When prayer comes between midday and 4pm, it’s peak heat. You can’t rehydrate or get shade. The heat quickly becomes dangerous. Volunteers give away cold water. I would get a bottle of water and down it in about five seconds, feeling like I’m going to pass out. I couldn’t believe how many water bottles were on the ground. The heat is so incredible, no one has the energy to talk. All you hear is stomping and plastic bottles crunching.

There’s a fight for any shade. There are people sleeping in the compartments where you put the luggage in buses. People are trying to find one little angle where the truck or the car will give you shade. That’s the difference between getting heatstroke and not. Elderly people are passing out under a tree or near the entrance of the mosques.

Normally when an elderly person trips on the street, everyone rushes: “Are you OK? Let me help you up.” Here, that instinct had gone. I saw people who collapsed in the arms of people that they love, realising: “Either I’m going to recover from this heatstroke or I won’t.” You see this resignation in the eyes. That’s the first time I’ve seen people give up on life.

In the places I passed, I remember seeing ambulances but no one coming to help. It just didn’t make any sense. What is their job other than to save people? A lot of people save up their entire life for the hajj and assume they’ll be looked after. But it turns out, here we are in the hottest place, and there’s not enough water, shade and doctors.

I didn’t want to lose my father. As an elderly man, to walk even a mile in the heat was dangerous. I realised I’m responsible for my father; I’ve become the father and he’s become the son. Because of the heat, I would leave him back at the hotel. He performed the essential rites himself. For others, I did them for him, as his son.

I remember feeling drowsy: “I just want to sit down for five minutes.” I remember thinking: “No, don’t sit down.” I’ve read about heatstroke. You don’t wake up from this. If I didn’t find shade, if I didn’t find water, I could easily pass out and I don’t think help would arrive. I’m surrounded by millions of people, but I could still die because of the heat. That’s such a bizarre feeling. My own weakness and vulnerability hit me. I remember my survival kicking in: “I need to just keep going, keep going.”

As the evening approaches, it starts to get a little bit cooler. About 4pm, I climbed Mount Arafat, near where the Prophet Muhammad gave his last sermon, to pray and ask God for forgiveness. Some people chose not to climb because it was hot, but I chose to. On the mountain, I look around and people are smiling, talking, praying. Hundreds of thousands of hands raised into the sky. Here, the heat is completely ignored. People have made peace with themselves, God, and death. This is the first time where I felt at peace. I’ve survived the hottest part of the day.

You spend that night sleeping outside in the open, on pebbles and dirt with thousands of people. We went from being very individualistic people into one cohesive body. At the start of the hajj, I’d seen people jumping queues to get on to buses and fighting. By the end of the five days, you realise: “No one else is going to help us. We have to help each other.” This is no longer: “I’m from country X, therefore I’m more eligible for this than you are.” You give advice, you give your umbrella, you give water. I realised this is what I came for.

Hajj is meant to expose certain pains in your life and you may feel vulnerable. You come back with relief. I watched some of the reporting about people losing their family. I remember feeling quite sad because I didn’t want the hajj to be a hardship in that sense. Historically, there have been many tragedies in hajj: overcrowding, cranes falling, rainstorms. But I’d never heard of so many casualties. These poor people are dying. Where I was, there wasn’t enough water, shade or medical help. Many of these deaths felt avoidable.

I don’t think climate change is something that most people pray about. But, opening your eyes to it, that’s important. In Islam, the world around us is full of God’s signs. Beautiful things point back to him. But we are losing his blessings. Even people who believe in climate change, you can sense there’s a nihilism: “I’m trying, but nothing’s really going to change. What’s really the point of this?” There’s very much a hands-off approach with everything. You say: “This is what God wanted.” But trusting God doesn’t mean doing nothing. The prophet said: “Tie your camel, then trust in God.”

This is climate breakdown was put together in collaboration with the Climate Disaster Project at University of Victoria, Canada. Read more.

Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 11:00:13 GMT

Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them

In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.”

With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field. They carried white lilies and all wore the same white shirts with a No 9 on the back, a black ribbon and the name of Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who died after a collision on the pitch five days earlier at the age of 30. At almost exactly the same time, 2,000km away to the west, Tenerife’s squad were walking out at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz. They did not have anyone alongside them, wore black suits not white shirts and did not have a game to play either, not this week.

Two days earlier Tenerife had been in Navahermosa, La Mancha, the tiny village their teammate’s family are from, carrying the coffin of the friend their captain called “our Demigol”. They were supposed to be in Granada on Saturday; instead, they were back on the island, in their home ground, to say goodbye and pay homage. Publicly, this time. Lilies had been laid on the pitch there too, a Tenerife shirt with them, and a stage built at one end. “We’ve seen how fragile life is,” the captain, Enric Gallego, said, offering words he said could never be enough, carrying the burden for all of them. “We think of the journeys, the wins, the losses, and hold on to those moments that seemed normal, but that now … a few days ago we shared that with you. To talk of you in the past tense is unfair. None of us are prepared to live what we’re living through.”

No one ever could be. Across Spain this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them. That, Budimir had told his teammates, was something they must think about but not think about too. The players’ union in which De Miguel had a role, a footballer there for others, had asked for the competition to stop. Respect demanded that it did, they said, requesting a judge intervene when the league did not hear them. But it had gone on. The only matches postponed were those involving Tenerife; Andorra, whose goalkeeper Jesús Owono had crashed into De Miguel; and Castellón, who he had taken to the second division, delivering them to segunda for the first time in 16 years and himself for the first time at all, aged 27.

On the eve of the game that opened this weekend’s fixtures, the Sevilla head coach, Luis García, said he thought they should wait. It was too soon, too raw, too theirs. His midfielder Giorgi Kochorashvili had missed training the day before: a former Castellón player, Kochorashvili had asked permission to go to the funeral, leaving early and returning late, his mind elsewhere. Of course he could, García had replied, “we are humans above all else”. And it was not just him. García had worked with Owono – “let’s not make two victims, we have had enough; he is in hell, for sure”, he had pleaded – and now he said: “If there’s a play that’s similar … what do I say to my goalkeeper?

“We need time,” García had said. “We need to reflect.”

Instead, they played. From Seville on Friday night to Madrid on Sunday, via stadiums everywhere. It was, some suggested, the best way to pay homage to De Miguel but no one truly knew. “We can’t ask him what he would have wanted,” José Mourinho said before Madrid went to Valencia and won 3-0, Tenerife’s flag flying at half-mast at Mestalla. He might not have wanted anything at all. “You never wanted any attention,” Gallego said, but this weekend he was on all their minds.

“Forever in our memories,” the league’s line read. At every game in the first and second divisions, the ritual was repeated. Teams came out together wearing the same white shirts bearing his name. Flowers were laid, a little uncomfortably, on the spot inside the centre circle where he had fallen and there was a minute’s silence, players and officials gathered around the wreath. As they stood before Cádiz-Oviedo, tears ran down the cheeks of the Tenerife-based referee Marta Huerta de Aza. On stadium screens, an image of De Miguel appeared. On television screens, a QR code did: a link to a crowdfunding campaign for the young family he left, set up by the former Tenerife player Fran Sol.

The games began and then, in the ninth minute or as near as the referee could manage, they paused again: the teams stopped, looking up to the screen, where a video of his best moments played out. It was not always an easy watch, and some preferred not to.

At Sevilla, where fans saw Antonio Puerta collapse on the pitch and pass away, applause still offered in the 16th minute every game, Kochorashvili stood by the bench, eyes lost somewhere his mind was not. At Espanyol, where in the 21st minute they applaud Dani Jarque, the captain who died during a pre-season tour and to whom Andrés Iniesta dedicated the winning goal at the 2010 World Cup final, Álex Calatrava and Álvaro González, teammates at Castellón and Tenerife respectively, looked about to break. In the ninth minute at the Metropolitano, the place was still rocking, the timing out of sync: Giuliano Simeone had just scored, so the referee Javier Alberola Rojas allowed a couple of minutes to pass, choosing his moment, Diego Simeone helping him impose silence on the stands when he finally stopped it. Then they started again, expected to carry on regardless.

In Pamplona, Alejandro Catena, who scored the late equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Athletic, raised an Osasuna shirt with De Miguel’s name and number on the back. Theirs was the game that felt most out of place, attention drawn from where it should have been, where it was. It would not be true to say that it did not matter, the Osasuna head coach, Jagoba Arrasate, admitting he had been carried along with it like everyone else, the calmness he thought they had found in the months out of the game soon abandoned again.

As they played, grateful for the grand day that they had before them, all the days they did, the tribute continued in Tenerife. The Heliodoro had filled early, access by every gate except eight and nine, engulfed by flowers and candles. De Miguel’s shirt lay on the turf where he had, lilies to one side, a spotlight on it. Another wreath occupied the bench. A giant shirt stretched across one end where the stage was, a lectern awaiting the speakers. A cross presided over it. Staff and players wore No 9 badges on their lapels. Supporters came in Tenerife shirts. And in the yellow shirts of rivals Las Palmas, whose president and captain Kirian, who had recovered after cancer, came. “This is the Canaries I want,” said Tenerife’s majority shareholder, Rayco García.

In the seats set up on the pitch, Tenerife’s players and De Miguel’s family sat, their eyes heavy. The archbishop, Eloy Alberto Santiago led a mass. The club’s president and majority shareholder spoke. He promised they would never allow María, De Miguel’s widow, to be alone. He also announced they would adopt Carla, his 14-month-old daughter, supporting her economically until she is 18. Gallego addressed her, football as family meaning something. “I hope one day you can look back and see who your dad was, be proud of him, not just for the footballer he was but the person: for his humility, his goodness,” he said.

Sniffing, his voice breaking, the captain paid homage to his teammate, his strike partner, his friend. The kind of person, he said, who did not seem to be there, and definitely did not demand that people notice he was, but always was. A man, he noted, so disinclined to put anyone out that when his car broke down he walked home from training rather than bother anyone for a lift. That, he insisted, might not seem like much, but it said much. “Today we don’t want to talk only of the player; we want to talk about you, Jesús, about the person that was behind the shirt,” he had begun. “Above any game, any team, what really remains is the person and the impact you leave. And you were a very special person.”

Gallego gave way to the archbishop, orations led by Tenerife staff, and as the act came to a close, difficult days ahead, the spotlight taken elsewhere, the drums began and the fans belted out a familiar tune, once more with more meaningful than ever before:

double quotation markWe have to sing with even more strength if you’re losing Even those who left us sing, from heaven This will never stop We will sing to eternity.”

Then Tenerife’s players departed. They have training on Monday and next week they play.

‘We did 10 takes of it!’ Kerr Smith on Dawson’s Creek and filming US TV’s first gay kiss

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 11:00:08 GMT

As he releases a memoir, the actor opens up about the late James Van Der Beek, the magic of the Creek, and facing homophobia for playing gay in the 90s

There are worse things to spend a couple of decades chasing than the feeling of being young, successful and surrounded by people who love you. For Kerr Smith, though, the particular magic of Dawson’s Creek has proved just about impossible to replicate.

“I’ve spent the last 25 years of my career trying to re-create that experience,” Smith says of the WB teen drama, on which he played the sensitive jock Jack McPhee for five seasons. “I’ve been trying to measure up to it my entire career.”

Speaking on a Zoom call this October, Smith is now 53, gray-haired and hatted with a brisk demeanor, Smith revisits that pursuit in his new memoir, I Don’t Want to Wait: My Life on Dawson’s Creek. Part oral history and part personal reckoning, the book draws on conversations with former castmates and colleagues, including big-hitters like Katie Holmes, to revisit the series, the protests that followed Jack’s coming-out storyline, and an episode of homophobic harassment Smith had never previously discussed. Highly rhapsodic and wistful about his experience on Dawson’s Creek, Kerr fully embraces the nostalgia in the memoir.

When Smith arrived on the set of Dawson’s Creek in 1998, he had only a handful of acting credits to his name, including a bit part in an episode of Baywatch and an uncredited role in CSI: Crime Scene Investigation. Introduced in Season two as a sexy interloper meant to stir up trouble between Dawson Leery (the late James Van Der Beek) and Joey Potter (Katie Holmes), he was getting his feet wet on set in Wilmington, North Carolina, with no reason to think the arrangement would change.

Then, about eight episodes into his run, creator Kevin Williamson asked him to get coffee. Smith remembers the invitation as ominous. “This is, like, two months into the job for me,” he says. “I’m thinking, ‘Oh crap. Am I getting fired?’”

On the walk to the coffee shop, he began to suspect otherwise. Smith had been thinking about how the show’s characters reflected different parts of Williamson himself: Joey represented one side of the writer, Joshua Jackson’s Pacey the jokester, Dawson the brainy one, and Michelle Williams’s Jen his wild side. But nobody represented Williamson’s sexuality. Still publicly closeted, the creator, Smith suspected, wanted to tell a story that would allow him to come out in some form beyond his family and friends.

At the coffee shop, Williamson confirmed his suspicions. “His exact words were, ‘Kerr, we wanna go down a different avenue with Jack.’” Smith’s immediate reaction was “holy crap,” though he kept that part to himself. He asked Williamson for a day or two to consult people whose opinions he respected. In 1998, playing a gay character on a hit network teen drama felt like a highly consequential proposition.

The decision transformed Jack into the center of the show’s groundbreaking gay coming-of-age story. It also made Smith half of what became the first kiss between two men on primetime network television in the United States, when Jack made out with college prep student Ethan (Adam Kaufman) in front of his dorm room in the third season’s finale.

“I was so nervous for that kiss,” Smith says of filming the scene with Kaufman. “We did ten takes of it. Ethan was nervous too, no matter what he says now.”

A director offered the actors a straightforward piece of advice: It didn’t matter whether the couple consisted of two men, two women, or a man and a woman. If the characters were attracted to each other and loved each other, they should simply kiss.

“He was right,” Smith says. “I thought about it, and I was like, ‘Yeah, it’s really that simple.’”

“There was a whole generation where that was a pivotal storyline for them and it was subsequent to them having their own coming out experience,” showrunner Greg Berlanti said in a 2020 interview. “It was nice to think that in some way we had sent a safety line to young people in a way that maybe hadn’t been there for us. It’s easy to forget about how valuable that is.”

Not everyone at the time was so accepting. Dawson’s Creek faced protests outside its Wilmington studio, and Smith remembers driving through crowds of demonstrators to get to work. He was frightened, though he found some reassurance in the fact that the protesters seemed to be directing their anger at the storyline rather than at him personally.

“I didn’t agree with the protests, but I respected that they weren’t actually throwing it at Kerr Smith, which was nice,” he says.

He tried to keep his attention on the work. “I put the blinders on,” he recalls. But the hostility wasn’t always confined to the studio gates. While filming horror film The Forsaken in Yuma, Arizona, around 2001, Smith returned to his car to find it covered in red graffiti, including homophobic slurs. He never discovered who had done it or how they had identified his vehicle.

For years, he kept the incident to himself. Writing about it in the memoir was the first time he’d put it down on paper.

“I had never mentioned that to anybody until I decided to write it down on the page,” he says. “As an actor, I like to be very vulnerable. But as a writer, when you’re writing about your own experiences, it’s a different thing, because it’s you. It’s actually you.”

The experience of writing the book also meant comparing his memories with those of his former colleagues. He came away with a realization: “One of the things that I learned is that no two people remember the same event the same way.”

During the show’s summer hiatuses, Smith deliberately sought roles that would put some distance between himself and Jack (in other words, aggressively straight). One was Final Destination, in which he played Carter Horton, a high school bully whose personality could hardly have been further from Jack’s. Carter, Smith says, was “a complete dick”.

He’s since lived a toned-down life, posting live-laugh-love-isms on Instagram and acting in a smattering of films and TV shows (including a brief stint in Riverdale, where he played, amazingly, the headmaster of a school named Stonewall Prep). But Jack’s story has followed him all the same. Smith was finishing the memoir when Van Der Beek died in February after colorectal cancer. Having already written about the cast’s September 2025 reunion at New York’s Richard Rodgers Theatre, a charity event supporting F Cancer, Smith added a final chapter inviting cast members, crew members, and friends to contribute short recollections of Van Der Beek. “I haven’t spoken with the cast again after his death,” Smith says. He hopes Van Der Beek would have approved of the addition.

More than 25 years later, the response from viewers has remained overwhelmingly positive, with a new generation of fans drawn to the show after it debuted on Netflix in 2020. People still approach Smith to tell him what Jack meant to them.

“The amount of people where that happens versus the negative things that happen is, no joke, a million to one,” he says with a proud smile. “People come up to me and say, ‘Hey, Jack, the storyline changed my life.’ I’ve even had people say, ‘I don’t know if I would be here today if it wasn’t for Dawson’s Creek.’”

I Don’t Want to Wait: My Life on Dawson’s Creek is out on 10 November in the US and Australia, and on 26 November in the UK

My son’s back home – and my mothering skills have gone out of the window

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 11:00:07 GMT

Like many graduates, he has been forced to return to the nest. How will he cope with my pigeon chat and dodgy dregs for dinner?

My graduate son has been back home for five months now. In this economy, he might be stuck here a while longer, meaning we’ve shifted from the extended holiday phase to a new normal. I feel like the William Munny of mothering – a creaky gunslinger dragged out of retirement for one last job, like Clint Eastwood’s character in Unforgiven. Having Seen Things and survived, I had settled into a dourly ascetic afterlife of silent staring and infrequent laundry, measuring out my life in coffee spoons of cholesterol-friendly flaxseed. How rusty am I at mothering? Will I go down in a hail of bullets?

Well, I can still wash, dry and fold multiple loads a week and ensure an uninterrupted supply of milk. It’s muscle memory, instinctive as breathing. I’ve lost other skills, though, like deciding what’s for dinner. I quit cooking the minute we dropped him off in halls in 2022 and wasn’t expecting to get my guns (guns = repertoire of five Meera Sodha recipes) out again. My husband and I have lost our conversational skills too, conversing in rambling, repetitive shorthand, and it’s unnerving having someone around to notice how much we talk about pigeons (constantly).

My worst old-timer trait? I’m realising that, to my shame, I’m a controlling curmudgeon now, with inflexible opinions about where things go, which bowls are acceptable and what should be eaten when. My son’s always catching me muttering crossly to myself as I move jars around, hide the pint glass I hate or re-sort the recycling. Despite that, I love him being here – he’s very fun company and extremely forgiving (except when I try to make him eat mouldy maple syrup). What an unimagined bonus to get extra time with one of my favourite people; shame it’s at the expense of his sanity. Here’s hoping Alan Milburn’s final Neet review works miracles and saves him and all his boomerang peers from more evenings of pigeon chat and dodgy fridge dregs for dinner.

Of course, when he does escape, as older friends remind me, if I’m lucky I might get another last job after this last job: grandparenting.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist
