Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 10:00:05 GMT

Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art

In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them.

After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong.

Yet, what’s interesting is that the studio’s ambitions were already straining against its cinematic influences. A cowboy adventure such as Red Dead Redemption might start with curated moments from spaghetti westerns – but the game itself would be eager to evoke everything from Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid to Warlock (the 1958 revisionist Old West novel by Oakley Hall) and the paintings of Frederic Remington.

Rockstar has since grown in stature so much that its newest game, Grand Theft Auto VI, had its first in-depth reveal in a Netflix special, with the added cachet of making Netflix’s own servers shudder a little on launch day.

So many video games deserve a place in the wider culture of the age from which they came. What are the 1980s without Pac-Man and Tetris? But with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this November, Rockstar finds itself in unprecedented territory. The numbers alone are dizzying. Grand Theft Auto V, which launched in 2013, has sold more than 230m copies, and GTA VI is said to have cost more than $1bn to make.

This is surely the biggest video game release of all time – one that has sent rival games rushing to find other street dates, and sent ripples through the rest of the media (and beyond). That raises a few questions. How did Rockstar get to this point with a game that initially explored the simple pleasures of running people over? What are the cultural touchstones ensuring GTA continues to fascinate so many people, regardless of whether they’ve ever picked up a game controller? And when it comes to art, where does GTA belong?

The first Grand Theft Auto was made by the Scottish developer DMA Design in 1997. Players would race around a series of fake US cities, stealing cars and colliding with pedestrians. The action was viewed from a top-down perspective and the tone was high-spirited, befitting a design heavily inspired by the penny victories of pinball.

Speaking to the Guardian in 2015, Paul Farley, one of the game’s designers, explained that there was no budget for a fact-finding trip to the US, and there was only one PC with internet access in the whole studio. “We’d come in on a Monday and say: ‘What movies did you watch at the weekend? What music are you listening to?’” Nonetheless, what can now be seen as the GTA experience was already starting to form. Here was a game offering freedom, a heightened sense of place, and sharp stabs of dark humour. The cars that players could steal had names such as Impaler and Mundano, reminiscent of the Culprits, Autocrats and Fiascos parked outside hotels in Martin Amis’ novel Money. Amis was already a useful reference in broader ways, too. As one online commentator said, Amis deals in “great ugliness described with surprising beauty”. That certainly sounds like GTA.

Grand Theft Auto 2 offered a polite expansion on these central ideas, but by the time of Grand Theft Auto III in 2001, the series was evolving. GTA III was the first game in the series to offer players a 3D world to explore, which meant the skyscrapers of Liberty City, based on New York, now rose overhead, while the pedestrians wandering its streets looked recognisably human, and reacted with horror as you sent them scattering.

The game was a gigantic hit, in part because of its references to films such as Goodfellas, and its promise of placing players within their own Scorsese movie. But the real thrill came from being in a world that had been so richly observed. GTA III was overwhelming.

“It’s real simple,” says Christopher Byrd, a literary critic who writes for the New Yorker and the New York Review of Books, and covers games for the New York Times. “I’d never seen an urban landscape rendered like that in a game.”

GTA III’s approach, setting crime stories in a detailed open world in which the player could go wherever they wanted, came to define the series’ 3D games – as did the cinematic influences. Grand Theft Auto: Vice City took the action to Florida and was heavily inspired by Scarface and Miami Vice, while Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, set in a faded, sun-lasered version of southern California, borrowed from hip-hop culture and movies such as Boyz n the Hood.

This ensured that when Grand Theft Auto IV took the action back to an ersatz New York, an increasingly thoughtful tone was not the surprise it once would have been. We weren’t playing pinball any more. The game now focused on the immigrant experience of an eastern European protagonist, approaching Liberty City with a weathered eye on the American dream. It was still a game that understood the subversive thrill of stealing cars and running people over, but it was as much a response to the “war on terror” as it was to the films of Michael Mann and his contemporaries.

By GTA V, the series had become something larger and stranger. GTA V has plenty of cinematic and even literary influences, ticking off everything from The Sopranos to the likes of The Serial, that glorious skewering of so-Cal obliviousness by Cyra McFadden. But by this point, these references to other media felt like a small part of the overall proposition. The simulation elements, which had been growing since players of the first GTA got into a car and changed the radio station, were now taking over.

The city of Los Santos had convincing traffic flows and a working fire department that would respond to any accidents you might cause on your road towards riches. Outside pulling off heists, players could make a fortune on the stock market or real estate. These things are all hustles, the game seemed to suggest, so why discriminate?

The sheer breadth of the games Rockstar was making by this point was intoxicating. Talking to Game Informer in 2009, writer and producer Lazlow Jones revealed that “one of the best quotes we saw was from a reviewer who stopped at the internet cafe and surfed the spoof internet we created. They said something like, ‘I’m trying to find the bottom of this thing, and I can’t.’”

But if you’re trying to understand the appeal of a series like GTA, the criminal element is still important. As Leslie Benzies, then head of Rockstar’s Edinburgh studio, told Digital Trends in 2012: “We do not sit down for design meetings and say, ‘Let’s make the most appallingly violent game possible.’” Instead, he explained, the team is drawn to worlds in which violence is everyday life. “People know that games are no longer all about eating dots or blowing up spaceships,” he said. “They can be dark and edgy and challenging.”

This approach will never go out of style. “We’re never not going to have crime,” says Geoff Manaugh, the creator of the “architectural conjecture” website BLDGBLOG, and the author of A Burglar’s Guide to the City, a wildly good read that explores the relationship between urbanism and crime. “The minute you have a rule, someone’s going to want to break the rule.”

Sign up to Pushing Buttons

Keza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gaming

after newsletter promotion

Put like that, perhaps games like GTA are perfect for exploring criminality. “I’m only using this as an analogy, but crimes [like bank robbery] are almost like an IQ test,” Manaugh says. “In the sense that you’re presenting people with things in front of them, and then you’re asking them to connect them in a way that results in this goal.” To Manaugh, these crimes are often real games. “You are playing by the rules in a different way, and you’re solving the puzzle differently. On that level, there’s no mystery to me why games and crimes go together.”

GTA V riffed on various real-world crimes, including the work of the Hole in the Ground Gang, who drilled into a Los Angeles bank vault in 1986 before escaping underground and have never been caught. But the lurid appeal of the outlaw life still can’t entirely explain the appeal of GTA. After all, games have been violent since people shot their first Space Invader.

“The [non-gaming] public imagines that these games are nonstop kinetic affairs in which you’re always doing something, robbing someone, getting in a fight,” Byrd says. “And people who spend a great deal of time with them know that often it’s the ‘downtime’ between missions: that’s what stays with you the most. It’s the aimless driving or seeing the mountaintop and going up there and watching the sun cycle for 45 minutes. There’s a possibility of dwelling in the world that I think is unique … the Grand Theft Auto games are so stuffed with incidental details and little pieces of gameplay that you can create for yourselves. You’re just enjoying the purposeless beauty of it all.”

This is territory that GTA has marked out for itself. “The closest phenomenological experience that we’ve had before as human beings … is that moment when you leave the movie theatre and the illusion is still in your head,” Byrd says. “You just saw Tom Cruise in a film, and when you’re walking out of that movie theatre, you’re walking … as though you have your own Tom Cruise swag going on. That’s now in video games, but it’s really only this one series that’s done this.”

Manaugh is not surprised that recent GTA games seem to be all but overwhelmed by their detailed simulations of the cities in which they are set. “There are just so many overlapping things to pay attention to if you go into a city,” he says. “They are just constantly laminating different types of opportunities [on] top one another … They’re lands of fecundity and promise.”

In other words, GTA may be making the case that the city is now an artistic form in its own right. For Byrd, this makes the most recent GTA games something broader than a video game that is influenced by cinema and pop culture. It puts him in mind of the gesamtkunstwerk beloved by Wagner: a work that combines a range of disparate art forms into a cohesive whole. “[GTA’s] more of a totalising artwork that is bringing everything together,” he says. “The music is as much of a pillar as the driving, the shooting, the conversations.” He goes on to cite an online post he read arguing that games like GTA are the cathedrals of the 21st century. “You have teams of the most talented people coming together to create this glorious work that we can all be appreciative of, in which people can find something of interest to them, whether or not they’re in the church of video games.”

Games such as GTA V belong in the context of those journalistic 19th-century novels by the likes of Zola and Thackeray that used the widest lens possible to capture a time and place. They’re the equivalent of Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser’s own favourite novel, Middlemarch. They’re the equivalent of Dickens opening Bleak House with that unimprovable one-word sentence: “London.”

Such a glittering constellation of influences helps explain why GTA VI seems to have something in it for almost everyone. It’s a satire, a toybox, a knockabout updating of Bonnie and Clyde and a surprisingly sincere love story about its two heroes, Lucia and Jason, who are trying to make a life for themselves in an unkind world. Alongside the usual run of cinematic references, GTA VI seems fixated on social media, perhaps a canny understanding that Hollywood’s biggest rivals are now TikTok and Instagram.

In the run up to its release, it is easy to focus on the game’s lavish variety, but to say that you can simply do a lot of things in GTA these days – sky-diving, off-road racing, manning your own taxi cab, annoying alligators – is increasingly missing the point. The point instead lies with the density of every frame: the fuzzy edges of exposed drywall in an apartment that has been hastily refitted as a drug den, the brisk splatter of blood that appears on paintwork when someone’s face collides with it. And it goes beyond these vivid details into the realms of things you may only vaguely be aware of. Fly over the mountains in GTA V and the game delivers turbulence in little bursts of haptic feedback through the controller. You may not even notice it, but afterwards you might notice its absence in other games. They don’t pull you into their worlds as convincingly.

But perhaps the defining characteristic of GTA is not its wealth of details, but the contradictions that these details inevitably allow to percolate – contradictions as deeply rooted as those of the country it explores. GTA is a satire of consumerism that has itself made billions of dollars. It’s an underdog story from a gigantic company that is now fighting its dismissed former staff in court. It’s about criminals who scare us, except for the odd ingenious bank robber who we might feel is sticking it to the man. And GTA VI aims to deliver a textured depiction of a modern relationship in a world where the restaurants have names like Effluvia. It’s a representation of the modern American landscape, from fast food to talk radio, that was masterminded by a studio based in Edinburgh.

Maybe these internal contradictions, and that clarifying distance, are what are truly vital about this game. “A lot of us are jaded by the pressure that digital life has exerted upon us,” Byrd says. “We’re jaded by AI slop and the fact that life feels artificial. There is some kind of great paradox that we shouldn’t try to necessarily explain away: this is the one piece of a truly grand simulated reality that many of us are really hankering for.”

Grand Theft Auto VI is released on 19 November

‘I didn’t dance until I was 45’: how Jorge Drexler went from repressed doctor to rump-shaking Oscar-winner

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 08:00:04 GMT

How did a Uruguayan medic who grew up under an anti-music dictatorship win a best song Academy award? As he looks set to scoop up more prizes at the Latin Grammys, we meet the extraordinary Jorge Drexler

It makes sense that a Uruguayan doctor turned singer would write a song that begins: “Long live science! Long live poetry!” Guitar y Vos (Guitar and You) is also the first track that Jorge Drexler performs this afternoon at a music industry event in the basement of Madrid’s Movistar arena. The second is El Otro Lado del Rio (The Other Side of the River), which he composed for the Che Guevara road movie The Motorcycle Diaries. Drexler was still largely unknown when it won the best original song Oscar in 2005, so was not invited to perform at the ceremony. In a classy act of defiance, he delivered a short a cappella version in lieu of an acceptance speech.

That’s how he sings it today too, solo under a spotlight on the stairs, before joining his band on stage. Backed by three drummers playing in the Afro-Uruguayan candombe style, Drexler turns a corporate lunchtime gig into a midnight block party. From his latest album Taracá – nominated for eight Latin Grammys at the forthcoming awards on 12 November – comes Ante la Duda, Baila (When in Doubt, Dance). While his lyrics list Spanish kings and colonial governments who have banned various forms of dancing over the centuries, the singer duly shakes his ass and moves us to do the same.

“I grew up in a society that didn’t dance,” Drexler tells me later, across town in the timber-beamed apartment that serves as his studio. Now 62, handsomely grey-bearded and youthfully dressed in very loose jeans with very big cuffs, he has lived more than half his life in Madrid. Born and raised in Montevideo, he spent his formative years under a civic-military dictatorship that was actively hostile to musicians, artists and liberal-intellectual families like his own.

“Dictatorships end, but their effects don’t leave your body so easily. It took decades to shake them out of my joints by making a record called Bailar en la Cueva [Dancing in the Cave]. You could say I didn’t dance until I was 45.” Drexler started out as a moonlighter, writing and performing at night while studying medicine, and paying for his own first recordings with what little he earned in clinical practice.

Fellow musicians treated him as a hobbyist, he says, and fellow doctors as a weirdo with an earring. “Working in a hospital, I hid my guitar under my white coat. Playing in a bar, I hid my white coat in my guitar case.” As an ear, nose and throat specialist, did he find himself especially sensitive to the acoustic effects of striking certain chords? “Well, I know my frequencies,” he says. “At a show I’ll tell the engineer, ‘Bring it down 250 hertz.’” He was already in his 30s when Spanish musician Joaquín Sabina invited him to play in Madrid, where he soon met his first wife, and stayed to make his way as a singer-songwriter, or cantautor – a venerable tradition in Spain but somewhat restrictive.

Coming from a background of Uruguayan rock, pop and candombe, he found that niche a bad fit, and sales-wise his early albums were “complete failures”. Something felt off until he tried to reconcile his romantic or poetic impulses with his scientific interests. Instead of singing about life in the strictly personal sense, he broadened his scope to the cosmic, and the biological.

“Life is also a molecule passing through a membrane,” he says. A song fittingly titled Todo Se Transforma (Everything Changes), and based on Antoine Lavoisier’s Law of the Conservation of Mass, was his first to “fully resonate”. “It was also my first to be anything like a hit.” He’s had many hits since, with songs about the prehistory of human migration (Movimiento), or the origins of love on a cellular level (El Plan Maestro). Both of those won Latin Grammys too.

The new album Taracá is a belated return to the candombe sound of his homeland, partly inspired by the recent death of his father, who escaped Nazi Germany with his family as a child. “So his life had a horrible start, but a beautiful ending,” says Drexler. The record also features an ensemble cast of Latin American players, from 74-year-old classical guitarist Julio Cobelli to Puerto Rican rapper Young Miko. In Drexler’s view, this may be the most important time in history for Spanish-language music, with stars such as Bad Bunny smashing down the gateway to the wider world by way of the US.

“The US is a bilingual country now. That’s what scares the Trump administration, and that’s why ICE exists, but I think it’s too late for them to stop it.” Spanish is tricky to write songs in, he admits, having helped Colombian megastar Shakira (“A genius”) to translate some of hers. “You guys have all these amazing monosyllabic words like bricks to build with,” he says of English speakers. “We don’t have so many. I mean, Can’t Buy Me Love sounds a lot neater than No Puedes Comprarme el Amor, no?” Drexler is still much better known in one language than the other, but he has learned that such concerns only get in the way of songwriting, which is already difficult enough.

A scholar of the craft as much as a practitioner, he will casually draw on Spinoza or Homer while talking about it. “The Odyssey was not a book, it was a very long song,” he says. And from the fabulist writer Italo Calvino he got the idea that the myth of the Medusa makes a useful metaphor for fame: “Look the monster in the eye and you will turn to stone.” He keeps his prizes in a closed cabinet in the corner, and tries never to open it. “The word for success is éxito in Spanish,” he says, “derived from the Latin exitus.

“It means ‘the way out’. In medicine, it’s our code for death. ‘This patient is going to exitus.’ And so, to me, success means the end of the process. But I love this process, and I’m not ready for the way out.”

‘My father loved Duncan more than he loved us’: the 30-year passion at the heart of the Bloomsbury set – and the family raised in its image

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 08:00:03 GMT

As the work of Bloomsbury artist Duncan Grant features in a major exhibition, Cordelia Roche reflects on her father’s decades-long relationship with the painter – as friend, muse, but never lover

After Duncan Grant died in our house, in Aldermaston in Berkshire, at the age of 93, I remember my father’s knees buckling and him falling to the ground. It was 1978, the end of their 32-year relationship, and the end of an era.

My father Paul Roche, a poet, writer and translator of Greek plays, seemed to crumble before my eyes. He was 61, a father of five, and I was the youngest. Duncan, the painter, designer and a key figure of the Bloomsbury group, had been his beloved friend for more than half his life.

Everyone in our family accepted the fact that my father loved Duncan more than he loved us. Not one of us was jealous, least of all my mother, Clarissa. We knew the depth of their devotion to each other and we did not try to compete. Our only way in was to share our father, and we did so willingly.

None of us questioned what kind of love it was. It was only years later, when I read the words “boyfriend” and “lover” describing my father in an article about Duncan, that it struck me how people had misconstrued their relationship.

They met on a summer’s evening in London in 1946, not even a year after the war had ended. They were both trying to cross the road at Piccadilly Circus. Don (his full name was Donald Robert Paul Roche) was on his bicycle. At the time, he was a Roman Catholic priest. His job gave him joy but he was living a double life, tormented by the restrictions of a sexless vocation. He would slip off his dog collar and dress as a civilian or a sailor in his spare time. He met women at dances and told them he was in the navy, wearing his sailor’s outfit that he had sent off for from a catalogue. As a seminarist during the war, he was ashamed not to be fighting for his country.

On this evening in July – dressed in a sleeveless shirt and trousers – he and an elderly gentleman in a dishevelled, tailored suit were bemoaning to each other how difficult it was to cross the sea of traffic. Duncan asked Don if he would like to see some pictures. My father assumed he meant films. He said: “Why not?” Duncan was talking about paintings, of course.

They set off in a taxi, bundling the bicycle in, and bought a bottle of rum along the way. Duncan took him to the artist Edward Le Bas’s flat in Bedford Square, which he was borrowing at the time, and which housed an impressive collection of contemporary British art: Augustus and Gwen John, Walter Sickert, Paul Nash, Matthew Smith, Vanessa Bell, and Duncan’s own work. This was the beginning of three decades of friendship and my father’s introduction to the arts. He was an educated man, speaking fluent Latin, and with a degree in theology and philosophy. He wrote and even spoke ancient Greek, but he knew nothing about paintings, and little about ballet or opera.

Despite Don’s classical education, Duncan became his educator and his inspiration. A few years later my father left the priesthood and became a writer, a poet and a translator of Greek plays. As erudite and brilliant as Duncan’s literary and artistic friends were, Don was fascinating to him. Different. Yet also familiar. They had both spent their childhoods in India, both had fathers who were officers in the British army, both had a passion for gardening. Don’s father, Robert Roche, worked as an engineer for the Great Indian Peninsula Railway. His mother, Roberta Arathoon, tragically died of smallpox when he was nine, prompting the family to leave India for England.

Don started modelling for Duncan the day after they met. He also briefly modelled for Vanessa Bell, Duncan’s artistic partner and former lover, the sister of Virginia Woolf and wife of Clive Bell. My father later regretted that he had not made more effort with her.

Before long, Duncan had fallen in love with Don, and Vanessa’s disapproval of him only grew. He was not invited to stay at Charleston, the Bloomsbury group’s famed farmhouse retreat. Once, he set up a tent in a field on the Downs behind the house and Duncan brought him food and drink. After Vanessa found out, they could only meet in London. He told me: “Duncan cared a great deal about Vanessa’s feelings.”

Duncan’s relationship with Vanessa became problematic soon after their daughter Angelica was born in 1918. My father told me: “It had become a huge ordeal for him. He was torn in different directions. He couldn’t give her what she needed.”

In a strange way, my father’s relationship with Duncan mirrored the one that Duncan had with Vanessa: unrequited love – or at least, unrequited sexual love – paired with an unbreakable bond. Over the years, there has been so much speculation about my father and Duncan. He told me clearly: “As much as I loved him, I did not have any sexual feelings for him and we certainly never did the deed.” In one of his letters, Duncan writes: “Why oh why is it worthwhile to go on loving you? I should like to know. But you won’t be able to tell me.” He ends another with: “Even if not loved your loving D.”

My father has been described as Duncan’s “muse”, but Duncan was Don’s muse in equal measure. He was his mentor, his educator, the inspiration for his creativity. It was Duncan who told him he was a writer. My father had not imagined he could be a poet or an author. Only because of Duncan did he have the courage to leave the priesthood, telling the cardinal he had a dentist appointment then disappearing. He kept his past vocation a secret from his family. It wasn’t until I was in my 30s that I found out he was ordained.

If all my father had desired was to be with Duncan, his life would have been so much simpler, but in 1953 he met Mary Blundell, the mother of my eldest brother, Toby. She got pregnant after they met on the Côte d’Azur in France. But my mother, Clarissa Tanner, a 22-year-old American, was already in the picture. They had met in Paris a year earlier – now she had returned. My mother also became pregnant. She and my father left for the US and married. My older siblings, Pandora and then Martin (Potie), were born.

Don (now going by his third name, Paul) found to his relief that his academic career blossomed in the US. After a book of fables, The Rat and the Convent Dove and Other Tales & Fables, and a novel, O Pale Galilean – for which Duncan designed the book jacket – were published, Paul was offered a position in the English department at Smith College in Massachusetts.

He was one of the most popular professors, alongside Sylvia Plath who was also teaching there, but when he received a grant from the Bollingen Foundation to translate Greek tragedy, he was no longer allowed to teach, so he left Smith College and he and Clarissa moved to Mexico, where my sister Vanessa was born. Although his agent warned him that there was no money in the classics, Paul pursued it anyway, keeping the poetic incantation of Euripides, Sophocles and Aeschylus alive with his translations. These books have sold in the hundreds of thousands and are still in print.

It was the death of Vanessa Bell in 1961 that brought my father back to England. During his time away, letters to and from Duncan continued: Duncan wanting him to come home; my father resisting. But with Vanessa’s death, Duncan’s grief was so acute that my father returned. Eight years had passed since they had last seen each other, and Paul was now the father of four children. A year later, I was born.

Duncan was like a grandfather to me. He spent every Christmas with us and was a kingpin of our dysfunctional family. When Duncan was around, fights ceased, tempers were muted; we would all behave civilly. He brought us such happiness. Clarissa was elated when Duncan was staying. She was her best self: charming, vivacious and happy, brimming with interesting conversation. My mother and Duncan developed a singular relationship, exchanging postcards and phone calls, independent of my father. Sometimes she would show him off to her friends – the clever ones who would appreciate him. Christmas was extra special with Duncan there. I have a watercolour of a donkey he gave me one year. Another present was a piece of embroidery. We also each received a five-pound note inside a card, a fortune in those days.

Then one Christmas, he didn’t come. We missed Duncan desperately. Forlorn, we children wondered why he had abandoned us. “He’s spending time with his other family,” my mother explained. It seemed extraordinary that he had another family. Did they love him as much as we did? Did he love them as much as he loved us?

Our family learned so much from Duncan. I never tired of observing him. He worked every single day at his easel, painting or drawing. I believed from a young age that being a painter was natural, accessible. Not surprisingly, my sister Pandora, my brother Toby and I all went to art school. We learned by watching him. And no place in the world was more inspirational than Charleston. It was a magical universe of invention. No door, stool, box or cupboard, screen, tray or fireplace had escaped his or Vanessa Bell’s paintbrushes. To a young eye, it set in my imagination the notion that design and colour could be anywhere and everywhere. Observing him, I learned to look.

Duncan and my father adhered to a clockwork schedule revolving round work and meals. My father was at his desk by 5am. Duncan would paint in his studio, listening to classical music. Mozart was his favourite.

after newsletter promotion

Towards the end of his life, Duncan was in a wheelchair. We all loved pushing him around and he was quite jolly and never complained. He was capable of standing, but getting on with painting was far more important to him than battling with the walking problem.

My father had stopped teaching at various American universities and came back to care for Duncan full-time. Sometimes he would refer to himself as “nanny” and there was a lot of teasing between the two of them. My mother hated the nanny thing, yet Duncan took it all in jest.

I learned from him the power of words, especially when I was tasked by my parents with reading to him, something I took great pains to do well. I particularly remember Anna Karenina – which he pronounced Kare-neena. He would ask me to reread passages, and on occasion his eyes shone wet. It is a novel about love, but it is so much more than just a love story.

We live in an age where people want to pigeonhole love. Familial love, romantic love, sexual love. But what happens when what two people share is the wrong shape for any box? I often wonder what made their combination so devoutly special.

Lover? Boyfriend? Muse? Companion? Friend? None of these words describe the essence of their partnership. Beloved is the only word that seems to fit. Don was Duncan’s beloved, as Duncan was Don’s.

After Duncan died and my parents divorced, my father bought a house in Mallorca. He continued to write as usual, poised at his desk before dawn every day, on an erect wicker chair as if depriving himself of comfort. He also went back to teaching in the US, notably at the Catholic University of Notre Dame. In 1982, With Duncan Grant in Southern Turkey was published, a journal about a holiday together in 1973.

With Duncan no longer in my father’s life, it was his paintings that gave him solace and pleasure. His walls were adorned with them: Don, nude, washing his feet, or in a pose with his back to the viewer. Don typing, reading or writing. Don as Christ ascending, larger than life, a companion piece to the mural in the Russell Chantry of Lincoln Cathedral. Don as Christ the shepherd, where Duncan’s depictions of Christ had been considered too racy. These works in Mallorca lived amid landscapes and still lifes, and paintings and murals by his children and friends, all of us inspired by Duncan.

There was one painting I particularly liked at my father’s house and I put it on my bedroom wall. It was Duncan’s first painting of Don, in Edward Le Bas’s flat in Bedford Square, right after they met. Don is lying naked on the ground, half on his side, his cheek pressed to the floor, an arm crooked, his hand covering his mouth so the bottom half of his face is obscured. It almost looks as if he is sucking his thumb. A rich red rug is spread beneath him, his mop of blond hair falling to one side. The colours are vibrant – complementary greens and reds; the background, so typical of Duncan’s work, as eye-catching as his subject.

Certain people commented that it was weird that I had a painting of my nude father in my bedroom. I simply saw this painting objectively, as a beautiful piece of art. To me it was not sexual or erotic but soulful. It was only later that I understood why: it tells the story of a young man in the throes of a new friendship with an older man who was to become the most important person in his life.

What must it have been like for Don to be introduced to a new way of thinking, to a visionary world? Nude and vulnerable, an artist’s gaze scrutinising him? Don was being truly seen. Perhaps he saw himself for the first time through Duncan’s eyes, allowing himself to accept the person he was. Even love the person he was.

Duncan’s art runs through my veins. His blue eyes, alight with curiosity, still live with me. Some faces fade, but Duncan’s never has. His discipline taught me that the act of making art was serious, even though the result could be light. Nothing escaped his gaze, myself included. At the age of eight, sitting still seemed physically impossible. Posing for a painter is hard work. “You’ll be glad you did this one day,” my mother told me. She was right. I am grateful to have been Duncan’s subject, his eyes on me and my skittish, childish form.

He continued to paint until a few days before he died of pneumonia at our house. I was away at boarding school but came home immediately. My father had kissed him on the forehead and bid him good night, telling him that God loved him. Duncan sighed, apparently, as if relieved, though he was not religious. When my father came back into the room to stay by his side, Duncan had stopped breathing. It seemed inconceivable that he was no longer with us.

Picking my father up, his trembling legs unable to hold him, eyes blurred with tears, I knew we would never be the same. Duncan made us a family, and now we were on our own.

Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury is at Tate Britain, London, 12 November to 11 April.

The hill I will die on: Nobody just ‘rustles up’ a lasagne

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 08:00:03 GMT

We need to give up this pretence of effortlessness and start calling the dish what it is: a laborious meat-and-cheese architecture project

What is this “rustling up a lasagne” thing – apart from a straightforward contradiction? Nobody ever says they’re rustling up a shepherd’s pie, or a moussaka, or a three-layered chocolate cake. But a lasagne? Sure thing.

I have a clear memory of the moment when, only recently out of our student years, a friend first pulled this misrepresentation out of her hungover hat. It was the day after a party, with a big clear-up under way and an agreed need for carbs. There was exhaustion, there were bin liners in hands, but she was busy “rustling”. And then, a mere few hours of laborious cooking and construction later, there it was on the table: the absolutely standard lasagne, in its “oh this old thing” white baking dish.

Decades later, the sheet-pasta extravaganza retains its reputation as an effortless standby, despite involving multiple components, careful assembly and a baking time long enough to watch a Netflix episode. You could be at the office picnic, an “everyone bring a course” dinner, even a wake, and people will casually announce they’ve made a lasagne as if they’ve decided to boil an egg, not committed hours to a meat-and-cheese architecture project.

“It’s no bother,” they add. “You can even buy the ready-made pasta sheets and do the cheat’s version. You don’t have to make it from scratch.” The relief. You’re still building the house, but someone’s delivered some bricks.

Few things make me more aware of my half-Danish heritage than the British talking about lasagne as if it’s the culinary equivalent of putting the kettle on. There’s an admiration, it seems, for effort without the appearance of having made any. I’ve neither mastered nor ever related to this.

Lasagne is the perfect food for this contradiction. It looks generous and impressive without seeming pretentious. It can be made in advance, which allows the cook to present the evening as wonderfully relaxed. By serving time the subtext is: “This? Just a lasagne.” No. You browned meat, chopped vegetables, made two sauces (we’re talking sauce on sauce), assembled six strata of carbohydrates and dairy and monopolised the oven.

There’s a generational angle, too. For anyone who learned to cook in the 1980s and 90s, lasagne was a “proper homemade meal” – you absorbed the idea that producing one was what competent adults did when guests came round.

Online searches tell me the first mention of “lasagne” was in 13th-century Italy, and that the word’s origins are ancient Greek or Latin, depending on the source. (A little more filtering brings up recipes for “next-level lasagne”: a new tautology for a dish that is by definition entirely levels.) But the cultural roots of the “effortless” myth is surely British.

The true miracle of lasagne isn’t the layering. It’s that we’ve spent decades persuading ourselves that a dish requiring project management, structural engineering and a cooling-off period counts as something you’ve “just knocked together”.

‘A new age of climate extremes’: Earth accumulating heat at accelerating rate

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 07:30:02 GMT

Increased heat will supercharge extreme weather events, warns UN agency as Cop31 climate summit begins

Heat is accumulating in Earth’s systems at an accelerating rate, the UN’s weather agency has reported as the Cop31 climate change summit begins in Turkey, with 2026 on track to be one of the four warmest years on record.

The imbalance between incoming energy from the sun and energy leaving Earth reached its highest level since monitoring began, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in its State of the Global Climate update.

That imbalance and the accumulation of heat will supercharge extreme weather events such as heatwaves, droughts and tropical cyclones.

Around the world, the average surface temperature for January to September 2026 was about 1.47C above the preindustrial average, the agency said. Sea surface temperatures hit monthly records and sea level was the highest since records began. The ocean absorbs 90% of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases and 2026 is on track to be a 10th successive year of record ocean heat.

“We have entered a new age of climate extremes,” said António Guterres, the UN secretary general. “A supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising. And those least responsible are suffering first and worst.”

Diplomats and world leaders are meeting on Monday in the Turkish resort city of Antalya for the 31st conference of the parties (Cop) to the UN framework convention on climate change. In 1992, when the convention was signed, the atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide, the primary greenhouse gas, was 356.42 parts per million (ppm). In 2025 it was 426.8 ppm, the WMO said. Overall, since 1750, the onset of the Industrial Revolution, the concentration has increased 53%.

The WMO reported that ocean heat content estimates indicate Earth’s energy imbalance rose at a rate of 0.3W per sq metre each decade for the period 2001–2025, compared with 0.13W per sq metre between 1960 and 2025.

Accordingly, 2026 is on track to be one of the four warmest years on record globally, making 2023 to 2026 the four warmest years since records began.

The year started with La Niña conditions in the Pacific, which typically act as a brake on global temperatures, lowering the average by about 0.1-0.2C. A brewing El Niño, a phenomenon that warms global temperatures, and whose latest iteration is forecast to be stronger than any to have taken place in the past 1,000 years, makes it likely that the final mean temperature for 2026 will be higher than 1.47C above the pre-industrial average.

Heat in the upper 2,000 metres (6,500ft) of the ocean in 2025 was the highest in the observed record and was accelerating, the WMO said. “This warming is projected to continue, representing a change that is irreversible on centennial to millennial timescales,” according to the report.

after newsletter promotion

At the poles, Antarctic sea ice reached its third-lowest annual maximum ever in 2026, while the Arctic maximum was the lowest or second lowest. Elsewhere in the cryosphere, glaciers lost more than 400 gigatonnes of mass. It was the fourth consecutive year in which all 19 glacierised regions around the world experienced mass loss, the WMO said.

Bill McGuire, a professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at University College London, said there were “no surprises” from the report, “to the extent that every measure reported, whether it be global temperature, sea level rise or sea ice extent, points to the fact that we are in deep shit”.

He said: “Of most concern is the growing imbalance between the incoming energy from the sun and that leaving the planet. Increasing greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere mean that while the heat coming in stays the same, that going out is steadily decreasing as our world hangs on to more and more of it.

“It is this growing imbalance – rather than just emissions – that most accurately tracks global heating and how quickly our planet will continue to heat up in the decades to come. This is because natural feedbacks are now coming into play that are driving up the temperature more rapidly than 20 years ago.

“The latest research suggests we will cross the 1.5C limit permanently in 2028, and with the planet now heating at an extraordinary rate of 0.4C a decade, we can expect to smash through 2C in the late 2030s.

“The widely publicised idea that we are still on track for 2.6-2.8C by the end of the century now seems wildly optimistic, if not downright impossible.”

‘It’s a feeling of being screwed over’: once-quiet village despairs over ‘monster’ warehouse

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 07:00:03 GMT

Residents of Astley in Greater Manchester will tell public inquiry next week of ‘cacophony’ of noise causing sleep deprivation and depression

When Stephen Retford retired from the police in 2006, he looked forward to a quiet life after nearly three decades catching villains. But now the former detective has landed another big case – one that is extremely close to home.

“It’s the total injustice of it,” the 70-year-old seethed, staring up at the 18-metre-high mega-warehouse that looms over the quiet village of Astley in Greater Manchester. Residents are up in arms about the “monster” construction, likening it to having a “cruise ship in our back garden”.

Andy Burnham expressed concern over the development weeks before he became prime minister, and Bev Craig, his successor as Greater Manchester mayor, said she too was concerned. “Old industry wouldn’t have got that close to your house,” she said. “So why is it that new industry can?”

This week, villagers will attempt to block plans by Whistl, the distribution firm that operates the warehouse, to use dozens of HGVs and trailers for its round-the-clock operation. In a two-day public inquiry, they will describe how the “cacophony” of noise is already driving some to sleep deprivation and depression.

“It’s had a profound impact on the neighbourhood,” said Retford, a burly man with a booming voice who after so many years in the police is not easily shaken. “The noise wakes you up at 2am and you can’t get back to sleep. We’ve not had a proper night’s sleep in well over a year. It’s a living hell.”

This once-quiet village is now on the frontline in a nationwide fightback against superstructures springing up everywhere from Devon to Cardiff and the Scottish Borders. Plans were announced last week for Britain’s largest datacentre at the site of the Drax power plant in North Yorkshire, and a further 315 “hyperscale” datacentres are queueing to connect to the National Grid.

Down the road from Retford’s house, a woman looked out of her daughter’s bedroom window at the Whistl warehouse just metres away. The woman, a police officer who does not want to be named, said her 10-year-old son, who is autistic, refused to play in the garden because of the “continuously whirring” noise of the conveyor belts. Her eight-year-old daughter has become too scared to play in her bedroom.

“As soon as she comes home from school, those blinds will be shut because she doesn’t want anyone to see in,” she said, pointing to a CCTV camera on the warehouse facing their home. “She hates it. She does get scared about it.”

Like many of their neighbours, the woman and her husband moved to Astley before plans had been submitted by a firm part-owned by Peel Group, one of Britain’s biggest landowners, run by the billionaire John Whittaker.

Back then, they were surrounded by farmland where lambs, cows and horses grazed. Now their view is a giant hunk of grey steel that was named the worst new building in the UK this year. “It was a lovely view, so secluded,” she said. “When we saw the structure of this, it was like: oh my God, what is this?”

As mayor, Burnham said earlier this year that the development had not been managed properly and that key things “should have been done differently”. Wigan council said it acted properly in approving the superstructure despite objections from the local MP and dozens of residents. However, the council’s leader, Labour’s Nazia Rehman, admitted last month that “some lessons have been learned” and said that in future “consultations [with residents] will be proactive”. Local leaders have scrapped plans for four other giant warehouses in response to the backlash.

Helen Halbous, who moved to the estate seven years ago, said: “It’s a feeling of being screwed over by Wigan council, having been born and brought up here. People who had a voice of power [in the council] either made this awful decision or they looked away and let it happen. It was a little mining village and now we’re this industrial centre. It’s so wrong.”

Halbous, 47, said she and her partner, Sami Halbous, now felt trapped in a house they once loved and they feared they would be unable to sell up. “A neighbour had their home valued and they lost 30%, and that’s if they can sell,” she said.

Residents felt hoodwinked about the size of the structure and its closeness to their homes, Halbous said. “The plan in 2019 was it was to be used for employment. It was never to have an 18-metre-high warehouse. Those permissions were changed [before 2024] and changed really quietly. We wouldn’t have bought here and let ourselves get trapped like this.”

PLP, the land owner, said the size and scale of the buildings had not changed since its planning application in 2023. It said earlier plans for smaller units, submitted in 2017 by Peel, one of its biggest shareholders, had since lapsed.

Wigan council said it recognised the “strength of feeling in the community and do not underestimate the impact residents tell us the development has had on them”. It said an independent review found its planning process was “legally sound” and followed national guidelines but there were “lessons around engagement and transparency”. It said: “We have acknowledged those findings and have taken steps to improve our approach.”

Whistl, which began operating at the site in July, has responded to the concerns by promising to use quieter vehicles and stopping their use outside between midnight and 6am. The firm said it took residents’ concerns seriously and was “committed to meeting its licensing responsibilities and being a good neighbour”. A Whistl spokesperson said the noise mitigation measures would remain in place and the overnight pause on activity in the yard would continue while all parties tried to “identify a sustainable, long-term solution”.

Retford became so fed up with the disturbance that he began overnight observations to track the big vehicles clanking around near his home. He commissioned independent acoustics experts to produce a sound report, convinced that the “cacophony of rolling thunder, a booming sound”, breached regulations.

A fightback fund launched by residents has so far raised £78,000, much of which will be spent on lawyers for next week’s public inquiry.

For Retford and his wife, Carole, 71, the impact has been huge. “Bloody hell, there’s not a lot of things I’ve not seen in my life,” he said. “I don’t get easily shocked and I’m not a flaky character, but this has had a profound effect on me. We’re not fuddy-duddies or nimbies. This is big business riding over the little people like us, saying ‘screw the lot of you’.”

Retford and his wife have spoken to their doctor about sleep deprivation. “It’s a torture for a very good reason, because it just drains you – and that is the effect it’s having on us,” he said.

Carole became close to tears. Staring up at the warehouse, she said: “It’s changed our lives. Your moods go up and down to being very depressed and very emotional about it because there’s no way out at the minute. People use the ‘depression’ word too lightly, but if you feel there’s no way out, it does get to you.”

British people don’t trust Palantir – it’s not too late to reverse the NHS’s dependence on it

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 06:00:02 GMT

We can’t allow our health data to be locked into the control of a US tech firm. It won’t be easy, but next spring the job of clawing it back must begin

Ben Coleman is Labour MP for Chelsea and Fulham and a member of the health and social care committee

Next March, Palantir’s £330m contract to run NHS England’s federated data platform (FDP) ends. Ministers must decide by Christmas whether to extend it. They should move on from Palantir, and transition to new suppliers that put the NHS in full control of its technology and patient data.

I sit on the health and social care committee. In June, we recommended no extension – people don’t trust Palantir, its benefits are contested and other tools could deliver the same or similar advantages. The debate so far has been whether to drop Palantir. The harder question is what replaces it. The tempting solution is to hire a single British firm. But that would not give the NHS the control it lacks: the freedom to switch supplier without losing what it has built.

Currently, NHS teams build applications on Palantir’s software platform. The NHS owns the applications and rents the platform. The aim is to join up hospital data to manage waiting lists, plan operations and get patients home. We need clarity about what will happen if the Palantir contract ends. How easy would it be to move the applications to another supplier? Will there be disruption that affects patient care?

Ministers assure me the NHS is not locked into Palantir’s service. Local NHS data teams, British tech firms and thinktanks tell me they are not convinced. A ministerial response to the committee in August left questions open. It said the NHS owned, or had a right to use, the applications built on the platform, but that some arrangements would end with the contract. It did not say which. Owning your applications is useless if they won’t work elsewhere.

It also said the government would explore how to move the applications on to a different platform only if the contract ended, and it declined to audit which Palantir tools hospital trusts depend on. Surely ministers need to know this now?

The NHS’s dependence on Palantir worries the national data guardian, too. She told ministers this month that “concerns about interoperability, vendor lock-in and data sovereignty must be addressed”, including by considering open standards. Open standards are shared, published rules for how health information is recorded and labelled, so that software from different suppliers can work together, much as any UK plug fits any UK socket.

In an FDP based on national open standards, regions could choose their own suppliers to build the software they need, from in-house NHS developers to small British firms. Data would stay with each region and be shared only under strict permissions. Suppliers could be swapped without starting again.

Britain has the skills to do this. Nigel Shadbolt, co-founder of the Open Data Institute, told our committee there is “nothing to suggest that the UK lacks the talent or capability to produce an equivalent to what Palantir offers”. For example, Greater Manchester’s integrated care board already runs its own analytics platform, while NHS OneLondon joins up patient records across the capital.

It is not too late to reverse the dependence on Palantir. The Guardian reported recently that 16 trusts and health boards say they do not use the platform. Some tried it and reverted to old systems. The British Medical Journal says a third of signed-up trusts have never logged in and many barely use it. The case for change is about more than avoiding lock-in. A data platform works only if patients trust it, yet mistrust of Palantir means opt-outs are growing.

The FDP’s benefits are also uncertain. Palantir claims a 14% fall in discharge delays, but the Health Foundation has found no noticeable change. Just one trust, Chelsea and Westminster in my constituency, accounts for 84% of the claimed national cut in outpatient waiting lists. Even NHS England now says cause and effect are unproven. I’ve asked its chief executive, Jim Mackey, why it lets Palantir claim otherwise.

A full evaluation is not due until 2029. Mackey told our committee that an independent review now would be “helpful and necessary” but could not be done before the decision.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Then there is sovereignty. Britain needs to be able to build and control its own health tech, including AI, and not leave the NHS dependent on a US company.

Could an open system be ready by March? Probably not. So ministers should agree only a short transition, on new terms, while it is built. That transition should do four things. Freeze new applications on Palantir’s platform. Run it for at most two years, with leaving made easier over time. Publish what the FDP does and costs, which tools trusts depend on and how an exit would work so others can bid. And make Palantir prove there is no lock-in by moving one application off the platform within a year.

Beyond the FDP, the planned single patient record, which will bring each person’s health records together, must be open, too, or it will tie the NHS to a single supplier on a far larger scale.

Data sovereignty means more than keeping health data on British soil. If Britain wants sovereign AI in health, it needs a system it controls. A British Palantir would not give it that. Open standards would.

Ben Coleman is Labour MP for Chelsea and Fulham and a member of the health and social care committee

Democrats to attend Cop31 climate talks boosted by midterms and eager to make up for Trump-era setbacks

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 06:00:01 GMT

US government will have no official presence at UN’s annual climate summit, this year’s Cop31 held in Antalya, Turkey

The US will be absent from key UN climate talks that start on Monday, a further sign of Donald Trump’s scornful dismissal of the climate crisis. But Democrats’ crushing win in the US midterm elections has delivered a timely shot of optimism to countries now looking beyond the Trump era of climate obstruction.

For the second year in a row, there will be no official US government presence at the annual climate summit, this year known as Cop31 and held in Antalya, Turkey. While almost every other country in the world sends delegations to the talks, Trump has derided the climate crisis as a “hoax” and “bullshit” and triggered the withdrawal of the US from the entire international climate framework.

“This summit rejects reality by failing to acknowledge that extremist climate policies are destroying countries around the world,” a White House official said, confirming that the administration would not send anyone to Cop31.

The snub is so severe that about 20 members of the US Congress heading to the summit have been denied usual state department assistance, requiring them to turn to philanthropic funding for the trip. “I’m glad we found a way to get there, but it is insane,” said Sean Casten, a Democratic congressman who is attending Cop31. “We have a lot of rebuilding to do. It hinges on Congress to maintain diplomatic continuities at Cop and minimize the damage until adults are back in the White House.”

Trump’s active support of fossil fuels, evisceration of pollution limits and throttling of clean energy projects has caused the US to become an outlier among wealthy countries, a recent UN report found. While all the other 20 major economies reduced or slowed their carbon pollution last year, the US was a “major exception” by emitting an extra 133m tons of planet-heating gases from the burning of coal, oil and gas, the report states.

Despite the world rapidly surging past “safe” temperature thresholds because of such pollution, and escalating heatwaves, floods, droughts and other calamities, Trump has remained defiant. “If you don’t get away from this green scam, your country is going to fail,” the US president told other world leaders at the UN last year, adding that the climate crisis was “the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world”.

But the Democrats’ stunning success in the midterms last week, wresting control from Trump’s Republicans in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, has buoyed delegates gathering in Antalya. While this will be the last Cop with the US as an official party, after Trump exited the UN framework, the midterms have raised international confidence of a looming return and new, post-Trump chapter.

“This marks the beginning of the end of the Trump era,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa. “His grip on Congress has been broken and hopefully paves the way for a Democratic president in two years. For everyone fighting for a livable planet, this is a moment of renewed hope.”

Trump has done “enormous damage” to the climate but the midterms results, along with Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s recent electoral victory in Brazil, provides a major tonic, Adow said. “It opens the door to America returning to the climate fight with the seriousness its responsibility demands,” he said, adding that Cop31 would be the “perfect time to accelerate climate action and turn the tide on the Trump dark ages”.

US lawmakers arriving at Cop, all of them Democrats, are aware the world has long been subjected to wildly erratic US commitment to climate action, Casten acknowledged. “We go in with a fair amount of humility – as important as we are, the US has been an extremely unreliable partner on climate,” he said. “But going to Cop on the heels of these results feels a lot better. It can be a much more positive process now.”

Spanning two weeks of negotiations among 197 countries with an accompanying trade show-like jamboree of pavilions and side events interspersed by protests, the sprawling Cop process requires a sense of momentum. The electoral revolt in the US, the world’s largest historical emitter of greenhouse gases, should provide such a fillip, according to Susan Biniaz, a former longtime climate negotiator for the US at Cop.

“Much of the world is looking to the midterms for some kind of signal from the US electorate that they are unhappy with this administration,” Biniaz said. “This could elevate the mood. I don’t think the midterm elections will directly affect federal climate policy but they will help the spirit of the Cop.”

“There’s been a big shift since the midterms. I’m certainly more optimistic,” said Catherine McKenna, former environment minister of Canada. “Negotiations at Cop are important but it’s more important what happens at home and Trump has been incredibly disruptive. We will now have more Democrats acting on climate and talking about the solutions that will actually save people money.”

But what will a thumping Democratic majority in Congress be able to do on climate? Sweeping climate legislation, similar in scale to the Inflation Reduction Act signed by Joe Biden that was subsequently gutted by Republicans, is not likely given Trump’s veto power. Still, Democrats are exploring other avenues.

Investigative and subpoena powers will be used to probe parts of the administration, such as the Environmental Protection Agency, over staff cuts and what Democrats call the “unlawful” withholding of climate and clean energy spending. Trump’s attempt to pressure Europe into taking US gas will be scrutinized, as will the vulnerability of the insurance industry to the climate crisis and concerns over the US ceding clean tech industries to China.

Democrats will dominate the budget process and will likely reverse funding cuts to environmental programs and rein in datacenters, which have become highly contentious with the US public.

Some legislation, such as the speeding up of the permitting process to allow new clean energy production and transmission, may be possible with Republican support too. The midterms also delivered striking Democratic wins at the state level, bringing new governors to states such as Texas and Georgia, meaning widespread state-based action to shift away from fossil fuels will be possible.

Much of this will likely be framed as helping tackle the rising cost of living or government corruption, rather than the climate crisis itself. Some activists have criticized Democrats for so-called “climate hushing” even as most people in the US favor the end of the fossil fuel era, but Casten said emissions reductions will matter more to the new Congress than rhetoric.

“We are going to do everything – oversight, legislation and action through the courts,” he said. “There are things around the cost of gas, or housing and insurance that are climate conversations even if we don’t mention climate. It’s our job to understand how all those things are connected but we have to talk about climate change to people in a way that is salient to them. It’s not that we don’t want to talk about climate change at all.”

Regardless of how Democrats talk about the climate crisis, its effects are mounting. Scientists have warned, repeatedly, that sluggish progress in cutting emissions has left little time to avoid disastrous impacts.

The world is already set to overshoot the internationally agreed target of limiting the global temperature rise to 1.5C, locking in turmoil for people, wildlife and ecosystems around the world, and any lingering embrace of fossil fuels by major emitters like the US will only worsen this pain. When Democrats take over Congress in January, advocates will clamor for them to rapidly make up for lost time.

“They have to do more than hold the line – this was a sweeping mandate for change,” said Rachel Cleetus, program director with the climate program at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “The science is sobering. It’s not going to wait for the next election cycle. This is a reality that people are dealing with right now and responsible lawmakers have to recognize that. The world is eager for the US to step up.”

‘I’m going to tell the truth. Screw this!’ Billie Jean King at 82 on coming out, tearing up tennis – and her one big regret

The Guardian Mon, 09 Nov 2026 05:01:00 GMT

She was the world No 1, whose fight for equal prize money changed women’s lives. As competitive as ever in her ninth decade, she discusses sexuality, tenacity and what it was like to finally graduate college this year

Every day, Billie Jean King tries to come up with a “gratitude list” in her head, identifying the people who have played a part in making her life so fulfilling. On the day we speak, the list includes her nephew and her wife, Ilana Kloss, who like her is a decorated former tennis player. And, as ever, Susan Williams, who was in King’s fifth grade class at school in Long Beach, California, when she was 11 years old.

“Do you want to play tennis?” Williams asked one day. “What’s tennis?” King responded. She had always been a sporty child, and her parents, unusually for the time, encouraged her athletic ambitions just as much as they did her brother’s (he later became a major league baseball pitcher). Although basketball was a big part of her early childhood, Williams was the first person to tell her about tennis. “She said: ‘You get to run, jump and hit a ball.’ And I went: ‘Oh, three of my favourite things.’”

As soon as she tried it, King was hooked, and it wasn’t long before she was telling her parents she was going to be the No 1 player in the world, which indeed she became. Across her career, King won 39 grand slam titles: 12 singles titles, 16 doubles and 11 mixed doubles. Across disciplines, she won Wimbledon 20 times, a record matched only by Martina Navratilova. And that’s not to mention her off-court achievements, especially leading the fight to secure equal prize money for men and women.

A new documentary about her life, Give Me the Ball!, tells the story of the “original 9” female tennis players. In 1970, and driven largely by King, they founded the first major women’s professional tennis tour, famously signing symbolic $1 contracts with World Tennis publisher Gladys Heldman to protest against the gender inequality of prize money. Much of the film focuses on 1973, the year King beat self-identifying “male chauvinist pig” Bobby Riggs in the historic “Battle of the Sexes” exhibition match. It was, she says in the documentary, “the pivotal year in women’s tennis”, but she was “a mess, emotionally”. Her internal struggle with her sexuality (she now identifies as a lesbian) was coming to a head, and her marriage to the lawyer and sports promoter Larry King was becoming increasingly strained.

We speak via video call – King, 82, is at home in New York, while I’m in London – and she bursts on screen in a hot pink jacket and matching pink glasses, and immediately begins talking energetically. She tells me my name, Lucy, is a favourite of hers and Kloss’s. “We named our dog that,” she adds, which I think she means as a compliment. She cuts a stately figure, with dark brown hair immaculately coiffed, pearls around her neck and in her ears. On topics such as the state of the US (we are speaking on the day of the midterm elections) and the importance of access to sport, she is serious and authoritative. But she is also enormous fun, which shouldn’t come as a surprise, given the way she has thrown herself into all kinds of projects over the years: from a cameo role in the cult lesbian TV show The L Word to her more recent appearance on the US edition of The Masked Singer, in which she performed Philadelphia Freedom, the song her friend Elton John wrote about her, dressed as a giant hen.

Born Billie Jean Moffitt to a firefighter father and a housewife mother, King was “the goody-two-shoes of the family,” she says, an identity she has carried into adult life: she hates lying, doesn’t drink, and when the first women’s tennis tour was sponsored by cigarette brand Virginia Slims, she never once had a puff. For the first part of her life, she was a Christian too. Now, although she is “still spiritual” and continues to pray, King dislikes organised religion, because in many cases she thinks women are still treated “as second-class citizens”. But she attended church with her family as a child, where her pastor was the two-time Olympic pole-vaulting champion Bob Richards. She says she learned a lot from Richards, and it was easy to believe when she was young that there was a God looking out for her. “Look at all the unbelievable things that happened to me,” she says, pointing to the offer to play tennis from Williams, and the fact that she was able to access free tennis instruction from the professional player Clyde Walker at her city’s public courts.

After she retired from professional singles tennis in 1983, King repaid that good fortune, famously instructing the then-children, Serena and Venus Williams, at a tennis clinic they attended in 1988. Even at the age of six, Serena’s serve was “so beautiful”, King says. “I told her: ‘Don’t let anyone change a thing.’”

“That clinic had a big impact on my life,” Serena says, appearing in Give Me the Ball! alongside footage from the clinic. Although King remembered being filmed by a local newspaper at the time, she had never seen those videos before, and was delighted to finally have access to them. Tellingly, though, one of the first things she notes when we discuss it is her weight at the time, which she says had shot up because of medication she was on for heart issues.

King has opened up before about her struggles with a binge-eating disorder, which she thinks grew out of her discomfort with her sexuality. In recent years, she has started using small doses of a GLP-1 weight loss medication to help quiet the intrusive thoughts she experiences around eating. “I think it’s OK to worry about your health and your body,” King says. What isn’t healthy, she says, is our culture’s obsession with body image. “Women have always been taught we’re supposed to look a certain way,” when most of the time “we’re just great the way we are. Same with the men,” she says.

At times, King makes for a difficult interviewee – not because of any lack of openness, quite the opposite, but because she is so reluctant to have a one-way conversation, and keeps batting questions back at me after she has answered them. “We’re talking about you!” I have to remind her at one point. “I’m always interested in everybody else,” she says, adding that she has been told throughout her life that she asks “too many questions”.

“My friends just look at me like: ‘All right, stop.’ And then I laugh,” she says. But it’s just the way she is, she explains. “There’s always so much to learn.” Her appetite for broadening her knowledge is so great that last year she returned to the history degree she dropped out of in 1964, graduating earlier this year – just one example of King’s refusal to stop pushing herself. She says she thrives under pressure.

However, she deliberately chose not to ask too many questions during the making of Give Me the Ball!. When athletes and entertainers “have a lot of say” in documentaries about them, “I don’t think it comes out as good as it should or could,” she says. The resulting film doesn’t shy away from anything – not King’s abortion, which she had in 1971 because “I did not want to bring a baby into the world not knowing what was going to happen with Larry and me”, and which was made public the following year, against her will, when King, without asking her, agreed for her name to appear in a Ms magazine list of high-profile women who had had abortions. Nor the “mess” of being publicly outed, after her secret relationship with Los Angeles hairdresser Marilyn Barnett ended and Barnett sued her, threatening to make the love letters King had sent her public if her demands for a share of King’s property and earnings weren’t met.

Barnett and her law firm were betting on King handing over the money to avoid the story of the relationship coming out, King thinks. Her ex “knew how tough it was for us and how we had to stay quiet,” she says – had she revealed her sexuality earlier in her career “we wouldn’t have had a tour,” because sponsors wouldn’t have supported something associated with gay people. “So what do you think I’m going to do? I’m not going to say anything. I want the tour for everyone. This is when it’s not about yourself sometimes – it’s about the future of the sport.”

But when she started receiving legal threats from Barnett, she decided enough was enough. “This has just gone on too long,” she remembers thinking. “I’m going to tell the truth. Screw this.” Sure enough, after confirming the nature of her relationship with Barnett in a 1981 press conference, she “lost every endorsement overnight”. But finally, the lies were over.

King thinks the bravery to speak out came from her parents, who had always taught her “to thine own self be true”, which is ironic, given that they were “so homophobic”, she says. It took their “whole lifetime” to come round to the idea of their daughter being gay, King says. And even up to her death in 2014, King suspects her mother thought she should have stayed with Larry, “deep down in her heart of hearts”.

King doesn’t deny that a lot of her relationship with Larry was wonderful. She thinks part of the reason it took her so long to figure out her sexuality was because of her love for him. “If I hadn’t loved him, it would have been different. But he was so cute, man,” she says. Prior to meeting Larry, she had kissed one woman while she was at university, but had not given the possibility of being attracted to women much thought. “Well, actually, she kissed me,” King clarifies, explaining her theory that everyone, romantically, can be categorised into “seekers” and “soughts”.

“And I’m definitely a sought,” which she says surprises people, because of her “go get ’em” attitude to most other things in life. But when it comes to relationships, “everybody’s always come to me”. When she started dating Kloss more than four decades ago, “I knew she was my life life life partner,” she says in the documentary. But King was still married to Larry – she had first asked him for a divorce in 1969, but he didn’t agree until 1987. She says he apologised before he died earlier this year. “We had good closure,” she says.

Though neither Kloss nor King were bothered about having “a big wedding” (they turned down Elton John’s offer to play), they tied the knot in a lowkey ceremony in 2018. It felt important to get married, not just to “make sure Ilana gets everything” after she dies (King’s wife is 12 years her junior) but also to honour “the people that came before us”, who fought to get same-sex marriage legalised, King says. “I also worried that the rights would be taken away, and they still could be,” she adds.

“We can lose it overnight,” she says. “Look at Roe v Wade.” The US supreme court ruling, establishing a constitutional right to abortion, made in 1973 – two years after King had her own abortion – was overturned in 2022. “It’s gone full circle,” King says with a grimace. She namechecks her recently departed friends Gloria Steinem and Dolores Huerta, who fought for human rights in the 60s and 70s, and hopes a “new crop of leaders” will emerge to tackle the issues facing the world today.

King has long been vocal in her support for minority groups, from people of colour to the transgender community, who she says “have it really rough right now”. Although she thinks when it comes to elite sports “it’s not an easy fix”, she hopes a way to better include trans people can be found. “I want them to be OK, and I want people to just let them be,” she says.

Given her staunch support for LGBTQ+ rights, it has surprised some of her fans that she has been open to tennis’s engagement with Saudi Arabia, a country where same-sex sexual activity is punishable by death. In 2024, when the Women’s Tennis Association hosted its Finals event in Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, King was reported in the Telegraph as saying: “I don’t think you really change unless you engage.” Though she stands by her belief in engagement, “I also think that was a difficult one,” she tells me now. “I don’t know what I would have done if I’d been in charge.”

King is clearly still hyper-engaged with the tennis world, politics and feminism, and is determined to continue making her mark. But, as she approaches 83, she says: “I’m running out of time, which is really getting me upset. I have so much I want to do before I’m out of here.”

Probably her only regret, she says, is that she and Ilana don’t have children. “I wish we did,” but “it was too tough around the 80s” for two women to have a child together. “But we know so many young people … we have nieces, nephews,” and the nonprofits she has founded, the Women’s Sports Foundation and the Billie Jean King Foundation, have given the couple the opportunity to support the next generation. King and Kloss are also godparents to Larry’s children from his second marriage.

“Know what you like,” is her biggest piece of advice for young people figuring out what they want to do with their lives. And then whatever it is, try to do it “every day for the rest of your life”. Which brings us back to Susan Williams, who, on that day in the fifth grade, introduced King to the thing she came to like best in the world.

“She changed my life,” King says. The pair are still in touch, and she won’t let her friend forget what an impact she made, seven decades on. “Every time I see her, I go: ‘It’s all your fault.’”

Give Me the Ball! is streaming on Disney+ from 22 November and showing in select cinemas

Hegseth Impeachment Charges Say He Violated the Constitution

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Trump Administration
