Representative Thomas Massie, Republican of Kentucky, set in motion a vote that must be taken within two days.

By Robert Jimison

Reporting from the Capitol

Representative Thomas Massie, Republican of Kentucky, moved on Monday to force a vote this week on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of violating the Constitution and federal law by ignoring the will of Congress in his conduct of the war with Iran and other military operations.

The resolution, which includes eight articles of impeachment, sets up the first post-election test of Republican resolve and loyalty to the Trump administration in the aftermath of their devastating midterm losses.

Taking to the House floor shortly after lawmakers returned to session in Washington for the first time since the election, Mr. Massie reintroduced articles he had put forth in September against Mr. Hegseth. They charge the defense secretary with having “abused” his powers as defense secretary and “endangered members of the our armed forces” through a series of military operations, and usurped congressional authority over military conflict.

“By such conduct,” Mr. Massie said, quoting from his resolution, which was read in full on the House floor, Mr. Hegseth “has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office.”

The move starts a procedural clock that will force lawmakers to confront the question of impeachment within the next two days. Mr. Massie’s resolution was brought up over the objections of Republican leaders who have sought to avoid the vote against a senior member of Mr. Trump’s cabinet.

Democrats were widely expected to support the impeachment, and Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the minority leader, declared on Sunday that he was a “hard yes.” With Republicans holding a razor-thin majority, as few as three Republican defections or a few absences could be enough to allow the charges to advance.

Several Republicans have expressed frustration with the secretary without committing to impeachment. Representative French Hill, Republican of Arkansas, said Sunday that he wanted to hear the arguments but cautioned that poor performance alone did not necessarily constitute an impeachable offense.

Mr. Hegseth has rejected the allegations, calling the impeachment effort a political sham. He announced that he would hold a news conference on Tuesday to address the push to impeach him. President Trump has defended his defense secretary and said he intends to keep him in office.

Robert Jimison covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on defense issues and foreign policy.

Supreme Court Allows Construction of Trump’s Border Wall in Big Bend

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Supported by

The administration had asked the court to permit construction of a border wall in southwestern Texas, including areas within a national park.

By Abbie VanSickle

Reporting from Washington

The Supreme Court on Monday allowed the Trump administration to continue construction of a wall along the southern border in the Big Bend region of southwest Texas, including within a national park.

The decision by the court, which was unsigned, allows the administration to resume its efforts to erect barriers and put up surveillance equipment along a 500-mile stretch of the U. S. border with Mexico as a lower court battle over the project’s legality continues. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson noted a dissent.

The court’s order pauses a decision from a federal judge in October that had blocked construction while she weighed a legal challenge brought by a church preservation group, a river guide and an environmental organization.

The justices noted that the challengers had claimed that construction in the Big Bend Sector would “diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area.” But the majority found that federal law permitted the homeland security secretary to waive laws aimed at environmental protection and conservation, reflecting “a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms” raised by the challengers.

The ruling is a win for President Trump and the first test of a major administration policy at the Supreme Court since last week’s midterm elections.

Plans for construction in Big Bend National Park have drawn strong bipartisan opposition in Texas, uniting environmentalists and ranchers in the remote desert region.

The park, described by the National Park Service as “a geological marvel evidenced in sea fossils and dinosaur bones” and “a place where you can still hear the whispers of pioneers, ranchers, miners and Native Americans,” is named for a sweeping curve in the Rio Grande along the U. S.-Mexico border.

Critics have raised concerns that a border wall would alter the landscape, cutting off river access, threatening crops and cattle, and interfering with the largest dark sky reserve on Earth.

A coalition that opposes the project, which includes local landowners, sued in April to block the administration’s plans. The group argued that officials had overstepped their authority by issuing the project waivers that allowed construction to proceed despite federal statutes, including the Endangered Species Act and the National Environmental Policy Act, without congressional sign-off.

But in August, bulldozers appeared near one of the national park’s main attractions, the Santa Elena Canyon, and construction crews leveled the ground for more than a mile. Trump administration officials said that Customs and Border Protection planned to build an access road, install surveillance technology and put up four- to six-foot-tall vehicle barriers in the area.

In early October, a federal judge in El Paso temporarily halted border construction across the region. Judge Kathleen Cardone, who was appointed by President George W. Bush, agreed the groups’ challenge was likely to succeed on at least one of its claims.

Lawyers for the Trump administration then asked the judge to pause her ruling while they appealed to the Supreme Court. When the judge declined, the administration filed an emergency application to the justices.

In the application, Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the lower court decision “baseless,” arguing that stopping the project would leave “a 300-plus-mile gap in border defenses” and “act as a dangerous magnet for cartels and other bad actors to exploit.”

In response, the challengers asked the justices to block the plan, asserting that the Trump administration went to the Supreme Court because it wanted to “immediately resume blasting, bulldozing, road construction and other border barrier-related construction across one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States.”

A decision to allow construction, they argued, “would result in the permanent alteration of an irreplaceable landscape” and would “threaten unique historic and cultural resources,” along with “myriad private ranch lands.”

Abbie VanSickle covers the United States Supreme Court for The Times. She is a lawyer and has an extensive background in investigative reporting.

In addition to the Nvidia investigation, congressional inquiries are ramping up. Republicans on three key committees have demanded that Mr. Huang appear in a closed-door hearing to answer questions about his relationship with Ms. Huang and any potential leak of sensitive data.

I. chips and helping China get access to that technology. The U. S. government has blocked the most advanced Nvidia chips from being sold to China, a ban Mr. Huang has publicly opposed.

Her Death From Dengue May Signal That the Disease Is Here to Stay

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

In the past, Americans were infected with dengue after being bitten by mosquitoes while traveling. But now, most of the current transmission is from local mosquitoes.

By Anemona Hartocollis

On the last Friday in August, Gay Rabb Small went for her daily walk along the Tampa shore. Nearing 80, she was determined to stay healthy and walked at least five miles a day.

That night at dinner, her daughter, Anna Small, noticed that her mother seemed a little off. “I thought she had overdone it,” Ms. Small said.

By Saturday, Gay Small had developed a tremor, and her daughter took her to the emergency room, where she was diagnosed with dengue, a viral illness transmitted by mosquitoes. She died the following Friday, Sept. 4, her 80th birthday.

Gay Small got dengue from a mosquito bite, probably from one of her daily walks. She is so far the only fatality among hundreds of people in Florida who have been sickened in a dengue outbreak that scientists and public health officials are struggling to understand. The size of the outbreak, they say, indicates that dengue may be making a comeback in the continental United States at a level not seen for many decades.

“I think the dengue outbreaks will get worse over the coming years in the U. S.,” said Ira Longini, a biostatistician at the University of Florida.

In the continental United States, dengue cases are almost always traceable to mosquito bites from traveling. So it is especially foreboding, public health experts say, that most of the current transmission in Florida is coming from mosquito bites locally.

“It is very unusual to have transmission in the United States,” said Eva Harris, a professor of infectious diseases and vaccinology at the University of California, Berkeley. “This is so very much of an eye-opener.”

Most people infected by dengue show no symptoms, so they don’t even realize that they have it. But the illness can be very painful, causing high fever, joint and muscle aches, headaches and pain behind the eyes. Most patients with severe symptoms recover, but in a small number of cases, dengue can be fatal, leading to shock, hemorrhage and organ failure.

About 2,678 people have been infected with dengue in the United States and its territories so far this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Almost half the cases have been in Puerto Rico and American Samoa, where dengue is endemic.

But Florida is by far the hardest-hit state, with 880 cases. About 503 of those people were infected in the United States, up from a previous high of 189 people infected locally in 2023, according to the C. D. C. In 2025, Florida had 517 cases, and only 72 of them were infected locally, according to the C. D. C.

This year, the center of the outbreak moved from Miami-Dade County, with 254 cases, to Hillsborough County, which encompasses Tampa, with 417 cases. Of people who caught the virus where they lived, 395 were in Tampa and just 12 in Miami.

Public health officials are puzzling over what is causing the shift from southern to central Florida and why local transmission has risen.

“That is the $100 million question,” said Dr. Gabriela Paz-Bailey, chief of the dengue branch in the C. D. C.’s division of vector-borne diseases. “Maybe it is associated with higher introductions through travelers to the Caribbean. But we’re still trying to work out why we’re seeing more cases this year."

Dr. Paz-Bailey said she did not expect to see “explosive” outbreaks like in Puerto Rico because of the higher standard of living in the continental United States. “But I do think that we will continue to see locally acquired dengue — that this will become the norm,” she said.

There are some forces that are probably contributing to the dengue outbreak in Florida. Warm, wet weather helps mosquitoes breed. Torrential rains have flooded parking lots and playgrounds lately in southern Florida, leading health authorities to fear that mosquitoes will proliferate.

The natural habitat of the mosquitoes that carry dengue is in tropical and subtropical countries, so climate change may be a factor. Florida is also a major transit hub for tourists and other travelers to the Caribbean and Latin America, who may bring the virus back with them. Mosquitoes may stow away on boats and planes.

In recent years, local transmission has been recorded where it was scarce before, in Texas, Arizona, California and with one case this year, Virginia. Dengue attributed to travel has been reported as far north as Minnesota and Maine.

There is no vaccine for dengue that is currently approved in the United States, Dr. Paz-Bailey of the C. D. C. said. In any case, the vaccines that are available are not very effective, experts said, and there is a need for both more vaccine development and research into anti-viral drugs for dengue. The treatment now is to manage a patient’s pain and fluids.

The outbreak has led to emergency declarations in three Florida counties — Hillsborough, Pinellas and Pasco — and statewide support from the C. D. C., including $800,000 in emergency funds for things like mosquito surveillance and control.

On Oct. 10, Gov. Ron DeSantis issued an executive order adding mosquito control to an executive order to combat flooding because of Hurricane Isaias.

The outbreak has unfolded as Florida voters on Tuesday approved a property tax cut that critics assert will cost local governments billions in revenue and drastically reduce public services, including mosquito control.

Still, Dr. Longini said, the situation is not as dire as in other countries. “The size of the outbreaks in Florida compared to what we’ve seen in southern Mexico is quite small,” he said. “We’re not seeing tens of thousands of cases, we’re seeing hundreds.”

Infection is expected to decline as the weather cools down. Mosquitoes don’t breed as well and are less infectious in cooler weather.

The best way to prevent dengue is to avoid mosquitoes by wearing long sleeves and pants, applying insect repellents that contain DEET, using screens on windows and doors, turning on air conditioning and emptying standing water where mosquitoes breed.

General spraying “looks good politically,” but can be evaded by mosquitoes, Dr. Longini said. “It takes a lot of individual effort,” he said.

There are four different dengue virus types, and a second infection with a different type can lead to more severe disease.

The one fatality so far, Gay Small, may have had a repeat infection that made her illness worse, her family says. The cause of death was “multi-system organ failure secondary to dengue,” her daughter said.

Ms. Small had not traveled in the weeks before contracting the virus, her daughter said. Her family finds it paradoxical that she had traveled all over the world, often by bike, only to be infected by dengue in her hometown.

Now, part of her legacy may be the battle against the insect that killed her.

“They’ve been spraying like crazy,” Anna Small said. “Every night, I hear the helicopters over my house.”

David Ovalle contributed reporting. Georgia Gee contributed research.

For most people outside of places like Puerto Rico, where it is endemic, dengue is an exotic disease. Writing this piece was kind of like taking a crash course in the disease. I learned that dengue is a growing threat in Florida and the U. S. and that the last continental epidemic of dengue was reported in Louisiana in 1945.

Anna Small, whose mother, Gay Small, died in the current outbreak, had a similar reaction. “I was like, O. K., we can deal with that,” she told me. “My father was a statistician who had worked on a dengue vaccine that was unsuccessful. So we knew about dengue, that it was not a pleasant virus to have but better than a stroke. It was actually a relief when we found out she had dengue – initially, at least.”

Anemona Hartocollis is a national reporter for The Times, writing about public health.

‘Just Win, Baby!’ Despite Victories, Progressives Still Face Electability Questions

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

As Democrats prepare to take power in Congress, some centrists are brushing off the victories of left-wing candidates. The left is pushing back.

By Kellen Browning and Patricia Mazzei

Progressive Democrats won Senate seats in Michigan and Maine, a host of battleground House contests and the mayor’s race in Los Angeles.

Yet the movement’s triumphant midterm results last week did not put an end to questions about the left’s electability. And the stakes are now suddenly much higher, with Democratic factions jockeying for position as the party prepares to take power and set a policy agenda in the next Congress.

All over the airwaves and the internet, moderates are arguing that left-wing candidates underperformed, sharing statistics and charts to emphasize various margins of victory.

“Moderates outran Kamala Harris by an average of 21 percentage points,” read one tweet from Third Way, the centrist Democratic think tank. “Progressives by just five. Democrats should be cleareyed about who the majority makers were in these historic midterms.”

Representative Adam Gray of California, a leader of the Blue Dog Coalition, said in an interview that the group’s moderate-to-conservative slate of Democratic candidates “did better than their progressive counterparts. I think you’re going to see that in the data.”

Establishment Democrats have been discounting the left’s electability for decades. Progressives say they are irked but unsurprised by the continuing effort from within the party to undercut their movement. But they also say they’re less willing to cede the argument now, fresh off sweeping victories that helped give Democrats a giant majority in the House and at least 54 seats in the Senate.

“We cannot waste opportunity,” said Randy Villegas, who won a House race in a conservative, agricultural region of California with an unapologetically progressive message. The lesson of the midterms, he argued, was that Democrats must do more than oppose President Trump. They “need to be leading with a bold vision,” he said.

Underpinning the debate is the fast-arriving 2028 presidential primary, in which progressives hope to field a candidate who can build on the two presidential campaigns waged by Senator Bernie Sanders, which helped lay the groundwork for the modern left-wing movement.

After the midterm results, several progressive leaders also complained that their centrist rivals keep moving the goal posts.

When their candidates ran in competitive battlegrounds this spring, the centrists said they would lose their primaries. When many of them won anyway, the centrists said they would lose in the fall and cost the party control of Congress. Now, after a successful election night in which at least eight progressive candidates in House or Senate battlegrounds swept into office, some centrists have a new message: We would have won more seats, and by larger margins.

“They’re running around with that goal post; they’re doing zigzags,” said Maurice Mitchell, the national director of the progressive Working Families Party, which backed left-wing candidates around the country. “That wasn’t the standard before Tuesday. The standard was, ‘Can progressives even win in challenging turf?’ We know the answer to that now. It’s pretty clear. It’s definitive.”

Mr. Mitchell and other progressives have a warning for the party: Do not discount the role we played. And do not ignore the role you played, undercutting our message, supporting our opponents and depriving some of us of national funds that would have boosted our margins and possibly pushed even more of us across the finish line.

In Florida, Angie Nixon, a progressive, ran a spirited campaign for Senate that fell three percentage points short in a race that neither party had considered competitive at the start of the year. She lamented that national Democrats all but wrote off her candidacy, leaving her with too little money to run a single television ad in one of the most expensive states in which to run a campaign.

“We’re not going to win unless we have more investment,” she said.

In a handful of cases, left-wing candidates did lose what appeared to be winnable battleground districts. In Maine, Matt Dunlap, a progressive, appears headed for defeat in a congressional seat being vacated by Representative Jared Golden, a more conservative Democrat.

And centrist groups including the Blue Dog Coalition and the New Democrats made big gains as the party won races in conservative states such as Texas, South Carolina and Kentucky. With such a large House majority, moderate Democrats may be less inclined to prioritize central ambitions of the left such as “Medicare for all.”

That would be a huge mistake, some of the left’s leaders and strategists say.

“It would be a tragedy if we all misread this moment to understand that everything for the past two years — the bottoming out in 2024, the struggle through the wilderness — was all forgiven and forgotten by the electorate,” said Lauren Hitt, a Democratic strategist who has worked for progressives and moderates, as well as for the DSA Fund, the nonprofit arm of the Democratic Socialists of America. “This is much more an election, if you look at the data, that’s a rejection of the status quo than it’s any sort of affirmation of either wing of the Democratic Party.”

They also argue that the metrics pointing to underperformance in progressive races are flawed.

It’s true, for instance, that Abdul El-Sayed and Troy Jackson, progressive Senate candidates in Michigan and Maine, outperformed Vice President Kamala Harris in their states by smaller margins than those of most other Democratic Senate candidates who won.

But Mr. El-Sayed underperformed Jocelyn Benson, now the Democratic governor-elect in Michigan, by only a small margin. He also faced a last-minute betrayal from his moderate primary rival, who endorsed his Republican opponent in the race’s final days. Mr. Jackson, meantime, was facing Senator Susan Collins, perhaps the most formidable Republican incumbent anywhere on the map, and he got a late start, becoming the nominee in July after an unusual Democratic candidate switch.

In the House, Manny Rutinel, a Colorado progressive, ousted a Republican incumbent by about 15 percentage points, while Mr. Villegas of California’s Central Valley was declared the winner against a Republican congressman. Mr. Villegas was ahead by a whopping 33 percentage points with more than half of the vote tallied.

Then there was the financial disadvantage.

People downplaying progressive victories intentionally ignored “the millions of dollars that these candidates had to overcome,” Mr. Villegas said. In Michigan, for example, William Lawrence, a progressive, narrowly ousted his Republican opponent in a tighter race than many other battlegrounds. But he also faced a juggernaut of G. O. P. spending against him — more, in fact, than in all but one other House race.

Mr. Lawrence dismissed the chatter about margins of victory.

“Just win, baby!” he said. “Everybody runs their own race, and I think that this punditry, without exception, operates from absolute ignorance about the local conditions of each race.”

Even in losses, progressives saw signs of their movement taking hold in swing districts. In Tennessee, Justin Pearson, a left-wing activist and state legislator, lost a Memphis congressional district redrawn to heavily favor the G. O. P. by just about one percentage point.

In Florida, Ms. Nixon, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, did not perform as well as David Jolly, the moderate Democrat who ran unsuccessfully for governor. But she noted that she actually outperformed him by a hair in Miami-Dade County — where conservative Cuban Americans had criticized her D. S. A. ties — “because I had a constituency program that focused on Hispanic and Latino voters.”

Mr. Jolly came within about one point of flipping the governor’s mansion, a close result that prompted speculation about whether Alex Vindman, the moderate whom Ms. Nixon resoundingly defeated in the primary, might have been able to win the Senate race.

Ms. Nixon strongly rejected that suggestion.

“If I was not at the top of the ticket, we would not have gotten this far,” she said. “We had increased turnout, based on the last midterm, for young people and Black people.”

Since Tuesday, some Democrats have suggested that Ms. Nixon should run to lead the state party. She said she would “absolutely not,” but another run for Senate in 2028 was “not off the table.”

In some parts of the country, the blue wave was so big that it seemed to lift candidates across the political spectrum. And some victors did not fit neatly into one ideology. Sam Forstag, a Montana smokejumper who is considered a progressive and campaigned with Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, was also endorsed by the Blue Dogs. Bob Brooks, a retired firefighter and progressive, won in Pennsylvania with the support of both Gov. Josh Shapiro, a moderate, and Mr. Sanders.

Those on the left argued that their message of upending the status quo and delivering economic relief to the beleaguered working class had suffused Democratic gains all over the country, even in races where candidates did not label themselves as progressives.

“This was an antiwar, anti-Big Tech, pro-economic populist message,” said Usamah Andrabi, the communications director for Justice Democrats, a left-wing group that backed progressive candidates. “If that’s not the sort of overarching progressive playbook that we’ve been calling for for so long, then I don’t know what is.”

Reid J. Epstein contributed reporting.

Kellen Browning is a Times political reporter based in San Francisco.

Patricia Mazzei is a national political correspondent for The Times, based in Miami.

At 87, She’s Poised to Become the First Woman to Lead the Texas House

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Senfronia Thompson, of Houston, would also become the first Black lawmaker to serve as speaker.

By Lauren McGaughy

Reporting from Austin, Texas

Over more than 50 years in the Texas House, Senfronia Thompson has shaped dozens of state laws with an eye for the causes and people who are often overlooked, what she calls “the little dogs.”

Now, at 87, the Houston lawmaker is on the verge of upending a Texas political institution, becoming the speaker of the House.

Last week, Democrats swept into power across Texas, winning every top elected office. For the first time in 24 years, the party will also take control of the Texas House of Representatives.

On Friday, Ms. Thompson announced that she had the votes needed to lead the chamber. The vote will happen in January, just after the slate of new Democrats is sworn in. If chosen, Ms. Thompson would be the first Black lawmaker and first woman in the job. It would also mean the state’s three most powerful policymakers — the governor, lieutenant governor and speaker — would all be women for the first time in Texas history.

A legislative force whose tenure and demeanor command the respect — and sometimes fear — of members from both parties, Ms. Thompson is considered by Texas Democrats to be the natural choice to help them lead for the first time in a generation.

Ms. Thompson would inherit a House that, in recent years, has passed some of the most conservative laws in the state’s modern history, including a near total abortion ban, restrictions on L. G. B. T. Q. rights and a billion-dollar school voucher program. The Texas Senate, which still has a Republican majority, is expected to try to hold the line against any attempt to unravel these measures.

Tom Oliverson, the chairman of the Texas House Republican Caucus, said they will choose a Republican candidate for speaker to run against Ms. Thompson but said she would be a “pragmatic” leader.

“I certainly believe that she can govern from the middle,” he said.

At a packed gathering in the Capitol on Friday, she promised not to “punish” Republicans — with one caveat.

“I don’t have a dictatorship,” said Ms. Thompson, who is known as “Miss T” in the Capitol. “But we are going to be working to resolve the issues.” Her voice grew stern as she warned against fighting “about little ‘wee wee things’ that have no place within our legislative process.”

State Representative Jolanda Jones, another Houston Democrat, recalled a recent debate on the House floor in which, she said, a Republican lawmaker was acting disrespectfully during debate. In response, Ms. Jones said, Ms. Thompson killed his bill.

“That was gangsta,” Ms. Jones said.

When asked to describe Ms. Thompson in one word, several lawmakers said “skilled” or “resilient.” Charlie Geren, a Republican member of the Texas House who supports her for speaker, called Ms. Thompson “awesome.” Members of both parties, including Dustin Burrows, the current Republican speaker, have called her “the conscience of the House.”

“I’ve seen her do some amazing things up against some incredible odds in this building,” said State Representative Venton Jones, a Democrat from Dallas.

The granddaughter of sharecroppers, Ms. Thompson grew up in Houston and taught junior high and high school. She joined the Texas House in 1973 after the Sharpstown stock fraud scandal, a public corruption case that led to huge turnover across state government. Widowed after her first session, she put herself through law school while raising three children.

Over five decades, she helped pass Texas’ first law allowing court-ordered alimony and wrote the James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Act, named for a Black man murdered by white supremacists in East Texas in 1998. She also pushed to raise the minimum wage, sponsored smoking restrictions in public places and wrote a law requiring certain health plans to cover prescription contraceptives.

Rafael Anchia was a freshman lawmaker in 2005 when Ms. Thompson fought an amendment to the state’s constitution to define marriage as between one man and one woman. Many Democrats would not publicly oppose the move, he said, “but Miss T did.”

“She knows attacks on one community were attacks on all of us,” said Mr. Anchia, the former chairman of the Mexican American Legislative Caucus.

In 2025, Ms. Thompson worked with Republicans, including Angela Paxton, a state senator and the wife of the outgoing attorney general, to crack down on massage businesses suspected of human trafficking.

“I told you I was coming for the pimps,” Ms. Thompson said at the time. “I’m going to take their money, and I’m going to give it to the people they’ve been running over.”

Ms. Thompson announced she would run for speaker once before, in 2020, but Democrats failed to win the Texas House. This time, she said she already has the backing of a majority of members, including some Republicans.

Ms. Thompson will turn 88 in January, just before the vote. No questions about her age or ability were raised during her announcement last week. She held a massive wooden gavel given to her by another lawmaker and slammed it twice on the lectern before her.

“May I call you Madam Speaker Thompson?” one reporter asked.

“That name sounds really good,” she replied, smiling.

Lauren McGaughy is the Texas politics correspondent for The New York Times, writing about the ways that policymakers in the second largest state are changing lives for their citizens and influencing American politics.

Could the Voter Backlash Against A. I. Actually Help the Economy?

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Voter backlash could threaten the data center boom. Some economists think that could be a good thing.

By Ben CasselmanTony Romm and Colby Smith

Ben Casselman and Colby Smith reported from New York. Tony Romm reported from Washington.

The artificial intelligence boom has powered the U. S. economy through a period of tariffs, war and uncertainty. It has also pushed up prices, raised borrowing costs and set off fears of a financial bubble that could burst to devastating effect.

Americans made clear in last week’s midterm elections that they do not think the trade-off has been worth it.

Voters overwhelmingly supported ballot initiatives that aimed to rein in data center development, and they elected to office governors and legislators who promised to do the same.

Now the question for newly empowered Democrats, and for policymakers more broadly, is whether they can find a way to address voters’ concerns without derailing the economy.

Many economists are optimistic, arguing that slowing the frenetic pace of the A. I. build out could make it more sustainable, even if it causes some short-term hardship. Some of the A. I. skeptics who won office last week, including Gina Hinojosa, the newly elected Democratic governor of Texas, have said they want to ensure data center projects benefit their communities, not stop them entirely.

But the whipsawing of financial markets in the days after the 2026 election shows just how narrow a tightrope that is to walk. The mere suggestion of scrutiny in Washington has rattled both Silicon Valley and Wall Street, which enjoyed two years of lax regulation under Republicans’ watch.

That tension was evident again on Monday, when Nvidia, the chipmaker at the center of the A. I. ecosystem, descended into a maelstrom over its chief executive’s relationship with a woman whom U. S. intelligence agencies believe to be a Chinese spy. President Trump came to his defense, some in Congress have called for investigations and Nvidia’s share price fell sharply Monday morning.

The incident offered fresh evidence that the economy has become so dependent on A. I., and so much money has flooded into the sector, that deflating the bubble without popping it could prove difficult. Investors have made their bets on the assumption that the sector’s breakneck growth rate would continue for years, meaning that the market could be vulnerable if the pace slows even modestly.

“It’s not like you can scientifically calibrate this dial,” said Jared Bernstein, who served as a top economic adviser to President Joseph R. Biden Jr. “The likelihood that things deflate in some sort of orderly way are low.”

The challenge for Democrats is that A. I. — and the building boom that developing it requires — has become embedded into nearly every aspect of the U. S. economy.

Investors have pumped hundreds of billions of dollars of capital into companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, which have spent that money on microchips, data centers and the electricity to power them. The investments have filtered through the economy, lifting demand for steel, construction equipment and even the specialized gray paint used to coat the walls of data centers.

At the same time, the rising share prices of A. I.-related companies have helped swell Americans’ brokerage accounts and retirement portfolios, helping to prop up consumer spending when rising prices and slowing wage growth are taking a toll on many people’s finances.

Suppliers to the data centers have continued to add jobs even as the rest of the manufacturing industry has cut workers, according to an analysis by Devesh Kodnani, a fellow at the Economic Security Project, a progressive research organization. The story is similar in construction, where data center projects have helped make up for soft demand in housing, warehouses and office buildings.

But while the boom has helped keep growth on track, it has also soaked up resources from other sectors. Companies found themselves forced to pay more for materials and labor. Shortages of memory chips led to higher prices for consumer electronics. The A. I. industry’s demand for power drove up electricity prices, while its demand for capital pushed up interest rates.

“It’s almost as if corporate America has been so obsessed with this technology investment that it’s chosen to do so at the expense of other aspects of the economy,” said James Knightley, chief international economist at ING, an investment bank.

That sense of corporate impunity helps explain public opposition to data centers, and to A. I. more generally, said Asad Ramzanali, director of A. I. and technology policy at the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator, a research institute at Vanderbilt University.

Communities experience the costs of A. I. as noise, traffic and higher electricity bills, and even people who live nowhere near data centers worry about the effects that A. I. could have on their jobs, the climate or even the future of the human race. The benefits, on the other hand, seem mostly to be flowing to a relative handful of tech billionaires.

“They see all the costs, they feel all the cost, they bear all the cost, and the benefits are not accruing in a meaningful way,” Mr. Ramzanali said.

President Trump and his aides have shrugged off such criticisms, celebrating the potential riches to come from A. I. and the data centers that power the technology. The administration has also worked to ward off anything that might inhibit the development of those computing facilities — and their contribution to the economy’s growth.

“As President, I am 100 percent in favor of Super Intelligence (SI), and will work with the many States in the U. S. that want to become RICH by having them,” Mr. Trump said on social media, referring to data centers. “They are GOLD, and only foolish leadership will say ‘NO’ to the riches they bring!”

Within days of the midterm election, some Democrats quickly pledged that they would use their newfound political strength to regulate A. I. and curtail data center construction.

“One of the reasons the American people rose up against A. I. data centers is that they saw the A. I. industry was running wild, and the Trump administration was encouraging the A. I. industry to run wild,” said Representative Ted Lieu of California, a chair of a Democratic commission established in 2025 to study A. I.’s economic implications.

Mr. Lieu offered a roster of policy areas the new Democratic majority expected to explore: the national security issues posed by sales of advanced chips, the effects chatbots could have on children and the worker protections required if A. I. replaces human labor. But he rejected the notion that those guardrails would pose a threat to economic growth.

Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, pointed to the nearly four dozen moratoria on data center development across the country. Taking aim at what he called “Big Tech oligarchs,” he added on social media: “NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW.”

But even as Democrats have warned about the pitfalls of A. I., many of the party’s newly elected leaders have said they are looking to impose limits on the industry, not shut it down.

In an interview with The New York Times on Friday, Ms. Hinojosa, the Texas governor-elect, said she would delay permits for data centers “until we can protect Texans” but maintained her state’s pro-business reputation.

“These newly elected officials presumably don’t want to lose that much economic activity,” said Mr. Bernstein, the former Biden administration adviser. “It’s kind of the whole game now.”

Such dependence on one sector is risky, many economists say, and some moderation in the pace of the A. I. build out would be welcomed.

Policymakers at the Federal Reserve have become concerned that the building boom is contributing to inflation, and that until recently it seemed immune to the central bank’s usual tool for controlling price pressures: higher interest rates. If Democrats rein in A. I.’s growth, that could lessen the need for more aggressive rate hikes.

Limits on data center construction could also impose some discipline on an industry that has been building so quickly, and spending so much, that economists were becoming skeptical all the bets would pay off. Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, an economist at Columbia University, estimated in a recent paper that the A. I. build out was on track to become the largest infrastructure investment in U. S. history, surpassing episodes like the railroad construction boom of the 19th century, most of which ended in catastrophic busts.

New regulations would probably “take some of the wind out of the sails of that whole sector,” Mr. Van Nieuwerburgh said. “But I think it’s not a bad thing. The silver lining could be that a bit slower build-out might actually give us more time to assess whether we need all of it.”

But while letting the air out of a bubble is appealing in theory, history suggests it is difficult to do. Even before the election, there were signs that investors were becoming concerned that some of their A. I. bets would not pay off. If the threat of regulation causes a more widespread deterioration in investor sentiment, that could lead to a sharper decline in stock prices. That could cause wealthier households to pull back spending, potentially causing a recession.

The real risk is that a bursting of the A. I. bubble reveals vulnerabilities in the financial system that economists and policymakers were not aware of. That is what happened in 2008, when a crisis that had seemed contained to subprime mortgages nearly brought down the entire global economy.

“I think the concerning version is where there are some hidden exposures in the financial system that we don’t really know about,” said Gabriel Chodorow-Reich, an economist at Harvard.

The best way to prevent that outcome, Mr. Chodorow-Reich said, would be through careful regulation and scrutiny by the Treasury Department and the Fed.

Reining in the boom through a patchwork of local regulations “is a very second-best or third-best or maybe fifth-best way to do this,” he said, “but it could help.”

Ben Casselman is the chief economics correspondent for The Times. He has reported on the economy for nearly 20 years.

Tony Romm is a reporter covering economic policy and the Trump administration for The Times, based in Washington.

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve and the U. S. economy for The Times.

Congress Has Reined In the Presidency Before. Here’s How to Do It.

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

iDEas

History tells us that constitutional oversight can be a powerful tool — if wielded correctly.

By Emily Bazelon

In the midst of a wild election night on Nov. 3, Representative Robert Garcia, Democrat of California and the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, had a gleeful message for Trump officials: “Lawyer up.” When Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress in January, they would investigate corporate corruption, “the Trump crime family” and more, Garcia vowed.

The Constitution tells us what that accountability could look like. The framers gave Congress the authority to exercise oversight, including by investigating government corruption or failure in the executive branch. When the members of the next House and Senate take their seats in January, President Trump will still have his veto pen, which limits the laws they can pass. By contrast, their power to scrutinize his administration’s actions will be broad and independent. Lawmakers can investigate any problems they think they could address through legislation. Their power of inquiry is an “essential and appropriate auxiliary to the legislative function,” the Supreme Court said in 1927, a principle it has since consistently upheld.

As Garcia suggested, Trump’s brash approach to governing has provided many targets for Congress. Along with the stream of reports involving self-enrichment by Trump’s inner circle — including $500 million in agreed-upon payments from a firm linked to the government of the United Arab Emirates for a stake in the Trump family’s cryptocurrency firm — Democrats could look into the tactics of ICE, the defiance of court orders, the lethal boat strikes by the military against supposed drug traffickers in the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea, baseless prosecutions of the president’s perceived enemies and the dismantling of U. S. A. I. D. without the approval of Congress.

But a question looms: How does the next Congress deploy its investigative powers wisely, to serve the national interest rather than the cause of partisan revenge? If investigations become lawmakers’ main business, voters could think their new representatives are looking backward to settle scores rather than forward to improve their lives. In other words, the whole thing could backfire.

There is more at stake than just the legacy of the Trump era (and that in itself is a lot). For decades now, Congress has been increasingly weak and distrusted by the public. It’s the branch that’s most prone to be fractured and feckless, the one with a collective action problem as hundreds of people vie to set the agenda. If the next House and Senate conduct investigations wisely and well over the next two years, they could go a long way toward restoring public trust in their institution and righting the system of checks and balances that has tilted too far toward the presidency.

But Congress could also fritter away a huge opportunity. History offers lessons in both directions.

Congressional investigations of the executive branch have often given presidents “real trouble,” the political scientist David Mayhew has written. The scholars Eric Schickler and Douglas L. Kriner found that 80 percent of 30 investigations from 1947 to 2002 that received major news coverage resulted in legislation or a concession from the administration like the resignation of a high-level official. Congressional investigations also tended to depress presidential approval ratings, reducing the political leverage of the White House and supplying Congress with “at least a partial counterweight to presidential power.”

Watergate remains the potent example of Congress’s building a case to take down a president. At first, most Republicans didn’t see the 1972 break-in by Republican operatives at the Democratic National Committee’s headquarters as a serious scandal. But as Congress held hearings and major media outlets covered the mounting disclosures, Republican senators became more critical of the Nixon administration. Bipartisan agreement grew across professional Washington, signaling to the public that investigating Nixon was not partisan warfare. “Nixon’s approval rating declined by the same rate among Republicans as Democrats,” Schickler says. “That was key to his collapse.”

Sometimes, the exposure of wrongdoing is an end in itself. Against Nixon, however, Congress also effectively wielded the threat of impeachment. He resigned after a trio of Republican leaders in the Senate told him that if he did not leave on his own, he would be impeached in the House and convicted by the Senate.

Congress investigated the administrations that followed. But party loyalty increasingly mattered to members of Congress more than promoting the independence of their branch. A Democratic senator, J. William Fulbright, led the major probe into the Vietnam War when Lyndon B. Johnson was president. Republicans, by contrast, did little oversight of the Iraq war waged by George W. Bush when they controlled Congress. Serious bipartisan scrutiny of the president generally receded. Trump’s first term intensified this development. “We’re fighting all the subpoenas,” Trump said in 2019. When Democrats led the chamber, the administration withheld the president’s tax returns from one House committee and then refused to cooperate at all when the House investigated whether Trump pressured Ukraine to investigate Joseph R. Biden Jr. and his son Hunter.

On the Bidens and Ukraine, the House fought back by impeaching Trump for abusing his power and obstructing Congress. But the Senate acquitted him in February 2020 as the Republicans who controlled it rallied around their defiant leader. His poll numbers rose during impeachment. Congressional oversight could not transcend our era’s supercharged partisanship. “When one party rejects an investigation, the public doesn’t care about it as much,” Schickler says.

For many months after Trump returned to office in 2025, reports that he was abusing his power were frequent but glancing. His base excused him, and his approval ratings sagged but then slightly recovered. It seemed possible that Trump had rewritten the rules that applied to Nixon. His vice president said so directly. Speaking in June to an appreciative audience at the Richard M. Nixon Library, Vice President JD Vance said it was “crazy” that Watergate had taken down a presidency. “If Watergate happened tomorrow, it would be like a 12-hour news story.”

In Vance’s telling, it wasn’t Nixon who abused his power, but Congress and the special prosecutor who investigated the president. He was the target of a witch hunt, just like another president who sees himself as a victim. Like Trump, Vance argued, Nixon was targeted not by a coequal branch of government but by a “deep state” that overstepped its bounds. The characterization delegitimized oversight entirely.

The rout Republicans experienced in the 2026 midterm elections suggests that Vance read the electorate wrong. Trump’s party had its worst showing since the elections in 1974 and 1976 that followed Nixon’s disgrace. And there was a connection between giving Trump a free pass and taking a huge hit. Late-breaking polls showed that corruption topped voters’ concerns as Democrats linked the rising cost of living to profiteering in Trump’s circle, from the crypto deals to pay-to-play pardons. Now the new Congress has a chance to prove that Trump has not succeeded in rewriting the rules of accountability.

Democratic leaders can follow a model that they themselves built. In the summer of 2021, months after the House impeached Trump for a second time for his role in the Jan. 6 attack on the U. S. Capitol but the Senate declined to convict him, the House formed a committee to investigate him for overturning the 2020 election results. The House Select Committee on Jan. 6 worked with a television producer to present its case in hearings that were packaged as prime-time episodes, optimizing clips for social media and late-night audiences. Most Republicans attacked the hearings alongside Trump, but two of them in the House, Representative Lynn Cheney of Wyoming and Representative Adam Kinzinger of Illinois, played prominent roles. “The committee was really good at the plot twist and the surprise witness,” says Josh Chafetz, a law professor who writes about congressional power. “There’s good evidence that Democrats didn’t have as bad a midterm in 2022 as they might have because of the Jan. 6 hearings.”

Beyond polls and election outcomes, the larger principle is Congress’s retaining the capacity to constrain the president that the framers intended it to have. “The manner in which Congress exercises the investigative power,” the historian Arthur Schlesinger Jr. wrote in 1975, determines “whether the constitutional order will in the end oblige the American government to control itself.” Congressional investigations have not stopped power from tilting toward the presidency. They’re insufficient for that and sometimes off base. But they’re still necessary.

Now what? How do Democrats balance digging into the Trump administration with proving themselves to voters who care much more about the cost of living? Before the election, I called Representative Jamie Raskin, the Maryland congressman who helped steer the Jan. 6 House Select Committee, to ask how he was thinking about investigations. “The ideal cases to begin with are ones in which there is a fundamental corruption of government taking place, with officials in the Trump regime ripping off the taxpayers and preventing the nation from making real progress,” Raskin said.

Corruption is a theme, not a story line the way Jan. 6 was. To hold people’s attention, Democrats will have to avoid being scattershot as they choose targets. Private citizens can’t resist subpoenas the way government officials can. Calling corporate executives as witnesses could unearth details about the deals that have enriched Trump’s family and inner circle and deter companies from continuing to do this.

There will be pressure from parts of the Democratic base to punish the president rather than stop at exposing his wrongdoing. But impeaching Trump for a third time would return him to a role he savors — the aggrieved main character — and suck attention away from anything else Congress does. Raskin said that impeachment was neither a taboo nor a panacea. He also said that for the new Congress, restoring Medicaid and Obamacare subsidies would take immediate precedence over everything else.

When the election was over, Democratic leaders started signaling that their caucus is committed to investigating Trump but not turning him into a martyr. Going after a proxy figure, though, could flex their new muscle. At a post-election news conference, the incoming speaker of the House, Representative Hakeem Jeffries, said that no one in the Democratic caucus was talking to him about impeaching Trump; a few days later, he said yes to a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. “The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over,” he said. Congress holds the president accountable. And it gets to decide how to do so.

Source images for illustration above: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images​; Getty Images.

Emily Bazelon is a staff writer at The New York Times Magazine.

Russell Brand Sentenced to 10 and a Half Years in Prison for Rape

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A London judge said the former comedy star, who was convicted of rape and sexual assault last week, had shown a “casual, arrogant disregard” for women’s wishes.

By Alex Marshall

Reporting from Southwark Crown Court in London

Russell Brand, the comedian, actor and conspiracy-minded YouTuber, was sentenced on Monday to 10 and a half years in prison for the rape and sexual assaults that he was convicted of last week.

The presiding judge, Joel Bennathan, said in a sentencing hearing at Southwark Crown Court in London that Mr. Brand, 51, was “a sexual predator” with a “casual, arrogant disregard” for women’s wishes. “Your status protected you until 2023,” when accusations of assault were reported in the British news media, the judge said.

Under British sentencing guidelines, Mr. Bennathan could have sentenced Mr. Brand to life in prison for the rape conviction, but judges have significant leeway in issuing sentences, and those for rape are typically four to 19 years.

The decision came four days after a jury found Mr. Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, in a trial in which six women testified about episodes that they said occurred between 1999 and 2009.

The judge said the women’s testimony showed Mr. Brand’s “staggering arrogance” and his belief that “fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live.”

Mr. Brand denied all of the charges and said that either the events had not occurred or that the women were reinterpreting consensual sexual acts. The jury found Mr. Brand not guilty of two other counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Under British law, anyone who makes sexual assault accusations has lifelong anonymity outside the courtroom regardless of a jury’s verdict.

The rape charge he was convicted of concerned an encounter in 2009. The woman in question told the jury that she had gone to Mr. Brand’s house for consensual vaginal sex, but that Mr. Brand had at one point removed his condom and had anal sex with her without her consent, ignoring her pleas to stop and leaving her bleeding.

The three sexual assault convictions included a 2004 episode in which Mr. Brand grabbed a woman’s breasts at a London bar within a minute of their meeting; a 2005 episode in which he pinned a woman against a wall at a radio station and groped her; and a 2009 episode in which Mr. Brand’s team told a woman who was working with him that he would continue only if she gave him a massage, after which he thrust his face into her lap.

In his judgment, Mr. Bennathan said that Mr. Brand had told “a series of lies” in court.

During Monday’s hearing, the woman in the 2004 episode appeared in court, concealed by a screen, and said that her encounter with the comedian had caused her to lose “any love for myself for a long time.” She added that “it was impossible to escape” Mr. Brand because of his media profile, and that she often saw him “being celebrated for his disgusting behavior against women like it was all a joke.”

The woman he was convicted of raping said in a statement read out to the court that before the episode she had aspired to pursue stand-up comedy, but afterward she “felt unable to continue, because the thought of encountering Russell Brand, or even hearing his name, caused me anxiety and fear.” She said she had turned to alcohol to block out her “feelings and memories” of the rape.

The woman Mr. Brand was convicted of assaulting in 2005 described him in her statement as “a sexual predator who has no remorse for how his behavior has impacted my life.” She added, “I just hope that he is not allowed to hurt any more women.”

Ian Winter, Mr. Brand’s lawyer, told the court that Mr. Brand was “a fundamentally different person now” compared with who he was at time of the offenses. Mr. Winter said that Mr. Brand’s behavior at the time was perhaps a “consequence” of his increasing fame.

Mr. Winter also asked the judge to take into account Mr. Brand’s family, including his three young children. “We invite mercy,” the lawyer said, urging the judge to also consider Mr. Brand’s charitable work helping people recover from addiction.

In sentencing, Mr. Bennathan said that the prison term was a “sad loss” for Mr. Brand’s children, but that he had brought that on them himself.

Just before finishing his ruling, Mr. Bennathan paid tribute to “the determination and bravery” of the women who testified. Under questioning from Mr. Brand’s legal team, those women “had to face being confronted and being told they had lied, or twisted the truth,” the judge said, before directing a comment at Mr. Brand: “That was all done because of you, on your instructions.”

In April, Mr. Brand said in an interview with Piers Morgan, the former newspaper editor, that he would accept his fate if he received a prison sentence, because it would mean God had decided on that path for him. “That’s the deal we’ve got,” Mr. Brand said.

An earlier version of this article misstated the year of the encounter that led to the rape charge Russell Brand was convicted on. It was 2009, not 1999. Because of an editing error, the article also misstated the range of years in which six women said in their testimony that episodes had occurred. It was between 1999 and 2009, not 2004 and 2009.

Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

An investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore company that was buying advanced Nvidia A. I. chips, was transferred to the Justice Department after a top Nvidia executive reached out to Commerce Department officials.

By Ana Swanson and Devlin Barrett

Ana Swanson covers trade and the Commerce Department and Devlin Barrett covers the Justice Department. They reported from Washington

Investigators at the Commerce Department were deep into a monthslong investigation of a Singaporean company that they suspected of smuggling Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips into China when their work came to a sudden halt late last year.

The investigation centered on Megaspeed, a data center company led by an executive who U. S. officials now believe to be a Chinese spy who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang.

But the case was abruptly transferred to the Justice Department last year. The shift came after Commerce Department investigators working on the case received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel seeking information about the inquiry into Megaspeed.

It is not necessarily unusual for Commerce Department agents working on a case to speak with a company’s representatives about issues involving their firm. But what was unusual was the content of the message. Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, said that Jeff Kessler, a top official at the department, had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case.

The agents were alarmed that Nvidia had invoked the name of Mr. Kessler, their superior, who was nominated to his role by President Trump. Some viewed Mr. Kessler’s interaction with Nvidia as violating government procedure and potentially tainting the case, according to current and former government officials and others familiar with the incident.

It is not clear what led to Mr. Teter’s outreach to the department, but the recent revelations about Mr. Huang’s acknowledged affair with a Megaspeed executive have only intensified scrutiny of Nvidia’s role in influencing policy on chip sales to China. The New York Times reported last month that the U. S. government had concluded that Huang Le, or Alice Huang, a top executive at the firm, was a spy working on behalf of the Chinese government.

On Sunday, Nvidia said it was opening an investigation into Mr. Huang, after he acknowledged to the company’s board that he had been intimate with Ms. Huang. The pair, who are not related, had been photographed together on multiple occasions, including at a bar and a restaurant in Taiwan alongside other tech executives.

The incident raised questions about what Mr. Kessler, who reports directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, had discussed with Nvidia. It also raised the possibility that those discussions could become their own subject of inquiry.

Perhaps inadvertently, some officials said, Mr. Kessler had opened himself to accusations of undue influence and potentially jeopardized his department’s work on Megaspeed.

The case was quickly transferred to the Justice Department in an effort to avoid any potential compromise of the government’s investigation of Megaspeed, these people said. The Justice Department is conducting a criminal inquiry into Megaspeed, according to people familiar with the matter.

A Justice Department spokeswoman said the agency does not comment on continuing investigations. A Commerce Department spokesman said that department had been aggressively enforcing its rules and had conducted this and other actions strictly by the book.

John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, said the company consults with officials “to answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field, request their guidance and instructions and ask whether they have any follow-ups.”

The company works “to help government and our partners halt any would-be smugglers while serving the critical market of lawful customers that help America win worldwide,” he added.

A representative for Megaspeed said the company was conducting an internal investigation into allegations of chip diversion and had repeatedly offered to cooperate with the U. S. government but that those offers had gone unanswered.

The United States began investigating Megaspeed and Ms. Huang in 2024, after the company started importing billions of dollars’ worth of advanced Nvidia A. I. equipment into Malaysia. Megaspeed had been planning and constructing data centers around Southeast Asia to serve Chinese clients, including Alibaba, the Chinese tech giant. While that behavior is legal, U. S. officials were concerned that some of the Nvidia chips the company had bought were illegally routed into China.

The United States has imposed restrictions on which technologies could be sold to China through export controls, which ban certain chips from being sold there and require U. S. companies to get licenses to sell others. Nvidia has opposed those controls and argued for selling its products more freely.

In August 2025, officials at the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security who were pursuing the case received an email from Mr. Teter, the general counsel of Nvidia, people familiar with the incident said. In a message to the agents, Mr. Teter said that Mr. Kessler had given him permission to reach out about the case.

A Commerce Department official said that Nvidia had contacted the employees directly to request a meeting with one of them. When the employees declined the meeting, Mr. Teter responded to the employees by saying he was unsure what the issue was because Mr. Kessler had said Nvidia could communicate with the bureau’s employees.

The employees forwarded the email chain to Mr. Kessler. Hours later, Mr. Kessler responded, saying they should continue to handle the case strictly by the book, the official said.

Mr. Kessler did not order his employees to divulge information to Nvidia, and he did not weigh in with the agents on what meetings to take or what information to divulge, that official said.

Mr. Kessler did not respond to requests for comment.

As an under secretary, Mr. Kessler would typically be walled off from the finer details of such an investigation given that he might be called on to serve as a neutral arbiter in the case. Mr. Kessler’s interactions with Nvidia could also be subject to legal discovery or a subpoena if the department were to pursue future legal action against Megaspeed, officials said.

It is not clear if other factors contributed to the decision to suspend the Commerce Department’s work. That decision also coincided with the collection of U. S. intelligence that would conclude that Ms. Huang had spied for the Chinese government. Mr. Trump was briefed in October 2025 that Ms. Huang had a relationship with Mr. Huang and was presumed to be a spy, but the president chose not to do anything with that intelligence.

The Justice and Commerce Departments often pursue export control cases in tandem, but the Justice Department can take the lead in cases involving criminality and intelligence. The Justice Department can pursue criminal penalties that often require a higher burden of proof, while the Commerce Department levies civil penalties including fines.

But officials described the way the case was handed off from the Commerce Department as unusual and concerning.

Several officials, who requested anonymity to discuss a highly sensitive issue, questioned why the Commerce Department was discussing the case with Nvidia, a party that had not been ruled out as a subject of the investigation.

After the email from Mr. Teter, Commerce officials convened meetings to discuss the incident and rapidly disclosed it to partner law enforcement agencies. The Justice Department requested that the Commerce Department pause its work on the investigation, and Commerce complied, one person familiar with the case said.

The outcome was a source of frustration to agents investigating Megaspeed, who had spent months building a case. It may also have prevented the Commerce Department from taking quicker action to stop technology shipments to Megaspeed.

Government officials inside and outside the Commerce Department already had concerns about the Trump administration’s deference to Nvidia, a driving force behind America’s A. I. growth and the U. S. stock market. Mr. Huang has been an influential voice on export control policy with both Mr. Trump and Mr. Lutnick, the secretary in charge of the Commerce Department, which controls American technology exports.

The Trump administration, including the Justice Department, has also taken the view that the federal government should avoid making regulatory or enforcement decisions that limit American companies’ ability to dominate the artificial intelligence industry. Nvidia’s chips are a major driver of that industry.

Since Mr. Trump’s return to office, Mr. Kessler and other leaders at the department had mandated that any investigations into Nvidia and other outreach to the company first receive their approval. Mr. Kessler, who reports directly to Mr. Lutnick, has also maintained tight control over the licenses granted by the department, many of which involve Nvidia technology, as well as the department’s communications with the company.

While other agencies have proposed placing Megaspeed on the entity list, a trade blacklist overseen by the Commerce Department, though the department has not moved forward with the action. The department has not added a company to the entity list in over a year, the longest stretch without such a listing in 18 years.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

Devlin Barrett covers the Justice Department and the F. B. I. for The Times.

Trump Veers Back Into Claims of Rigged Election

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump, who initially said he would accept the midterm results, renewed his unsubstantiated claims that voting was manipulated.

By Luke Broadwater and Zolan Kanno-Youngs

Reporting from Washington

For years, President Trump has claimed without evidence that any election he lost or even feared losing was rigged. So it was a surprise to many when, on election night after his party was routed in the midterms last week, he said he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results.

That lasted less than a week.

“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” Mr. Trump wrote on Monday on social media, renewing his efforts to sow doubt about the outcome in the face of staggering Democratic wins. “How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!”

Mr. Trump has in recent days returned to his penchant for amplifying conspiracy theories about widespread election fraud. On Saturday, he had shared several posts from others questioning the results with convoluted mathematical theories about election rigging.

Election officials have said the vote went reasonably smoothly, with few major issues reported and no evidence of widespread fraud.

Mr. Trump had tried to lay the groundwork for claims of fraud before Election Day, mounting an intense campaign to assert more federal control over the election process and sow doubt about the outcome. Much of his campaign was blocked by the courts.

His administration directed federal agents to scour state rolls and federal databases to try to find noncitizen voters. The administration sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for refusing to cede to the federal government’s demands to turn over voter rolls. But his claims of large numbers of noncitizens illegally voting fell apart in court, and the administration lost more than two dozen of those cases.

The Supreme Court blocked Mr. Trump’s effort to have the U. S. Postal Service screen mail ballots. The administration even tried to pre-emptively challenge the certification of Alaska’s Senate election if the Republican candidate were to narrowly lose, essentially trying to nullify an opponent’s potential win before the votes were tallied. A federal judge dismissed that lawsuit.

Mr. Trump’s focus on voting machines in his social media post on Monday was notable, given his administration’s efforts in recent months to cast doubt on whether the machines can be trusted. Mr. Trump’s homeland security secretary asked the Justice Department in September to examine whether a commonly used voting machine could be counted on to create a verifiable record.

And Mr. Trump last month hosted in the Oval Office Tina Peters, a former Colorado county clerk who was convicted of tampering with voting machines after the 2020 election. Ms. Peters has called on Mr. Trump to inspect or seize voting machines — a move that legal experts say would be an overreach of federal authority.

Election machines are already heavily monitored and regulated through testing and certification by federal agencies, states, local election offices and private labs.

Mr. Trump’s posts in recent days follow a long pattern.

He once objected to the results of the Emmys. He falsely claimed that President Barack Obama had not won the popular vote in 2012. He asserted that Senator Ted Cruz of Texas “stole” a primary victory from him in Iowa in 2016. He predicted, before he defeated Hillary Clinton that year to win the presidency, that the general election would be “rigged.” Leading up to the 2020 election, Mr. Trump again predicted that he would be cheated out of a victory and refused to commit to a peaceful transfer of power, leading up to the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the Capitol.

Democrats denounced Mr. Trump’s reversion to form.

“Donald Trump’s pathetic return to election denialism was inevitable,” Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, wrote on social media. “He can whine all he wants, but nothing will stop this inescapable truth: For the last two years of his presidency, Trump will face the largest Democratic congressional majorities in decades, all because he has been an unprecedented failure.”

Mr. Trump’s turn toward election denialism received a chilly reaction even from some on the right. Megyn Kelly, the conservative commentator, wrote two words in response to Mr. Trump’s post: “Just stop.”

Luke Broadwater covers the White House for The Times.

Zolan Kanno-Youngs is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.
