It’s Roy Cohn All Over Again

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark

Mr. Bird and Ms. Goldmark are the authors of “American Scoundrel: Roy Cohn’s Dark Journey from Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump.”

“Where’s my Roy Cohn?” Donald Trump cried out early in his first term in the White House. Mr. Cohn, the lawyer and fixer who mentored Mr. Trump during his ascent through New York real estate — and who taught him never to back down, never to apologize and always to threaten opponents with multimillion-dollar lawsuits — was then dead for 31 years. Mr. Trump clearly longed for his ruthless loyalty and his abrasive, no-holds-barred defiance of the American establishment. “Wouldn’t Roy love to see this moment?” Mr. Trump asked Roger Stone, another member of Mr. Cohn’s circle, just after the 2016 election. “Boy, do we miss him.”

In his first term, Mr. Trump appointed a chief of staff from deep within the political establishment: Reince Priebus, the head of the Republican National Committee. He lasted half a year. When Mr. Trump took office a second time, he went in a different direction, appointing Susie Wiles, a mostly behind-the-scenes consultant known for her understated managerial competence. In the wake of the Republican Party’s midterm calamity, most politicians would tack toward conciliation. Mr. Trump instead did what he was taught: He doubled down, replacing Ms. Wiles with Stephen Miller, the dedicated consigliere and attack dog who was the architect of some of Mr. Trump’s most divisive policies. Forty years after his mentor’s death, Mr. Trump found his Roy Cohn.

The similarities are almost spooky.

Both Mr. Cohn and Mr. Miller came from privileged backgrounds. Mr. Cohn was the son of a Bronx judge, and Mr. Miller’s father was a Santa Monica lawyer and real estate investor. Raised in liberal Jewish communities, Mr. Cohn and Mr. Miller both rebelled against their roots. Mr. Cohn in his 20s played a critical role in sending Julius and Ethel Rosenberg to the electric chair, and was rewarded by becoming chief counsel for Senator Joe McCarthy’s notorious subcommittee on investigations. While still in high school, Mr. Miller made a point of taunting Latino students and became a protégé of the conservative writer and activist David Horowitz.

Mr. Cohn came of professional age in the era of McCarthyism, the strain of Republican thought that morphed during the Trump presidency into a nativist, “America first” politics of resentments against the old bipartisan establishment — against multiculturalism, globalization and liberal culture. He hated affirmative action and the very notion of diversity. He once told the journalist Peter Manso, “I don’t want to be operated on by a Black who had lousier marks or who is a poorer doctor than a white who was excluded because we wanted to make room for the Black at Harvard Medical School because of some kind of affirmative action to pay for our past sins in suppressing Blacks. I want the best doctor.”

Similarly, Mr. Miller has used his position to oppose diversity, equity and inclusion, and has expressed the view that the “white youth population” is “disappearing.” His foundation, America First Legal, has demanded to know, “When did racism against white people become OK?”

Mr. Cohn led a witch hunt against gay people in the government and suspected Communist subversives, and Mr. Miller is the architect of a witch hunt against illegal immigrants. More closely than anyone else in Mr. Trump’s administration, he follows Mr. Cohn’s playbook of aggressive, unapologetic defiance. Mr. Miller even looks and sounds like Mr. Cohn, displaying the same hooded-eye scowls and snarling demeanor.

The quality Mr. Trump most obviously values, however, is absolute loyalty. It’s a trait that served Mr. Cohn well in his dealings with Mafia clients including Anthony “Fat Tony” Salerno, John Gotti and Carmine Galante. “Roy Cohn was a man that if he liked you,” the president said in a 2005 interview, “he was an unbelievable, loyal friend.”

Mr. Miller has shown Mr. Trump the same fealty. Most of the country has abandoned the president, but Mr. Miller will be by his side, enabling his worst instincts. “I pledge to you, Mr. President,” Mr. Miller said after being tapped for this new position, “my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment and my total devotion to your success and the success of this country.”

This is the level of devotion required by a deeply narcissistic, insecure braggart in his waning years. Mr. Cohn understood, as his relationship with Mr. Trump matured, that his onetime acolyte expected an increasing degree of obsequiousness. After a dozen years of collaboration, however, Mr. Trump began to distance himself when it became clear that his old friend and mentor was suffering from AIDS. In his last weeks of life, Mr. Cohn underwent the public humiliation of being disbarred for unethical and unprofessional conduct.

Mr. Miller now has the job of advancing an agenda that Americans rejected. We can expect him to do so as Mr. Cohn did, subsuming his identity, his morality and his professional credibility in service of a mercurial leader who does not reciprocate the loyalty he demands. Count on the Miller White House to fight any attempts to constrain its outrageous power grabs, deploying even more threats, bigger lawsuits, angrier campaigns of retribution and more aggressive anti-immigrant policies than we saw in the last two years.

When it ends badly, as it no doubt will, Mr. Miller should expect to be among those the president blames. Then the eager acolyte will join the long list of people who have embraced the president only to be pitilessly abandoned or destroyed.

Still, Mr. Miller may take heart. After freezing out his mentor, Mr. Trump did invite Mr. Cohn to a farewell dinner at Mar-a-Lago, and showed up at his disbarment hearing to attest to his good character. “He is a very loyal person,” Mr. Trump said, “extremely loyal and extremely honest.” Mr. Cohn died in 1986. A journalist saw Mr. Trump at the memorial service, weeping.

Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark are the authors of “American Scoundrel: Roy Cohn’s Dark Journey from Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump,”

A. I. Turned Mundane Chipmakers Into Tech Celebrities

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

As chips became essential components for A. I., executives like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang saw their personal wealth and profiles soar in a way the industry has not experienced before.

By Don Clark

Reporting from San Francisco

Before Jensen Huang and Nvidia changed the technology landscape, the semiconductor business was conspicuously short of stars. Wealth, infidelity and politics seldom figured in discussions of the chip industry’s leaders.

But Mr. Huang changed Silicon Valley, starting in the middle of the past decade, by single-mindedly pursuing the silicon chips that power generative artificial intelligence and related innovations. Extraordinary riches followed for the Taiwan-born executive and many of his peers, in some cases eclipsing the fortunes of high-profile software or internet entrepreneurs.

With that money and influence came attention from powerful people in Washington, notably President Trump, and opportunities for the kinds of entanglements that Mr. Huang on Sunday admitted to with a Chinese executive who goes by Alice Huang. U. S. intelligence has determined that Ms. Huang, who could not be reached for comment, was a Chinese spy. A Nvidia spokeswoman declined to comment.

“Before generative A. I., semiconductors were not a sexy business, and were never a place for C. E. O. s to make fast money,” said David Yoffie, a Harvard Business School professor who has closely tracked the chip business.

Mr. Huang largely seemed to fit this mold until 2023, Mr. Yoffie said, when generative intelligence driven by Nvidia chips exploded and turned the semiconductors — which can perform calculations and other tasks — into essential components.

“In the last three years, he became a rock star, which apparently attracted the same kind of attention as all rock stars,” Mr. Yoffie said.

Not that Mr. Huang, 63, is known for throwing his money around wildly by Silicon Valley standards, where fancy houses and fast cars are commonplace. But he could afford to splurge.

The value of his Nvidia stock holdings skyrocketed from about $659 million in 2017 — when the company was best known for chips called graphics processing units that were used in video games — to about $143 billion, factoring in a decline in the shares Monday following the news.

The most famous chip leader before Mr. Huang — Andy Grove, the former chief executive of Intel — never held shares worth more than a few hundred million dollars. Among the chip industry’s pioneers, Gordon Moore, who co-founded Intel, was the one prominent billionaire. Mr. Grove and Mr. Moore, as well as many of their peers, were known for long marriages and sedate lifestyles.

But Intel never experienced such a rapid surge in revenue or stock-market value as Nvidia, which makes chips that carry out the bulk of number-crunching in popular A. I. applications. The Silicon Valley company, which was founded in 1993 and in 2017 eclipsed $100 billion in value, became the first $1 trillion chip maker in 2023 and later the first public company to break $5 trillion.

A few other chip companies also saw their fortunes soar. One is Broadcom, which sells networking chips needed for A. I. data centers and helps companies design chips for A. I. calculations. Henry Samueli, one of its co-founders, holds shares worth about $26 billion.

Other big winners are suppliers of memory chips, which store vast amounts of data needed for A. I. calculations. Micron Technology, the sole U. S. maker of both kinds of chips, has been transformed from a frequent money-loser into a $1 trillion company before a recent market sell-off.

But Sanjay Mehotra, its chief executive, does not hold founder-size equity in the company. Neither does Hock Tan, Broadcom’s chief. Both hold shares worth hundreds of millions of dollars, according to public findings.

The chip industry has not been immune from scandals. In 2018, Intel forced out its chief executive, Brian Krzanich, over a relationship with a subordinate.

And there have been some chip executives who liked to show off their wealth. Jerry Sanders, the co-founder and former chief of Advanced Micro Devices, bought flashy houses in Beverly Hills and Malibu and at times was driven around in Rolls-Royces.

Mr. Moore, who died in 2023, built a 10,000-square-foot home on the big island of Hawaii toward the end of his life. But he is much better known for his philanthropy and an oft-quoted prediction about the pace of improvements in manufacturing semiconductors. He never bought a Hawaiian island, unlike Larry Ellison, co-founder of the software giant Oracle.

Signs of exorbitant spending by semiconductor executives may become less likely now, partly because of a recent stock-market slump over fears that spending on A. I. data center hardware will slow.

Still, chip makers are reporting robust income statements and enjoying a sales surge that executives and analysts expect to last longer than past cycles. The industry’s annual sales surpassed $1 trillion for the first time in August, a figure that until recently was expected to be reached in 2030. That month, Gartner, a market research firm, predicted $1.6 trillion in revenue for 2026, up 92 percent from 2025.

“I have not seen this kind of growth,” said Ajit Monocha, the chief executive of the trade group SEMI, in kicking off its annual conference in San Francisco last month. “It’s the most exciting time of the industry.”

‘Talafreako’ Is, Accidentally, the Campaign Song of the Moment

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Critic’s Notebook

An impromptu song by a Texas rapper has helped immortalize the frisky nickname of Senator-elect James Talarico.

By Jon Caramanica

In political campaigns, theme songs are carefully chosen, vetted to make sure they embody just that right amount of triumph and hope.

But sometimes, a song does the choosing. Such is the case with “Talafreako,” a tossed-off bit of filthy partisan exuberance by an until-now unheralded Texas rapper, Lil Texxan.

In just over a week, “Talafreako” — the full title is “Talafreako (Ken Paxton Diss)” — has become an accidental political anthem, less an elegant song than an emblematic and effective one. It’s a celebration of James Talarico, who was elected to the U. S. Senate last week, beating the Republican state attorney general Ken Paxton, who was backed by President Trump and is the subject of the song’s far less flattering sections.

Talafreako the word has a bit of a lurid backstory. Trump began using it as a pejorative in speeches attacking the candidate. But then Talarico himself took it on and flipped the meaning, essentially turning it into the moniker for his stan army. The campaign even began selling “I’m a Talafreako” T-shirts.

The song’s anchor is a simple, almost instinctual rhyme in the chorus: “She a freak ho for James Talarico.” It’s silly and improbable, and Lil Texxan has an air of stand-up comedy in his delivery. After a couple of lewd lines, it’s followed by a boisterous, bitter chant against Paxton that’s shouted six times, for emphasis.

The production is largely centered around a keyboard line that juxtaposes an ominous, pugnacious figure against a sweetly tinkling rejoinder. It threads seriousness with freedom, curiosity with certainty.

The song has all the hallmarks of great Dallas rap — loose, shouty and highly rhythmic, with ample space for dancing. Appropriately, since it came out shortly before Election Day, it’s been bubbling around the social internet, largely as a soundtrack for videos of people bending, which is a dance style specific to the Dallas-Fort Worth area, one of the great dance-rap regions in the country.

In a phone interview on Friday, Lil Texxan — 33 years old and born Shaqulle Standberry — said he made it in one freestyle session with nothing written beforehand, using a beat he found on YouTube by the producer Laa4beatz. (The beat was made in the style of JhonnieDamnD’s “Murda Bend,” a local bending anthem.)

“I pulled up to the studio and somebody had a Talarico sign in the front yard, and I was like, Hey, that’s a catchy last name,” he recalled. “Plus, he’s a great guy in my opinion.”

Lil Texxan is from Dallas and now lives in Austin. He said he wasn’t a fan of Paxton; the song mentions Paxton’s 2015 fraud allegation and includes some uncharitable assessments of his appearance. And Lil Texxan sensed that Talarico was aligned with his values. “I know what’s right and what’s wrong,” Lil Texxan said. “I voted for that boy Talarico.”

Lil Texxan said he’d had no contact with the Talarico campaign before making the song: “I don’t know them folks!”

Over the weekend, though, the Team Talarico Instagram account — part of the campaign’s digital arm — posted a clip of Talarico’s surprise appearance on “Saturday Night Live” soundtracked by, and captioned, “Talafreako.” (Lil Texxan said he was planning to make a clean version of the song, so that it might be used and heard more widely.)

This grass roots reclamation has been developing in tandem with a surge of A. I. memes of Talarico that include clips of him strutting into a restaurant, bounding out of a courthouse or dominating someone in basketball while shooting them a middle finger. These fake clips are a lighthearted variation on digital blackface, inserting Talarico, who comes off as a lanky schoolboy in his blue blazer, into unlikely cultural and social milieus. (The ones of him dancing with A. I. Barack Obama are especially funny.)

These A. I. memes and the video clips soundtracked by “Talafreako” all together serve as a kind of modern digital folk art — immediate, topical, endlessly iterating on a common theme — and seemingly organic street-team marketing.

They’re alluring on their own as low-touch art, but they also meet unfulfilled demand for political conversation that might not be happening from the top down. Making one of these videos, or even just posting one, reflects how political sentiment actually functions on the micro scale; it’s the online equivalent of a campaign yard sign.

Though “Talafreako” emerged organically, it may set a worrisome template. TikTok and Instagram are littered with enthusiastic sponsored content — some overt, some sub rosa — designed to pass for genuine support. Political campaigns do the same thing, of course, with traditional influencers. But the “Talafreako” lightbulb moment might have them conscripting local rappers (or singers, or bands) to whip off a few ditties and post them online, in hopes of astroturfing one into the viral slipstream.

It’s a grim proposition, but engineered virality never quite feels like the real thing. And Lil Texxan’s sense of timing, play and political mood will be tough to duplicate by fiat.

“I didn’t pay for nothing. I didn’t pay for it to get reposted or nothing,” Lil Texxan said. “I’m just off the dome with it.”

Jon Caramanica is a pop music critic who hosts “Popcast,” The Times’s music podcast.

Congress to Vote on Far-Reaching Plan to Speed Up Energy Projects

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The sprawling bill, which has divided Democrats, would overhaul major environmental laws to streamline the permitting process.

By Brad Plumer

Reporting from Washington

As Democrats return to Capitol Hill after stunning midterm victories, one of their first tough decisions is whether to back a sweeping, contentious plan to make it easier to build power plants, gas pipelines, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure.

The Senate is scheduled to take an initial procedural vote on Monday evening on the bipartisan permitting-reform bill, which would overhaul longstanding environmental laws to speed development of fossil fuels and renewable energy alike.

Business groups, energy developers and labor unions all back the legislation, as does President Trump. The United States is struggling to build enough power sources to keep up with soaring electricity demand, especially for A. I. data centers. Cutting red tape, proponents say, could increase supplies and lower electricity prices.

Yet the 494-page bill has divided Democrats, whose votes are needed in the lame-duck session. Supporters say the bill would bolster clean energy technologies that could reduce planet-warming emissions. But environmentalists have sharply criticized provisions that would benefit oil and gas and make it harder to sue to block polluting facilities.

Last week’s “blue tsunami” could complicate passage. Some Democrats have said the party should negotiate a new bill next year, when they’ll have large majorities. Others counter that this bill took years to negotiate with Senate Republicans and the White House, and a better deal is unlikely anytime soon.

“We don’t have more years to lose as clean energy projects sit on the sidelines, and there’s no guarantee Congress would ever find another compromise that would be able to pass the Senate,” said Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island, one of the authors of the bill. “Democrats ran and won on affordability, and this bill lowers costs for families and will allow us to start delivering on our election promises. It’s a bird in the hand. We’d be fools not to take it.”

Here’s a rundown of the bill’s major provisions.

Many energy companies have complained that it’s gotten increasingly difficult and expensive to build large infrastructure in the United States. A giant wind farm and power line in New Mexico took 17 years to complete after numerous lawsuits and route changes. Regulatory challenges delayed a 303-mile natural gas pipeline through Virginia and West Virginia for a decade.

Some experts say federal environmental laws are one major factor. Big energy projects often have to navigate a thicket of rules that require extensive reviews and allow lawsuits that can cause unpredictable delays. These laws were enacted in the 1970s to encourage public participation and transparency. But some politicians say they have become too restrictive.

Energy has also become increasingly partisan. Democratic-led states like New York have used clean-water rules to block natural gas pipelines, while the Biden administration tried to stifle oil drilling on public lands. The Trump administration has sought to revoke permits for offshore wind and bury wind and solar projects in red tape.

The permitting reform bill — known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA — would streamline federal approvals and make it harder for presidents to unilaterally block energy projects.

The complex measure was negotiated after months of closed-door sessions between senators from both parties and the Trump administration. While Republicans have long favored shrinking environmental regulations, a growing number of Democrats like Mr. Whitehouse now say it’s impossible to reduce planet-warming emissions without being able to build many more long-distance power lines or large solar arrays. That requires permitting changes.

The legislation would overhaul several landmark environmental laws to make it easier for the federal government to approve all sorts of projects, from gas pipelines to subway expansions.

“This bill would certainly be the biggest change to environmental permitting in decades,” said Michael Gerrard, director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia.

For example, the National Environmental Policy Act of 1970, or NEPA, requires many projects with federal involvement to go through lengthy reviews of potential impacts on air and water. The bill would exempt certain projects from these reviews, such as expansions of pipelines or power lines along existing routes, while setting tighter deadlines and restricting the ability of environmental groups and communities to sue.

Notably, the bill would prevent courts from halting projects if they found an environmental review inadequate. Judges could only order federal agencies to update their reviews while construction proceeds.

Supporters say that NEPA often ties up projects in years of litigation that does little to improve environmental outcomes. They note that energy facilities still have to follow other laws, such as the Clean Air Act.

“Whether you’re talking about solar or wind or gas, it takes five to seven years to get through permitting,” said Ray Long, president of the American Council on Renewable Energy, a trade group. “That’s too long. We should be able to get it down to 24 months while still preserving the right of communities to weigh in.”

Yet environmentalists who frequently use the law to sue oil and gas projects have argued that the changes could render NEPA toothless, removing a key tool for communities to understand the effects of new developments.

The bill makes other major changes, such as limiting states’ ability to object to gas pipelines under the Clean Water Act. It also streamlines reviews required by the National Historic Preservation Act of how infrastructure projects could affect historically or culturally important sites, a big consideration for tribal nations.

The bill also limits the ability of presidents to revoke already-issued federal permits, while allowing companies to sue federal agencies that hold up energy projects for an “unreasonable” length of time. Some Democrats sought those provisions to make it harder for the Trump administration to slow wind and solar farms, though they could also prevent future Democratic administrations from delaying oil and gas permits.

Several far-reaching provisions would push regional grid operators to plan for more large power lines while giving federal regulators stronger authority to authorize new ones.

That provision has been of particular interest to renewable energy groups. One huge roadblock for more wind and solar power has been a lack of long-distance lines that can connect the windy Great Plains and sunny Southwest with population centers. When lines do get proposed, states and localities in their paths often hold them up. The bill, experts say, could lead to a large expansion of the electric grid.

The legislation would also require data centers to pay a larger share of the costs of new power plants and transmission lines. It’s a nod to widespread voter anger over data centers for A. I., with many communities worried that the massive energy-hungry facilities could raise costs for ordinary households.

Other provisions would streamline permitting for geothermal energy. Many start-ups are trying to adopt advanced drilling techniques from the oil and gas industry to harvest clean energy from underground heat, yet they often face hurdles to explore federal land in the West.

Various groups have tried to model the bill’s provisions and found that it could help lower electricity costs and expand renewable energy, though the magnitude is uncertain.

The Rhodium Group, a research firm, estimated that the bill could cut U. S. electricity prices by 3 to 5 percent and potentially reduce domestic greenhouse gas emissions modestly as both natural gas and wind and solar power expand. The bill would quite likely free up more gas for U. S. companies to export, though the group did not estimate the emissions impact of that.

One wild card for emissions, said Ben King, a director at Rhodium Group, is whether tech companies might build more data centers on the grid or use more polluting off-grid equipment if the bill passes. Other impacts are hard to model: If the legislation boosts advanced geothermal, that could create a major new source of clean energy, though that wouldn’t affect emissions immediately.

Influential green groups like the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council have praised provisions that would expand the electric grid but have criticized the environmental rollbacks. They oppose the current bill.

Some are concerned that the plan would enable Mr. Trump to approve a slew of fossil-fuel projects — new gas pipelines, mining, data centers on public lands — that would be difficult for a future president to undo. Conservation groups have also opposed the bill on the grounds that it could lead to more water pollution or harm endangered species, effects that don’t show up in modeling.

“To just say we’re going to let anyone build anything as fast as they can and lock it in with President Trump?” said Abigail Dillen, president of Earthjustice, an environmental group that opposes the bill. “That’s a dangerous prescription.”

By contrast, some climate groups like Evergreen Action say those trade-offs are worth it for a bill that would make it much easier to build clean energy.

The divide underscores a broader debate about how much environmentalists should focus on blocking fossil fuels versus working to expand less-polluting alternatives as quickly as possible. Supporters of permitting changes note that the Biden administration often ran into bureaucratic constraints while trying to expand wind and solar power, while arguing that states like New York have struggled to cut emissions by blocking gas pipelines.

“I don’t think we have any evidence that blocking fossil fuel projects with permitting has been an effective tool in reducing global emissions,” said Jane Flegal, a senior fellow at the Searchlight Institute and former climate official in the Biden administration. “It raises costs, it’s bad politics and it doesn’t work.”

Most energy companies, including fossil fuel and renewable energy trade groups and electric utilities, have backed the bill. A group of former economic officials from the Trump, Biden and Obama administrations also urged passage, saying that the United States could lose the technology race against China without big changes to energy permitting.

Some tribal nations had criticized the bill’s changes to the National Historic Preservation Act, and the bill’s authors revised the text recently in an effort to address those concerns.

It’s far from certain that the legislation will pass during the brief lame-duck session. The bill needs 60 votes in the Senate and would also need to be taken up by the House while lawmakers still have many other priorities — including funding the government.

Brad Plumer is a Times reporter who covers technology and policy efforts to address global warming.

How Tension Over Trump Fractured American Diabetes Research

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

It began with a protest at an American Diabetes Association conference. Now a resulting boycott has caused a scientific slowdown, with no end in sight.

By Eric Boodman

Eric Boodman is The Times’s national science correspondent.

The plan was for a polite, academic act of dissent.

For its biggest conference, the American Diabetes Association had invited Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, director of the National Institutes of Health, as keynote speaker, and scientists were mad. Here was one of the officials behind slashed research grants, an existential threat to American science, some thought, and he was being billed as the star of their scientific meeting?

There was talk of a walkout. Dr. Steven Kahn, director of the University of Washington’s diabetes research center, had another idea. Before the speech, he and other scientists would distribute copies of an editorial he had coauthored decrying federal funding cuts — a quiet counterpoint, given that audience questions would not be allowed.

“Don’t want this to be a big deal,” one of the action’s participants, Dr. Desmond Schatz, told the A. D. A.’s then chief scientific and medical officer, Dr. Rita Kalyani, by text. “You may want to CALL Steve and tell him where he can and can’t give out his copies. Should not in any way be disruptive.”

“Thanks Des,” Dr. Kalyani responded. “I’m on plane and will find out details of where it can be given out when I land.”

But Dr. Kahn says the association never reached out.

On the morning of June 5, he divided 1,000 printouts of the editorial among a dozen colleagues, and they fanned out around the lecture hall.

The A. D. A.’s Scientific Sessions is the Super Bowl of diabetes research. Data on household-name drugs like Ozempic are often unveiled there. The Banting Medal, among the field’s highest honors, is presented there. Diabetes Care, the A. D. A.’s most prestigious journal, has its annual meeting there. This year, over 12,000 attendees were expected.

It didn’t take long for police and security to notice “disruptions,” as the A. D. A.’s chief executive, Charles Henderson, would later describe them. Guards — some with guns and handcuffs on their belts — yanked away editorials, grabbed researchers and escorted them outside. Five scientists were expelled. When a few returned, they were kicked out again and threatened with arrest.

The event laid bare long-simmering tension between a formidable nonprofit and the scientists it works with to fight a disease that affects more than 40 million Americans.

To the New Orleans Five — as the ejected researchers call themselves — the struggle is about righting an institution gone rogue. “The A. D. A. is a microcosm of the Trump administration,” Dr. Kahn said. To Aaron Kelly, a University of Minnesota physiologist who was among those expelled, the organization’s response embodies nothing less than “a quelling of dissent in the United States of America.”

Researchers have accused the nonprofit of censorship. A. D. A. officials have resigned. Donors have excised the association from their wills. And since September, Dr. Kahn has been coleading a boycott of the organization, with nearly 1,200 experts refusing to work with the A. D. A.’s medical journals or present at its conferences. At Diabetes Care, editors have stopped editing and submissions have slowed.

By now, the conflict is less about the expulsion and more about what it represents. Dr. Kalyani said she had no hand in the researchers’ ejection and agreed with their editorial. The A. D. A. declined to answer questions beyond a report released last month that said the association had received threats of disruption before the conference, creating security concerns and that no constitutional rights had been violated because free speech is not protected in privately leased spaces. Still, it conceded that three of the New Orleans Five “likely shouldn’t have been removed.”

But that partial apology wasn’t enough to end the standoff and bring American diabetes research back to normal. International scientists who usually clamored to speak at the A. D. A.’s meeting wondered whether it would be worth traveling to the United States in 2027 at all.

Look at the résumés of top diabetes researchers and you’ll see “A. D. A.” appear and reappear as a three-letter leitmotif. Many of the field’s stars have both given and received support. By its own count, last year, the association invested $27.5 million in research and introduced 70 pieces of legislation. According to its latest public tax filings, in 2024, the C. E. O.’s total compensation package neared $1.3 million. It’s not the Gates Foundation, but it isn’t a neighborhood nonprofit, either.

Dr. Kahn first joined in the 1980s, soon after arriving in the United States from South Africa. His emigration was a pilgrimage of sorts. The National Institutes of Health was the biggest funder of biomedical research on earth, the United States a scientific mecca. Dr. Kahn wanted in and the A. D. A. was instrumental, giving him an early grant to study the genetics of diabetes. In the 2000s, he served on the organization’s board. In 2023, he became editor in chief of Diabetes Care. Last year, he received the Banting Medal.

But suddenly, he was on the sidewalk outside the association’s biggest conference and told not to come back.

“‘What do I do now? I’m supposed to chair a session,’” he remembered writing to an A. D. A. leader. “I never heard back from her. Not a word. They whitewashed my name from the program.”

The story might have ended there. Dr. Bhattacharya, the N. I. H. director, hadn’t even shown up; he sent a deputy instead. If A. D. A. leaders had apologized, met with the ejected researchers and returned their badges, the episode might have been a blip. That was what Dr. Mark Atkinson, volunteer chair of the Scientific Sessions planning committee, had proposed on June 5.

Instead, the next day, the A. D. A. sent an email blast saying that Dr. Kahn and his peers had “violated conference policies regarding unauthorized distribution of materials.” It was signed with Mr. Henderson’s name — but also Dr. Atkinson’s.

“I did not agree to sign that letter,” Dr. Atkinson said. He resigned as chair that evening and booked the next flight out, he said, too ashamed to show his face at the event he had helped organize.

Though Mr. Henderson eventually released a video apology, the situation had become a tug of war over the truth. Dr. Kahn and his fellow editors at Diabetes Care compiled a post-mortem on the incident, but the A. D. A. blocked its publication. Dr. Kahn cried censorship. The A. D. A. said it was waiting for “authenticated facts” established by an “arms-length review.” Dr. Kahn and his colleagues were dismayed that the review was run by current and former A. D. A. board members, including a lawyer representing the association in court.

In early September, when Mr. Henderson announced that the investigation was complete and deemed the removals appropriate, Dr. Kahn’s camp was incensed. The researchers wanted to see both the full report and the A. D. A. bylaws governing such internal investigations. The organization refused.

There was a sense on both sides that this conflict had become a distraction. “This is not a moment our community can afford to spend fighting itself,” Mr. Henderson wrote in an editorial for STAT.

“I, personally, was really tired of hearing about the New Orleans Five, really tired of hearing about how horrible the A. D. A. is and really just wanted to get a resolution so that we could move on and fight the good fight,” said Dr. Jane Reusch, professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz, who had distributed editorials but was not expelled.

More important, to her, was a broader pattern of A. D. A. decisions that undermined its scientific integrity. She wanted that fixed so everyone could focus on Trump’s dismantling of American science. “The current administration wins when we’re fighting ourselves like this,” she said.

It was that very animosity from the Trump administration toward academia that kept researchers from backing down. “We expect our leaders to have a spine and stand up and not take part in this anticipatory obedience,” said Dr. Kelly, the University of Minnesota physiologist.

Last year, he had watched Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents grab people in Minneapolis with impunity; the lack of legal recourse felt overwhelming. Here was a squashing of dissent he could make a difference against. Here was an executive branch he could hold to account.

“I really wrestled with this,” said Michael Donnelly-Boylen, a patient advocate with Type 2 diabetes and obesity. He had been invited to join an A. D. A. advisory committee and was scheduled to moderate a webinar for the organization soon after the boycott began. His participation felt important. Too often, people with obesity were left out of decisions that affected their own bodies.

He couldn’t stand the idea of researchers being thrown out by police for distributing an editorial. But he worried that the chance to shape diabetes care could be lost if he spoke up. As he understood it, he was among the first patients to be invited to join the A. D. A.’s obesity and weight management advisory group. “Would patients in the future be given the same opportunity I was?”

Though he ultimately honored the boycott, his nervousness was a testament to the A. D. A.’s outsize influence. The whole operation was based in mutualism. The prestige of its journals depended on peer review, its clinical guidelines on knowledgeable experts writing them. In turn, the organization gave weight and credibility to those in its orbit. The controversy threatened that circular economy.

Last month, the A. D. A. sent invitations to speak at next year’s Scientific Sessions. Many worried that the boycott would put recent graduates in a bind. “For the junior scientists, this may be the biggest opportunity that has ever happened to them,” said Dr. Reusch. “They might be going up for promotion this year and require national recognition.”

On Oct. 22, the A. D. A. published its review of the June incident, which differed from the organization’s previous accounts of what had happened. The report recognized that the association had gotten its own code of conduct wrong when accusing the New Orleans Five of breaking rules. It apologized to three of them, including Dr. Kahn.

But there were still points of contention. The independence of the investigation. The disregard for evidence. The A. D. A.’s suggestion that Dr. Kelly had posed a security threat, which he called “a baldfaced lie.”

When asked about these and other issues, the A. D. A. said, “Our focus is now on the work ahead: rebuilding trust within the diabetes community through meaningful action.”

The report, though, hadn’t accomplished that. “It was close to the truth, but it was not all the truth,” Dr. Kahn said. He wanted the association’s bylaws released publicly. He wanted a meeting with its board.

By Nov. 6, Dr. Kalyani had resigned. The A. D. A.’s vice president for publications announced his resignation, too, citing worries about editorial independence and scientific integrity after the organization insisted on appointing interim editors for Diabetes Care while the official editors were not working.

Amid all this, pre-boycott submissions to Diabetes Care had come out. One probed links between disruptions in the microbiome and Type 1 diabetes. Another examined the risks and survival rates of patients whose blood sugar had so damaged the vessels in their feet that they needed amputation.

Like so much of science, the findings were incremental, data that yielded new questions and more data, which at some point might become an intervention that could change people’s lives. Depending on how negotiations go, Diabetes Care’s editors might resume work any day now. Or these might be among its last contributions for a while.

As the Country Swung Left, Independent Senate Candidates Stalled

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Democratic Party threw its support behind independent Senate candidates in deep-red states, but they came up short.

By Luke Vrotsos

Despite Democrats’ high hopes for a group of independent candidates they backed in deep-red states, the candidates were unable to significantly outperform the Democratic Party as a whole.

Four major independent candidates ran for Senate and lost: Brian Bengs in South Dakota, Dan Osborn in Nebraska, Todd Achilles in Idaho and Seth Bodnar in Montana. Of that group, Mr. Osborn was widely considered to have the best chance of victory.

In some recent Senate elections, independent candidates, including Mr. Osborn, have been able to run ahead of Democrats in red states by shedding the Democratic label. In 2024, Mr. Osborn lost to Senator Deb Fischer, a Republican incumbent, by 6.7 percentage points. That was nearly 14 percentage points better than Kamala Harris’s vote margin in the state — a larger outperformance than that of any Democratic Senate candidate in the country. Similarly, Evan McMullin, an independent who ran for Senate in Utah in 2022, performed 20 percentage points better than the average Democratic candidate for the House in his state.

Those types of performances were not repeated in 2026, with the independent candidates running much closer to other Democrats. Mr. Osborn and Mr. Achilles outperformed the candidates for governor in their states by just under two percentage points, and Mr. Achilles ran behind his state’s Democratic candidate for attorney general. Mr. Bengs accounted for a slightly larger gap, outperforming Dan Ahlers, the Democratic candidate for governor in South Dakota, by six percentage points.

Arrows show how counties shifted toward Dan Osborn or Republicans

Note: Data as of Monday, Nov. 9 at 11 a. m. Eastern time. Source: Associated Press Albert Sun/The New York Times

Mr. Osborn’s result was particularly disappointing for Democrats given the large shifts toward the party in similar races. The average House vote in Nebraska shifted nine percentage points to the left from 2024 to 2026. The Democratic candidates for Senate in neighboring Kansas and Iowa won, outperforming Ms. Harris’s 2024 vote margin by 21 and 17 percentage points. Mr. Osborn’s result in Nebraska, however, barely changed, with his vote margin improving by less than a point compared with his last Senate run. He also underperformed the polls of the race, even as Democrats nationwide outperformed the polls in competitive Senate races.

Mr. Osborn’s strong performance in 2024 came largely as a result of drawing support from Republicans and independents in rural parts of the state. He lost support among these voters in 2026, with many rural counties shifting 10 percentage points or more against him. He did make gains in Democratic-leaning suburban and urban areas, such as Douglas County, which includes Omaha.

One possible reason for Mr. Osborn’s failure to gain more support is that Nebraska voters were skeptical of his status as an independent, negating much of the advantage that Democrats sought by avoiding the party label. In a Times/Siena poll of the race, 55 percent of Nebraska voters said they thought of Mr. Osborn as more similar to Democrats, compared with 33 percent who thought of him as more of an independent. Among Republicans, 72 percent viewed him as a Democrat.

While the candidates identified as independents, and may have intended to remain that way politically, the Democratic Party’s embrace of them was clear, with party leaders pushing them forward as a path to making inroads in deep-red states. In Nebraska, Idaho and South Dakota, the Democratic candidate exited the race to consolidate support behind the independent. And three of the four candidates — Mr. Osborn, Mr. Bengs and Mr. Bodnar — relied on the party’s campaign infrastructure, using ActBlue, the Democratic-leaning fund-raising platform, to accept donations.

In Montana, the Democratic nominee, Alani Bankhead, refused to drop out amid pressure from some inside her own party. She received 12 percent of the vote, and Mr. Bodnar received 38 percent. The Republican incumbent, Kurt Alme, won with 48 percent of the vote. If either Mr. Bodnar or Ms. Bankhead had run alone and been able to consolidate nearly all of that combined support, that candidate potentially had a path to victory.

Luke Vrotsos is an elections analyst at The New York Times who covers American elections and public opinion using a range of data sources.

Nvidia’s Stock Drops After Board Opens Investigation Into C. E. O.

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

The chipmaker’s size and significance to the A. I. trade means that Jensen Huang’s admission of a relationship with a businesswoman suspected of spying for China could reverberate across Wall Street.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

By Joe Rennison and Jason Karaian

Nvidia’s stock price sank on Monday, after the company announced it would open an investigation into its chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with a business executive who U. S. intelligence determined was a Chinese spy.

Shares of Nvidia dropped roughly 5 percent on Monday. That stood out against a broader market rally, with the S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite index both rising about 2 percent in midmorning trading.

Nvidia’s board has said that it has no reason to believe national security or the company’s own trade secrets have been compromised, but the chipmaker’s sheer size and significance to the A. I. trade means that the news will reverberate across Wall Street.

Nvidia and Mr. Huang initially said there was nothing problematic or unusual about his relationship with Alice Huang, who became a U. S. government concern after surveillance revealed that she was feeding information directly to Beijing. Ms. Huang is a top executive at a Singapore-based data center company that had become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia.

Investors were already reeling from a sharp sell-off in many of the tech companies that have driven the development of artificial intelligence, like Nvidia. Those fears picked up again last week as the initial relief rally following the midterm election results turned to a sharp sell-off, with investors anticipating that state and local governments controlled by Democrats could lead to a slowdown in A. I infrastructure projects.

Nvidia’s stock fell nearly 9 percent last week and is now about 25 percent below its peak at the start of October, a decline that erased some $1 trillion in market value. The sharp fall put the company in a bear market, defined as a drop of 20 percent or more from a recent high.

“We believe demand for the company’s products seems unlikely to be affected, but it seems plausible to postulate increased risks” for the A. I. industry’s momentum, analysts from Bernstein wrote in a note on Monday, “as A. I. build-outs become an increasingly political issue.” The scandal engulfing Mr. Huang also highlighted what’s known as “key man risk” for Nvidia, the analysts added, given how tightly associated he is with the company he co-founded more than 30 years ago. “Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary C. E. O.,” they wrote.

Nvidia became the world’s largest public company, by market value, for the first time in 2024, exerting an outsize influence over major indexes like the S&P 500. The rapid run-up in Nvidia’s share price put it at the forefront of an exclusive club of tech giants known as the “Magnificent Seven,” which now dominate the stock market.

It was the first company to hit $4 trillion and then $5 trillion in value, as it rode the A. I. boom to dizzying heights. Analysts expect the company to make a profit of well over $200 billion this year, with its chips in high demand as tech companies rush to build giant A. I. data centers.

But as investors have recently turned more wary of sky-high A. I. valuations and the seemingly circular investments of the industry’s largest players, Nvidia’s stock has stumbled. During last week’s market turmoil, Nvidia fell below Apple as the world’s biggest company.

The company’s shares are now roughly flat for the year, although remain significantly higher over longer time periods. Analysts remain bullish, with more than 90 percent of those who cover the stock rating it a “buy,” according to a compilation by FactSet, with an average price target nearly 80 percent higher than where it closed trading on Friday.

“This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum,” Dan Ives, the senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, wrote in a research note on Sunday. The analyst, who is known for being consistently upbeat about tech stocks, warned that the revelations would “create an overhang on the stock.”

Joe Rennison writes about financial markets, a beat that ranges from chronicling the vagaries of the stock market to explaining the often-inscrutable trading decisions of Wall Street insiders.

Jason Karaian is a deputy business editor at The Times, based in London.

Megyn Kelly, Elon Musk and Others Defend Russell Brand After Rape Conviction

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The former star, whom a British judge sentenced to 10 and a half years in prison on Monday, became an anti-establishment flag-bearer through conspiracy-minded commentary.

By Alex Marshall

Reporting from London

Just minutes after a British jury found Russell Brand guilty of rape and sexual assault last week, Megyn Kelly, the former Fox News host, went live to her 4.1 million subscribers on YouTube and expressed her shock at the verdict.

“I don’t believe the charges,” Kelly said, “and I don’t have to believe them just because the jury came through with the opposite conclusion.” She added, “I feel indignant that this obvious conservative stalwart has been targeted.”

A day later, Elon Musk chimed in. Replying to another user’s post on X mocking Brand’s conviction for offenses more than a decade old, the tech mogul called it an example of “a crazy legal standard.” (England does not have a statute of limitations for rape or sexual assault.)

Although Brand, a former comedy and movie star who was born in Britain, may not be a household name in the United States, his conspiracy-minded videos on YouTube, where he has over 6.6 million subscribers, has to some Americans made him an anti-establishment flag-bearer. Brand also posted clips to X, where he has more than 10 million followers, and to Rumble, the video-sharing platform that pitches itself as a home for free speech.

On Monday, a British judge sentenced Brand to 10 and a half years in prison for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. The episodes included one in which Brand had anal sex with a woman without her consent, she said, leaving her bleeding and in pain (Brand said the woman had consented).

Brand was found not guilty of two other counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Kelly, in her recent live YouTube video, called Brand a “conservative commentator the size of Joe Rogan,” although she said his politics were “closer to” Tucker Carlson’s.

Brand often interviewed, or was interviewed by, U. S. political commentators like Carlson, Ben Shapiro and Candace Owens who are less well known in Britain. He frequently riffed on issues that have become hobbyhorses of those skeptical of creeping government authority, including Covid-19 vaccination campaigns and efforts to digitalize society.

Robert Topinka, a researcher at Birkbeck, University of London, who has studied Brand’s YouTube output, said in an interview that the comedian’s videos seemed aimed at reaching Americans who believe “the mainstream media and elites and big corporations are combining to control us.”

Since Brand’s conviction, some X users have posted that they believe the case was politically motivated, or to claim that Brand was being persecuted, in part, because he is a Christian. The conservative commentator Ryan Samuels pointed to a lack of forensic evidence to argue that the verdict was a “shameful display of justice.”

As Topinka noted, both Brand and some of his high-profile supporters have long claimed that the accusations against him were part of a news media and political conspiracy.

In 2024, Donald Trump Jr. said in an interview with Brand that similar sex accusations had “happened to my father.” In April, Carlson told Brand that he believed the star was facing “a real jail term” because he “spoke against the people in power.”

Unlike Kelly and Musk, Carlson has so far remained silent on the verdict against Brand. A representative for Carlson did not respond to several interview requests.

Brand had a twisty route to his position. Rico Isaacs, an academic at the University of Lincoln in England who has published a study of Brand’s YouTube videos, said in an interview that a decade ago Brand was widely perceived as a left-wing figure. In 2013, appearing on the prominent BBC News program “Newsnight,” Brand said Britain should adopt a “socialist egalitarian” political system to benefit “underserved, impoverished populations.”

That interview excited many British political commentators and, in 2014, Brand started a YouTube series called “The Trews.” There, he discussed the news and political ideas with guests, including a prominent British environmentalist and Ed Miliband, who was then the leader of the Labour Party in Britain.

That same year, Brand returned to “Newsnight” to discuss “Revolution,” his book that expanded on his calls for social change. “Let me be absolutely clear,” he said. “I don’t trust politicians — no one does.”

Isaacs said that it was really only during the coronavirus pandemic that Brand’s videos became more conservative and conspiratorial. About that time, Brand also leaned more toward a U. S. audience by regularly interviewing prominent figures like Carlson.

In the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, Brand appeared at a rally featuring other anti-establishment figures, including Robert F. Kennedy Jr. In September, Brand shared a stage with high-ranking U. S. health officials, including Mehmet Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

A spokesman for Kennedy did not respond to a request for comment.

Isaacs said Brand’s reach was helped by his conversion to Christianity in 2024, adding that as his trial approached, Brand increasingly focused on issues of faith in his videos.

Isaacs said he could not see Brand’s followers leaving him over the conviction. “Once he’s got true believers,” he said, “he’s got true believers.”

Before Brand was sentenced on Monday, a group of his supporters held a large banner outside the courthouse proclaiming his innocence. “Christ was crucified for telling the truth,” the banner said: “Russell is the truth.”

Alex Marshall is a Times reporter covering European culture. He is based in London.

A Father’s Dream of Antarctica and a Son’s Unfinished Quest

The New York Times November 09, 2026

A decade after Max Worsley’s father died crossing the continent, he embarks this month on his own journey into the lonely land his father loved.

A decade after Max Worsley’s father died crossing the continent, he embarks this month on his own journey into the lonely land his father loved.

Credit...

Supported by

By Raymond Zhong

Photographs by Nicholas J. R. White

A few days before Henry Worsley died, he called his son, Max.

Max was 21 and asleep at home in France, where it was the middle of the night. He hadn’t seen his father in two months. Henry, 55, was 9,000 miles away, in the brutal icy wilderness of Antarctica. Henry was on his third South Pole expedition, his longest and most grueling one yet: He wanted to become the first person to cross the entire continent on his own. But after nearly 70 days of skiing through blinding snowstorms while pulling a sled loaded with all his food and fuel, he was worn out and in pain.

“I just wanted to hear your voice,” Henry said to Max by satellite phone. He repeated it again and again. “I just wanted to hear your voice.”

“Dad, you’ve done enough,” Max told him. “You’ve made everyone so proud. You need to call it in.”

Max’s father acknowledged his words but didn’t say what he would do next. Max’s mind was racing as he fell back asleep. Soon after, Henry called for a rescue and was flown to Chile, where doctors discovered an infection in his abdomen. He died of organ failure two days later, on Jan. 24, 2016.

Max had just been starting to get to know his father better. He spent most of his childhood at boarding schools, and Henry, an officer in the British Army, had often been posted overseas. Henry could be lively and sociable in the right settings, but he struggled at times to connect with Max on an emotional level. This, Max knew, was just his upbringing: When Henry interacted with his own father, a decorated general, there were no hugs, no I love yous. Just handshakes.

Henry’s death left unfulfilled a promise he had made: that he and Max would someday trek through Antarctica together. It would have been Henry’s next expedition, the trip that would solidify his bond with his son.

Max knew that if he ever wanted to feel closer to his father, he would have to venture into the bleak, beautiful, lonely land that had been his all-consuming passion. He would have to attempt a South Pole journey of his own.

Henry Worsley was a figure from another age: a soldier, writer and artist who loved Rudyard Kipling’s poetry and idolized Ernest Shackleton, the 20th-century polar explorer famed for his grit.

Henry’s first South Pole expedition retraced a journey that Shackleton had failed to complete exactly a century earlier. For his third trip, he wanted to follow in his hero’s tracks by pursuing a trans-Antarctic crossing, which Shackleton had called “the last great polar journey that can be made.” Shackleton set off with a team in 1914 when their ship, the Endurance, was crushed by sea ice, kicking off one of the greatest survival stories in the history of exploration.

Henry, though, was making his journey alone — an ultimate test of his mettle and wits. After he died, the journalist David Grann wrote a book about his fateful final quest. Prince William declared that he would “remain a source of inspiration to us all.”

Max and his younger sister, Alicia, had grown up steeped in their father’s love for Antarctica. Their home was filled with Henry’s collection of polar memorabilia: autographed books and diaries, black-and-white photos and faded maps, commemorative comic books and jigsaw puzzles. They absorbed so much of their father’s passion for the frozen continent that even his death didn’t taint their enchantment. “Because I know how much he loved it,” Alicia said. “And I loved him.”

Max yearned to experience the adventures his father had conjured for him in his youth. He longed to feel the blissful solitude Henry felt — the feeling, as Henry once described it, of being “this atom on an ice cube in the middle of nowhere.”

Around three years ago, Max finally felt ready to make it happen.

He would ski the same route his father had skied to the pole. And he would do it alone, to feel a deeper communion with his father. He knew, though, that if he wanted even a chance of pulling it off, he needed to prepare.

Before trying his solo crossing, Henry had undergone military training and completed two polar expeditions. Max had barely done any cross-country skiing and had never pulled a sled. He had started mountaineering and climbing in his teens and made several dayslong treks through the Alps, but never in Antarctica.

He decided to consult one source that might contain some practical wisdom for his journey: his father’s leather-bound diary from his final expedition. His mother, Joanna, kept it in a safe in her London apartment. She and Alicia had refused to read it, fearing it would upset them too much. Max had flipped through it before, but he was also apprehensive about delving into his father’s state of mind during his final weeks.

In just the first few pages, he saw how anxious his father had been about one key aspect of his trip: his sled. At roughly 325 pounds, it was heavier than the ones he had hauled during his first two expeditions, which were only to the pole, not all the way across the continent.

“General anxiety over weight and wait,” Henry wrote on Nov. 11, 2015, a day after he had arrived at the Antarctic logistics hub from which, weather permitting, he would be flown to the starting point for his journey.

When he set off two days later, his spirits were high. But as Max kept reading, he noticed something else he hadn’t known: His father first felt pains in his midsection weeks before calling for help.

Day 35: “Woke this morning to a very severe stomachache. I set off in trepidation and after 10 mins could go no further.”

Day 56: “Woke feeling really terrible. Something I ate didn’t agree.”

Henry’s jottings grew spare, haunted. Max found them hard to read, both for their ragged handwriting and for the misery they described.

Day 63: “Fingers still a worry. A number on the verge and I wonder how long they will last.”

Day 68: “Very low.” “Took painkillers.”

Day 69: “Just want it all to end.”

After Henry’s death, his family and friends wondered why he hadn’t called for a rescue sooner. Now, reading the diary confirmed for Max something he had long believed: His father was so fixated on reaching his goal that he waved away warning signs about his condition.

His judgment was further clouded, Max believed, by his deep experience in uncomfortable situations. Henry was so used to physical and mental strain that it hindered “his ability to know when something was too much,” Max said.

Max didn’t have that issue. He wouldn’t make the same mistakes.

His training began in Singapore, where he was living at the time. He was working for an ocean robotics company and preparing for Antarctica became a second job: intense lower body workouts in the gym, runs through a humid city park, many painful sessions on an Assault Bike. He laid out a fitness plan on spreadsheets. He flew to Norway to learn cross-country skiing and visit a sports lab, where the trainers filmed him roller-skiing on an enormous treadmill to analyze his technique.

He set his sights on starting his journey around November 2026, during the Antarctic summer.

For the Norwegians, expeditions were all about technique, Max said. His father was the opposite. He thought that the real test was mental, that Antarctica was traversed by putting one ski in front of the other, hour after backbreaking hour, day after punishing day.

Max understood that, over hundreds of miles, shaving even a tiny amount off his stride could cut down his journey time significantly. But he also thought that technique would count for little if, feeling battered and forlorn on the ice, he couldn’t silence the doubts that might be rattling around his head: What am I doing here? Why am I subjecting myself to this?

Max began discussing his plans with close friends. When he told his sister, she said she trusted and supported him, but added, “Gosh, good luck telling Mum.” About a year into his training, he had told his mother he was planning an expedition. He just didn’t mention it would be a solo one.

For Joanna, Antarctica had been Henry’s “mistress,” one that had taken him away from her again and again. Even when he wasn’t on the ice, his thoughts were consumed by it. He would return from an Army posting in Afghanistan, she said, only to tell her, “Oh darling, I’m really, really sorry, but I really need to go to Norway and train.” After his first expedition, he hid himself away to write a book about it, titled “In Shackleton’s Footsteps.”

“I didn’t mind,” Joanna remembered. “I loved his passion for it. But when he died, I did mind.”

Max felt guilty about putting his mother through so much pain again. Still, he couldn’t hide his plans forever.

One day early last year, he and his mother were discussing his trip on the phone when she asked the question he had been trying to dance around.

“Who are you planning on doing it with?” she asked.

The words came tumbling out.

“Oh,” Max said. “Actually, I really want to do it solo.”

She went quiet, very quiet.

Their call ended quickly after that. Max agreed to give his mother some time to think. Really, though, her silence had told him everything he needed to know.

He realized that, since Henry’s death, the thought of a loved one alone at the end of the Earth, with no one to help for hundreds of miles, had not left his mother’s mind. He could see that making this trip solo would be agony for her.

And so, not long after their call, Max told his mother he wouldn’t retrace his father’s last expedition alone.

As it happened, he had recently been introduced to a potential partner at a pub in Oslo. Martin Nesse, a 35-year-old software developer, had skied across Greenland but was struggling to find the money for a South Pole expedition. He had considered doing what many Norwegian adventurers do to finance their Antarctic exploits: sell his apartment.

At the pub, Nesse was impressed by Max’s detailed plan for raising funds, including from a few sponsors that had also supported Henry. He was glad to find someone who was as serious about reaching the pole as he was.

They kicked their preparations into high gear. Max took a job that allowed him to live on an island in Scotland, where he trained by pulling tires across gravel or grass for one to two hours, sometimes longer, three times a week. He worked with a nutritionist to optimize his diet. He and Nesse practiced hauling sleds across Norway’s mountain plateaus. They took a crevasse rescue training course in the Alps and a wilderness medicine course in England.

“I have definitely felt like I needed to not just tick every box, but tick it twice,” Max said. “And tick double the amount of boxes than I needed to. For Mum, really. And for me.”

Max kept his mother informed of his preparations, but delicately. “He will tell me anything if I ask him, but I don’t really want to know much,” Joanna said. The mere thought of Max going to Antarctica still stirred within her a dark cauldron of emotions. “I feel like I’m just holding it together,” she said.

Still, she would never have dreamed of stopping her son from going, she said. Even if he had insisted on going solo.

“I really do have this belief that your children either do crazy things with your love and support, or without your love and support,” Joanna said. And “with,” she added, is better for parent and child alike.

On a sunny September morning, Joanna sat in her London apartment with Alicia. Henry’s skis from Antarctica were mounted on the kitchen walls.

Max would be arriving soon, but for now, mother and daughter took stock of his journey, two months before he was set to depart.

Alicia was 19 when her father set off for the last time, too young to understand the risks he was taking. Even though she felt mostly at ease about her brother’s expedition, “I don’t want to think it’s a given that Max is coming back,” she said. “So that worry exists. That didn’t with Dad.”

Joanna liked Max’s dedication to honoring her husband’s legacy, though it did make it somewhat harder for her to push past the pain of his death. “In my heart, I still miss Henry, and I still am very sad,” she said.

She looked out the window. Max was here. “He won’t want me to cry,” she said. “So I have to pull myself together.”

Max plopped down on the pink herringbone sofa next to his sister. The mood was light at first. He began talking about how “desperately hard” he had been working to put on weight. He was six feet tall and 170 pounds before he started training. His target was around 195 pounds, every ounce of which he would need once he was on the ice and burning thousands of calories a day skiing.

“It’s exhausting, eating 4,500 calories a day,” Max said.

Joanna gasped. “Do you really?” She was relieved to see Max’s commitment to bulking up. She had long thought Henry hadn’t gained enough weight before his last expedition.

Nesse’s weight gain strategy was simple: He chugged a cup of cream every morning. Max’s involved round-the-clock work, he explained. Three big meals, plus salami, nuts and other snacks, plus two bagels midmorning.

“Two bagels, or one halved?” Alicia asked.

“No, two bagels,” Max said. “And then a protein shake.” Everyone laughed.

“I like you being adventurous,” Joanna said. “I’m just not relishing when you’re going to be down there.” She would probably wake up at night thinking about crevasses, she said.

That sent the conversation down a darker path. Toward Henry.

“That last expedition I was always nervous of,” Joanna said. “There was something different about it.”

Max mentioned learning that his father’s sled had been much heavier on his last trip.

“I’ve never thought about that,” Joanna said.

“Because he was there alone, and he was doing a much longer expedition,” Max said.

“Oh dear, you know that makes me so depressed,” she said. “You see, he should have been doubly trained, and he wasn’t.”

She couldn’t hold it together any longer. She began to weep. Alicia got up and put her arms around her mother’s shoulders.

Henry would have been 66 this year. Max was still filled with sadness not knowing how his relationship with his father might have blossomed if he had only come home. He would be living in the countryside today, Max said. Keeping bees, growing vegetables. “He’d have a little artist’s studio, doing his painting,” Max said. “Maybe he’d write another book about his life.”

When Max thought about his own trip, he knew coming home to his mother and Alicia had to be the priority. If it were just him, “maybe I’d push myself slightly further,” he said. With them in the picture, though, nothing else he might gain or learn by taking additional risks seemed worth it.

On Nov. 2, two days before Max would leave to start his journey in Punta Arenas, near the southern tip of Chile, he sat down with Alicia and his mother for the Christmas dinner he would miss while he was in Antarctica.

In previous years, the family sometimes celebrated Christmas even earlier, before Henry left on long Army tours. He felt it was wrong for officers to take their leave from Afghanistan over Christmas, Joanna said, “so he always stayed.”

The anniversary of Henry’s death had long made the end of the year an emotional time for her. Max’s trip was making this one exceptionally tough. As he talked through his gear and his plans, she tried to keep bad thoughts at bay.

“Trauma, however much you try to shove it into a river and drown it, it just comes to the surface,” she said.

In Punta Arenas, Max explained, he and Nesse will spend days weighing and prepping every morsel of food they will eat during their two months on the ice, down to the sugar and dates they will sprinkle on their oatmeal. On Nov. 12, they will fly to an Antarctic logistics hub. Then, after a day or two, if weather allows, they will be dropped off by plane at the Antarctic coast and begin skiing south. At the start, their sleds, loaded with all their food, fuel and gear, will weigh around 265 pounds each. Eight hundred miles of icy nothingness will separate them and the pole.

Max will be carrying some of his father’s things — his diary, his hat, his goggles. Every evening in their tent, Max and Nesse will take turns sending voice updates that will be transmitted by satellite and posted online. Max will read out snippets from his father’s diary.

The family hadn’t discussed how often Max would call home. “I was thinking like once a week or something,” he said. “Could be more. Could be less.”

“No, I think more,” Joanna said, gently.

“More,” Max said. “OK.” He gave her a reassuring look.

On the ice, he will feel … what, exactly? He wasn’t quite sure. He was ready for the exquisite silence. What his father’s spirit might say to him in those quiet moments remained to be seen.

I’ve gotten to know Max Worsley over the past few months as he prepares to make a journey a decade in the making. Any South Pole expedition is a huge undertaking, but I hadn’t fully appreciated just how much work is involved, even for a trip as intensely personal as his.

This has been “the most stressful, difficult year” of his life, he told me last week, before he got on a plane to Chile. “The next bit is really simple,” he said, even if it won’t exactly be easy. “I’ve literally just got to put one ski in front of the other for 65 days. That’s it.”

Raymond Zhong reports on climate and environmental issues for The Times.
