‘You Can See Everything’ Puts ‘The Dropout’ on Trial

The New York Times November 09, 2026

What to Watch

Advertisement

Supported by

As they dissect Elizabeth Holmes’s persona, Nathan Fielder and Amanda Seyfried confront the nature of truth.

By Caroline Darya Framke

Elizabeth Holmes and Amanda Seyfried have at least one thing in common besides their uncanny ability to keep from blinking: They both really hate watching “The Dropout.”

Hulu’s 2022 limited series, starring Seyfried as Holmes, has had a resurgence in popularity since the release of “You Can See Everything.” The much-hyped documentary, by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, was shot largely in the weeks before Holmes went to prison over her fraudulent claims about Theranos’s supposedly revolutionary diagnostic technology.

The film was so secret that its first trailer came as a huge surprise. When it finally came out in mid-October, one of its biggest shocks was Fielder’s bringing in Seyfried to anchor the second half.

“The Dropout” traces Holmes’s life from her teenage years to her rapid ascent as the Theranos chief executive to her spectacular collapse when the science behind the company’s key invention fails to stand up to scrutiny. Seyfried’s performance as Holmes, one of her best to date, won her an Emmy.

It wasn’t just about the accuracy of her Holmes impression (although it was excellent). It was the fact that Seyfried, alongside the “Dropout” creator Elizabeth Meriwether, created a portrait of Holmes that considers the complexity of her experience without excusing her actions.

The show traces the arc of Holmes’s all-consuming ambition but also examines the roots of her frustration and fury when people fail to take her seriously. It also treats her sexual assault while at Stanford as more than a fleeting moment on the way to stardom, as many accounts of Holmes’s life tend to do. Where others may have sensationalized the story, “The Dropout” dug deeper into its nuance.

The real-life Holmes, or at least the one portrayed in “You Can See Everything,” cuts a frustratingly slippery figure. Her default answer to tricky questions is most often a legally sound “I don’t remember.” In conversation, her penetrating stare becomes even more unnerving when paired with her unwavering placidity. But when Fielder asks her to watch “The Dropout,” she reacts with visceral distaste.

Holmes tenses up watching Seyfried, the glossy Hollywood version of herself, bouncing around a set of her childhood bedroom. She curls up into herself during a later episode as Seyfried dances robotically to Lil Wayne. She groans aloud at a scene of Seyfried’s facsimile having a nasty argument with Naveen Andrews’s Sunny Balwani, who was then Holmes’s partner in both business and life.

“I really don’t want to watch this,” she protests, turning away from the screen and covering her face to hide her tears. Maybe she doesn’t recognize the show’s interpretation of events; maybe she just hates seeing it play out on TV. Either way, it is perhaps the only time in the documentary that Holmes has a recognizable emotional reaction.

With the second half of “You Can See Everything” unfolding after Holmes goes to prison, it is Seyfried’s turn to confront her past. Fielder initially brings in the actress as a kind of expert witness — she’s one of the few people who have thought as much as he has about Holmes’s motivations.

Seyfried, fascinated by Fielder’s insight into her post-trial life, admits she still sometimes feels “a little haunted” by Holmes. When Fielder shows her the footage of Holmes watching “The Dropout,” however, her fascination curdles into horror. While Holmes cringes at her dancing, Seyfried practically crawls out of her own skin. When she sees Holmes lie back in tears, she calls it “heartbreaking.”

Plenty of actors have portrayed real-life figures onscreen, but few have seen the aftermath of it as Seyfried does in “You Can See Everything.” Forced to face the subject of her performance head-on, she can’t help but empathize. When she and Fielder visit Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, in the film’s most explosive scene, Seyfried’s suspicion of him leads to a passionate defense of Holmes’s dignity. Fielder doesn’t comment, but he can’t keep from smiling as their composure unravels.

As with Fielder’s TV shows “The Rehearsal” and “The Curse,” “You Can See Everything” is preoccupied with performance and perception — how they shape and inform one another, why they shift and who it affects. In all his projects, Fielder invites scrutiny about his own perceptions and motivations. In “You Can See Everything,” the result is an unsettling Möbius strip that leaves viewers wondering whether any of it is authentic or true, and what that might actually mean.

Seyfried soon falls even further through the looking glass. She slips back into Holmes’s skin, deep voice, chapped lips and all, to recreate Fielder’s recollections of events that weren’t captured on camera. Seeing Seyfried re-enact moments from the film’s first half with Holmes’s benign smile plastered on her face is genuinely spooky. It’s also kind of a relief. After spending two hours of “You Can See Everything” with Holmes herself, there’s some comfort in regaining the distance of a scripted performance.

That doesn’t last for long. Fielder’s usual tricks and techniques keep hitting the wall of Holmes’s eerie calm, even when performed by Seyfried. Neither of them can crack her code, and their opposing reactions to their frustration seem to take them both by surprise.

After confronting Evans and re-enacting several scenes opposite Fielder, Seyfried becomes far less sympathetic to Holmes’s unease. Playing Holmes from a script again gives her more room to treat her as a character to interpret, an approach Fielder tries to resist.

Their final scene together, in which they grapple with Fielder’s final interaction with Holmes, is tense. Each challenges the other’s interpretation of events. Seyfried questions whether Fielder is misleading her in order to protect Holmes. Fielder suggests that a key scene in “The Dropout” leaves no room for the possibility of her innocence, which he says would make it a lie.

At this point, Seyfried has had enough. “They’re not lies,” she snaps. “It’s [expletive] TV. You know.”

Fielder is indeed no stranger to people questioning the veracity of his TV shows. But he still can’t square his experience of Holmes with Seyfried’s idea of her, which leaves them at an impasse. In “The Dropout,” Seyfried synthesized reality, research and performance to create what she seems to believe was a truthful representation of Holmes. To Fielder, the only way to ensure accuracy is to be entirely honest — but what does “honest” even mean?

Neither of them can say. By the end of “You Can See Everything,” the only thing they know for sure is that no one’s truth will ever match their own.

Caroline Darya Framke is a TV critic and the host of the Watching newsletter at The New York Times.

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

OpinionThe Editorial Board

Credit... Photo Illustration by Tam Stockton for The New York Times

Supported by

By The Editorial Board

The editorial board is a group of opinion journalists whose views are informed by expertise, research, debate and certain longstanding values. It is separate from the newsroom.

President Trump’s unpopularity was clearly the main engine of Democratic Party’s resounding midterm victory. But his unpopularity alone did not deliver the scale of the Democrats triumph. To win in places like Kansas, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, Democratic candidates needed to persuade many voters who had previously considered their party unacceptable. The candidates’ success offers a road map to a sensible future for the party.

How did they do it? The simplest summary is that they ran as economic populists and cultural moderates.

That combination is consistent with American public opinion, which leans center-left on many economic issues and center-right on many social issues. By taking this approach, candidates were able to present themselves as beholden to neither of the country’s two political parties, both of which remain unpopular. The heterodox combination also has much to recommend it substantively. It meets the moment, after years of disappointing laissez-faire economic policies and a decade of cultural excesses by the progressive left.

On the economy, this year’s Democrats offered a strikingly populist message. They promised to raise taxes on the wealthy and criticized billionaires for corrupting the political system. They called for higher minimum wages, lower health care costs and expanded government programs. They raised concerns about artificial intelligence and data centers. They did not sound like the triangulating Democratic moderates of an earlier generation who championed Wall Street and free trade.

Nor did they sound like the progressives who shaped the party during the 2010s and early 2020s. This year’s candidates frequently denounced ideas — on immigration, energy, policing, gender and voter ID — that have taken hold in elite left-leaning circles and alienated many working-class Americans of all races. Winning candidates often took a middle ground between a censorious left and an extremist Republican Party. If you do not live in a place with a 2026 battleground campaign, you may not realize how strongly the Democrats turned toward social moderation.

Adam Hamilton, a pastor who became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Kansas since 1932, captured the mood in an ad in which he spoke directly to the camera while standing on a farm. “America is being torn apart by politicians on both extremes,” he said, placing himself in the populist middle, in contrast to his Republican opponent, Senator Roger Marshall. “On one side, the far left pushes socialism and open borders,” Mr. Hamilton said. “On the other side, Roger Marshall gives us higher gas and grocery prices while slashing our health care.”

Our editorial board does not agree with every message that came from a Democrat this year, and we lament that the party did not do more to lay out an affirmative agenda for lifting Americans’ living standards. Democrats should urgently begin that work. Nonetheless, the 2026 campaign represented meaningful progress for the party.

Even as the factional battles between the party’s left and center will no doubt continue, the Democrats who won difficult races this year largely borrowed the strongest messages from each side. They demonstrated an admirable pragmatism and a willingness to compromise that are central to maintaining democracy in a diverse nation. As Rob Sand, Iowa’s governor-elect, said during his campaign, “I think a lot of people are tired of division, tired of being told that anyone that they love or who’s a friend of theirs that’s in the other party is somehow their enemy.”

Coalescing around a similar big-tent strategy will be crucial in 2028. The competition between Democratic and Republican candidates today is not merely one about policy. It is, unfortunately, a contest between a party that supports democracy and one that has enabled corruption, lawbreaking and autocratic behavior. The country would be far better off if the Republicans pivoted and nominated a candidate in 2028 who rejected Trumpism. Until Republicans return to being a normal political party, however, the effectiveness of the Democratic Party will remain more than a partisan question. It will affect the health of American democracy.

For most of the 21st century, most Americans have been unhappy with the country’s direction. The reasons are complex and varied, including failed foreign wars, alienation caused by digital technology, slow-growing living standards and deep anxiety about the future. The country is stuck in a long malaise.

Americans’ view of how things are going in the U. S.

Source: Gallup, Oct. 2026

This dissatisfaction extends to voters’ views of the two major political parties. Only 38 percent of Americans had a favorable view of the Republican Party heading into the midterms, according to the Real Clear Politics polling average. The Democratic Party’s favorability was barely better, at 39 percent. Many voters say neither party is sufficiently focused on the concerns of ordinary people. Swing voters tend to consider the Republican Party too right wing and the Democratic Party too left wing.

Share of Americans who think the Democratic Party is …

Share of Americans who think the Republican Party is …

Source: Gallup, Oct. 2026

As a result, successful candidates in modern politics often present themselves as being distinct from both parties. They emphasize their disagreements with their own party and highlight their openness to working with anybody who has a good idea. That was a theme among Democrats who won tough races this year.

“It’s time to stop the nonsense from both extremes and start to focus on lowering costs for Iowans,” said Josh Turek, who calls himself a “common-sense prairie populist” and became the first Democrat to win an Iowa Senate race in 18 years. Another Turek ad boasted that he had voted with Republicans more than 700 times in the state legislature. In Ohio, Representative Marcy Kaptur, who won a House district that Mr. Trump easily won two years ago, told voters, “I’ve repeatedly said no to my own party.” In Alaska, Mary Peltola, who leads her Senate race pending a final vote count, said, “When both parties are attacking you, you’re doing something right.”

To demonstrate independence, this year’s Democratic winners took positions on hot-button culture issues at odds with recent progressive consensus. On each one, they rejected the excesses of both sides and found a sensible middle. Five issues stood out:

1. Immigration

One candidate after another criticized the laxness of President Joe Biden’s immigration policy. “A disaster,” said Mr. Hamilton. “Really terrible,” said Paige Cognetti, who defeated a Republican congressman in northeast Pennsylvania. “Out of control,” said Chris Pappas, a senator-elect in New Hampshire, adding that it “made America less safe.”

In Texas, Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect, went so far as to praise the Trump border policy. “There is no question that crossings are way down, and there is no question it is because of President Trump,” she said. Even Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive senator-elect from Michigan, criticized the party’s loose earlier approach to border enforcement. “We got that wrong,” he said on “60 Minutes.”

Democrats combined these acknowledgments with tough criticism of the Trump administration’s brutal, lawless use of immigration agents. This mix — neither Mr. Trump’s cruelty nor Mr. Biden’s incompetence — is right. Immigration policy should combine a secure border, humane enforcement of laws, clear rules for legal immigration and a citizenship process for some people who entered the country illegally.

Listen to James Talarico, the senator-elect from Texas. At a town hall last month, he called out “the utter chaos” of the “failed” Biden policy as well as the “extremism” of a Trump policy that includes “kidnapping our neighbors off our street.” Then he said: “We have to build a pathway to citizenship for our neighbors who have been here for years and decades. They should pay a fine. They should pay back taxes. They should learn English. And if they can do all those things, I think they deserve a shot at joining our communities as full citizens.”

2. Crime

The emphasis on border security was part of an embrace of law enforcement that served as a rebuke to the anti-police sentiment of many on the left.

In an ad for Roy Cooper, the former North Carolina governor who handily won a Senate race there, the narrator declared, “He bucked his party to oppose defunding the police, worked with Republicans to strengthen bail laws and partnered with President Trump to crack down on fentanyl.” In Arizona, Amish Shah, a winning House candidate, said that he had worked as a state legislator to “fully fund Arizona’s police.”

In the Mississippi Senate race, former President Barack Obama recorded an ad praising the crime-fighting record of Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee. “Guided by his Christian faith, Scott made his communities safer, prosecuting violent crimes as district attorney and fighting corruption,” Mr. Obama said. Mr. Colom, who also played up his support for gun rights, now leads his race by about 2,500 votes.

Police officers and prosecutors must be held accountable when they abuse their authority — and communities need well-funded police departments, as most Americans believe.

3. Voter ID

Republican politicians have long tried to exploit voter identification as an issue and falsely suggested that fraud is a major problem. It is not. Yet most Americans support voter ID laws for understandable reasons. People must present an ID to do many things less solemn than voting, such as checking into a hotel, renting a car or traveling on an airplane.

Require all voters to show a government-issued photo ID to vote

Source: Pew Research Center, Aug. 2025

Many other democracies require voter ID, too. If U. S. states are going to require it, the key is ensuring that it is easy to obtain. Several of this year’s Democratic winners took this position, supporting both ID requirements and easier access.

Amy Acton, the governor-elect in Ohio, announced that she backed a ballot initiative enshrining an ID requirement in the state Constitution. (It passed with 65 percent of the vote.) She also said she would fight to make sure that all eligible voters could obtain ID “easily and at no cost.” Mr. Colom and Mr. Talarico took a similar approach. Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia and Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, two landslide re-election winners last week and potential 2028 presidential candidates, also spoke positively about voter ID.

4. Energy

Mr. Trump has pursued a self-defeating policy that restricts the development of clean energy and raises costs. Prominent environmental activists have made the opposite mistake and opposed the use of oil and natural gas. This year’s Democratic stars took a smarter approach, advocating an all-of-the-above energy strategy that can both hold down costs and limit carbon emissions.

“If the Democratic Party is going after the good-paying oil and gas jobs here in Texas, I’m going to stand up against them,” Mr. Talarico said. Bobby Pulido, a Tejano musician who crushed an incumbent House Republican in South Texas, celebrated the importance of oil and gas jobs. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola promised to buck national Democrats who opposed “resource development.” In Kansas, Mr. Hamilton said, “Stop the war on domestic energy projects.” Each of these candidates also called for expansions of clean energy.

5. Gender

Along with immigration, gender issues may have been the most frequent source of Democratic repositioning in 2026. Many on the left have urged Democrats to avoid this issue and try to change the subject, but voters can often sense when politicians are trying to hide something. This year’s candidates instead engaged with the subject, even running their own ads about it.

In Texas, Ms. Hinojosa poked fun at the practice of announcing one’s pronouns by closing one ad with, “My pronouns are mom, Texan, and, soon to be, governor.” And the list of candidates who said they opposed trans girls or women playing female sports was long, including Aaron Ford, the governor-elect in Nevada; Annie Andrews, who won a shocking Senate victory in South Carolina; Mr. Sand and Mr. Turek in Iowa; and Ms. Acton and Ms. Kaptur in Ohio.

We are dismayed that some Democrats used harsh and inaccurate language, such as describing trans girls as boys. Still, much of the repositioning on gender is justified. People born with male biology are taller, faster and stronger on average, and most Americans believe that the differences create an unfair advantage in girls’ sports. Too many progressives equate this recognition with bigotry.

The candidates who struck the best balance were those who spoke out against Mr. Trump’s vilification of trans Americans and opposed discrimination in employment, while acknowledging difficult trade-offs in other areas. Mr. Ford, for example, opposed trans girls playing girls’ sports. He also criticized his Republican opponent for “beating up on one of the most vulnerable populations we have in our country, punching down on a group of individuals that don’t deserve to be political pawns in an effort to increase his voter turnout.”

It was another reminder that on many hot-button issues today, there is a middle ground that is both reasonable and popular.

The mistake among some centrists has been believing that the right answer to every policy question lies in the middle of the two parties’ historical positions. In truth, the country needs bold action on many issues. Americans, frustrated by slow-growing living standards and government dysfunction, are hungry for action on the economy.

Do you think people with $100 billion or more generally …

Do you think the federal government should try to reduce wealth inequality?

Source: YouGov, Jan. 2026 and June 2026

Many of this year’s winning Democrats promised such action. They called for tax increases on corporations and billionaires, along with a smorgasbord of policies to reduce costs and increase opportunities for most Americans. The all-of-the-above position on energy helps as well.

Mr. Shapiro, often described as a moderate, supported more than doubling Pennsylvania’s minimum wage, to $15. Mr. Turek called for indexing the federal minimum wage to inflation and making it easier for workers to join unions. Ms. Peltola called for a big increase in the child tax credit and tax incentives for companies that pay decent wages. Mr. Hamilton said Medicare should expand to include dental and vision coverage. Mr. Pulido called for breaking up health-care conglomerates. “The people in office have sold us out,” he said. “They’ve allowed these companies to prey on us.”

Along the way, many candidates, including Mr. El-Sayed, drew a limit on their economic progressivism and said that they were not socialists. They described themselves as capitalists who wanted to ensure that American capitalism delivered better results for its citizens.

Democrats still do not have anything close to a comprehensive economic agenda. Many of their ideas remain small-bore or even dubious, especially on housing, where the party is not focused enough on building more homes. It has also failed to produce a plan to reduce the alarming federal debt. The party should raise its ambitions and spend the coming months developing an agenda that will reduce housing and health care costs, regulate A. I., put the country on a sustainable fiscal path and more.

This project will not be easy, but it does not need to tear the party apart. The progressive and centrist wings of the party agree much more on economic issues than they disagree.

Two years ago, the situation was bleak for the Democratic Party. Its ineffectiveness and unpopularity enabled Mr. Trump’s return to the White House, and many Democrats were in denial about why they lost. The party has rebounded from that nadir.

This year, it fielded a diverse array of savvy, appealing and authentic candidates, and they won astonishing victories. Their combination of economic populism and cultural moderation offers the party an opportunity to change its image among working-class Americans who have long viewed it as out of touch and condescending. Common-sense populism presents the most promising path to building an enduring Democratic majority in Washington. Yes, the party still has a long way to go before it can govern the country well and force the Republican Party to return to reasonableness. But the victors of 2026 have started to point the way.

Source photograph by John Tully for The New York Times.

Americans Hunt for Holiday Deals That Stay in Their Own Closet

The New York Times November 09, 2026

U. S. Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

Shoppers strained by high costs of living are expected to put a priority on value this season, whether they’re buying gifts or everyday items for themselves.

By Kim Bhasin

Americans are expected to take advantage of steep Black Friday discounts to buy everyday household items as higher costs have eroded their discretionary budgets.

Shoppers will still buy gifts. But, according to a report from Adobe Research, they’ll also stock up on basics, such as self-care products, pet supplies, baby essentials and cleaning goods.

The firm predicted that online sales of basic clothing would surge 210 percent from last year, and personal hygiene products 150 percent, during the five days from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday, Nov. 30.

“Consumers, especially the value-seeking ones, have become very savvy and know that these promotional windows are great times to get even better deals than they may find throughout the rest of the year,” said Brian McCarthy, a principal of retail strategy at Deloitte, an advisory firm.

It is the latest sign of how people are finding ways to cope with stubbornly high inflation, which has been accelerating for months as the war with Iran continues to push up prices.

Holiday retail sales in the United States are expected to rise 4.5 percent from last year, according to Visa Business and Economics Insights. Adjusted for inflation, however, the growth in holiday sales is expected to be only 1.1 percent.

“It’s a good number, but I think it masks some of the underlying trends,” said Michael Brown, the principal U. S. economist at Visa.

The cost of living is higher and Americans are paying more for groceries and gas. Annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September.

Consumer spending has remained resilient over the past year, and retailers across the United States have worked to lower and stabilize prices to keep shoppers coming back. But in September, U. S. retail sales rose just 0.8 percent, down from a 1.3 percent jump the previous month. That’s why top executives at Walmart, Costco and Target have stressed that it’s crucial to provide shoppers with value in this economic environment.

“We’re investing heavily in price because customers need us to and because we believe it drives market share gains over time,” John Furner, the chief executive of Walmart, said on a conference call with analysts and investors in August.

Retailers have already begun holding pre-Black Friday sales. They expect gift boxes to be particularly popular, because shoppers see more value in bundled items. Kohl’s has raised the number of gift sets that it offers across the store’s departments and will sell more than 400 types of beauty boxes through its partnership with Sephora.

“It’s a unique moment, where the customer is,” said Arianne Parisi, the chief customer officer of Kohl’s. “We’re thinking about how pinched consumers are.”

Consumers are expected to be more aggressive when comparison shopping. They’re looking for deals, redeeming rewards points and buying more private labels. About a third of consumers who earn less than $100,000 a year said they would trade down to cheaper brands or stores this holiday season, according to Visa.

Shoppers have more tools now to find the lowest price, with artificial intelligence able to parse several websites simultaneously, make purchase recommendations and ease checkout.

To pay for gifts, about a third of American households are taking steps to cut costs elsewhere, according to the National Retail Federation. Even double-digit percentages of households with incomes of about $150,000 plan to cut back on spending on themselves, open more credit cards or use “buy now, pay later” services to ensure they get their holiday shopping done, the group said.

“Once you’ve finished paying off your utility bills and you can’t shave off any more money on your grocery bill, then you are going to go into the store to look for deep discounts,” said Priya Raghubir, a professor of marketing at New York University. “At that stage, just stock up.”

Kim Bhasin is a business reporter covering the retail industry for The Times.

King’s Lost Draft of ‘I Have a Dream’ Emerges From a Desk Drawer

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The document, hand written by Martin Luther King Jr., will be auctioned in January at Christie’s, which expects it to fetch more than $10 million.

By Jennifer Schuessler

On Aug. 28, 1963, the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. stood on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial and delivered a speech whose refrain — “I have a dream” — has soared into the canon of American oratory.

But the night before, he was a man alone in a Washington hotel room, wrestling with what exactly he would say.

For days, King had been brainstorming with aides, who had compiled various themes and motifs into preliminary drafts. Now, he wrote out his version by hand on a yellow pad, heavily crossing out words and whole paragraphs before sending it to be typed up.

King’s draft had long been assumed to have been discarded. But more than six decades later, it has surfaced from a desk drawer of a former aide, Edward T. Clayton, and will be auctioned at Christie’s in January.

The auction house said it expected the document — the only handwritten final draft of the speech known to survive — to fetch more than $10 million. The proceeds will benefit the King Center in Atlanta and other philanthropic causes chosen by the consignor, the aide’s widow, Xernona Clayton.

Spread across a table at Christie’s offices in Manhattan last month, the document looked unassuming — just seven pages filled with blue ink and the rusted ghost of a paper clip in the upper left corner. But the $10 million-plus price, if reached, would put it in a stratosphere associated with rare copies of the nation’s founding documents.

Peter Klarnet, Christie’s manuscript specialist, said that when he first saw it, his jaw hit the table.

“This is the most important manuscript I’ve ever had the honor to handle,” he said. “I can’t imagine anything better.” He paused, before adding: “That I wouldn’t have to steal out of the National Archives.”

The draft is very close to the typescript King carried to the lectern, roughly 20 copies of which are known to survive. Like the typed version, it does not include the words “I have a dream,” part of the ringing second half of the speech that King famously improvised.

It’s unclear whether the densely crossed-out passages, which fill half of some pages, will yield significant new insights into King’s ideas. But scholars who inspected a digital scan of the document provided by Christie’s said it was an extraordinary find.

“When they called me, I was almost in disbelief,” Lerone A. Martin, the director of the Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute at Stanford and the senior editor of the Martin Luther King, Jr. Papers Project. “It’s almost like it gives us a chance to get between King’s ears, to get in his mind.”

Drew D. Hansen, the author of “The Dream,” a detailed study of the speech published in 2003, said the document gave him “actual chills.”

“I’ve read the speech a thousand times,” he said. “But seeing some of these refrains in his own hand is electrifying.”

Today, “I Have a Dream” is American political scripture, on par with the Declaration of Independence and the Gettysburg Address, both of which King’s text invokes. But before the March on Washington, few Americans had heard King give a full speech.

He and his aides were keenly aware of the high stakes of the march, which was held barely two months after President John F. Kennedy sent the proposed Civil Rights Act to Congress. They were also mindful of the more mundane request that all speakers — including King, who spoke last — limit their remarks to five minutes.

The composition process, according to Hansen’s book, started five days before the march, as King sat with Clayton, Stanley Levison, Clarence Jones and other advisers in New York, Atlanta and Washington, trying out ideas and refrains, including some already in King’s repertoire.

Three typed preliminary drafts produced by aides, which King drew on in the final speech, are known to survive. But until now, Hansen said, there was nothing in King’s own hand beyond a few sentences written on the back of one of the aides’ drafts.

For King, drafting speeches was a collective effort, but the final poetry was all his.

“I don’t mind you criticizing my ideas,” King once said to the civil rights leader Bayard Rustin, who had made an unwelcome edit on another speech. “But I don’t like your criticizing my words, because I’m better at words than you are.”

Hansen, who is not involved with the auction, said the closeness of the manuscript to the final typescript supported that it was a final draft written between the late hours of Aug. 27, when King retreated to his suite at the Willard Hotel after a final meeting with aides in the lobby, and around 4 a. m., when he sent the speech to be typed.

So does the fact, Hansen said, that there are extensive heavily crossed-out passages, with some word choices crossed out multiple times.

“That’s unusual for King in general,” said Hansen, who for his book interviewed four people who helped with the speech’s composition. “But it’s consistent with what people who were there that night saw.”

Hansen noted King’s edits on the third page, where he warns of “the tranquilizing drug of gradualism.” First, he wrote “tokenism” and then crossed it out and wrote “waitism,” before landing on “gradualism.”

“You really see that care for individual words,” Hansen said.

The handwritten draft, like the typed version, includes no trace of King’s most famous edit — the impromptu insertion on the podium of the lengthy “I have a dream” section, which King and his aides had discussed using but ruled out because of time constraints. It does include the famous closing words, “Free at last.”

Hansen said the textual evidence was enough to convince him the document is King’s draft. And then there’s the document’s provenance from Clayton, the public relations director at King’s organization, the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, who is known to have helped with the speech.

“This is not coming from some random file drawer,” Hansen said.

Klarnet, of Christie’s, said he first viewed the document in Xernona Clayton’s office in Atlanta. In a video interview last month, Clayton, who recently turned 96, described how she had found it in her husband’s desk, which she had left largely untouched for decades after his death in 1966.

“He saved everything,” she said.

She first came across the manuscript in the late 1990s, she said, inside an envelope labeled “speech.” She recognized the words immediately but didn’t fully grasp the document’s significance as King’s own draft. She put it back in the desk, she said.

Clayton, who organized events for the S. C. L. C., was close with King and his wife, Coretta Scott King. Film footage shows her presenting a smiling Dr. King with a gift on his 39th birthday, in January 1968. Less than three months later, she helped Mrs. King buy a dress for his funeral, and has described touching up a spot on Dr. King’s cheek with makeup as friends and family approached the open casket.

Over the years, Clayton said, she was frequently asked whether she had King memorabilia to display or sell. But she said she didn’t want to be seen as disrespecting the memory of “a man I loved a lot.”

In recent years, she said, she changed her mind, and in 2024 showed the document to Eddie Bridgeman, her financial manager, who helped arrange the auction.

“Now that I’m older, I’m wiser, and it just seems like something that important ought to be shared,” she said.

The document is being offered by the Still Marching Irrevocable Charitable Unitrust, which Clayton has created to promote causes she champions. Bridgeman, its trustee, said that all proceeds from the sale would support philanthropic efforts, including a museum highlighting her legacy as an activist, broadcaster and community leader.

In the 1960s, Clayton contributed to the campaign to desegregate Atlanta’s hospitals, and in the 1970s, she became one of the first African Americans in the South to host a prime time talk show. She also helped create the International Civil Rights Walk of Fame in Atlanta and founded the Trumpet Awards, to honor African American achievements.

“You don’t have to be Martin Luther King,” Clayton said. “You can help those who are deprived just by being yourself. Just help where there’s a need for help. That’s been my life, and I’m still doing it.”

James L. Walker Jr., a lawyer advising Clayton, declined to comment on the division of proceeds with the King Center or on any discussions with King’s two surviving children, who are known for vigorously enforcing the copyrights on his words and have sometimes fought legal battles with family associates, and one another, over ownership of artifacts.

The King Center, through a spokesman, also declined to comment on financial arrangements. But King’s children are backing the Christie’s sale.

“It is poetic that the past will protect the future,” Martin Luther King III said in a statement included in a Christie’s news release.

“We are also grateful to join with Mrs. Clayton to ensure that the sale of this draft helps support the great work of the King Center and our mother, Mrs. Coretta Scott King, who would be 100 this upcoming year,” Bernice King, the chief executive of the King Center, said in the release.

On Nov. 16, the document will go on public view at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta, followed by displays in Chicago and New York. Clayton said she hoped the sale would drive new appreciation of King’s ideals.

“I think people need to hear Martin Luther King’s words fresh,” she said. “They are good words.”

Jennifer Schuessler is a reporter for the Culture section of The Times who covers intellectual life and the world of ideas.

Why Colorado Is at the Epicenter of So Many Supreme Court Clashes

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Supported by

In three recent cases, the conservative-dominated bench has ruled against the state and in favor of the rights of Christian business owners.

By Ann E. Marimow

Reporting from Denver and Washington

First, there was the baker from Lakewood, Colo., whose refusal to make a wedding cake for a same-sex couple landed him before the Supreme Court. Next, a graphic designer from nearby Littleton, who wanted to limit her wedding-related services to celebrations of heterosexual unions.

Last year, the court heard the case of a therapist from Colorado Springs who sought to counsel young L. G. B. T. Q. people to change their sexual orientation or gender identity.

And last week, the justices heard arguments about a Colorado Catholic preschool. It says it should not have to admit the children of gay or transgender parents to get public funding from the state.

The Supreme Court reviews thousands of petitions each term and agrees to schedule only about 60 for oral argument on its formal merits docket. But again and again, cases from the same Western state, with just over six million residents, have come before the court.

The reason, according to local lawyers, academics and former elected officials, says a lot about the shifting politics and demographics of Colorado and a little about how a local legal dispute can evolve into a precedent-setting case heard by the Supreme Court.

They also cited Colorado’s complicated history with gay rights and the ease with which citizens can propose ballot measures to amend the state’s Constitution.

Once a Republican stronghold, Colorado is now decidedly Democratic, but also the home base of well-funded, organized evangelical Christian think tanks and political groups with a long history in the state. A steady flood of ballot measures, including two that Colorado considered on Tuesday dealing with transgender issues, has also made the state a fertile testing ground for ideological battles.

And as Colorado has become increasingly liberal, the Supreme Court has moved in the opposite direction, with the addition of three justices nominated by President Trump, creating a powerful motivation for conservative groups to try to find test cases that challenge what they see as the state’s boundary-pushing policies.

“We are simultaneously a state where much of the population is at the forefront of ensuring equal rights and at the same time, we are home to a well-organized Christian-right structure, which generates strategies and plaintiffs to serve as the faces behind the battles against social equity,” said Mari Newman, a civil rights lawyer in Denver.

The Supreme Court’s new term opened in October with a groundbreaking lawsuit filed by the liberal college town of Boulder, Colo., targeting oil companies over their role in climate change. Two years ago, the justices also shut down an effort by Colorado voters to disqualify Mr. Trump from the state’s Republican primary.

Colorado is now so ubiquitous before the Supreme Court that it has become a laugh line for practitioners and even the justices themselves.

“You guys write, here in Colorado, a new constitutional amendment every three seconds,” Justice Neil M. Gorsuch, a Denver native, teased during a fireside chat with a fellow judge at a legal conference this fall at a resort in the foothills of the Rocky Mountains.

“They usually end up in my court,” Justice Gorsuch continued, to knowing laughter from the crowd. Justice Gorsuch served for more than a decade on the Colorado-based appeals court before his Supreme Court nomination.

Kristen Waggoner, the chief counsel of the influential Christian conservative legal organization Alliance Defending Freedom, owns a T-shirt sporting the state’s flag in the shape of a heart and the message “I love suing Colorado.” On the back is a list of more than a dozen lawsuits the organization has filed against the state and school district officials since 2014.

She insisted it is the Colorado legislature that is picking fights, by passing anti-discrimination laws that in her view impermissibly impose the government’s favored speech on its residents.

“We believe Colorado is at war with the First Amendment and that Denver is essentially trying to dictate what the right to speak freely means, and what the right to practice one’s faith means,” Ms. Waggoner said.

A former Colorado solicitor general, Eric Olson, rejected that assessment. He noted that in two of the cases the alliance brought in recent years, government officials took no action against the business owners who claimed they were discriminated against by state law. Instead, the businesses sued preemptively to block the chance they could be targeted — and potentially to win new precedents on religious speech issues from the court.

“It’s unfortunate that Colorado’s efforts to create a place where everyone can thrive is selectively attacked by those who wish to exclude members of our community from full participation,” Mr. Olson said.

Colorado’s unique history is part of what has brought it to this place.

Three decades ago, when the state’s population was smaller, whiter and more conservative, the group Focus on the Family established its headquarters in Colorado Springs and became a powerhouse of Christian conservative activism. The founder, James Dobson, helped start Alliance Defending Freedom as a counterweight to the American Civil Liberties Union.

In 1992, another Colorado Springs group, with support from Focus on the Family, got a measure on the state ballot that would have prohibited state and local lawmakers from passing anti-discrimination protections for gays and lesbians. It passed with 53 percent of the vote, giving Colorado a reputation among civil rights activists nationally as the “Hate State” and provoking a legal fight that set it on a path to the Supreme Court.

Ultimately, the justices struck down the measure, with Justice Anthony M. Kennedy writing for a six-member majority in 1996 that Colorado had impermissibly placed the state’s gay and lesbian citizens “in a solitary class,” making them unequal to everyone else. Justice Kennedy, a Republican nominee, would go on to write many of the court’s major decisions to protect gays and lesbians, including the 2015 decision legalizing same-sex marriage.

Pat Steadman, a former state senator, lawyer and longtime gay-rights advocate, recalled sleeping on the sidewalk outside the Supreme Court overnight to secure a seat for oral arguments in 1995. He was so moved by the court’s decision that he tattooed his right forearm with one of Justice Kennedy’s closing lines: “A state cannot so deem a class of persons a stranger to its laws.”

He said the fight mobilized Colorado’s civil rights community to pass new protections for the L. G. B. T. Q. community.

In the years since, an influx of left-leaning residents from other states has also turned Colorado solidly blue. The state has two Democratic senators and elected the nation’s first openly gay man as governor, Jared Polis, who is finishing his second term. The state has not elected a Republican governor in more than 20 years.

But the black ink on Mr. Steadman’s right arm has now faded and blurred. And his feelings about the court have changed, too.

In recent years, the state and L. G. B. T. Q. rights have been on a losing streak at the Supreme Court. In the cases of the Colorado baker, the graphic designer and the therapist, the conservative-dominated bench ruled against the state and in favor of the Christian business owners.

Mr. Steadman said he was preparing for the possibility that the state would lose once again in the case heard last week involving publicly funded preschools. He now sees the justices as political actors, particularly after the court’s 2022 decision to overturn Roe v. Wade.

“Back then, I thought we were making progress,” Mr. Steadman said of the 1990s case. But, he said, “we took a hard rightward step backward.”

In the case of the baker who turned away a gay couple, it was Justice Kennedy who ruled against Colorado and wrote for the majority.

Justice Kennedy found that members of a state board, the Colorado Civil Rights Commission, had treated the case with “clear and impermissible hostility” to the baker’s sincerely held religious beliefs. The justice cited the words of one of the commissioners, who had claimed that freedom of religion had “been used to justify all kinds of discrimination throughout history, whether it be slavery, whether it be the Holocaust.”

Melissa Hart, a former State Supreme Court justice, who died in October, said in an interview this fall that the opinion’s focus on the comments was unfair and made her worry that the conservative majority had concluded the state was hostile to religious interests, hurting its prospects at the U. S. Supreme Court.

“It put a target on the state that has had long-term consequences,” Ms. Hart said. “The reputation is ill deserved.”

At oral argument on Tuesday, those cases re-emerged in the latest litigation involving the Catholic preschool. Justices Amy Coney Barrett and Samuel A. Alito Jr. both recounted Colorado’s long list of disputes with religious entities and suggested the state should have anticipated a challenge to its anti-discrimination rules.

“It’s hard to imagine that Colorado couldn’t have seen this coming,” Justice Barrett said. “I mean, especially given the history.”

From Ms. Waggoner’s perspective, the state has “doubled down” even after its losses. Her organization is already back in court with new challenges to transgender protections that she said violate the First Amendment rights of business owners — cases that could put Colorado back before the Supreme Court.

Former Gov. Bill Ritter, a Democrat who served from 2007 to 2011, when the state was more purple than blue, said “the ideological center has moved left in Colorado as the ideological center of the court has moved right.”

He predicted, “We have not seen the end of the ways in which Colorado will find itself in these cross hairs.”

Noel Black contributed reporting.

Ann E. Marimow covers the Supreme Court for The Times from Washington.

The Best VPNs to Protect Yourself Online

Wired November 05, 2026

Hundreds of VPNs are at your disposal. They all want you to believe they’re the best VPN you can buy. All of them claim to have the biggest network or a no-logging policy. And they all promise your internet traffic is safe on the network of servers they’ve rented. Only some of them are telling the truth.

VPNs are only growing in popularity due to age-verification laws in the UK and in several states in the US. Even if you don’t want a VPN, you might need one. If you’re hesitant, I get it. VPN providers have been deep in murky waters for years, constantly caught lying about their practices, handing over user data that was never supposed to be logged, and serving as safe havens for large cybercriminal organizations.

I wanted to find the VPN services that actually work; the ones that keep their promises even in the face of potential prosecution, and the ones that have a proven track record of reliable performance. Some of the picks in this guide aren’t conventional, and some of the services I suggest you avoid might be controversial. But these are the top VPNs I’d use day to day.

Read our other VPN guides, including how to set up a VPN on your router and how to use a VPN to watch Netflix when you travel abroad.

If your looking to get a VPN deal, Proton, our top VPN pick (read more below), is running an early Black Friday sale: 75 percent off the regular price for two years. You can get Proton VPN Plus for $2.49 a month (regularly $10 a month); billed at $60 for 24 months. VPN Plus protects up to 10 devices and gives you access to more than 20,000 servers, plus it blocks ads, trackers, and malware. You can also snag one year of Proton Unlimited for $6.50 a month (regularly $13 a month); billed at $78 for 12 months, which adds Proton’s mail, calendar, and password manager software, plus 500 GB of cloud storage. We don’t know when this deal expires, but we imagine it will last through Cyber Monday.

What Does a VPN Do? And How Does It Work?

VPN stands for virtual private network. A VPN provides a tunnel through which all of your internet traffic passes. Instead of connecting to your internet service provider's servers, you connect to a VPN's server before connecting to the broader internet. Because most VPN services operate this way, your browsing data isn't stored, essentially making you anonymous online.

The linchpin in this system is a VPN protocol. Today, nearly all internet traffic is encrypted, but that encryption happens only after you've established a connection with a website. A VPN protocol encrypts traffic before it reaches the VPN server, adding extra security on untrusted networks like public Wi-Fi at a coffee shop or airport. It doesn't help much on your personal network unless there is an intruder.

What Are VPNs Used For?

Although VPNs are often marketed as security tools, they serve a better purpose for privacy and bypassing geo-restrictions. By anonymizing your traffic through a VPN server, your browsing can't be traced back to you. The internet is full of cookies, and you might be surprised by how much of your traffic online is tracked via browser fingerprinting. That includes hiding what sites you visit (and what you do on those sites) from your internet service provider (ISP).

By routing your traffic through a server in another location, you can also bypass geo-restrictions online, such as the content libraries available in different countries on Netflix or checking product availability in other regions of the world.

VPNs can also be important when connecting to public Wi-Fi. If you're doing anything remotely sensitive on your computer at a coffee shop, a VPN is a good idea to protect your personal data.

How Much Do VPNs Cost?

VPN prices vary widely, but most providers cost around $10 per month for a monthly plan. Pricing changes if you buy several months at once, and it gets even more complicated with full security suites, such as those offered by Nord Security and Proton.

Most prominent VPN services offer multi-month or even multiyear discounts. These plans are often the best way to get your foot in the door, but some VPNs have recently faced class-action lawsuits over their auto-renewal practices. Although a handful of lawsuits have been filed, that doesn't mean these services necessarily engaged in illegal practices.

Free VPNs exist, as well, but you should avoid most of them. Some restrictive free plans from Proton and Windscribe are useful, but you should approach most free VPNs with skepticism.

VPN Terms and Features, Explained

You'll come across a few of these terms in this guide as you generally shop for a VPN. Here's what they mean.

Double-hop: Connecting to two (or more) VPN servers in succession. This provides an extra layer of privacy if someone traces your network path, but it will vastly reduce speeds.

Split tunneling: Allows you to choose which apps use the VPN tunnel. Useful if you want some apps (like your browser) to use the VPN tunnel but not others.

Kill switch: A security feature in VPNs that will disable your internet connection if the VPN connection drops. A kill switch can prevent internet traffic from leaking if the VPN fails.

IP and domain block list: A list of IP addresses or domain names that are blocked inside the VPN tunnel. Some VPNs offer Domain Name System (DNS) blocking, too, which can block ads served from particular DNS servers.

Static IP: Most VPNs assign you a random IP address, or even rotate the IP address while you’re connected. If you need external access to your network with a network-wide VPN, you'll need a static IP address.

Port forwarding: Allows you to forward a port on your private network, bypassing the VPN tunnel. Useful when you need external network access with a network-wide VPN, such as running a media server.

NetShield: A feature specific to Proton VPN that blocks ads and trackers while connected to the VPN. Other services, such as Windscribe and NordVPN, offer similar features.

Dark web monitoring: A feature available in some VPNs, such as NordVPN and ProtonVPN, that will monitor the dark web for your email address or other personal information. You'll be notified if the information shows up on the dark web or as part of a breach.

DAITA: A feature of Mullvad VPN that will introduce background noise to your connection, combating AI-assisted network analysis. Windscribe, NordVPN, and ProtonVPN offer similar features.

Are VPNs Illegal?

Short of a few exceptions, VPNs are legal around the world. That includes the US, UK, Canada, Australia, the EU, South Africa, and many countries in Central and South America. Places such as North Korea and Turkmenistan have VPN bans in place, but due to the extreme censorship in those countries, it's hard to verify what laws are on the books (and how they're enforced). You can probably guess the North Korean government's stance on bypassing censorship, though.

For everyone else, VPN legality only comes into play based on which VPN you use and what you use it for. Countries such as India and Russia call for compliance with the government, forcing providers like NordVPN to shut down servers in those regions. And, regardless of what country you're in, engaging in illegal activity while connected to a VPN is still illegal.

Proton (Free)

Proton VPN (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is the best VPN you can buy. Its Plus service was the fastest I tested across the US and UK. It has a generous free plan if you'd like to try it out first. The features are unmatched, and the pricing is excellent, especially if you bundle Proton VPN with the company's other software (Proton Unlimited). After testing all of these services, Proton is what I personally use now.

What sent Proton over the edge was its commitment to transparency. It has maintained a transparency report since 2017, undergone third-party audits annually since 2022, and open-sourced its applications five years ago. That last bit is huge, as bugs within the application can pose a security risk, and handing those applications over to the open-source community can surface those bugs much faster. There are no real compromises here, with features like split tunneling, port forwarding, and double-hop connections.

Proton is a rare example of a VPN service that gets it. Every VPN engages in the same marketing practices, touting their security, speed, and privacy. But Proton puts its money where its mouth is, all while offering a remarkably easy-to-use and feature-rich VPN application.

Black Friday is a good time to sign up for Proton VPN. The company is offering 75 percent off the regular price for two years.

NordVPN

NordVPN (2-Year)

NordVPN (1-Year)

NordVPN (Monthly)

NordVPN has a long history, and it's one of the most prominent VPN services on the market. It comes with one of the largest VPN networks available, enough features to make Surfshark blush, and decent (though not the best) speeds. It's a little more expensive than I'd hoped for, but that's the price you pay for such an extensive network and feature set.

That feature set is where NordVPN stands apart. Its Basic plan will get you access to the VPN, but I recommend going with at least the Plus plan. It opens up an ad blocker and gives you access to one of the best password managers around, NordPass.

Nord backs up security and privacy credentials with independent audits of the company’s no-log policy and the service’s security. Like Proton, Nord lets you scale up your protection with encrypted cloud storage, but Nord leans further into security while Proton focuses on privacy-focused productivity. With NordVPN, you can upgrade to unlock NordProtect, an identity theft protection service, as well as Incogni to remove your data online.

These extras wouldn't mean much on their own, but the core of NordVPN is still an excellent VPN service. It's been on the bleeding edge of VPN security and features for years, and that hasn't changed.

Windscribe

Windscribe (Pro, Yearly)

Shop at

Windscribe (Free)

You should generally avoid free VPNs, but Windscribe is one of the few worth considering. You get 10 GB of data across 10 server locations and unlimited connections, and you can even unlock more data if you refer friends or post on social media about Windscribe. There are a few similar offers from services like Proton, but Windscribe provides a pleasant on-ramp for subscribing.

If you do decide to pay, you can build your own plan. Unlimited data runs an extra $3 per month, and you can add server locations for an extra $1 per server per month. It's fantastic. Most people don't need VPN servers in Ghana, Cambodia, and Peru, so rather than charge for all those locations, you can pick out your locations piecemeal. If you want everything, that's available at a discounted rate, too.

The pricing model is what sets Windscribe apart, but it's an excellent VPN in its own right. It offers additional packet obfuscation to combat network analysis, and it's loaded with features like split tunneling and port forwarding. It's fast, too, dropping just 15.6 percent of my speed when connected in the US.

Like the other providers I've included, Windscribe has undergone a third-party audit. But unlike the other options, it's also been taken to court. Windscribe CEO Yegor Sak was personally charged with a crime in Greece in relation to a user's activity on Windscribe-operated servers, essentially tying activity on the network to Sak personally. It was dismissed. VPNs are subpoenaed all the time, but the fact that Windscribe wasn't able to produce logs even when the CEO of the company was facing criminal prosecution speaks volumes.

Windscribe added random hashed login in December 2025, which makes it possible to create an anonymous account. Windscribe doesn’t record the random hash, so if you lose it, you’ll also lose account access—but it can help to keep your identity private. This is similar to how Mullvad and IVPN handle accounts. Windscribe accepts cryptocurrency payments as well.

Mullvad

Mullvad VPN (Monthly)

Any VPN worth its salt claims a no-logs policy, but almost all of them keep some logs. Those logs shouldn't have anything to do with your browsing data, and they should be anonymized, but most VPNs need to at least keep logs of information like your email and payment method. But not Mullvad.

Mullvad doesn't do multi-year subscriptions, referral links, or social sign-on. You generate an account number to sign up, and you add time to that account with the payment method of your choice, including a credit card, PayPal, crypto, or cold, hard cash (via mail). If you want to go through the hassle, you can stay fully anonymous in the eyes of Mullvad. If that wasn't enough, Mullvad even claims it was raided by Swedish police and still didn't produce logs.

It's not as fast as Proton, Windscribe, or Surfshark, but it's not bad, either—around a 24 percent drop in the US compared to 19 percent with Surfshark—and it lacks some features like port forwarding. But the pricing is good at roughly $6 a month, depending on exchange rates (Mullvad charges a flat €5 regardless of location).

Mullvad is on the cutting edge of privacy, too, building RAM-only servers starting in 2022 and introducing defense against AI-guided traffic analysis (DAITA) last year. DAITA protects against AI traffic analysis, introducing network noise and sending consistent packet sizes to obfuscate your encrypted traffic further.

Bitdefender

Bitdefender

While the built-in, free Bitdefender VPN is usable, it's too limited for what most people will want. The company's paid option, Bitdefender VPN Premium, gets you support for up to 10 devices, and it's plenty reliable and fast—without the data restrictions. Its biggest draw is its first-year price: it's only $30, which is a great value for a VPN like this. It goes up to $70 after the first year, though, which is a bit more expensive than ProtonVPN. But that first-year price comes out to just $2.92 per month, making it an especially good VPN for beginners to try.

Our VPN reviewer, Matthew Smith, was also impressed by the app experience, which is supported on Windows, Mac, iOS, and Android. It's clean, and all the important information is right up front—including the kill switch. A couple of platforms are missing, such as TVs and Linux, so be aware of that. So, while Bitdefender VPN Premium might not be the ultimate privacy tool, as it's missing some more of the advanced features, it's a user-friendly and dependable VPN with a killer first-year price. —Luke Larsen

ExpressVPN

ExpressVPN (2 Years)

ExpressVPN (Yearly)

ExpressVPN (Monthly)

ExpressVPN has had a rough few years, but it finally seems to be on solid footing. It was purchased a few years back for almost $1 billion by Kape Technologies, a firm that owns several VPNs, including CyberGhost and Private Internet Access. A revolving door of executives followed the sale, but ExpressVPN's leadership is solid enough now that it's worth recommending.

That's because the service itself hasn't degraded in the past few years. ExpressVPN is still insanely fast, packed with features, and dead-simple to use across desktop and mobile. It can go toe-to-toe with the top dogs, and it's always been able to. That hasn't changed.

However, I'm recommending it here due to recent changes ExpressVPN made to its membership options. Its core service is still intact, offering 10 simultaneous connections and full access to the ExpressVPN network. You can push higher, though, with the Advanced plan offering 12 connections and the Pro plan offering 14. The Advanced plan is best for most people, not only due to the higher connection limit but also because it comes with a password manager and 50 percent off one of ExpressVPN’s AirCove routers.

Surfshark: I've used Surfshark personally for a few years, and I'd still be using it if Proton didn't impress me so much. Surfshark is dead simple to use. It pops up and connects before swiftly getting out of my way so I can get on with my day. If you spring for a two-year plan, it's cheap. You can score over two years for around $54 with the Starter plan.

If you want to dig in deeper, you can. Surfshark is one of the most feature-rich VPNs I've used, sporting the basics like a double-hop connection and split tunneling, as well as an ad blocker and email masking. Like Proton, Surfshark offers other security tools like antivirus and dark web monitoring if you pick up a more expensive plan. Surfshark loses out just a bit when it comes to privacy, however. It has a no-logs policy, and it maintains a transparency report and a warrant canary, so it’s not bad in this regard. However, it doesn't have open-source applications, so you’ll need a bit more faith in Surfshark’s app security than with some other VPN services.

EventVPN: This is a free, ad-supported VPN from ExpressVPN. Ads and VPNs don't really mix, but EventVPN says it's able to offer a free service via Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT) and Identifier for Advertisers (IDFA), basically allowing it to serve ads without harvesting your personal data. The problem is the pervasiveness of ads. A banner lives at the top of the app at all times, and you'll need to sit through a 30-second ad each time you connect or disconnect; a big problem when some servers post unreasonably slow speeds. I'll admit EventVPN is a unique concept, but I see nothing better than ProtonVPN or Windscribe for a free VPN service. And when it comes to the inconvenience of sitting through ads, it's straight-up worse.

IVPN: This privacy-focused VPN provider is similar to Mullvad. It does not ask you to create an account with a username, password, and email, but instead generates a random ID, which you use to log in. That helps preserve your anonymity, since that information can’t be tied to your usage even if IVPN suffered a security incident. IVPN also accepts cryptocurrency payments (Bitcoin and Monero). Unlike Mullvad, IVPN offers one-year, two-year, and three-year plan options, as well as an unusual weekly option, which might be nice if you want a VPN while on vacation (IVPN standard is $2 per week). These can be more affordable than Mullvad’s monthly fee. However, IVPN lacks some privacy features you will find with Mullvad, such as RAM-less servers. IVPN scheduled a security audit for 2025, but as of January 2026, the results have not been posted. IVPN also has a tight two-device limit on the Standard plan. The Pro plan raises that to seven, but the Pro plan’s price is $10 per month, so it’s more expensive than Mullvad, which has a five-device limit. That remains true even if you go with a multi-year IVPN plan. Still, IVPN is a fine alternative if you want annual plan options. And while most VPN apps serve their purpose, I do think IVPN’s app is both more attractive and easier to use than Mullvad’s. —Matthew S. Smith

Private Internet Access (PIA): With its long history in the VPN space, PIA has maintained a track record of defending user privacy—even in the face of actual criminal activity. In 2016, a criminal complaint was filed in Florida against Preston Alexander McWaters for threats made online. McWaters was eventually convicted and sentenced to 42 months in prison. Investigators traced the online threats back to PIA's servers and subpoenaed the company. As the complaint reads, “A subpoena was sent to [Private Internet Access], and the only information they could provide is that the cluster of IP addresses being used was from the east coast of the United States.” According to the complaint, McWaters engaged in several other identifying activities, but PIA wasn't among them. Despite such a clear view of a VPN provider upholding its no-logging policy, PIA didn't impress me during my tests. It delivered the worst speeds out of any VPN I tested, with more than a 50 percent drop on the closest US server. (Windscribe, for context, only dropped 15.6 percent of my speed.)

MysteriumVPN: This is the go-to dVPN, or decentralized VPN, as far as I can tell. The concept of a decentralized VPN has existed for a while, but it's really gained traction over the last couple of years. The idea is to have a network of residential IP addresses that make up the network, routing your traffic through normal IP addresses to get around the increasingly common block lists for VPN servers. Mysterium accomplishes this network with MystNodes. It's a crypto node. People buy the node to earn crypto, and they're put into the Mysterium network. It's not inherently bad, but routing your traffic through a single residential IP is a little worrisome. Even without the decentralized kick, Mysterium was slow, and it doesn't maintain any sort of privacy materials, be it a third-party audit, warranty canary, or transparency report.

PrivadoVPN: A popular option to recommend as a free VPN, offering a decent free service, with a handful of full-speed servers and 10 GB of data per month. You'll have to suffer through four—yes, four—redirects begging you to pay for a subscription before signing up, but the free plan works. The problem is how new PrivadoVPN is. There's no transparency report or audit available, and although the speeds are decent, they aren't as good as Proton, Windscribe, or Surfshark. PrivadoVPN isn't bad, but it's hard to recommend when Proton and Windscribe exist with free plans that are equally as good.

You'll find dozens of free VPNs all claiming to protect your privacy. Most of them don't. There are plenty of VPNs I don’t recommend, but these are a few I've tested that are worth mentioning.

Hola is an infamous name in the VPN industry, but it's been close to a decade since its very public debacle. Hola is free, and it's able to stay free because it uses a peer-to-peer network. Hola also owns Bright Data (formerly Luminati), which is a data collection company. In 2015, Hola sold access to the network of its free users (via Luminati), which was used in a distributed denial-of-service attack on 8chan. It's been a decade since that incident, but Hola still operates in a similar way. If you don't pay, you could be used as an exit node in Bright Data's network, and the privacy policy makes it clear that Hola logs data about your usage, including your IP address, the pages you visit, and timestamps.

X-VPN is available on desktop, but it primarily shows up in results on the Apple App Store and Google Play, targeting mobile users with a free offering. X-VPN hasn't done anything explicitly wrong like Hola, but it has way too many inconsistencies to recommend. For starters, it uses a proprietary VPN protocol, which it obfuscates within the app. Proprietary protocols like NordVPN's NordLynx and ExpressVPN's Lightway are based on existing, open-source protocols. Further, X-VPN was highlighted in a Tech Transparency Project report about free VPNs with links to the Chinese government; X-VPN is based in Hong Kong. There's no smoking gun with X-VPN, but there doesn't need to be. The speeds aren't the best, the app lacks basic features like split tunneling, and the pricing for a paid plan is in line with top providers.

Functionally, a VPN should do two things: keep your internet speed reasonably fast, and actually protect your browsing data. That's where I focused my testing. Extra features, a comfy UI, and customization settings are great, but they don't matter if the core service is broken.

Speed testing requires spot-checking, as the time of day, the network you're connected to, and the specific VPN server you're using can all influence speeds. Because of that, I always set a baseline speed on my unprotected connection directly before recording results, and I ran the test three times across both US and UK servers. With those baseline drops, I spot-checked at different times of the day over the course of a week to see if the speed decrease was similar.

Security is a bit more involved. For starters, I checked for DNS, WebRTC, and IP leaks every time I connected to a server using Browser Leaks. I also ran brief tests sniffing my connection with Wireshark to ensure all of the packets being sent were secured with the VPN protocol in use.

On the privacy front, the top-recommended services included on this list have been independently audited, and they all maintain some sort of transparency report. In most cases, there's a proper report, but in others, such as Windscribe, that transparency is exposed through legal proceedings.

How Elon Musk and Big Tech Poured Millions Into the Midterms, and Lost

Wired November 05, 2026

This week on Uncanny Valley, Hugo Lowell, David Gilbert, and Vittoria Elliott from WIRED’s politics team join Leah Feiger to break down how Democrats flipped both the House and the Senate, and why the MAGA base is pinning the losses on Trump and the Iran war. We look at how more than $400 million from Elon Musk’s super PAC largely came up empty, why voters restricted 39 of 40 data center ballot measures in what WIRED called the data center referendum, why election deniers suddenly went quiet, and what it all means for 2028.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

You can follow Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger, Hugo Lowell on Bluesky at @hugolowell, David Gilbert on Bluesky at @davidgilbert, and Vittoria Elliott on Bluesky at @telliotter. Write to us at uncannyvalley@wired. com.

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

I am Leah Feiger, director of politics and science. This week we're bringing you a special midterms episode. I'm joined by three of my WIRED colleagues, Hugo Lowell, a senior correspondent covering the Trump White House.

Leah Feiger: David Gilbert, senior reporter who focuses on disinformation and extremism.

Hugo Lowell: Yeah, I agree with Tori. South Carolina, Darline Graham was handpicked by Trump and endorsed by him to win that race. And it was not this close in previous cycles.

Leah Feiger: To inherit her brother's seat.

Hugo Lowell: Insane. And she ended up losing it.
